policy since the entry into force of the treaty. however, after some forty years of existence, these rules began to show signs of fatigue. modernisation was therefore urgently needed and was particularly necessary in five areas: the authorisation system, decentralised enforcement, procedural rules, judicial enforcement and excessive formalism. the authorisation system needed a rapid reform, which was unanimously requested by companies, researchers and specialist lawyers. i have not attended any competition law forum where there was no call for a change in the system. a system which offers such a limited number of decisions, both authorising and prohibiting, as the one in force, is anything but a good system. articles 81 (1) and 82 have long been applicable to national competition authorities. however, they could not apply article 81 (3), which to a certain extent prevented a consistent application of article 81 (1). ladies and gentlemen, you are aware that two questions from german courts are currently pending before the court of justice. the question is whether it is possible to apply article 81 (1) without being able to apply article 81 (3). the commission's proposal was therefore also subject to reform. the competition procedure is essentially contained in regulation no 17/62. the amendment was unanimously required. the fact that it did not define a genuine procedure, that no time limits were established, that access to the files of the persons concerned was not regulated or that the rights of the defence were not adequately recognised, are all reasons which explain the unanimity of this request. the court of justice has long since accepted that community competition law can be applied by the courts of the member states and the commission already published a communication on the subject in 1994. it was therefore necessary to facilitate this route. one of the most frequently voiced criticisms of community competition law is that it is too formal. it follows from the continental legal tradition that the anti-competitive character of certain agreements depends more on the analysis of their clauses than on the effects they produce on the market. the introduction of economic analysis was therefore necessary. the white paper claims to solve these problems, which is why we support the proposals contained in it. it is true that there are some shortcomings in this report which have been highlighted. for example, to begin with, it focuses exclusively on article 81 and not article 82, although it is a question of modernising both articles. in an era when the processes of company mergers and privatisation of monopolies have preserved and even strengthened dominant positions, the continuation of abusive practices is of particular importance. secondly, regulation no 17/62 must be repealed and replaced by a new regulation. we shall support the report in this sense. however, if certain amendments, in particular those tabled by the epp group, were to be adopted, we would consider that the report would be distorted, that it would be a contradictory document lacking in rigour, and we would then reconsider our support.

the rapporteur. - (de) mr president, year after year we find out, mainly through the court of auditors' report, that funds from the european union budget are being misused, either because of disappearances, mismanagement, irregularities or suspicions of gross fraud. these anomalies have long prompted parliament to take action which should help to protect the money of european taxpayers, which in fact feeds the entire union budget. in this connection, the fight against fraud, its detection, its condemnation and its prevention, deserve particular attention. the creation of uclaf, the task force and the establishment of the office for the fight against fraud, olaf, were important steps, as was the regulation on the protection of the community's financial interests and on on-the-spot checks. the union may only impose administrative sanctions on confirmed cases. so far, the commission has had only relative success in recovering funds wrongfully collected. criminal measures are the responsibility of the member states. as these two legal aspects often overlap and as cross-border attacks on the union budget are increasing - and also as a result of organised crime - the distribution of competences between member states is not clear. in addition, there are differences between national legal provisions and requests for mutual legal assistance which are dragging on or are not being answered. the convention on the protection of the european communities' financial interests, signed by the european council in 1995, and the two protocols relating thereto have not changed anything. the convention must be ratified by each of the 15 member states before it can enter into force. after five years, only four did. this inaction, which threatens to undermine the union's credibility, has led parliament to call for the creation of a european public prosecutor's office. in doing so, there is no question of creating a transnational criminal and judicial order. the aim is rather to provide the union with specific instruments to protect its financial interests, while respecting subsidiarity. we are now revitalising this idea and urging the commission to come forward with legislative proposals to achieve this objective. in this connection, the requests made in the opinions of the committee on legal affairs and the internal market and the committee on civil liberties and internal affairs are fully taken into account. we express two recommendations which follow from the creation of olaf and should guarantee its operational and legal efficiency, its transparency and the protection of individual freedoms. to this end, we need - first recommendation - a legal act that anchors offences against the financial interests of the union and the guiding principles. in an amendment i would suggest setting 30 september as the deadline by which the commission must make its proposal. the second recommendation concerns criminal procedure. the commission should propose - and i am proposing, again by amendment, to set the deadline at 31 may 2000 - a legal act on the creation of an independent body, institutionally linked to the commission, responsible for coordinating and monitoring the regularity of olaf's investigative activities. the existing supervisory committee can only monitor the independence of the director of the office. such a proposal should contain an independent statute for that body and define its tasks, which are limited to olaf's internal investigations and prosecutions of offences against the union's financial interests and its relations with national authorities. it remains impossible to influence the judiciary in the member states. the court of justice must review the legality of acts. we also call on the next intergovernmental conference to start the debate on the creation of a european public prosecutor's office to protect the financial interests of the union, if possible on the basis of the now widely recognised study produced by renowned experts, the famous corpus juris, and the feasibility studies that followed. further recommendations on this approach are also contained in the second report of the committee of wise men. the commission, represented by mr barnier and mr vitorino, and some member states are also strongly in favour of this. i would ask you, ladies and gentlemen, to vote in favour of this report, which was adopted by a large majority in the committee on budgetary control. we can once again show that this parliament is active in preventing mismanagement and, in particular, fraud and condemning where necessary. the commission has already submitted a proposal for a directive amending the directive on working time for doctors in training employed in hospitals. the content of the proposal concerns the average weekly working time of 48 hours for these doctors, with the possibility, after negotiation, that it be increased to 54 hours. on this question, there is agreement between the council, the commission and parliament on the content, and disagreement on the transitional period before the directive enters into force. the parliament's proposal is for four years, the commission's for seven years and the council's for 13 years. the proposal is still being discussed between the council and parliament under the codecision procedure. despite this divergence, it should be stressed that there is agreement between the three institutions on the substance and that efforts are being made, to the extent possible, to find a common solution to this important and sensitive question, which concerns a very large number of doctors working throughout europe.

- question no 39 by emmanouil bakopoulos (h-0807/99): the equal community initiative was adopted by the commission on 13 october 1999 to promote crossborder cooperation and to identify and develop new ways of combating discrimination and inequality in the labour market. it is mainly aimed at asylum seekers. under this initiative, each member state will submit proposals through a community initiative programme covering its territory. on what criteria will the commission accept or reject member states' programmes? what community institution will monitor the financing of the steering group and the supervisory committee and the correct implementation of the programmes? since the contributions to the european social fund will amount to eur 2.487 billion for the period 2000-06, and the equal initiative is co-financed by the member states, what percentage will greece contribute?
commission. - (el) first of all, i would say that you would really help us, since we are at the stage of preparing it in parliament, if you would put forward concrete proposals that we would take into consideration. secondly, i should like to make it clear that the equal initiative is not intended to reduce unemployment, that it cannot even tackle this issue or provide employment support. to do this, there is the european employment strategy, there is the social fund, with considerable amounts, especially for countries like greece. the equal initiative has a clear mission: to encourage, help promote, create statistical data, carry out studies and set up bodies to support groups facing discrimination. what we are asking for is cooperation between groups and local authorities, between countries, so that we can exchange experiences. this is what we are seeking above all: that each country pass on its experience to the other so that it can be replicated. the initiative has been structured in this way, its budget has been set accordingly, and our aim is to involve as much as possible the development actors, non-governmental organisations, local authorities, in order to make it as close as possible to the citizens.
- question no 40 by mr michael cashman (h-0808/99): subject: article 13 of the teu and employment the commission's draft directive on the establishment of a general framework for equal treatment in employment provides for a derogation for religious organisations (article 4 (2)). could the commission indicate to parliament in what circumstances and to which groups, in the context of article 13 teu, such a derogation might apply?
commission - (el) i would point out that this derogation cannot take the form of refusal of employment for one reason or another. for sexual orientation - as in the case you mentioned - for ethnic discrimination or whatever. it allows a choice only in cases where special skills are required which are directly related to the activity. in other words, it is positive discrimination. in the example you gave of the catholic school, it makes sense that the teacher would be a catholic. and only this form of derogation can be accepted.

question no 45 by mr krarup (h-0006/00) subject: implementation of directive 96/71/ec on the posting of workers denmark has not yet implemented the directive on the posting of workers oj l 18, 21.1.1997, p. 1. despite the expiry of the deadline for this purpose. the bill presented to the folketing contains no provisions governing the rights of employees arising from collective agreements. article 3 (8) of the directive requires that working and employment conditions be in accordance with 'collective agreements concluded by the most representative social partner organisations at national level and applied throughout the national territory'. however, the application of an agreement in this sense, i.e. outside its individual scope, cannot be imposed on the social partners without a legal basis. the directive is therefore not applicable to denmark, or denmark is obliged to make provision for conventions of general application. would the commission confirm that the posting of workers directive cannot be applied in denmark in respect of 'collective agreements ... of general application' (article 3 (1)) in so far as such agreements do not exist in danish law and, if not, would it indicate how the directive should be implemented in this respect?
commission. - (el) first of all, there is no attempt to change the system in denmark any more than in any other country. as i said earlier, there is always a problem of interpretation of the european commission directives, because they are a very general framework and the systems differ greatly from one country to another. as regards the point you have raised, denmark is not the only country with this problem, with unresolved questions. five countries have transposed the directive into national law, and the others are still discussing it. what needs to be done, and this is why there has been consultation and discussion between the commission and denmark, as with the other governments, is to find the best way for a decision which has been taken at european level by all the countries and which constitutes a general framework to apply to workers from other countries who are posted to denmark. and we expect a step in this direction from the danish government and from nine other governments.

president of the committee on budgetary control. - (de) mr president, the decision on discharge for the 1997 financial year was postponed because the previous commission had already resigned on the date for that decision and was now only dealing with current affairs. now mrs van der laan, who deserves to be honoured for all the work she has done, asks us in her report to give the commission a discharge for 1997. it may be asked why the present commission should receive a discharge for the implementation of the general budget of the previous commission - mr camre also mentioned this - especially since the discharge for 1996 was refused. but it's the way it is. since taking office, the new commission has had to take responsibility for the acts but also for the failures of the past. since the system of collective responsibility in the commission allows us to take three decisions on discharge altogether, namely granting, postponing or refusing, the fact that four commissioners from the previous commission are now back in the commission has no bearing on the matter. this question should have been asked when the new commission was inaugurated. if parliament approves the proposal made by the committee on budgetary control this week and grants discharge, the commission would be wrong to regard this decision as a blank cheque. i believe that the third part of mrs van der laan's report, the motion for a resolution, is the most important. the obligations contained in it, which are set out in eight different titles, form an integral part of the discharge. it is on its execution that our decision depends. during the discharge for the following financial year - 1998 is already under consideration - parliament will have to check very carefully whether it has not congratulated the commission a little too prematurely. we will have the benchmarks when the commission presents its reform programme. the discharge for 1998 will tell us whether efficiency, transparency, accountability and an open attitude towards discharge authorities prevail.
president of the committee on budgetary control. - (de) mr president, when it comes to internal reform, the european commission is in a bind. after the cases which led to the resignation of the previous commission, expectations are high. i sometimes get the impression that the proposals made in this house are applauded all the more because they are radical. on the other hand, circumstances cannot be changed overnight. as soon as it comes to putting things into practice, as soon as we have to discuss a few details, we see that difficulties arise very quickly. this is probably why the committee on budgetary control has had to face more difficulties than expected on this point. however, we are not ashamed of the result as it presents itself to you today. i would like to take this opportunity to thank mr van hulten for his work on this report. if this report is not watered down by the adoption of several amendments, it will make it possible to give the commission clear and unambiguous instructions on several key points. let's start with the most important education. we do not want the removal of financial controls. the financial controller must still be given the opportunity to do his job before payments are made, not in all circumstances but in cases where uncertainties and risks exist. the commission is sending the wrong signal by renaming the directorate-general for financial control into the directorate-general for audit. the commission's establishment plan can easily be changed, but the task becomes more difficult when it is necessary to stick to the legal texts and, in this case, the financial regulation. i have not made an exhaustive list, but the community's financial regulation and the implementing provisions refer to the financial controller, his independence and the tasks assigned to him in more than a hundred different passages. this regulation cannot be ignored or circumvented, not even by means of a so-called soft law, as one of my colleagues said at a committee meeting. apart from these legal considerations, it would be an unforgivable mistake to abolish financial control in its traditional sense at the very moment when those responsible for it in the commission may no longer be isolated for very long and may finally become the link in a chain with effective control mechanisms. in our view, three control mechanisms will in future interlink: the a priori control carried out independently by the financial controller, the a posteriori control carried out by the verification service to be set up, also called the audit service, and finally the detection of irregularities by olaf, the office for the fight against fraud. it is good that mr van hulten's report establishes the link between the three mechanisms and makes it clear where the major shortcomings are which need to be addressed. as a reminder, i would just add that disciplinary procedures do not work, especially when it comes to financial sanctions for officials for their failures. as regards criminal sanctions, there are still some areas of uncertainty and the promises we have received from the commission remain rather vague. i can only stress that this is the most difficult problem, one that we will eventually have to tackle.

his programme be courageous, because if it is, i can assure him that parliament will be on the commission's side in this reform process. we want a strong commission, which can exercise its functions with complete independence and neutrality, but which has a political orientation. the commissioners must not see themselves as high officials but as politicians in office. this is why the report counsel. - (pt) mr president, the question of transparency is of course a question of the institutions. this intergovernmental conference is a conference which, at least at the outset, is based on the idea of a better functioning of the institutions, especially in view of our common desire that these institutions should be more democratic, more transparent and more efficient. all within the general framework of the overall acceptability of all the solutions we can find to carry out these three desiderata. it goes without saying that the question of transparency will remain on the european agenda and will be on the agenda of this intergovernmental conference. i can assure you that the portuguese presidency will not tire of asking the member states and the representatives of the preparatory group for the conference this question. it must be able to count on the support of the members of the european parliament, who will no doubt mobilise to support this proposal. we shall then see at ministerial level what further action we can take. it should be noted, however, that we have just concluded an amsterdam treaty, adopted in may last year, which contains a set of implementing measures on transparency. the question is whether it is not premature to embark on a new process of transparency. nevertheless, i think that this issue should remain on the agenda, because it is clear that public opinion is sensitive to it and that it is really about the need to make the bodies of the european institutions accountable to the citizens. as far as we are concerned, it will be so. we shall see if there is consensus on this.
- question no 5 by mr josu ortuondo larrea (h-0785/99): subject: proposal for a regulation fixing the total allowable catches for certain fish stocks in the year 2000 (specific case of anchovy) according to the latest reports of the international council for the exploration of the sea, the anchovy stock in ices division viii is currently in a critical state. however, have the fisheries council and the commission assessed the impact on the anchovy stock in ices division viii of the transfer of the quota of ices divisions ix, x and copace 34.1.1 from portugal to france (overfishing of 5000 tonnes per year) and its role in the current situation of this stock and the possible future socio-economic consequences for this fishery? does the council consider it admissible to continue overfishing in breach of the total allowable catch originally set at 33 000 tonnes per year, given the obvious crisis currently affecting this resource? what measures does the council intend to adopt, and according to what timetable, to reconcile the critical state of the anchovy stock with the abovementioned surrender of quota and the principle of relative stability?
counsel. - (pt) mr president, the portuguese presidency has every interest in answering this question in full, because it deals with a problem which affects portugal positively and i will explain why. the council is well aware of the critical situation of anchovy stocks in the cantabrian sea to which the honourable member refers. however, at the last fisheries council of last year, held on 16 and 17 december, the member states involved in this fishery - france, spain and portugal - considered that the precautionary principle, which sets a tac reduced from 5 000 tonnes to 2 000 tonnes on the basis of a commission proposal, was being applied in an excessively cautious manner. a compromise was found to balance the need to reduce biological risks to fish species and the socioeconomic difficulties caused by a limitation of fishing, with the tac being set at the intermediate level of 16 000 tonnes instead of the 33 000 tonnes planned for 1999. it was also planned to revise the figures in the light of new scientific information concerning the conservation of species. we should have these elements available during the first half of this year. the tac for the southern anchovy stock in cim and 9a was set at 10 000 tonnes for the whole of 2000, compared with 13 000 tonnes in 1999. trade in fishing rights between portugal and france has been proportionally reduced from 5 800 tonnes in 1999 to 3 000 tonnes in 2000, which will have to be fished in french waters. i would like to say that this transfer will not increase the pressure on the whole of the anchovy stock, in the context of the whole of the community fishing area. in accordance with the principle of relative stability, the allocation key for anchovy in the cantabrian sea allocates 90% of the stock to spain and only 10% to france. without the transfer of portuguese waters, the tac level of the cantabrian sea would have increased tenfold to allow france to fish adequately. that is why i think there is a positive element in the portuguese case. it is obvious that this solution would be even more damaging to the stock situation than the risk mentioned by the honourable member, which we understand nonetheless.
- (es) mr president-in-office of the council, i must say that i am not at all satisfied with your statements. i understand that portugal is involved in this. but it seems illogical and absurd to me that 80% of the anchovy that was fished in portugal's banks until 1995, according to an agreement between that member state - portugal - and france, is going to be fished in the bay of biscay and that the council of ministers continues to assert that this has no impact on the anchovy population of the bay of biscay. it has been proved, since we have been denouncing it since 1995, that this change is a mistake and if portugal and france want to reach an agreement, that seems very good to us, but these anchovies must be fished in the banks of portugal and not in those of the bay of biscay. today, scientific studies show that the anchovy population in the bay of biscay is threatened with extinction. and today comes the measures to restrict the amount of anchovy that can be caught in the bay of biscay. i do not know whether you, gentlemen of the council of ministers, are aware of the responsibility you have assumed in these years and for the year 2000 in relation to the thousands of families who live off the anchovy fishery in the north of the iberian peninsula.
- council (pt) i would like to say, mr president, that in its judgment of 5 october 1999, the court of justice of the european communities ruled that this transfer, which was approved, was in accordance with the principles laid down in council regulation 37/60/92 and in particular article 9 (1), which provides for the possibility for member states to exchange all or part of their fishing rights. the court also held that the principle of relative stability had not been infringed since the quota of anchovies allocated to spain in subdivision 8 was maintained at 90% and the french quota at 10%. in addition, mr president, the court is of the opinion that the transfer between portugal and france does not infringe the principle of rational and responsible exploitation of living marine and aquatic resources, since the pressure of fishing on subdivisions 8 and 9 does not increase or adversely affect the overall quota of resources allocated to spain. the council therefore reiterates its view that without the transfer in question, france's fishing rights for anchovy in the bay of biscay would be higher. the council therefore considers, mr president, that the pressure on fisheries would be even greater and harmful to the fish stocks without this solution. in concrete terms, 3 000 tonnes represented 57.5% of portugal's fishing rights in 2000, compared with 5 008 tonnes in 1999, or 73.9%. in our view and in the council's perspective, these figures represent a real improvement in terms of conservation, compared to the 80% level set by council regulation 685/95.

commission - (nl) madam president, the basis for the tobin tax would be very short-term foreign exchange transactions. these transactions, it is argued, are only very loosely linked to the fundamental economic variables, as mr désir has just pointed out. its supporters, like mr désir, also believe that the international application of the tobin tax would in principle reduce speculative transactions and hence exchange rate instability and would improve economic prosperity. given the considerable size of short-term financial flows, even a nominal low tobin tax would bring in large sums of tax revenue. in reality, the reason for the growing interest in the tobin tax and other sources of international finance in the mid-1990s was not economic in nature. rather, it was the ability of the tax to generate revenue for international public programmes at a time when the demand for such funds was growing rapidly and funding was becoming increasingly difficult to find. recently, the commission has shown a renewed interest in a global tax such as the tobin tax as a means of achieving what could be described as socially acceptable globalisation. mr desir also mentioned the growing interest from all sides. however, if the tobin tax were unilaterally introduced to prevent any attack on a specific currency, it could not be effective and could even harm the internal financial market. in addition, in the long run, large funds may be able to avoid the tax by transferring foreign exchange transactions to offshore financial centres. in this case, the tax could result in a net loss of total economic prosperity. the tobin tax can therefore only be effective if a sufficient number of industrialized countries are willing to participate. finally, although the tobin tax is designed to curb currency speculation, it may also affect non-speculative flows, which is not the intended purpose. for these reasons, i do not see the need for a european tobin tax. the commission is in any case opposed to any attempt to restrict the movement of capital within the european union. moreover, in so far as this provision could be described as an indirect restriction on capital flows, it would be contrary to the treaty of rome. in my view, the correct approach to speculation is to eliminate the real causes of financial confusion and not to try to suppress its symptoms by creating barriers to the proper functioning of the markets.

- (es) mr president, the time i have will allow me, mr president and mr commissioner, to try the didactic approach of the following example: once upon a time, before the treaty of amsterdam, a council was discussing the amendment of the brussels and lugano conventions: for those who are not familiar with these technical questions, this is a question of jurisdiction. the problem is which judge to refer to in the event of a crossborder conflict. the council, unanimously and within the framework of intergovernmental cooperation, i.e. very little community cooperation, very close to public international law, had reached an initial agreement. but now the treaty of amsterdam has come into force and, in accordance with article 65, this amendment to the brussels and lugano conventions had to be made community law and transformed into a community act: a regulation. the commission then came on the scene and, in order to take advantage of the new amsterdam treaty, decided that the community status of an act simply consisted in changing its title: where it was written convention, it had to be read regulation. and that's all there is to it. the commission, without any prior consultation, without any consultation between the various directorates-general, has therefore launched a draft regulation on these questions of jurisdiction. today in parliament the report is being examined - for a mere opinion, since parliament has only limited powers in this area - under the chairmanship of mrs diana wallis, who i hope will address the subject. but from this observation - and that's where my story ends - we have to draw some conclusions: firstly, the lack of coordination in the council. the council is not the council, it is the council in its 'justice' form. it is not all in the training of experts, professors of private international law, who are the ones who have negotiated these international treaties which, in the end, deal with this specific field. the internal market and general affairs councils were also not consulted. but also - and this is more important for the future - there was a lack of coordination on the part of the commission, which was going through a very difficult period - it was a resigning commission - but there was a lack of coordination in the end because, mr president, the hearing on this matter took place after the publication of the proposal for a regulation, which is contrary to the most basic criteria of efficiency and respect for the citizens and this house, among other problems. i think that this example also highlights the difficult and compromised situation, or the challenge - as you would like to call it, mr president - that we are facing: internal market criteria, criteria of private international law. in short, does the communitizing of an act, and we shall have to do so very often, simply mean indicating a regulation where it is indicated as a convention? in the opinion of the committee on legal affairs and the internal market, the answer is no, and i hope that parliament will feel the same way. to make a measure a community act means first and foremost to examine each of its legislative proposals concerning the fundamental principles of the internal market. in particular, the principle of mutual recognition and the principle of control in the state of origin. community-orientation is in fact respect for the internal market. this is very important because, at present, completing the internal market means tackling this frontier area which encompasses the standards already in force and which, being anchored in the procedure, and of course in many areas of this private international law, lacks a clear definition. if we lose the criteria which inform the internal market, we are indirectly emptying the internal market of its content and heading towards an extremely dangerous situation. another danger is added. it turns out that in this situation of digital revolution, there is a certain tendency to say "we are global, the internal market has become too small, let's regulate the world, why the internal market, let's go beyond the internal market". well, let us remember that european integration was based on the internal market and that we are also obliged, under a treaty, to respect the principles which underlie and shape this reality. now you may ask me, "what about the consumers in all this?" well, in the example i gave, it turns out that they claim to protect consumers by giving them the opportunity to seek justice from the judge next door, the judge closest to their home. is this how we protect them? no, sir, i did not. i want to prove that consumers don't complain when they buy a small device, when they buy something in the store next door. why? because it's very expensive and because it's a very long process. in short, if we want to protect consumers, let us take action. for example, the two initiatives launched by the commission, the small claims procedure and the out-of-court settlement of consumer disputes. this protects consumers: procedures are quick, cheap and efficient. in addition, mr president, protecting consumers also means treating them as adults, not thinking that consumers are incapable of making choices. i think that one of the great challenges facing europe in this digital revolution is to change the culture and the principles of consumer protection. we must protect consumers, but we must protect them in reality, not in a formal way, and we must adopt a culture of risk, of calculated risk for the consumer, that is, that he can make a conscious choice. i will conclude, mr president. europe must defend its values, but europe has another challenge: the balance between public legislation and self-regulation. for the protection of consumers, we need a strong and protective framework of public legislation, but also a space in which, starting from civil society, systems are established that are more adapted to our times than those that public institutions can establish. the other day, at the madrid summit, someone said to me: 'mrs palacio, on the internet, a year is two months. a directive that you take four years to draw up is a long time". let us move faster, let us keep our values, but above all let us understand that our internal market must be a priority.

- the next item is the report (a5-0094/1999) by mrs rosa miguélez ramos, on behalf of the committee on fisheries, on the proposal for a council regulation (com (99) 382 - c5-0145/1999 - 1999/0163 (cns)) on the strengthening of the dialogue with industry and the parties concerned on the common fisheries policy.
the rapporteur. - (es) mr president, the regulation we are considering today is intended to strengthen the dialogue with industry and the sectors concerned on the common fisheries policy. the commission thus wishes to ensure that information on the needs of the professional sector is well received and to promote the dissemination within this sector of community regulations and decisions adopted in the field of the common fisheries policy. the committee on fisheries supports this proposal for a regulation, to say the least. the european commission needs to know the reality of the sector through dialogue with the professionals involved in it in order to formulate proposals and exercise its powers. this proposal for a regulation was preceded by the reform of the advisory committee on fisheries and aquaculture, a consultative body set up in 1971 and bringing together all the professional sectors. the reform essentially involved updating the body by integrating other actors who in recent years have played an increasingly important role in managing the rational exploitation of resources: development ngos, environmental groups, consumers and also scientists. the reform also strengthened the presence of certain sectors that were previously under-represented, such as aquaculture and the marketing of products. the number of members of the committee's plenary was changed and specialised working groups were set up. the main point of this reform of the advisory committee is, in my view, the priority given to representative organizations at community level so that the committee does not merely relay national positions. the committee on fisheries of this parliament and in particular myself, as rapporteur, have been very critical of the fact that we have not been consulted on the reform of this committee. this means that we must today confine ourselves to giving our opinion on this proposal for a regulation, which i would venture to call minor. as regards the concrete elements of this commission proposal to promote the dissemination of information on the cfp, namely its objectives, mechanisms and legislative provisions concerning the sector, we fully support them. nothing would please us more than to see the commission finally decide to make this effort to provide information. the commissioner himself, in his last appearance before the committee, acknowledged that this was absolutely necessary. mr fischler said that we had a marketing problem and that we needed to inform and defend our model better: information to the inside, to the sector itself, which often knows little or nothing about its own situation, and also information to the outside. as a member of the committee on fisheries, i have often been surprised by the general public's profound ignorance of a common policy (fisheries) which is of enormous importance to many member states and to the union as a whole. as regards information to the sector itself, we ask the commission to be aware of the realities faced by many fishermen. ladies and gentlemen, since not everyone has access to new technologies, information and dissemination campaigns must use all available means, including the most traditional. i would like to highlight the work of the printed press, which is increasingly concerned about the future of fisheries in europe, and of radio and television, which are democratic means of communication available to everyone. i would like to conclude by drawing the commission's attention to the representativeness of the organisations which are members of the advisory committee. the dialogue between the commission and the professionals in the sector is essential. however, for this dialogue to bear fruit, it is necessary that the professionals involved are genuinely representative of the different sectors involved in the common fisheries policy. neither the commission proposal nor the advisory committee regulation provides for mechanisms to ensure that this is the case. in such a fragmented sector, marked by considerable geographical dispersion and little impregnated with a culture of association, it is very difficult to ensure that the commission's interlocutors at community level are valid representatives of the sector concerned. thus, in order to increase their representativeness, it may be appropriate for the commission, in addition to the actions it has undertaken, to take initiatives to promote the membership rate of the trade organisations that exist today. the representatives of the sector, who are elected as the commission's interlocutors and thus the members of the advisory committee, are required to represent the common interest.

commission - (el) mr president, i should like to say in the preamble that the frequency of legislative amendments in the common fisheries policy is a sign of the dynamism of this sector. this is a dynamic that could not be expressed in the way the previous advisory committee on fisheries operated, and that is why the legislative proposal under consideration was tabled. it aims to create a more effective and solid relationship between the commission and the advisory committee. the commission has spent three years working on this proposal. in 1997 an independent study was commissioned. two conclusions emerged from this. firstly, that fisheries policy should go beyond the interests of the sector and now concern the concerns of society itself. that is something we must bear in mind. secondly, the way in which the advisory committee operated did not meet the needs of managing complex issues. the legislative proposal is divided into three parts: the first is the reform of the advisory committee, which now has 20 members instead of 45, with the participation of the trade organisations at 60%, industrial and commercial enterprises at 25% and environmental organisations at 15%. the commission has therefore been asked to consult not only professionals and businessmen but also society itself. the second part of the legislative proposal consists of measures to assist professional organisations in the sectors concerned by the common fisheries policy, in particular european professional organisations in the fisheries sector. the third part concerns support for the communication activities of the dg fisheries with these groups. the legislative proposal mentions these last two points, but i would like to reiterate that the final version was preceded by a long consultation on the composition of the committee. on 26 october the proposal was examined for the first time by the council, which is awaiting parliament's opinion to continue its work. i would like to thank mrs ramos in particular for the outstanding quality of her work and the committee on fisheries of this parliament for the excellent cooperation and work on this text. i come now to the comments on the amendments and the commission's position. three amendments have been drawn up in the committee on fisheries of parliament. the first expresses parliament's wish to exercise precise control over the expenditure of professional organisations so that they meet exactly the objectives set by the legislative proposal. the commission agrees with this amendment and considers it admissible. the commission naturally shares parliament's view on the second amendment, which is that parliament wants to be fully informed of the work of the committee and its many contacts. but the preparation of an annual report listing all these activities is an extremely heavy task for a community fisheries directorate whose programme is already heavily loaded, without the benefit being obvious. the third amendment takes up the substance of the second and refers to the representativeness of the advisory committee, in other words to the participation of all nationalities. we agree that the committee must ensure the representativeness of the whole sector in a balanced way, but we dispute - as has been shown by the studies and the dialogue - the idea that this balance should be based on nationality. the commission has asked for help from european organizations which are perfectly capable of ensuring their own national representation or the representation of particular categories, when they consider it necessary. in conclusion, the commission accepts amendment no 1, which calls for the community to strengthen financial control, but for the reasons i have just indicated, it considers it appropriate to reject amendments nos 2 and 3.

- (es) mr president, i do not want to dramatize, because i know that many civilians are victims of violence in armed conflicts in different countries, but 131 un workers, humanitarian staff and human rights activists were murdered in conflict zones between 1992 and 1997. there were 35 incidents between 1 january 1994 and 17 march 1997, in which 119 aid workers and humanitarian personnel were abducted. in 1992 it was estimated that one un official died violently every month. in 1993 this was increased to two per month and in 1994 to one per week. nine workers died in the first two months of 1997. in 1996, 153 delegates of the international committee of the red cross were victims of incidents, including assassinations and kidnappings. i would like to recall in particular the death of three members of médecins du monde spain in rwanda in 1997. finally, as we say in the compromise resolution with which we wish to conclude this debate, the murder of the peace and third world workers iñigo eguiluz and jorge luis mazo, who died on 18 november in quibdó, 500 km north of bogotá, on the atrato river in colombia, is only the latest in a long series of attacks directed not against the integrity of these people but against human rights, international humanitarian law and, within the latter, the right of victims of conflict to be helped, against the judgment of the perpetrators of these acts and against the reparations necessary so that such crimes do not go unpunished. the recent insecurity of humanitarian personnel is due, among other things, to the increase in conflict, the exponential growth of humanitarian organizations and, above all, the nature of current conflicts. it is no longer a conflict between regular armed forces under political control and guerrilla movements with a hierarchy of command and a defined ideology in which the parties to the conflict were in some way responsible for the protection of humanitarian personnel for the benefit of the populations. these references no longer exist today. humanitarian and cooperating personnel are exposed to banditry; the civilian population is seen as an additional element of the conflict and is part of the strategy both politically and militarily. humanitarian action thus becomes an obstacle to the objectives of the parties to the conflict, which frequently consist in eliminating part of the civilian population for ethnic, religious or cultural reasons. in the face of this reality, the safety of humanitarian personnel is a wide-ranging issue of concern to parliament and should be of concern to the commission, which funds more than 180 ngos active in conflict zones, and also to the council, which is striving to pursue a foreign policy in accordance with the treaties and to promote human rights and a security policy which, for the time being, is concretized precisely in humanitarian action. we therefore ask that parliament's concerns be shared by the other institutions. the commission, by drawing up a communication on the safety of cooperating and humanitarian personnel and by adopting measures to ensure the safety of our cooperating personnel. before we come to the measures proposed by some governments, such as military protection for their collaborators, we must propose other measures which are more effective in situations of conflict. the council, through the promotion, through the cfsp, of international humanitarian law and perhaps through the possible creation of a european civil peace corps. in 1999, we commemorated the 50th anniversary of the geneva convention on international humanitarian law, which protects civilians in armed conflict and guarantees their access to international aid. these instruments are legally binding on states and yet they are systematically ignored. we ask the secretary-general of the council to use the new capacity of the european union for external action to promote these principles of the european union. the secretary-general of the united nations recently asked the security council to enforce international humanitarian law by applying chapters 5, 6 and 7 of the un charter. what we are asking for here today is simply that awareness be raised and that the necessary steps be taken to deal with a problem which concerns not only ngos but also the very foundations of our conception of the world order.
the commission is deeply saddened by this tragic event, one of those which occur every day in the world and which the honourable member has mentioned. the commission is therefore expressing its regret and would like to emphasize once again the courage and dedication of these humanitarian workers who are working in such dangerous areas all over the world. in the specific case of colombia, the commission has repeatedly and forcefully expressed its concern to the authorities of that country. we are continuing to monitor the situation and are in close and constant contact with the embassies of the member states in bogota. as regards the murder of inigo eguiluz, who was working on echo projects, and the murder of the priest, the commission and the member states have urged the colombian authorities to investigate the crime. the european commission and the spanish ambassador met with the colombian vice-president and insist that those responsible for this crime be brought to justice. the safeguarding and protection of life in these exceptional circumstances is an integral part of humanitarian law. the role of the echo office in colombia and other countries is to monitor the humanitarian situation there, but also, and especially in colombia, the situation of people who are displaced against their will, and efforts are being made at all times to monitor the application of humanitarian laws. the honourable member is quite right to stress the need for special measures and special actions by the commission to ensure the safety of staff. you mentioned that there is already a commission document on the safety of assistance staff, which was submitted in may 1998 and sets out the priorities by specifying the actions. in view of the deteriorating situation, the echo office of the commission organized a seminar on security with the international committee of the red cross in april 1999, and all organizations in colombia were asked to have a security policy and to notify the international committee of the red cross in advance of their travels, in order to ensure that members of the various armed groups were informed of the humanitarian nature of the mission. i should also point out that apart from planning, intervention measures and staff training, there are also financing needs. the implementation of humanitarian aid is not without cost. the commission therefore not only encourages humanitarian aid practices but also funds activities to train and raise the risk awareness of those involved in these missions. let me give some recent and past examples of initiatives taken to this end: the presentation of documents on humanitarian aid, the seminar on security with partners held in lisbon, the workshop on security issues organised in brussels for staff, the inclusion of staff security issues in echo manuals and the meeting of echo correspondents to be held in february and march 2000 to this end. naturally, the european parliament's proposals will be taken into account, and since this is a very delicate and multifaceted matter, close cooperation, new ideas and proposals are also very important for the commission's action.

it is important for us to ensure its success. any failure would be catastrophic for the union. we must therefore ensure that the final results of the work of this conference are sufficiently acceptable to all public opinion and all political frameworks in the various countries. i think that the mechanism we have proposed for this conference has been very well received by the various governments. the creation of the preparatory group, which i chair, is also a response to the concerns expressed by the european parliament about the degree of involvement of its representatives at institutional questions which may be connected with them. in this context, there is of course the work connected with the community institutions, the bodies of the union; the problem of enhanced cooperation, which is closely linked to left overs; but there are also issues such as the legal personality of the union, the simplification of the treaties, and other types of issues which are organically linked to a revision of the treaty on european union and which we consider important, such as those concerning, for example, the very structure of parliament in a post-enlargement scenario, the transitional measures to be implemented in the event of enlargement taking place before the end of this parliamentary term, and the individual responsibility of commissioners. finally, a whole series of subjects which we believe should and can be included on the agenda of this conference. we have seen an openness on the part of the member states to this possibility. i would like to say that during the portuguese presidency i have heard that initiatives are being born and are being launched quickly with substantial work. i do not intend to start the work of the preparatory group merely as a small review of the subjects, as a notary - to use the expression of mr napolitano - of the positions of the various member states. i do not intend to be a notary, i intend to make concrete proposals on specific issues, at the risk of not being accepted. i would like to say that we intend to divide the work of the preparatory group into two cycles, during which all the themes will be analysed. in a first round, we will begin with qualified majority voting, then we will try to identify the institutional issues related to the leftovers and we will deal only afterwards with the question of the commission and the weighting of votes. we shall include the questions of enhanced cooperation in the institutional questions. in the last part, or in the second round, we will take up all the issues that have been dealt with in the meantime, which will be dealt with at the ministerial meetings, and we will also try to identify all the new issues that could be added to the agenda. it is at this stage that it is important to know whether the security and defence issues will already be ripe for inclusion in the final phase of the conference. the same is true of the charter of fundamental rights. we shall then see whether the debates on this specific question will lead us to include this theme in the intergovernmental conference, particularly in the second half of this year. that is the presidency's intention in principle. we will report to the european council in lisbon, a report which will of course be factual, since it will be in march, whereas the conference will start in february. we hope that the second report which the presidency will present on its own responsibility at the second european council will be more substantial and will already contain some more concrete elements, concrete in terms of the texts of the treaties, if possible. we take note of the commission's proposals. as the presidency, we accept these proposals and will submit them to the appropriate treatment in the debates of our conference, regardless of what each member state may think of the solutions put forward by the commission in its proposal. we hope to be as soon as possible in order to avoid any delay. of course, the conference will always be open to suggestions from the member states, but we would like them to define their positions as soon as presidency, as far as the intergovernmental conference is concerned, will produce effective and serious work. we hope to be able to convey to the french presidency something tangible and as - (es) mr president, we have been discussing this directive since 1997. it was time we came to an agreement. as i broadly agree with what my colleague mr sjöstedt and the green group representative, mr de roo, have said, i shall not use the two minutes i have and will merely raise two questions. firstly, and perhaps this is the fundamental element of this proposal, the idea, inherent in the recycling and use of waste, of using materials which subsequently pollute less. another important point is that waste containing lead, cadmium and mercury, as well as waste containing pvc, should not be incinerated or crushed. parliament is discussing this in another area. the second question is who should bear the costs. i agree with the previous speakers that the polluter should pay, and even more so in the case of this proposal. it is the producers who have to pay, even though we know that eventually the cost may be passed on to consumer prices, and they have to bear these costs before 2006, as some amendments propose. we are more in favour of the amendment at first reading. it is also important to set the percentage of recyclable materials that vehicles must contain and the date from which this percentage must be applied. in my view, the proposal provides for very long time limits. finally, mr president, i believe that the creation of small and mediumsized enterprises should be encouraged, which, if they are properly approved and duly authorized, can encourage job creation in this vital sector, so as to avoid monopolies by large enterprises.
commission. - (sv) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, thank you for this interesting debate and for the many important arguments which have been put forward. would you be so kind as to bear with me for a few minutes? let me explain briefly some of the starting points and principles behind this directive. let me also comment and respond to some of the most important arguments put forward in this debate. first of all, i think we need to repeat some of the basic elements that mr florenz and others have already mentioned. we are talking about the fact that almost ten million cars are destroyed every year in the european union, which produces about as many millions of tonnes of waste. this means that almost ten million tons of waste are produced by these vehicles and that about 7 percent of it is dumped in nature. they also release the worst environmental hazards. about 10 percent of lead production comes from cars, but there is also cadmium, chromium, mercury, and other very dangerous substances. we already know all this, but i want to repeat it for those who will listen. the growth of these waste streams is one of the fastest we have in europe. we know that waste is there, we know how to deal with it, and we have no excuse for not doing something. the directive has three objectives: firstly, we want to put an end to the use of dangerous heavy metals in the manufacture of new cars. on the other hand, we want to establish the responsibilities of the builders. we cannot take matters into our own hands any longer at the end of a product's life cycle, but we must avoid producing so much waste. we must ensure that the various components of products are recycled as much as possible. finally, we want to achieve the recycling target set in this directive. these are the three main objectives of the directive. this is because there is a waste of resources due to the lack of recycling of the material in the cars. it is primarily the resources of the manufacturers that we waste if we do not tackle the life cycle of a car. two main issues have been raised here - there are of course many more, but i would like to focus on two of the most important. on the one hand, who will pay? secondly: does this proposal harm the competitiveness of the european automobile industry? the first question is therefore who will pay. the directive states that the costs must be borne largely by the manufacturers, in accordance with the principles laid down in the eu treaty on producer responsibility and on polluters having to pay. it is clear, however, that these costs will be borne collectively by producers and consumers. we have calculated that the cost of recycling vehicles is no more than one percent of the price of a new car. do we think that the costs will disappear if we do not adopt this directive? no, it is clear that we will all have to bear the costs if the environment is damaged, but they will be much higher. there will also be costs later on. so the costs will not go away, but we are now clarifying the responsibilities and how the costs should be shared. is this a car industry in crisis? is it a badly profitable industry that we really need to help by not imposing a lot of burdens on it? so the car industry has absolutely no means? is the motive really to undermine the competitiveness of the european automobile industry? no, of course not! it's the opposite! do you think consumer demands for clean cars and fuel efficient cars will decrease in the future? what do you think your children and grandchildren will demand of cars or that legislators in the future will demand of cars? of course they have to be green, they have to be recyclable, they have to consume less, they have to not pollute our environment. only in this way can we build a future for the automobile industry. we need to create a healthy driving force, one that ensures that we take care of waste, that we recycle materials and that we compete with cleaner, less fuel-consuming cars. the fact that we have a highly developed european automobile industry already makes up for the fact that there are indeed several vehicles on the road in europe for which it has to answer. it's not an insurmountable cost or an impossible mission. if we create such driving forces, i am quite confident that the market forces and the people with interests in the automobile industry will see to it that a system develops which supports both. everything will certainly be put in place, from insurance to an efficient and judicious system of destruction and recycling. the industry itself will see to it that this happens in europe. these are not insurmountable costs for the european automobile industry. it will, on the contrary, help industry to cope with the need to produce cars that are less polluting and consume less fuel. we have to do this for the environment. the costs don't go away, nor does the waste. otherwise, we will all have to pay the bill as taxpayers or as citizens of the community; in addition, it will cost much more if we delay doing so, and therefore if we wait longer. that's what i wanted to say as an introduction. i would also like to comment on the question of the retroactivity of legislation. if we calculate that the average life of a car is 11 years, do the members or others mean that we should wait 11 years before we tackle this problem? are you saying that when we legislate on chemicals we should ignore chemicals that are already on the market and only make laws for those that will be made later? it is clear that we must look at the problem now and the challenge of existing car fleets. it's not an insurmountable problem yet. we can handle it. we already have the infrastructure. we have everything we need to load up on old vehicles. i naturally hope that the result of today's vote will be positive. i would also like to thank karl-heinz florenz, if i have not already done so, for the hard work he has put into this proposal in the committee on the environment. it is indeed innovative in many respects with regard to reuse and manufacturers' liability. i think that this will have many positive and tangible consequences for the environment. we cannot continue to turn a blind eye. as has been said, we have the knowledge and the means to solve this problem. after the first reading in the european parliament in 1999, the commission proposal found itself in a difficult political situation in the council. however, we reached a well-balanced common position in july under the finnish presidency. we must now ensure that this legislative process is completed successfully. in all, 48 amendments were tabled. the commission may adopt 10 of them in full. three amendments can be adopted in part and one can be adopted in principle. some amendments concern improvements to the commission proposal which we have already accepted at first reading or reintroduce into the directive elements of the original proposal which the council deleted. this is the case with amendments nos 5, without the first part, 8, 9, first part, 10, 12, third part, 15, 16, 20, 22, 24 and 25. all these amendments can be adopted. amendments nos 6 and 21 are new; the commission can accept them. it can also vote for amendment no 26 with certain changes in the wording. i would point out that some of the remaining amendments to the basic principles of the proposal involve a significant reduction in the level of environmental protection which is the objective of the common position. we cannot therefore adopt them. parliament has traditionally made a major contribution to strengthening environmental legislation in europe. i'd be surprised and disappointed if it wasn't today. i am concerned about certain amendments in parliament which call into question the absolute basis of this proposal. this includes the disposal of heavy metals, the responsibility of manufacturers and the need for recycling. i would like to refute these amendments as a group. amendments nos 4, 11, 12, 13, 28, 30, 32, 37, 42 and 48 concern the removal of heavy metals. amendment no 12 implies that the entry into force of the provision is postponed for at least 10 years. amendments nos 13, 28, 32, 37, 42 and 48 concern the introduction of superfluous conditions and exceptions. this means that the process of replacing dangerous substances would be a long one. amendments nos 4, 11 and 30 involve the separation of heavy metals and waste before recycling. the commission considers that the elimination proposed in the common position is easier to implement from a technical point of view. amendments nos 17, 18, 27, 34, 36, 38, 44 and 45 concern the liability of manufacturers. the compromise reached by the council is fair, but fragile. the commission does not believe that the amendments can improve the balance without creating tensions at the same time. i regret the confusion which has recently arisen because of the misuse of internal commission documents, which has led to uncertainty about the commission's position on the matter. i would like to stress that the commission had already proposed a special clause on manufacturers' liability in 1997 and that it fully supports the common position. there are no disproportionate costs to the manufacturers, far from it. amendments nos 39, 40, 46 and 47 concern the quantified objectives. the high level of protection sought by the common position would lose much of its meaning if the 2006 recycling target were rejected. these amendments would also make the targets difficult to process and control. let me also comment - listen carefully to what i am about to say now, because i have heard this repeatedly in the debate - on the question of historic and collector cars which are mentioned in amendments nos 3, 7, 9, part two, and 35. such vehicles are not covered by the definition of waste and therefore do not fall within the scope of the directive. so, despite what has been said here, historic cars and motorcycles are not covered by the directive. we do not think that amendments nos 2 and 14 add anything to the directive. amendment no 23 implies that the commission must adopt quality standards for reused components. that is not covered by the directive. this would therefore require an ad hoc directive from the european parliament and the council. amendments nos 29, 31 and 41 relax the requirements for dismantling. in particular, amendments nos 31 and 41 risk reducing the possibilities for recycling plastic, tyres and glass to nothing. finally, the commission cannot accept amendments nos 1 and 33 because of the need for legal clarity, and amendment no 19, which the commission considers to be unnecessary at this stage. amendment no 43 is also out of place within the scope of the directive.

- question no 41 by mr paul a.a.j.g. lannoye (h-0021/00): the council has not yet adopted the common position on the proposal for a directive on the approximation of the laws of the member states relating to the protection of employees in the event of the insolvency of their employer. the european union is faced each year with an increasing volume of waste electrical and electronic equipment (6 million tonnes in 1998) due in particular to the accelerated obsolescence of equipment. the environmental problems associated with the incineration and landfill of this waste are mainly due to the presence of hazardous substances (lead, cadmium, mercury, hexavalent chromium, pvc and halogenated flame retardants). a preliminary draft directive to regulate the management of such waste has been the subject of three successive versions, the latest of which was adopted in july 1999. can the commission explain the long gestation of this project, which was supposed to be completed in 1998? is it true that the us government disputes the main provisions of the current draft and even threatens to take action against the world trade organisation (in violation of article xi of gatt and article 2.2 of the agreement on technical barriers to trade) if it is adopted?
commission - (sv) the commission agrees with the honourable member that the treatment of electrical and electronic waste in the european union is causing major environmental problems. the commission has therefore decided to draw up a proposal on this subject and has been working on it since 1997 with all the parties concerned. the results of this debate and of the extensive research being carried out in this field are currently being studied by the commission. parts of the proposal have been criticised, including the prohibition of certain heavy metals and bromine flame retardants, and the application of the principle that the manufacturer is responsible for the treatment of such electrical and electronic waste. the united states delegation to the european union expressed its scepticism on certain points in the latest document resulting from our consultation, namely on the prohibition of the substances i have just mentioned and on certain issues related to the principle of manufacturer's responsibility. the main argument put forward by the us in this context is that these provisions would be incompatible with international trade law. the commission is currently examining this argument. let me add that i intend to submit to the commission before easter a proposal on the treatment of electrical and electronic waste.
commission. - thank you for your supplementary question. it is important that i have the opportunity to respond to it. it is clear that in a reflection process such as this, which concerns a very large flow of electrical and electronic waste in europe, the various parties involved are in constant dialogue. during this discussion we had a positive exchange and we worked out a proposal. some paragraphs have been strengthened, and others have perhaps been revised downwards a little too much, in a spirit of compromise. we are still drafting the texts and the dialogue between the various bodies involved has continued right up to the very last minutes. i would like to say that i believe that the united states' intervention must not have the effect of steering our decisions towards measures which are inadequate from the point of view of the environment. i am really against the fact that the wto and trade rules can be constantly invoked to prevent the eu from taking radical environmental measures. i'm assuming we have to do it. however, i am prepared to listen to all the arguments. for example, i recently met with representatives of the electronics industry. they made suggestions - including practical ones - on how we could improve our proposal. i would like to say that i am not in favour of the idea that the united states should be the one to decide what form our directive will take. i think we must show the way forward, and that will be the spirit of our final proposal.
- question no 42 by mrs maj britt theorin (h-0026/00) subject: women and the environment almost all the parties involved in the rio and kyoto processes - organisations, citizens' movements, governments, the world bank, the united nations and charitable organisations - felt that women should have a greater say in environmental decisions. the appointment of more women to senior positions in environmental bodies would allow the mainly male decision-makers to go beyond business issues to include issues of social justice. will the commission adopt an action plan to increase the active participation of women in environmental decision-making?
commission - (sv) mr president, in 1998 the commission launched an action programme to promote equal opportunities for men and women. the current programme, which runs from 1997 to 2000, aims to create a work culture which places both men and women in their respective roles and takes account of the specific needs of both sexes. one of the objectives of this programme is to develop methods, strategies and measures to promote equal participation of both sexes in decision-making processes, particularly in the highest functions of society, and to study the results. each directorate-general shall develop its own action plan under this programme. one of the aims of these various action plans is to increase the number of women in positions of responsibility. the new commission intends to double the number of female heads of unit during its term of office. the directorate-general for the environment is working particularly actively in this direction. at present, 60% of management positions and 20% of unit heads are held by women. our policy is to encourage the recruitment of women in administrative services, in order to build up a pool of competent candidates for future management vacancies. at present, 24.5% of our category a civil servants are women. we hope that this number will continue to increase. we also try to involve qualified women in the consultative forums we organise. as far as our external partners are concerned, we can only set a good example and encourage their own efforts to democratize decision-making processes. as regards the more general questions of integrating this gender perspective into our work, you will no doubt be aware that the principle is contained in the treaty of amsterdam. article 3 of the treaty states that the community, in all the activities referred to in that article, shall aim to promote equality between men and women and to redress existing inequalities. the commission fully supports the efforts being made in this respect and is currently studying whether specific measures can be taken in the field of the environment. i must of course tell you how much i appreciate the role played here by the parliamentary committee on women's rights and equal opportunities, and in particular its chairwoman.
commission. - (sv) i of course see mainstreaming as a principle which must apply to all our work. gender issues play a very important role in the project being developed in my department. i am also prepared to make a personal commitment, for example by leading seminars on management responsibilities, or other topics, to encourage women to take on new roles within the commission. if we want to motivate all women civil servants, i think it's very important that this message is conveyed to all levels, top to bottom or bottom to top, as we prefer. it seems to me that environmental work, in general, is very often dominated by women. this trend should be continued so that women can also obtain positions of responsibility or move up the hierarchy of bodies working on the environment. i would say that our action plan reflects that will, but it could certainly be improved. i have some experience in the field of project implementation and monitoring. i hope she can be useful.

commission - the question of excise duties, to which the honourable member refers, is a matter for the member state concerned. the commission has no instrument at its disposal to impose any reduction or increase in excise duties on alcoholic or other products. at the end of this year the commission will present a report on the differences in excise duties between member states. this report will undoubtedly initiate a debate with the parliament and the council on this situation, which clearly shows that there are many differences between member states in excise duty rates. for example - and i think the honourable member was referring to this - france does not apply excise duties on wine, whereas the united kingdom does. this leads to a distortion of the internal market as wine is smuggled from france to the uk. the question specifically referred to the link between the excise duty and the alcoholic strength of the products subject to the excise duty. the commission has no power to influence this. in the case of sweden, excise duties are actually used to reduce alcohol consumption. although this results in a disparity in excise duties between sweden and other eu member states - and as such increases cross-border smuggling of alcoholic products - it is a legitimate instrument to reduce alcohol consumption. of course, there is the elasticity of demand; in this case, the price elasticity of demand. i'm not entirely sure of its value but it's not a zero and so it must have an effect.
the commission. let me confirm to mr maccormick and other members of this house that the present situation, in which excise duties differ between member states, is not really conducive to the proper functioning of the internal market. we must not limit ourselves to alcoholic products. if we look at petrol, for example, we see that the excise duties in germany are different from those in the netherlands, which means that dutch drivers cross the border and fill up in germany. this is indeed a distortion of the internal market. if it were up to me, i would use a magic wand to harmonize excise duties in europe. this would put an end to all smuggling, unless products are inherently more expensive in some member states. but i don't have a magic wand, and it's not just me. it is a unanimous area, as mr maccormick knows, and unless all the member states agree on the harmonization of excise duties, it will not take place. once again, the commission will be submitting a report on the state of play in the field of excise duties towards the end of the year and i am naturally open to any discussion with parliament on this report.
