in writing. - (es) we have seen the transformation of a report that was primarily concerned with the quality of europe's water into an instrument of trade war. we all agree that water quality is a priority, especially in view of the adverse impact on nature of the development of the accelerated industrial growth model. it is clear that the private profit logic of this model has been harmful, and therefore the polluter pays principle is adequate to deal with these consequences. but beyond these principles, water must be considered as a common good which cannot be subject to market rules. surprisingly, i imagine with the best of intentions, this ecological objective has been turned into an instrument of commercial warfare by making consumers, especially in the agricultural sector, bear the cost of facilities and procedures to ensure good quality water. in effect, water becomes a commodity subject to the laws of the market. the neoliberal model is thus applied to water. when we do not distinguish between countries and regions where water is abundant and poses no problem, and regions where drought and low rainfall make it scarce, limiting their possibilities for minimal economic and social development, we are already altering the ecological principle to make it a devastating weapon. in the same vein, it is somewhat ironic to make it difficult to share this good, which is rare in some areas, while those living in areas with abundant water give advice on water restriction to those living in areas affected by drought. it is this lack of sensitivity and solidarity which motivated my vote as a member of parliament from one of the dry mediterranean agricultural regions but with prospects such as the region of murcia.

the rapporteur. - (es) mr president, i also have the pleasure of greeting the spanish commissioner, mr solbes, whom i have congratulated on several occasions, both inside and outside parliament, for the excellent work he has done in the kingdom of spain in the field of european convergence. the proposal to amend this regulation, concerning the application of the protocol on the excessive deficit procedure annexed to the treaty establishing the european community, raises a fundamental question concerning the adaptation to the european system of accounts (esa 95) which, as you know, replaces the previous system of accounts integrated in 1979, and above all a question concerning the emergence of new ranges of financial products, the consistency in the calculation of the ratios between the public deficit and gross domestic product in the light of this european system of accounts for 1995, and, finally, the taking into account of the importance of the calculation of interest expenditure and its consistency with this new methodology. in my view, the purpose of the proposal for a regulation is to update the definitions and assessments of certain economic transactions involved in the calculation of the deficit within the meaning of the maastricht treaty, which sets maximum percentages for the general government deficit in relation to gdp at market prices in the various states. until now, member states have calculated this gdp in accordance with the esa 79 methodology. the last estimate we have is the one submitted in september 1999 and which referred to the 1998 accounting year. therefore, if this regulation is approved, the estimate corresponding to march 2000, the first estimate of the deficit for the 1999 accounting year, will already be made in accordance with this new system. it is known that the member states have done their homework, so to speak, and have calculated and drawn up their national accounts in accordance with esa 95, and their corresponding estimates are already published. this has meant, in addition to the incorporation of the new methodology, the nominal revision of most of the accounting aggregates and operations due to the methodological changes and more refined statistical information incorporated in the estimates. of course, these changes are likely to alter the public deficits in terms of national accounts of the member states. and very briefly, i will say what are the five areas that are perhaps the most important changes. first, the adjustments in the delimitation of what is meant by the institutional sector of general government according to the esa 95. this is important because the government deficit refers to what all public administrations get in this case. the absence of precise criteria for their definition would produce discrepancies in the estimates of member states' government deficits. second, the public deficit - or, if appropriate, the surplus - is equal to the balance of the general government sector of the esa 95, called the financing need or capacity. thirdly, public investment is equivalent to gross fixed capital formation, according to the esa 95 for the general government sector. fourth, government debt is defined in accordance with esa 95, as are flows or interest arising from this liability or asset. fifth and lastly, the aggregate to which the government deficit will refer will be gross domestic product at current market prices, estimated in accordance with the definitions of the european system of accounts 1995. in sum, this commission proposal represents, in my view, a correct and practical adaptation of the criteria laid down in the european system of accounts 95 and i therefore approve it in its entirety, as expressed by the commission.

commission - mr president, i should like to begin by thanking the rapporteur, mr viceconte, and congratulating him on his report. i think we all recognise the economic, social and environmental importance of tourism in europe as it has developed so far and its extraordinary potential for growth and jobs. i am glad to see that the commission and parliament are going in the same direction on this point. employment is now the main concern in tourism. to make progress in this area, it is essential that cooperation with member states and industry and other partners be as fruitful as possible. the success of our work will depend on it. it is obvious that the commission will seek to ensure that there is good coordination with employment policies. this will also be important in the run-up to the march summit, where the importance of tourism in job creation will certainly be mentioned. the coordination of community tourism activities with other important issues such as regional policy, transport, employment, the environment, culture and competition must involve the member states and the tourism industry itself. as regards specific policies, i would just like to emphasize one, which the draft resolution insists on: regional policy. the commission's text containing the guidelines for the structural programmes for the new programming period already indicates that tourism is one of the areas which offers considerable potential for job creation through the competitiveness of its enterprises. the commission hopes that the member states will place greater emphasis on measures relating to tourism when they draw up their plans and projects. quality, sustainability and innovation are at the forefront of the commission's policy and are priorities recognised by the council of ministers. quality products to improve competitiveness, sustainability to protect resources and innovation in particular through information technology. the european environment agency and the commission have already started work on sustainability indicators. i would like to stress, as others have already done today, that tourism based on natural and cultural heritage is expected to be the type of tourism in europe that will grow the most over the next two decades. it is imperative that we exploit this potential. mr provan said that i often talk about tourism and information technology. i am personally convinced that information and communication technologies will play a key innovative role in european tourism. the travel and tourism sector is at the forefront of the use of information and communication technology tools. it will profoundly change the way he operates. marketing, booking and transport are expected to be the areas that will undergo the greatest changes and improvements. the use of these technologies opens up a whole new dimension in the field of travel and tourism. direct contact between the consumer and the firm will complement, and sometimes also reduce, the current and almost exclusive business-to-business relationship. the tourist offer will be broader and better and new products of better quality will be created. to do this, the commission believes that action in the field of tourism must be closely linked to measures to promote the adoption of information and communication technologies by the tourism industry, in particular through the technological innovation programme and the technological programme for an innovative society, both of which are within my remit. the new strategy set out in the commission communication on tourism and employment and approved by the council focuses on the collection and dissemination of tourism information and good practice. the implementation of the statistics directive aims to improve knowledge of the structures and trends of the european tourism market and the sector concerned. the commission's decisions have advanced the methodological approach. the report on the experience gained in the work carried out under this directive is part of our work programme for the current year. additional work on the social and economic impact of tourism is currently underway in collaboration with international organisations such as the world tourism organisation. the european community's primary role is to provide a framework which enables and encourages stakeholders and authorities at all levels to optimise and realise the potential of the tourism sector for growth and employment. such a european strategy will be achieved by building on the commitment of the member states and the commission to cooperate in a number of priority areas: exchange and dissemination of information, including through new technologies; training to improve skills; quality of tourism products and sustainable development in the tourism sector. the commission will report in the autumn on progress in this respect. in about two years' time, a report on the work to be undertaken jointly with the member states and the tourism sector should be available. depending on the results of this work, a wider debate could then take place, which could well be the starting point for even more comprehensive policy initiatives. mr medina ortega asked me some very specific questions. as regards the role of tourism policy in the communities concerned, we must understand that many policy sectors have a huge impact on the structure of tourism. specific, targeted tourism measures are not the only ones to be imported; there are also other horizontal actions in the transport sector. at present, congestion of airways and roads is the fundamental problem. in the field of the environment, we are looking at methods of cooperation with mrs wallström; in the field of regional policy, mr barnier pays great attention to this sector. we need a streamlined approach to tourism, covering all policies. i am sure that we will make progress in this area in the future, when we have a good report from the high-level working group, the support of your report and also when the tourism sector is brought under the umbrella of business policy. why is it so important in this business? because in the enterprise policy the main emphasis will be on support for the creation of new enterprises, on how to help young people to set up their own enterprises more easily. that's where the potential lies. if we can remove barriers and lower the cost of starting a business, make access to finance easier and change the attitude of society to have a more positive entrepreneurial spirit, i am sure that the tourism sector will be the first to benefit. there is a problem i hesitate to mention today because i am new to this business. i have worked in all sectors of industry and services, but when you look at the organizational structure of the tourism sector, it's almost impossible. it is very difficult for a commissioner to try to work in a sector with dozens of organisations whose representativeness must be checked every time. to strengthen the role of tourism in europe, organisations should do what has been done in most economic sectors: seek better convergence, coordination and concentration of activities. then we can start a serious dialogue in our daily work. this is the main difficulty we have to overcome. as far as the treaty is concerned, the intergovernmental conference started this week and we do not yet know the outcome. i want to be very frank: i have not seen much enthusiasm for this conference or for the proposal to expand the powers of the eu. tourism is also on the list of subjects which are not among the new areas of eu competence. we shall see what happens, but for the moment it does not seem to be the case. finally, the commission welcomes the resolution which is in line with the high level group, the commission communication on increasing the employment potential of tourism and the council conclusions on this. the general agreement reached between the two institutions in this area should not prevent the commission from taking the most pragmatic approach to achieving our common objectives. - the next item is the oral question (b5-0010/2000) by mr hatzidakis, on behalf of the committee on regional policy, transport and tourism, to the commission, on european postal services.
- mr. markov, you'll have a few minutes in five or six minutes. i'd appreciate it if you wouldn't interrupt your colleagues.
- (es) like mr radwan, i am glad that commissioner monti is here today in place of mr bolkestein, because i think he can shed light on certain aspects of competition. i do not know whether mr monti is aware of the judgment of the court of justice of the european communities last week, namely on 10 february, which envisages the possibility of a dominant position on the part of the german postal service, as a consequence of the existence of the postal monopoly. before the next liberalisation on 1 january 2003, competition will undoubtedly have to be introduced in this sector, as postal trade is currently being diverted through countries with very low rates. this has an effect on free competition between the different postal administrations. assuming that liberalisation is achieved throughout the european union, what consequences could this have for free competition? so far as we know, in the only country where it has been implemented, sweden, the liberalisation has resulted in a 59% increase in the price of postal services. but we do not know what will happen in each of the countries where liberalization is going to take place. it is foreseeable that postal liberalisation will lead to greater differences in the cost of postal services between countries, with likely consequences for competition, not only on the cost of postal services but also on the establishment of facilities. for example, today there are companies that set up in the netherlands because postal rates are lower there than in germany, and similar situations may occur in the future. in this connection, i wonder whether the package of measures which the commission will present on postal liberalisation includes provisions on the maintenance of free competition, since it is very likely that postal liberalisation in this sector - as has happened in most sectors of the present community - will lead to concentrations of large companies which will eventually eliminate the benefits of theoretical liberalisation. at present, in theoretically non-liberalised services - such as national postal services - there is a fundamental liberalisation, which is being developed through the system of the universal postal union allowing low rates. in a theoretically liberalised service, free competition may disappear because of concentration of the service in large entities through abuse of a dominant position or because of agreements between companies and other similar problems. i would therefore advise commissioner monti to look at the issue of postal liberalisation from the strictly free-competition point of view, because i think that in the future this will become a matter of concern. i believe that liberalized postal services will probably be much less competitive than the current public postal services.
commission - mr president, i consider it a privilege to be taking the place of my colleague, commissioner bolkestein, in a debate of such quality on postal services. i shall try to answer this debate on the basis of the information which commissioner bolkestein has given me. let me repeat that he will be available to the committee on regional policy, transport and tourism this monday. some members, such as mr stenmarck, complain about the delays in the new proposal. others think that, after all, it is not so bad to take a short break after the first stage of liberalization. this is the position expressed by mr berthu, for example. the commission's position is that the delays in the new proposal are mainly due to internal problems within the commission which i am sure parliament is not totally unaware of. but we feel we have a legal obligation to make a proposal. commissioner bolkestein intends to submit such a proposal to the commission for adoption during the first half of this year. the date for implementation of the next steps, 1 january 2003, remains realistic. the proposal will take account of the studies undertaken and will examine in particular each question such as universal service, to which i shall return in a moment. as regards the existing directive and its implementation, most member states have taken the necessary legal measures to transpose the directive. a number of problems exist with regard to the structure of the regulator and its independence. the deadline for member states to implement the directive expires in january 2003. liberalisation will continue thereafter. some areas, such as the courier and express sectors, are already subject to competition. in general, the quality of services has improved, particularly at cross-border level. the quality of services, which is so important to consumers, was a key concern for all the speakers, some of whom, including mr rübig, were very explicit on this point. the experience of more advanced countries on the path to liberalisation, such as sweden, finland or the netherlands, shows that when liberalisation is carried out in an organised way, the requirements of national regulations for higher quality of services and the monitoring of these can lead to improved quality of services. it is not a question of selling the service or its quality. frequently, liberalisation leads to guaranteed standards and continuous standardisation of service quality assessment also contributes to this, as these standards will better reflect actual performance. this will allow for a serious performance assessment and better customer orientation by the responsible operator as a result of the combined pressure from regulators, competitors and customers. we can see, dear responsible operators, in the post offices a change in culture which i do not think anyone can regard as negative if the current trend of focusing on the needs of the customer is maintained. the concerns expressed this morning by members of this house will be at the heart of the work of my colleague and the whole commission in preparing the next proposal. this proposal will take full account of the need to guarantee universal service, develop effective safeguards for consumers and create a climate conducive to new jobs - not job losses - in the context of a gradual, gradual evolution. the question of universal service was raised by mrs isler béguin, by mr miller - whom i thank for his personal message - and by many others. we are all aware of the extreme importance of social and structural cohesion, particularly in the sparsely populated rural areas, one of which was particularly strongly and overwhelmingly represented in this morning's debate. we believe that universal service is a pillar and i am confident that my colleague will be able to give assurances to the appropriate parliamentary committee. mrs gillig, and others such as mr markov and mr esclopé, expressed concern about employment. experience in other sectors shows a kind of u-curve: a phase of declining employment begins just before liberalisation, the existing operator naturally preparing to be competitive. in a second phase, employment stabilises, with the jobs created by the new operators offsetting the potential further reductions in employment. finally, there is a third phase of net job creation, both for the responsible operator and for new ones, at a time when the benefits of liberalisation are reaching users and market development is accelerating. in the postal sector, the first phase has already begun, with universal service providers having embarked on a process of modernisation. rather than the process of liberalisation of the sector, it is new technologies and logistics which are the main factors influencing employment. as regards the availability of the studies, which was raised by mr staes and other members, copies of each of these studies were sent to parliament in september 1999. they have all been available on the commission's website since august 1999 and the commission is prepared to provide a copy to anyone interested. the studies have been the subject of some criticism, particularly from the public postal services. i am aware that all the studies that have been undertaken have had difficulties in collecting adequate data. this was not surprising to us, as universal service operators do not always have detailed mail collection systems. does that not say a lot about management ability? no single methodology for accessing the cost and financing of universal service is accepted by all parties. nevertheless, mr bolkestein is convinced that the studies undertaken are sufficiently clear and precise to form the basis of the decision-making process. i come now to three speeches on a subject which i am supposed to know better than the postal services: competition. mr purvis, i found your methodologically provocative comment on the tender interesting and certainly worth exploring. mr medina ortega, i am as convinced as you are that we will have to be more vigilant even after liberalisation, because we do not want the disappearance of public monopolies to give rise, in the absence of control over concentrations, to private operators. this applies to the postal sector as well as to other sectors. if i may give you an example of this kind of vigilance, i will mention the case of deutsche post, for which the commission, following complaints and legal action, opened a formal state aid investigation procedure in july. we have just received the german government's reply to the comments. the state aid procedure covers the issue of cross-subsidisation between monopoly postal services and commercial courier activities and the financing of the recent and numerous acquisitions of deutsche post. i will not go into detail because of the lack of time, but perhaps this illustrates, among other things, the fact that the commission does not stop its work with the progress of liberalization. in a sense, that's where his work begins. finally, mr radwan, it is clear that there must be limits to competition, and there are limits. if we look in particular at the question of competition and services of general interest, when a member state defines a public service mission, it is important to quantify the costs of that mission and state aid compensating for those costs is certainly not a violation of competition. i do not entirely agree with the terms you used, mr radwan, when you said that it was time to consider the needs of citizens rather than the need for competition alone. that is a concept which i firmly reject because competition is for citizens and citizens alone. most companies hate competition. competition is implemented and managed in the interests of citizens, in their economic interest and for their freedom. the examples of liberalisation and competition in air transport and telephone services in europe show that citizens have benefited. i can only repeat that commissioner bolkestein will be able to address all these concerns in a more competent and detailed manner next monday in the appropriate committee.

counsel. - (pt) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the celebration of international women's day is an imperative that is adapted to the process of women's accession to the place that has always been theirs and which is intrinsically linked to their dignity. the celebration of this day must therefore combine two fundamental aspects: the aspect of remembrance, the ability to link us to the past of this cause and to all those who have associated themselves with it, among whom i would highlight the non-governmental organisations to be quite fair, and, on the other hand, the symbolic aspect, the potential of the cause of equal opportunities between men and women, as regards the future. it is by bringing out what has been in the shadows that this holiday will help men and women to see themselves as the starting point and the end point of their own dignity, in a process where it is not so much a question of sanctifying time, but of purging it of any prejudice. a celebration of this kind is all the more appropriate because by recalling the past we help to get rid of the millennia-old stigmas that have marked women in their forced cohabitation with poverty, in their inferiority in education, in their natural fragility that exposes them to gratuitous violence, in their forced removal from power and the decision-making framework, in their health affected by the circumstances of motherhood, or by violence, or even exploitation, in the weight that society imposes on them in terms of family responsibility, economic fragility and in terms of employment, in the lack of time to devote to their own person and still in the status of a complex object that is their own in terms of social communication, in trafficking and sexual exploitation, finally in the endless list of violated human rights. the foresight of ancient greece has given us the natural heritage of the identification between equality and justice. aristotle is very clear when he says that what is just is what conforms to laws and observes equality, what is just makes us conform to laws and equality, what is unjust leads us to lawlessness and inequality. but two thousand years after him, voltaire warns us against the apparent simplicity of this thought, telling us that equality is the most natural cause, but at the same time the most chimerical. since men are exaggerated in everything, as soon as they can they exaggerate inequalities. modernity and the democratic regime on which it is based rests on the idea of the social contract, the form of association which, according to rousseau, defends and protects, with all the common force, the person and property of each partner and by which each one, binding himself to all the others, obeys only himself and remains as free as before. as each one gives himself completely, the condition is the same for all. the same conditions apply to all, so it is in no one's interest to make it a burden on others. however, we know that this condition of universal equality did not include women. in postmodernity, after having declared the inadequacy of rousseau's social contract, we must apply a new form of contract, richer and more enriching because it is more in line with the nature of the human being in his polarity of male-female integration. we need to move towards a new gender social contract, but this proposal stems from democracy itself. we live in an age where politics is devalued, where democracies suffer from a lack of political engagement by citizens. we must understand this fact from the implications of the binomial citizenship-democracy, concepts and realities that are mutually determining. the exclusion of women from the full exercise of citizenship rights is, in my view, one of the determining factors in the crisis of democracy, which only an integrated policy of gender equality can help to reverse. it aims at the goal of parity, which must be realized in the emergence of a parity democracy, a new paradigm that will result from the realization of the new gender social contract, a path or shortcut to an inclusive society. globalisation has various implications for democracy. it shows the need for a new ethic, the insufficiency of personal and social ethics having been amply demonstrated. the concepts of fluidity, mobility and speed are finally established at a stage never seen before: that of the planet. concepts and realities such as transnationalism, regionalism and tribalism have definitely landed in our daily lives, posing a problem and a question sometimes in a drastic way. as for the irreversible path towards the establishment of democracy on a global scale, which seems to be a given, we have discovered at the same time the extent of the social suffering resulting from the flow of globalization in the most fragile layers of humanity and, therefore, for women, since poverty is taking on the name and face of women. in fact, the accumulation of wealth and power has increased the number of those who are excluded. technological progress has created and multiplied the number of unemployed. the globalisation of the economy and the financial system has removed certain attributes that previously belonged to the state, which has been reduced to the dimension of a parallel state. the reality of nomadism emerges simultaneously and consequently, which aggravates the problems of social inclusion, a new situation which reinforces the factors mentioned above. in short, exclusion is becoming multiform, it is a fact, and it is everywhere. it is the shame of our regime, which then becomes the democracy of our discontent, a process of exclusion, disaffection, stigmatization and social disqualification without equal in time and space. in the context of the portuguese presidency, taking into account the efforts and contributions of the various member states, the extraordinary summit in lisbon, which will have as its theme 'employment, economic reforms and social cohesion for a new europe of innovation and knowledge', aims to counteract these risks, which history tells us are only getting worse for women, especially in the areas most directly linked to the specific nature of the proposed theme. we therefore aim to adopt measures which create the conditions for access to knowledge, continuing training and the overcoming of the constraints which keep people away from technological advances, with all their implications. the aim is to renew the european social model, while at the same time strengthening the employment dimension and social cohesion. we are thus taking a position which reverses the traditional exclusion of women, which is determined by the responsibilities traditionally assumed by women. this is only possible with a new social contract in which the reconciliation of family and working life is of strategic importance and the keyword is 'sharing'. but it is in the political sphere that women's exclusion is most pronounced. this is why the choice of today's theme is so relevant, since it is a decisive factor for the future, since equality has been established in legal terms. the introduction of the feminine is essential to combat the complexity of modern life. it is clear that the lack of effective equality reveals the lack of legitimacy of political structures, their lack of representativeness. all this shows the inadequacy of the mere establishment of legal equality, which, while it was intended to guarantee equality from the outset, was not able to guarantee it in its results. the so-called universalism of the texts of the founding fathers of modern democracy, as i said, did not include women as citizens. women were not thought of as subjects of law. since genuine democracy presupposes and implies equal participation by all citizens, the gender difference leads to a significant deepening of the democratic regime on the basis of this evidence. the human race is twofold and requires a system in which men and women participate in debate and decision-making in a balanced way. parity means a balance of men and women in the structure of social and political representation. being a woman is one of the essential ways of being human. being a woman or a man are divisions of the human race that separate as much as they unite, which is why they are creators of an eternal game of polarity. the concept of parity democracy, based on this observation, takes advantage of managed creativity and puts it at the service of decisions that are more correct, more just and more adapted to the problems it is trying to solve. that is why i believe in parity, a new form of gender equality, which replaces universalism in its truth and within the politically organized society. the beijing platform is a historic milestone on the long journey we are discussing today. the evaluation of the programme, which is currently under way, cannot be used as a pretext for any retreat. this is not a new declaration but simply an assessment of the implementation of the declaration by the signatory states. it must be preserved in its principles, in the values it holds dear, in the objectives it claims to pursue. it can be deep, but never diminished. this is the position that the european union must take. the conclusions of the european evaluation process in geneva last january go in this direction and reaffirm the need for full implementation of the 12 identified areas. the process leading to the launch of the fifth community programme for gender equality 2001/2005 is also underway. our knowledge of the process clearly shows that the continuation and strengthening of the policy of equality between men and women at community level is essential because, despite the progress and work done, there are also significant situations of disparity between men and women in the economic, political, social and civil spheres. portugal, as the eu presidency, welcomes and wishes full success to this programme for the construction of a europe which offers equal opportunities for all. through their polarity, women and men constitute and structure the societies in which they live. it is a new way of thinking about the public and private spheres, a proposal to combat mistrust of politicians and their way of acting, an alternative to overcome mistrust of the functioning of democratic structures and their transparency, and a process to minimise the disaffection of certain sections of the population with regard to traditional political parties and their respective way of doing politics. gender equality policy has value-added aspects that benefit both women and men in terms of personal, social and professional fulfilment, and that contribute greatly to social progress by recognising and enhancing the specific resources of each gender, by contributing to the deepening of democracy, by bringing the decision-making process closer to voters, by introducing new dimensions of women-specific values into the political arena, by contributing to the improvement of the quality of life and the deepening of democracy. in his reflection on the subject of equality, a portuguese thinker pointed out in 1922 that "the necessary condition for equality of rights is equality of power". no one can deny the far-sightedness of his thinking and, in acknowledging it, no one can deny that it is inherent in the essence of democracy. let 's build it . only in this way can we truly say that humanity is a solidarity that extends throughout history. (applause) i would like to thank
commission. - (el) mr president, two centuries ago, at the time of the french revolution, a very famous woman, olympe de gouges, was executed and considered insane for advocating equal rights for men and women. two centuries later, europe has achieved many successes. in the last century, we have gone through three phases. the first was marked by institutional changes, the transformation of the legal framework, major constitutional conquests in all the member states, thanks to the struggles of the women's movement, the great decisions of progressive parties and the action of enlightened women and men. then we had a second phase in which female role models came to the fore. women are everywhere. prime ministers, mps, bankers, ministers and, in the professional arena, doctors, lawyers, pilots, generals. we are now in the third phase, where the composition of the bodies that exercise political and economic power must be transformed. the composition, the transformation of the composition will also lead to changes in policies, which must take into account the values and experiences of both sexes. ladies and gentlemen, the first months of the new millennium were marked by two important events: first, the election of finland's president, mrs halonen. in finland, for the first time, there were more female candidates than male candidates. and it's a woman who's been elected. the other event concerns france, where a law was passed to ensure that women and men are equally represented, following the declaration made in april 1999 at the 'women and men in power' congress. the ministers concerned committed themselves to taking concrete measures and policies that would change the balance of power. we must congratulate the prime minister, mr jospin, for having endorsed this commitment in the clearest and most formal way. (applause) i would like to thank many statements have been made and policies pursued in the member states. the figures are true. and the figures for europe are still problematic. women represent 24% of the members of governments and on average 22% of the members of national parliaments, ranging from 6% in some member states to 40% in others. the number of women in committees that exercise power, that make policy, is very small. even in countries such as germany and belgium, which have specific legal obligations regarding the number of representatives of both sexes, the participation rate of - the next item is the commission statement on the floods in mozambique. i call commissioner patten on behalf of the commission.
mr president, i am not going to go into the details of the situation in mozambique. the continuous torrential rains throughout the southern africa region, exacerbated by cyclone eline, have caused the displacement of a large number of people and considerable damage to homes and infrastructure. it is estimated that 800,000 people have been affected by the floods; about 300,000 people are in urgent need of food and other humanitarian aid. many people have been killed, missing or injured. the government of mozambique has appealed for humanitarian aid from third countries. the international community, including the united states, switzerland, south africa, ireland, norway, denmark, italy, sweden and the netherlands, has so far provided substantial assistance. this afternoon my colleague, mr poul nielson, accompanied by the portuguese secretary of state, is on his way to mozambique to assess the situation on the ground. mr nielson will be happy to report to parliament on the results of his mission. before i talk about the help echo has provided so far, perhaps you will allow me to make three rather personal remarks. first, from 1986 to 1989, i was minister for overseas development and developed a special relationship with the people of mozambique. in those days they courageously faced the enormous problems of the environment and politics, the problems of poverty, and the aftermath of a bloody war. if any country deserves the help of donors, it is mozambique. secondly, this sentiment has been reinforced by the real efforts made by mozambique in recent years to build a strong and prosperous economy and a stable society. thirdly, we have spent much of this afternoon in this chamber discussing conflict prevention, how to prevent crises from breaking out or how to respond to them more effectively. we have spoken of the importance of the commission developing a series of major objectives in non-military crisis-related action and i think i can say that if there is one case that is relevant in this respect, it is the disaster that struck mozambique. let me address the assistance provided so far. last week echo decided to allocate €1 million for flood relief, €600,000 of which will be distributed through the spanish red cross, €150,000 through msf luxembourg for operations in mozambique and €250,000 in botswana through the german red cross. these ngos will address the most urgent need, namely to move people in danger to safer areas, as well as to provide health care, water and sanitation facilities. echo is currently preparing a second decision for an additional eur 2 million. this decision will be implemented through unicef, action against hunger, cosv, nuova frontera and vireaid, pending, of course, the receipt and examination of their final proposals. these ngos will focus on water and sanitation, the provision of shelters, plastic tarps, cans, blankets and similar equipment. they will focus on the resettlement of displaced people, the continued prevention of malaria, cholera and other contagious disease outbreaks, the provision of additional food for malnourished and at-risk children, the provision of seeds and tools, food security, the rehabilitation of vital animal health facilities and the training of people responsible for the organisation of livestock in villages. a third decision will be considered in the light of commissioner nielson's mission. the commission is also preparing a medium-term community response combining ngo co-financing with operations under the european development fund, with a view to helping mozambique to respond to the crisis situation by restoring the rapid growth rate that mozambique had struggled to achieve. it is expected that this response will encompass the current emergency phase and reconstruction for a period of three to four years. at such times, we all realize the extra effort we must make to prevent disasters and to deal promptly with those we cannot prevent. i am not sure at this stage that i can add much to the analysis of what has not worked or what we can improve but it is obvious that we must learn from this terrible calamity. i repeat, commissioner nielson will be happy to report to parliament when he returns from mozambique and the disaster site.

scientific research into the nature of the disease. i agree that such research is necessary and i believe i know that the united kingdom is currently setting up such an organisation. i will be studies but is based on the results of research carried out in the member states. i can also partially accept the passage of amendment no 6 which states that directive 93/53 should be amended in the reasons have been put forward to explain this decline: pollution, overfishing, climate change, etc. to date, it cannot be excluded that iuu fishing may have an impact on wild fish stocks. fish leakage from aquaculture sites has been reported in the past and the virus has been detected in wild fish stocks. in this context, a number of scientific questions which can only be resolved by further research remain open. for this reason, a cautious approach to the control of the ais is necessary. sick fish should not be kept on farms and i am prepared to look into this to avoid unnecessary spread of the virus into the environment. to this end, i propose to amend our original proposal to ensure that rural programmes drawn up by the competent authorities must be approved by the commission, in order to avoid excessive withdrawal periods. i also propose that we require that fish with clinical signs of the disease be removed immediately. the procedures for establishing additional control measures, which already exist in community legislation, will be used to implement withdrawal schemes based on the health status of fish, in order to minimise any impact on the environment. in view of this, i can accept amendments nos 7 and 8 with a minor amendment to the latter. i also welcome amendment no 9, but i think it could be better formulated, so that environmental concerns, disease control and eradication strategies are brought together. i do not think i am in a position to accept amendments nos 12 and 13. i believe that these amendments are aimed at achieving zero risk. i think that this objective is very difficult to achieve without closing the sector concerned, namely salmon farms. i look forward to parliament's opinion on these amendments and will take them into due consideration if you think that is the best way forward. i can accept amendment no 11 in part. finally, i would like to stress that we are continuing our efforts to achieve a high level of health protection in accordance with our obligations under the treaty. i believe that measures commensurate with this objective are the way forward. we remain committed to eradicating the disease, which will benefit both the environment and salmon farming. i hope that by accepting our proposal the european parliament will recognise our commitment and i would be very grateful to it.

commission - (pt) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, first of all, the commission would like to stress that the proposal for a regulation under consideration this evening is only and above all a new wording of the 1995 convention on insolvency proceedings. it is well known that the convention in question was the result of long years of often difficult and laborious debate and that it therefore represents a compromise between the principles of unity and territoriality, that is to say, between the structural principles of the various bankruptcy legal systems in each of our member states. the fact that we are aware that the changing world economic situation and, above all, the internal market may require more frequent recourse to bankruptcy proceedings, which often have the character of cross-border proceedings, fully justifies the union as such having the necessary binding legal instruments to ensure that insolvency proceedings are conducted in accordance with a set of common structuring principles and with guarantees of prompt execution. fortunately or unfortunately, corporate bankruptcy will increasingly become a normal circumstance of our everyday economic life. it will also be a factor in the renewal of the fabric of enterprises, which should not be hampered by the existence of slow bureaucratic procedures or by obstacles that prolong the agony of enterprises that are no longer viable. this is why it is important to try to find a legal framework of reference which adapts to the new requirements of the globalised economy. the proposal for a regulation was not put forward by the commission but was a joint initiative of two member states - germany and finland - in the framework of their right of initiative in this field, which they share with the commission. the commission considers that this regulation does not alter the substance of the text of the convention. as early as 1981, the commission expressed its position in favour of the clear adoption of the principle of unity of bankruptcy. this perspective was also taken into account in the commission's proposals for a parallel procedure for the winding-up of undertakings. the 1995 convention, on the other hand, eventually authorises the opening of secondary procedures and thus creates situations of exception to the general rule which the commission would like to see adopted. following the entry into force of the treaty of amsterdam, the commission would have preferred the adoption of a new text expressly enshrining the unity thesis. however, i do not think that this is the time to call into question the agreement reached on the 1995 convention after 30 years of negotiations. the commission therefore refrained from submitting a proposal and confined itself to concentrating its opinions on institutional matters. that is also why the commission does not think it should table an amended proposal for the regulation, but wants to express its views on the amendments tabled. the commission agrees with amendments nos 1, 2, 3 and 5 proposed by the rapporteur, mr lechner. however, it does not agree with amendment no 4. the commission considers that parliament should rather support amendment no 4 by the committee on civil liberties and human rights in order to allow the commission to amend the annexes to the regulation, with the help of a regulatory committee in accordance with the procedure laid down in article 5 of decision 1999/468. the commission therefore agrees with amendments nos 3 and 4, but not with amendments nos 1 and 2 concerning the concept of the 'centre of the debtor's main interests'. in fact, as regards the centre of a company's or a collective person's main interests, the concept is perfectly defined in article 3. in all other cases, which are not directly envisaged, the reference to recital 13 seems to us to be sufficient.

commission - we are finally coming to the end of a process which began a year ago, under the previous parliament. apart from the importance of the subject itself, this regulation and the annex to it on tropical forests are the first two regulations on development cooperation to be examined under the codecision procedure. so for many of us, it's an interesting learning experience. the previous regulation expired at the end of 1999. since the beginning of the year the commission has been unable to make any financial commitments under these budget lines. this puts the commission and europe in an increasingly difficult position. which explains our desire to complete the adoption process in the near future. in this context, we have supported the informal negotiations between the council presidency and the rapporteur of parliament with the aim of reaching a proposal which could be accepted by both sides. the main stumbling blocks were the financial reference amounts, the comitology and the duration of the settlement. i should like to make a brief comment on each of these points. as regards the financial reference amount, we accept the compromise proposals made in amendment no 11. as regards comitology: our position has been to advocate an advisory procedure rather than a management procedure for the implementation of the regulation, in accordance with council decision 1999/468/ec of 28 june 1999 which states that 'the management procedure should be used for management measures such as those relating to the application of the common agricultural policy and the common fisheries policy or those relating to the implementation of programmes with significant budgetary implications'. in our view, the programme to be financed under the regulation has no significant budgetary implications and does not therefore merit a management procedure, a consultative procedure being more appropriate. however, in view of the council's opinion on this matter and in order to avoid conciliation, we support the compromise proposal put forward by parliament for a separate comitology procedure whereby decisions on the strategic guidelines for the actions to be financed would be subject to a management procedure, while the approval of projects, for the limited number of projects above eur 2 million, would be subject to a consultative procedure. the commission therefore supports amendment no 16 in principle, but prefers the wording of amendments nos 19, 20 and 21. as regards the duration of the regulation, we are in favour of an indefinite duration, subject to periodic review after the evaluations have been carried out. we are nevertheless aware that if an indefinite period were to be approved here, it would inevitably lead to a conciliation procedure. in this context, we think that a seven-year period proposed by the council is perfectly appropriate and, in order to avoid conciliation, we do not support amendment no 18, which provides for an indefinite period for the regulation. the last important issue which is common to this regulation and the forestry regulation concerns the amendments relating to bank guarantees. we share the parliament's view that the commission should not put bureaucratic barriers to access for certain ngos to funding from community funds. for this reason, the commission decided in july 1999 to require bank guarantees only for advance payments of more than eur 1 million. this largely solves the problem. the commission also considers that these issues are easier to resolve horizontally than through specific regulations. that is why the commission does not support amendment no 10 on bank guarantees. the other amendments to the environmental regulation can be divided into two categories: on the one hand, amendments which consist of reformulating certain elements of the scope of the proposed act or its means of intervention; the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the commission's position on these two types of amendments is as follows. in order to find a compromise solution which might avoid conciliation, the commission could support amendments nos 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8, although in its view they add little value to the text as a whole. a careful reading of the common position shows that most of the concerns underlying these amendments have been taken into account, but in accordance with the structure of the regulation. the second type of amendments is more problematic for the commission, which does not support them. amendment no 9 - coordination with local partners, as formulated in the report - is not supported by the commission, not because it does not agree with the principle, but because the article in question is formulated in the context of the treaty, which refers only to coordination with the member states. amendment no 12 proposes to increase the amount of projects for consideration by the council from eur 2 million to eur 5 million. the commission has already proposed a number of amendments to the proposal, including a number of amendments to the proposal for a directive on the protection of the environment. we are also concerned that its adoption may lead to a conciliation procedure. the commission therefore does not support it. the amendments on supply and market access - amendments 13 and 14 - would be a departure from the carefully agreed standard formulations. in any event, the commission does not consider it appropriate, as in the case of bank guarantees, for these issues to be resolved through special provisions in specific regulations and prefers that they be resolved in a horizontal manner. we oppose amendment no 15 on the creation of an environmental monitoring unit, since we believe that this is an internal organisational issue within the commission which should not be resolved by means of a regulation. this unit is, in fact, already operational although we wanted to strengthen it. finally, we do not support amendment no 17 because it is not in accordance with the rules or the terms of the usual regulations and is considered redundant.
the rapporteur. - (es) mr president, as commissioner nielson has said, we are inaugurating with this debate the new powers of the committee on development and cooperation in the area of codecision. the regulation under discussion today is intended to create measures to promote the conservation and sustainable management of tropical forests in developing countries, so as to be able to guarantee the financial means necessary to maintain and extend the actions and projects which, with this objective, have been launched since the approval of regulation 3062 in force until december 1999. this financial instrument enables the union to fulfil its obligations under the convention on biological diversity, the framework convention on climate change and the convention to combat desertification. all these conventions emphasize the need to support developing countries in finding solutions to problems concerning their forest resources. between 1990 and 1995, more than 56 million hectares of forest, unevenly distributed but certainly affecting developing countries in particular, were lost as a result of increased land use for agriculture, infrastructure construction, natural disasters and fires. we are therefore faced with a problem of primary importance, not only for the developing countries but also for the whole planet and the living beings that inhabit it, a problem on which parliament already gave its opinion at first reading at the end of the previous parliamentary term on 5 may 1999. since then, a long and sometimes difficult negotiation process has taken place within the council, which only resulted in a common position in december 1999 between the council, the commission and parliament, in the search for the necessary consensus. all this is conditional on the approval of a budget which imposed limitations in several areas, particularly the need to allocate funds to set up the special plan for the reconstruction of kosovo. parliament has already approved a total of 34 amendments at first reading, 18 of which have been incorporated in whole or in part into the council's common position. of the remaining 16 amendments, some of them, in particular amendments nos 5 and 6, no longer have any reason to exist after the interinstitutional agreement on the budget for the year 2000. the discussions and negotiations we have had with the council and the commission have been on three issues: the budget, the timetable and comitology. the rapporteur would particularly like to highlight the effort and flexibility that everyone has shown in bringing budgetary positions closer together, so that from an initial allocation of eur 9 million for line b7-6201, which meant a total of eur 73 million for the whole period, we have reached an agreement providing for the provision of eur 249 million for the whole of the next seven years, on top of the eur 30 million already provided for in the 2000 budget. from that budgetary agreement - which also implies an agreement on the timetable - the differences mainly concerned the comitology aspects arising from the historical positions of parliament and the council, which in the future, in my view - and not to stress the problems highlighted in mr wijkman's speech - should be revised in an interinstitutional agreement in order to make the parliamentary legislative process faster and more fluid. i would like to conclude by asking the house to support amendments nos 1, 7, 9, 10, 11 and 12 and to vote against the other amendments, which, if adopted, would end the agreement reached in the discussions with the commission and the council, which would force us to start the whole negotiation process again, paralyse certain projects and actions to be carried out and probably cause serious problems in the policy of conservation and rehabilitation of tropical forests which we want to develop.

definition of the objectives of social policy in the treaty and the community acquired its own competences, complementary to those of the member states. in nice, before the great enlargement, i ask you to look at this text carefully, i beg you to look at it prospectively. as we are today, we could function well or badly and continue to live together. but that is not what we are talking about, mr president, i would like to ask you to take the time to answer the two questions. i am particularly pleased to have the opportunity today to reply to mr van de bos on the subject of anti-personnel mines. i shall also take the opportunity to answer mrs carlotti's question. the commissioners adopted a communication and a draft regulation on eu action to combat landmines with the aim of achieving greater coherence, efficiency and visibility of the very important actions in this field in which we are already engaged. in doing so, we are responding to the parliament's initiative, on which we are basing ourselves, to create a specific budget line for mine action. landmines have caused terrible losses in many of the world's poorest regions. not only do they represent a constant and insidious threat to life, but they also impede economic development and the implementation of a series of community programmes of aid for reconstruction, rehabilitation and development. that is why the union is already strongly committed to the fight against landmines throughout the world and why we are also active in the negotiation and conclusion of the ottawa convention on the prohibition and destruction of anti-personnel mines, which entered into force a year ago. over the past eight years, the european community has allocated more than eur 180 million to the fight against landmines. we've been all over the world. we have supported the actions of local authorities, international organisations, particularly ngos. we helped to clear and destroy mines and to assist the victims and to research new techniques of mine clearance. but so far we have not had a coherent overall approach to our mine action. to make the most of the diversity of our instruments and funding mechanisms, we need to ensure that we have a structure within which we can formulate the priorities and horizontal guidelines to ensure the effectiveness and coherence of our actions. funding for mine action under regional cooperation programmes and from the budget line of such programmes will continue. mine clearance and other mine action are often a preliminary step to any sensible development programme. they should therefore be part of national or regional reconstruction and rehabilitation programmes. the new regulation and the special budget line will support and complement the geographical line by promoting the overall structure of the policy and by functioning as a general reserve and a source of funding for international programmes. the budget we have for mine action should remain unchanged in real terms, as we have been able to do in recent years, i.e. it should be around 30 million euros per year. regular programmes for the removal and destruction of mines under our new policy should benefit mainly the countries which have signed the ottawa convention. but we must also be prepared to provide exceptional assistance to mine victims in their homes or elsewhere when they have been displaced, even when they are unlucky enough to be in a non-signatory country. finally, the european union is recognised as one of the leading funders of mine action in the international community. the entry into force of the ottawa convention a year ago has given us a powerful new instrument and a set of ambitious objectives for the years ahead. we have set ourselves the objective of eliminating all landmines in the world within 10 to 15 years. this will require determination, consistency, and perseverance. with the funding and coordination mechanisms under the new regulation and the communication, we are well placed to meet this challenge.
the commission has already submitted to the council and parliament a report on the implementation of the new regulation. a breakdown of eu funding for mine action by country from 1992 to 1999 and projects over the past year is attached to the communication and we will also continue to provide this type of financial information. how can i say how much i thank the honourable member and other members of this house for their encouragement and support and for the way in which they have handled this matter, which is of enormous importance as we are sadly continuing to discover.
commission - what we obviously need to do is to make very clear what we have. we have created a website which will, i hope, allow us to inform ngos and other organisations very clearly about what we have. we are trying to establish a multiannual work programme. we'll talk about it on our website. so i hope that the ngos will feel involved in what we are doing. much depends on their active support and understanding. i would like to mention another subject which concerns them, although they are not always so directly associated with it, namely research as a whole, for which we spent 17 million euros out of more than 40 million in the last full year, 1998. but in general, i can assure the honourable member that we will involve the ngos as much as possible. they have much to contribute to this important work.

commission. - the commission, mr clegg, recognises that the agreement on china's accession to the wto is an extremely important decision. this is precisely the type of agreement which would be subject to parliament's assent procedure if the commission's proposals to the intergovernmental conference were accepted by the member states. however, at this stage these are only proposals and the commission cannot go against the rules in force laid down by the treaty establishing the communities or anticipate the decisions taken by the member states at the intergovernmental conference. i would remind mr clegg, if necessary, that in view of its service-related aspects, the china accession agreement would, however, in principle be subject to the article 300 consultation procedure. this means that parliament, under rule 300, should have the opportunity to give its opinion on this agreement. of course, as usual, it is the council's job to consult the european parliament. that is the legal and institutional answer to your question, mr clegg. as regards the more practical aspects, i would like to reiterate my willingness to seek with the european parliament the means of making its voice heard in these negotiations. i have said this on several occasions and i think this is important for relations between the commission and parliament and also important for the effectiveness and scope of the negotiator in a case of this kind. i am therefore quite prepared, as usual, to have this subject discussed in some depth before the committee responsible in parliament.
commission - i share your view, mr clegg, that china's accession to the wto would be, will be, at any given moment, of the utmost importance. however, i do not think that your comparison with the uruguay round is entirely justified. there was in the uruguay round, and particularly with the creation of the dispute settlement mechanism, an institutional leap forward in the international legal order which justified, in the light of an unquestionable reading of the treaties, the existence of the assent. as far as china is concerned, we are legally in a process of accession to the wto, which is a relatively well-calibrated, well-known process, and which has not been contested so far. i therefore assume that the council will hesitate to ask for assent because it is not the council's custom to go much further than what the treaties require it to do in consulting parliament. what is important, from our common point of view, is that when the time comes, we can, either in committee or in plenary, discuss the conditions, which i hope will be those we have agreed with the people's republic of china, and that we do so in full transparency. i am quite prepared and i know that at that time i will be asked questions of a slightly more political nature. i think that's normal and i expect it.
commission. - that is a good question. i claim authorship of this expression: 80 to 20 percent. it is there to try to make it clear that indeed a good part of the way has already been done since what the one who negotiated before you gets, you get through the most favoured nation clause. but there is still 20%, madam, for very simple reasons. in a bilateral negotiation, each party tries to focus on the areas where it is least competitive, with the understanding that the rest is left to the others. that is why, on a number of subjects, the united states has concluded a bilateral agreement with the chinese which we benefit from, but which, on a number of points, is not as favourable to us as if we had negotiated it ourselves. that's one reason. it is up to us, as far as possible - and i am working on it - to ensure that what is generally a good deal between the americans and the chinese is also a good deal for the europeans. and so that 20 percent -- it's only 20 percent -- but you know, in a negotiation, it's often the last percentage points that make all the difference, and that's where we are. there is another reason, more technical, that calls for some nuance. under names which are more or less similar, there may be very different tariff positions. i take the example of alcohol: bourbon and gin are not treated in the same way as whiskey and cognac. while all of these alcohols are, on the surface, the same thing, well there are cases where the tariff positions are not the same. these are more technical considerations but all these aspects must be looked at and negotiated in detail. it's not quite over. i have indicated that i will go to beijing in the last week of march to try to resolve what i consider to be the real difficulties in this negotiation. this is the political part on which the chinese authorities have expressed a number of reservations. these are the reservations which i have been given the mandate to try to overcome and i shall try to do so.

- question no 50 by mrs carmen fraga estévez (h-0190/00): the council has not yet adopted the common position on the proposal for a directive on the approximation of the laws of the member states relating to the protection of employees in the event of the insolvency of their employer. subject: commission proposals to achieve a better balance between northern and southern fisheries agreements in october 1997, the council of fisheries ministers considered the imbalance between northern and southern fisheries agreements: shipowners covered by southern agreements have to co-finance them in an increasing proportion, while northern agreements cost nothing to the shipowners concerned. ministers also discussed the under-utilisation of the nordic agreements, despite the interest shown by other member states in making the most of these opportunities. the council therefore invited the commission to consider measures which would allow the transfer of quotas from one member state to another and to consider how the costs of agreements between the community and shipowners could be allocated 'in a fair and non-discriminatory manner'. what studies have been carried out on the possible transfer of quotas? what have been the results? what decisions are being taken to balance the financial burden of the north-south agreements? what is the opinion of the commissioner responsible for the sector of imbalance mentioned above?
commission - (de) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, on the substance of the matter, the commission is of the opinion that the fishing opportunities granted to a third country under a fisheries agreement should be fully exploited and that appropriate mechanisms should be established for the transfer of unused or unused quotas, without, however, calling into question the principle of relative stability. the commission would point out that an incomplete exploitation problem has arisen only in the case of the greenland agreement, the only agreement concluded in the nordic region. however, mr fraga estévez certainly knows that a number of member states consider any transfer of quotas to be an infringement of the principle of relative stability. consequently, and despite all efforts, the legal mechanisms provided for in community law, which in principle allow such a transfer of quotas, have not yet been able to enter into force. the commission therefore considers that this thorny issue can only be dealt with in the context of a broader and more comprehensive review of the common fisheries policy. it is common knowledge that this examination will have to be undertaken in connection with the reform of the common fisheries policy. when you speak of a disproportion between agreements with third countries in the northern hemisphere and those with third countries in the southern hemisphere, i would draw your attention to the following situation: the community and the member states do not pay any licence fees under the agreements for the northern hemisphere because the third countries in that region have not requested it and these agreements, with the exception of the agreement with greenland, are based on reciprocity - that is to say, a fish for a fish - and have no impact whatsoever on the community budget. on the other hand, the third countries in the southern hemisphere are demanding duties from the community and from the shipowners. moreover, such licence fees were already provided for in the bilateral agreement between spain and third countries concluded before spain's accession to the community. so you will understand that we will not voluntarily propose to include licensing rights in the agreement with greenland or other states in the northern hemisphere unless our partners demand it. apart from that, other third states also fish in the waters of these northern states and they do not pay licence fees either. we would of course like to avoid any inequality of treatment between our fishermen and those of third countries fishing in the same waters. however, this is what would happen if we proposed to pay licence fees on our own initiative. another difference between the agreements in the two hemispheres is that in the agreement with the northern hemisphere, the fishing opportunities granted to the community are expressed in terms of total catch. the same cannot be said for the agreement with the southern hemisphere. our possibilities are directly expressed in terms of the number of fishing vessels or the number of licences. it is therefore naturally possible to provide in the agreement for licensing rights for shipowners. so you see that there are good reasons for doing things differently in the agreements with both hemispheres.
