- the agenda calls for the council statement on the 50th anniversary of the geneva conventions - humanitarian rights.
counsel. - (pt) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, a few months ago we commemorated the 50th anniversary of the geneva convention for the protection of civilian persons in time of war. fifty years ago, 63 countries signed the four conventions and two protocols that still serve as the basis for international humanitarian law. it is worth recalling that these international legal instruments were born in the period immediately following the second world war and that they reflected the deep concern of the international conscience, still pained by the devastating effects of that conflict. the events since then have proved the case of all those who felt that it was essential to strengthen the rights of people in conflict zones, whether civilians or military personnel not directly involved in the conflict. the belligerents were required to adopt a new ethic of behaviour, in line with the reinforcement of the dignity of life, which was gradually enshrined in international regulations in other fields. unfortunately, the facts have shown that the binding nature of the conventions and the way in which they are made effective are far from meeting the requirements of the situations they purport to defend. we are still witnessing acts of war marked by barbarism, by the total denial of the rights of civilians and military personnel outside the battlefield. many belligerent states or forces behave without any principle and only in the interests of the ends they pursue. it is not uncommon to find that civilian populations are the prime targets of military action, either through some forms of terrorism or as an instrument of political pressure. moreover, the atypical nature of some conflicts, especially those in the form of civil war, seems to serve as an excuse for the most serious crimes, often committed under the cover of a lack of information from the outside and a kind of scorched earth policy aimed at victory at any cost, including genocide. in this case, all the actions affecting the most vulnerable social groups take on a special significance and are even more shocking. the inability of these groups to defend themselves ultimately exposes them to all kinds of inhuman treatment. children and the elderly now appear as the central victims of a certain type of conflict. they even seem to be selected as examples. the question of humanitarian organizations comes into play here, their work often seems to suffer from intolerable behaviour on the part of the belligerents, who cynically seek to gain time to assert their victories or promote reprisals against the populations at risk. the capacity of these organisations to act freely and to defend humanitarian workers must continue to be strengthened. in this connection, i would like to draw particular attention to the case of the international committee of the red cross, which already stresses in its reports on specific action the need to improve its own framework for the application of the geneva conventions. if it were not for social communication and the new role that social communication plays in the disclosure of conflicts - and the shocking nature of some of these conflicts as a result of the mobilisation of the international community - the situation we are experiencing today in some war zones would be worse and the degree of impunity would be even greater. mr president, the european union, which defends and practices an order of values which is proudly at the forefront of the international community, has emphasized the vital importance of respect for the geneva conventions. in its external relations, the union promotes these same values and ensures that they are constantly reflected in its political action. we are therefore alert to any breach of the principles which unite us in this area and we constantly denounce any violation of the common foreign and security policy. we are trying to use all the instruments at our disposal to ensure that the pressure we apply is effective in time and in its effects. we are aware that we have often fallen short of our desired targets, but we are determined to continue our efforts in the future. mr president, despite the seriousness and frequency of the violations of human rights, which the geneva conventions and their protocols seek to protect, i believe that the new millennium does offer some elements of hope. this hope lies essentially in the gradual stabilisation of an international order of values which is already beginning to have some difficulty in taking refuge behind outdated criteria, such as cultural differences and certain national peculiarities. slowly but surely, we are undoubtedly moving towards this new international order of values that the globalization of information is promoting and helping to install in the collective consciousness of our societies. we must make sure that our citizens internalize this action so that there is an automatic reaction in the event of actions that do not respect the basic principles that must now be considered our common heritage. by setting up international tribunals such as those now in place for the former yugoslavia and rwanda, we are taking a step forward in making life more difficult for those who promote acts that undermine the values of the geneva conventions. these individuals need to know that the world has become a place where impunity is not a bet. if this message is passed on, we will certainly contribute to the strengthening of humanitarian law and to the necessary credibility and effectiveness of the principles that the geneva conventions and their protocols have tried to protect.
- (es) i congratulate the president on a point of order and i now speak on behalf of the socialist group in the following debate on what we consider to be a satisfactory statement by the council on the geneva conventions, with a preliminary explanation of why my group tabled a resolution on the same subject at the last plenary session of parliament in 1999, a resolution which was not debated for reasons which should not be mentioned here. it seems to us quite appropriate that the european parliament should express itself on standards which have enriched the legal acquis of mankind, since every opportunity should be taken to recall and strengthen the force of these instruments because of the protection they offer and the rights they guarantee. another argument for approving a resolution such as the one we are presenting is that much of the work done by the european institutions is aimed at seeking balance and fairness, and these concepts are little or not compatible with situations of armed conflict. the main victims of conflict - children, women, the general population - are more exposed to threats and suffering, and we cannot fail to make their protection a priority in our action. the more we fight against violations of international humanitarian law, the more we remind other states - taking advantage of all the opportunities offered by our external relations - of the need to ratify and respect the geneva conventions, the more we will help those people who are more exposed to threats. and the more we avoid suffering, the less we have to do to correct the great imperfections of war. what more can be done to improve compliance with international humanitarian law and thus alleviate the suffering of the victims? for example, to make this right known, especially to society itself, to the youth, to mass organizations and to the armed and security forces. we must also develop a passion for peace in our citizens through education. the european union must be a first-class peace-keeping agent in this respect, but it must also be a key partner in the efforts of the organisations to which the international community has entrusted the responsibility for protecting the victims of conflict and defending their rights. among these organizations, the international committee of the red cross is noteworthy. all the institutions of the european union must firmly support the work of the icrc, for its role is simply paramount. finally, i think it is unacceptable to say, as the commission said to me a few months ago in response to a question i had put, that it did not have the necessary competence and resources to carry out actions to promote international humanitarian law, thus expressing a fundamentally bureaucratic point of view and a sensitivity very different from that envisaged by the council in its reply to another question where i expressed a similar concern, and different from the sensitivity shown by the council in its intervention today. in this area, the institutions of the european union - including the commission, of course - have a general responsibility, because it is a matter of spreading and supporting essential values which, moreover, are identical to those inspired by our european project. i therefore ask you, mr president, ladies and gentlemen, to support the resolution which we have before us, which takes up the main points of the proposal put forward by the socialist group at the end of last year.
commission - (da) mr president, i fully agree with the council's statement that the geneva conventions have represented a very important step forward in the development of humanitarian legislation. i also agree that these conventions are as important today as they were 50 years ago. let me take this opportunity to express my full appreciation of the enormous humanitarian work carried out by the international red cross and other humanitarian organizations, both in spreading the knowledge of the humanitarian principles enshrined in the geneva conventions and in helping the victims of wars throughout the world. i feel that the geneva conventions present two main problems at the moment. firstly, there is the gap between the principles and their application and secondly, there are important areas which are not covered by the conventions. to illustrate the ever-widening gap between the principles contained in the conventions and the actual application of those principles, i would point out that ten times as many civilians as soldiers have been killed in conflicts over the last ten years. this is the reverse of what happened in the first world war. this widening gap between principles and their application is, i believe, the result of a change in the nature of warfare over the last 50 years. many wars are still fought in anarchic conditions, in the absence of stable structures and in the absence of government control of the war-affected areas. the world has also seen an increasing number of wars in which weapons are deliberately directed against civilians and aimed at eliminating certain social groups. under such conditions, humanitarian aid to the victims is obviously not welcome, leaving the world with a terrible dilemma. on the other hand, the geneva conventions do not sufficiently target actions carried out by humanitarian actors. although the geneva conventions contain provisions authorising the provision of humanitarian aid in crisis situations, they also stipulate that this right requires the consent of the government of the country concerned. this is especially true when it comes to internal conflicts. the principle of being able to provide humanitarian aid or enable the international community to help and protect people in distress if a state is unable - or unwilling - to do so itself is therefore not universally applicable. this is a serious violation of the humanitarian principle and, in some cases, a fatal shortcoming, with many victims on the conscience. it is precisely and mainly to enable humanitarian organisations to have normal access to the war-torn regions that i went to chechnya at the beginning of february. one of the main problems that arise at the moment, in my view, is to what extent circumstances require a revision of the geneva conventions and in what ways they will have to be revised. i think we have two possibilities, which are not mutually exclusive. the first possibility would be to amend the conventions to enable them to better address the complex crises we are experiencing today, for example by establishing the right to provide humanitarian aid to people in need. the second possibility would be to ensure that humanitarian principles, as defined in the geneva conventions, are actually respected, for example by improving the mechanisms for enforcing these conventions. the first option, i.e. revising the content of the conventions to fill in the gaps, is complex and involves risks. it is complex because the nature of war is constantly changing and it is also fraught with danger because it cannot be ruled out that a new agreement may not be reached once the conventions have been reviewed. but i want to make it very clear: i am sincerely in favour of consolidating the principle of allowing access to humanitarian aid in all situations and of strengthening the right of people in need to receive humanitarian aid. as regards the second possibility, namely to ensure better compliance with existing principles, i believe that one of the best ways would be to allow the prosecution of offenders. the obligation for states to prosecute war criminals is enshrined in the geneva conventions, but this is clearly not enough. that is why i wholeheartedly support the point calling for the speedy ratification of the statute of the international criminal court. this point was also stressed in today's debate. i am in favour of working together to find a solution to this problem so that it can become a legal reality.

president, the debate on xenophobia and racism is a deeply political and social debate. the ludford report contains very acceptable points which every democrat can and should endorse, but also other points which go beyond political and even legal rigor. european citizenship is an abstract concept which lacks legal virtuality. member states regulate the political rights of their citizens under hernández mollar. i shall therefore begin, madam president. the existence of a panoply of fundamental civil, economic, social and political rights, fully guaranteed by constitutional regulation and public authorities, is one of the essential elements of modern western civilization. the various charters and declarations of human rights which mark the history of european-american politics first and then world politics are milestones which ennoble the collective life of humanity, bringing it to the triumph of christian values and the philosophical spirit of the enlightenment up to the present democratic ideal. the european union has always considered respect for fundamental human rights to be one of the fundamental pillars of its inspirational spirit and has made it the frontispiece of its constitutional treaties. without this indispensable component of our moral conception of social organisation, the very existence of the union would be meaningless, for in addition to articulating a vast area of economic freedom, the citizens of the 15 member states want above all to offer the rest of the world an example of scrupulous respect for these rights. but this firm and unequivocal will must be exercised with legal rigor and above all with common sense. nationals of non-eu states legally resident in our territory must be treated on an equal footing with nationals of member states as regards access to education, health and social security. this is done by respecting their religious beliefs and specific cultural traits. any act of racism, intolerance or xenophobia must be immediately repressed in any member state where it occurs. but the administrative status of resident is one thing and the political status of citizen is another. citizens of the union are, at political level, citizens of one of the member states and this enables them to participate fully in political life, including voting in elections, holding representative offices in elections or standing for permanent posts in public administrations. the artificial construction of a european citizenship which is foreign to the indispensable precondition of being a citizen of a member state, a european citizenship floating in the constitutions of the states which make up the union, without a solid legal or political basis, hastily granted to holders of passports of third countries, even if they are residents, represents a great deal of confusion and a risk of infringement of the rights of citizens of the 15 member states. the european union must be a generous place of welcome, open to all those who come to contribute with their efforts and work to the general prosperity or who seek asylum and refuge, fleeing oppression or persecution. but full political citizenship must be acquired in accordance with what has been established in the legal framework of each member state. in his famous lecture at the sorbonne entitled "what is a nation?" ernest renan warned us: "let us not abandon this fundamental principle, that man is a reasonable and moral being, before he is a student of this or that language, before he is a member of this or that race, a member of this or that culture". many of the tragedies that have befallen europe in the 20th century are due to the fact that this wise counsel has been forgotten. let us refresh our memory in the sense indicated by renan, but commission - madam president, as my colleague, mr chris patten, has made clear, it is for me to express the commission's position on the other two reports before us this afternoon: the haarder report and the ludford report. first of all, i would like to say that the commission shares the view of the european parliament that the new legal context following the adoption of the treaty of amsterdam gives the union increased powers and responsibilities in the field of human rights. in this context, the commission welcomes the european council's initiative to draw up a charter of fundamental rights of the european union which will give greater visibility to these rights and also, i hope, greater legal certainty, at least if, as parliament and, as i have already said, the commission wish, this charter becomes a legally binding instrument and under judicial supervision. in this context, and as the personal representative of the president of the commission in the convention responsible for drawing up the charter, i intend to defend the view that the benefit of the charter should be extended to third-country nationals legally resident in the territory of the member states. the commission notes with satisfaction that its views and those of the european parliament on the nature and content of the charter are very similar. that is the case with the debate we had yesterday on the duff and voggenhuber report and it is also the case with the conclusions of mr haarder's report, which i warmly welcome. the commission shares the concern, not just rhetorical, but also practical, to bring a certain consistency to the standards applied in the field of human rights by national courts, the court of human rights in strasbourg and the court of justice of the european communities. in this respect, we are certain that the accession of the european union to the european convention on human rights would clarify the hierarchy of case-law and provide external protection in matters of community law, as is already the case for the legal order of the member states. we believe that this accession is not incompatible with the drawing up of a binding charter of fundamental rights. as regards the content of mr haarder's report, i shall concentrate my contribution to the debate on the areas which are directly within my competence in the commission. i believe that the conclusions of the tampere european council provide a very clear political framework for the european union's policy on respecting and promoting the rights of migrants in the broadest sense. the heads of state or government stressed that the common immigration and asylum policies to be developed on the basis of the treaty of amsterdam should be based on principles that are both clear to citizens and offer guarantees to those seeking protection in the european union or seeking access to its territory. the presidency conclusions also set out the four pillars which will form the basis of the future common european asylum and immigration policy: a partnership with the countries of origin, a common european asylum system, fair treatment for third-country nationals and more effective management of migration flows. i would like to stress above all the need for the european union to have a comprehensive approach to immigration that addresses the political aspects, human rights and development issues in the countries and regions of origin and transit: the fight against poverty, the improvement of living conditions and employment opportunities, the prevention of conflicts, the consolidation of democratic states and respect for human rights, including those of minorities. i would like to reiterate the importance which the union and its member states attach to the absolute respect for the right to seek asylum on the basis of full and comprehensive application of the geneva convention. i would also like to stress the ambition to develop a vigorous policy on the integration of third-country nationals legally residing in the territory of the member states of the union. finally, it must be recognized that while these measures are necessary to guarantee social peace in our member states, we must also strengthen the fight against illegal immigration and guarantee the protection of the rights of the victims of the criminal networks which organise this immigration, with particular attention to the situation of the rights of women and children. i therefore share the concerns of the rapporteur and, i hope, of parliament. the commission would like to draw your attention to the fact that, in order to respond to your concerns, our concerns and the requirements of the tampere mandate, we intend, during the year 2000, to present to parliament and the council all the main instruments of asylum policy: common procedures, revision of the dublin convention and the final instrument of eurodac. but at the same time, the commission intends to present to parliament in the autumn a communication on immigration policy in the european union. we believe that the 1994 communication should be revised and the approach to migration policy in the union updated in the light of the conclusions of the tampere council. as regards the shortcomings of the judicial services which were highlighted during the debate, the commission does not intend to address some of these theoretical and practical issues, which are very interesting, such as the career structure of national magistrates or the length of trials in several member states, because i believe that in this respect the principle of subsidiarity must be respected and that the choice of the essential options is a matter for each member state. the commission would like to stress in this connection that a green paper on legal aid is a good contribution to the need to define common rules on the protection of the accused, such as the guarantee of the assistance of interpreters and translators in cross-border trials, and to the establishment of a more comprehensive programme for the mutual recognition of judicial decisions. as regards civil justice, we believe that the communitization of several civil justice instruments is an effective way of ensuring the effective justiciability of human rights. the commission has already proposed the communityisation of all existing conventions which are not in force, in particular the one on the transmission of documents, to which are added the brussels ii convention and the bankruptcy convention. we have also proposed that the very important 1968 brussels convention on jurisdiction and the recognition and enforcement of judgments in civil and commercial matters be converted into a regulation. all these instruments are currently under examination by the council. even the united kingdom and ireland have decided to join the member states, and denmark, which does not have the same possibility of participating in the work of judicial cooperation in civil matters, is also looking for solutions, which are being examined. finally, as regards the chapters on the rights of the child and women, although they deal mainly with matters within the competence of the member states, i think i can remind the house that the commission and i have committed ourselves to presenting a package of measures on these matters by the end of the year. these measures will be designed to go beyond the joint action of february 1997. they will cover definitions, criminalisation and sanctions relating to the fight against trafficking in human beings for the purpose of sexual exploitation and the sexual exploitation of children.

the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the animal health requirements for the importation of bovine animals are met. i would like to thank mr graefe zu baringdorf in particular for his report on this proposal and the members of the committee on agriculture and rural development for their support for most of the amendments proposed by the commission and for the amendments in the original report of the committee. the member states encountered serious trade problems when the health rules for intra-community trade were updated in directive 64/432, which came into force on 1 july last year. in order to facilitate the transition to the new rules, the commission, under articles 37 and 152 of the treaty, proposed amendments to the directive introducing transitional measures to address the most acute trade problems, minor corrections and clarifications in the annexes and a general mandate to the commission to establish transitional measures in accordance with the new comitology procedure included in the proposal. the committee on agriculture and rural development of the european parliament accepted two amendments tabled by mr graefe zu baringdorf amending the commission proposal. the first amendment calls on the member states to ensure full implementation of the directive and on the member states and the commission to carry out checks on implementation. the second amendment aims to reduce the period of application of the transitional measures to two years. the commission can accept these two amendments, amendments nos 1 and 2, and must therefore reject the amendment tabled by mrs auroi to abolish the transitional measures. i am sorry, however, that i cannot accept amendment no 3, which was tabled by mr graefe zu baringdorf last week. it amended the comitology procedure by proposing the introduction of a management procedure with a right of review for the implementation of the measures relating to article 37. this is in direct contradiction to article 2 of council decision 99/468 on comitology which provides for regulatory committees for matters relating to animal health and it seems that mr graefe zu baringdorf, after lengthy discussions with my office, does not accept this position. but i understand that mr graefe zu baringdorf may have misinterpreted the comitology and is trying to amend it once again in this plenary session. let me express my surprise and concern in this regard. i regret that i cannot accept your new amendment which aims to replace articles 17 and 17a by a new article which covers the whole comitology procedure. it introduces a regulatory committee with the right of control for parliament and, i quote the letter it sent me, 'in the case of a codecision procedure on the basis of article 251 and article 8' - namely article 8 of council decision 99/468 on comitology. i can assure you that i attach great importance to the role of parliament in the legislative process, particularly as regards comitology in the codecision procedure. the overall objective is to achieve rapid and effective results in order to translate policies into legislation. the council decision referred to above clearly establishes the framework for the comitology procedure. the right of parliament to scrutinise is provided for in areas related to codecision, namely article 8. directive 64/432 as amended is based on articles 37 and 152 of the treaty. the new provision on the commission's implementing powers to establish transitional measures may have a direct effect on public health. that is why the commission proposes, in this case, article 17a which mentions a regulatory committee with a right of scrutiny for parliament. i would refer you in particular to article 3 of the directive which amends article 16 of the original directive and which provides that 'where this proves necessary to facilitate the transition to the new arrangements provided for in this directive, the commission may adopt, in accordance with the procedure laid down in article 17a, transitional measures applicable for a period not exceeding three years'. the legal department that advises me thinks that's the appropriate way to handle this matter. where a basic legislative provision provides for amendment by a comitology procedure, the actual comitology procedure must be introduced in the basic provision. the individual provisions envisaging such an amendment should therefore clearly identify the procedure. consequently, the power given to the commission to extend the period provided for in article 3 clearly identifies that it is article 17a which must deal with this problem, which includes article 8 of the council decision of last june, thus giving parliament full power of control over any such proposal. when the current version of directive 64/432 refers to article 17, it is only very slightly and in very few cases referring to implementing measures concerning animal health, on the basis of article 37, which do not concern public health. these measures should therefore not be subject to parliament's right of scrutiny. for example, those implementing measures relate to the approval of cleaning and disinfection procedures and sites, the form for notifying diseases, the approval of assembly centres, the definition of additional guarantees for member states free of diseases not transmissible to humans such as infectious bovine rhinotracheitis or transmissible gastro-enteritis in pigs. i now want to make a few remarks on the implications of the amendment on institutional balance. the commission's implementing powers are set out in the third indent of article 202 of the ec treaty, together with the council decision 99/468 which i have already mentioned, the appropriate council decision laying down the appropriate comitology procedure. this system clearly aims to define precisely the respective roles of the executive and the legislature in the basic legislative instrument. therefore, the basic legislative act must, from the outset, clearly define which implementing measures are based on the co-decision procedure, namely article 152, and which provisions do not have the direct objective of protecting public health and would therefore not be subject to parliament's right of scrutiny. the basic legislative provision to be amended by comitology must clearly define the procedure. any formulation which leaves room for negotiation on a case-by-case basis would compromise the fragile institutional balance and seriously undermine transparency. the wording proposed in the new amendment for the regulatory procedure with the right of scrutiny, i quote 'in the case of a codecision procedure on the basis of article 251 and article 8 thereof', leads to legal uncertainty and is contrary to the implementation of the council decision on comitology. i will quote the document which mr graefe zu baringdorf distributed this afternoon, in which he states his intention to table an amendment at this stage. he said: 'i do not think it is necessary to include two almost identical references to the comitology procedure, just to make sure that the european parliament does not claim rights it does not have.' let me say to the european parliament that i do not intend, by establishing these two procedures - articles 17 and 17a - to ensure that the european parliament does not claim rights it does not have. i am a strong supporter of the codecision procedure and the procedures provided for in the comitology. i strongly support the idea that parliament should have a right of full scrutiny over the commission's proposals where the legal structures of the european union, namely the treaty and the directives, allow it. to deviate from this would be to defy the european court, which i must avoid. i must also reply to mr graefe zu baringdorf that the two almost identical references to the comitology procedure are not in fact identical. they are quite different and should be treated separately. however, it is in the interest of all the institutions that procedures are clearly defined and transparent for all. in addition, the adoption of this amendment would imply a further slowing down of the legislative procedure, which otherwise could be completed after the first reading. in conclusion, i would like to confirm that i accept amendments nos 1 and 2 by mr graefe zu baringdorf, but not his amendment on the comitology procedure which he proposed this afternoon. i cannot therefore accept mrs auroi's amendment. i now counsel. - (pt) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, first of all i would like to point out that the member states of the european union played a very important role at the beijing conference in 1995 in drawing up its platform for action. after its adoption, the european institutions and the member states have been actively involved in its implementation both at national and european union level. as regards the specific issue of trafficking in women, which is dealt with in the chapter on violence against women, the objectives are very clear. the measures to be taken by the governments of the countries of origin, transit and destination of the regional and international organisations are varied and the honourable member is quite right to mention the violation of the safety and dignity of women in europe in the face of the threat posed by this trafficking. it can be sure that the other institutions are considering this matter very seriously and that, in fact, some measures to combat this trafficking have already been taken. i would like to present them as synthetically as possible. firstly, it should be noted that since november 1993 the justice and home affairs council has adopted a series of recommendations on trafficking in human beings for the purpose of prostitution. these measures are intended to combat trafficking in human beings. two years later, your parliament adopted this theme; in addition to adopting certain resolutions, it produced a report and a specific resolution on human trafficking. the commission published its first communication on the issue of trafficking in women and launched the stop programme, which was endowed with €6.5 million per year in 1996, just one year after the adoption of the beijing platform. i think that the importance of this programme should not be underestimated, as it helps to finance many projects and has proved to be very effective. thirdly, the commission and the international organisation for migration organised a conference in vienna in 1996 which proposed an interdisciplinary approach, bringing together elements from the member states, the institutions, the european union, academia and various non-governmental organisations. a number of conclusions are drawn from this work. finally, in 1996, the council approved a joint action to combat trafficking in human beings and the sexual exploitation of children. in 1997, the hague ministerial conference led to the hague ministerial declaration on european directives on effective measures to prevent and combat trafficking in women for the purpose of sexual exploitation. finally, in 1998, the commission adopted a new communication on further action to combat trafficking in women. i would also like to point out that this issue is periodically analysed in the context of the transatlantic dialogue, because this phenomenon also affects countries such as canada and the united states, it is not limited to the specific dimension of the immediate proximity of the european union. we believe that the exchange of views with other countries of destination is increasingly important in order to compare or evaluate the phenomenon and to develop a set of harmonized forms of control. it goes without saying that this issue is regularly on the agenda of contacts with the countries of central and eastern europe, which are transit countries and even countries of origin for a large part of this traffic. in this area, campaigns are financed by the phare programme, some with the help of the international organisation for migration. the council does not wish to comment - i would like this to be clear - on the figure of 300 000 women who are victims of this trafficking in europe, a figure put forward by the swiss foreign minister. there are no such precise statistics on the subject, and we are forced to work on the basis of figures which are very difficult to obtain, since they concern the problems of illegal immigration on the one hand and illegal work on the other. we obviously think that this figure is quite high, we think that an effort should be made to assess it more accurately and we should not, however, dwell on an assessment of this kind, which seems to us to be unfounded. in any case, the problem must be taken very seriously, not only because of the number of people involved, but also because trafficking in women is a type of organized crime that is clearly on the rise worldwide, because it generates considerable profits for a relatively low risk taking by traffickers. some of this trafficking is on a small scale, but there are large international companies and networks that are in the process of creating a sophisticated and well-organised sector with political support and economic resources in the countries of origin, transit and destination. that is why this issue must be tackled at the highest level, in particular in cooperation with the united nations. the honourable member is certainly aware that a draft protocol to prevent, suppress and punish trafficking in persons, especially women and children, is being discussed as a supplement to the united nations convention against organised crime. to this end, the council recently adopted a decision specifically authorizing the commission to negotiate this protocol. the member states of the european union also play a very active role in the session of the united nations commission on the status of women, which is preparing the special session of the united nations general assembly on women. in conclusion, i would like to reiterate the importance which the council continues to attach to this issue of trafficking in children and women, and i hope that i have succeeded in reassuring the honourable member somewhat, at least as regards the council's involvement in this issue.

- question no 2 by mr dupuis, substituted by mr casaca (h-0148/00): subject: articles 6 and 7 of the eu treaty on 2 february the council stated that it would monitor the situation in austria following the entry of the fpö into government, under articles 6 and 7 of the eu treaty. in its resolution of 3 february, the ep 'calls on the council and the commission to prepare themselves, in the event of a serious and persistent breach by any member state of the principles set out in article 6 (1) of the eu treaty, to act under article 7 of the treaty'. in its reply to question h-0826/99 annex to the full report of the proceedings of 21 january 2000, p. 16. the fact that italy is the country most condemned by the court of human rights for the slowness and dysfunctions of its judicial system and that in belgium the trials related to paedophilia are progressing with a worrying slowness and silence, the commission had indicated that "the union must not intervene in the organization of justice in the member states", that it "has established an administrative structure" which, "if necessary, will be responsible for examining cases of serious and persistent violations by a member state of fundamental rights" by applying "the criteria and principles already developed by the european court of human rights and by the court of justice of the european communities". it added that "at the moment, no examination of cases of serious and persistent violation of human rights by a member state is under way". can the council exclude that the above facts constitute serious and persistent violations of fundamental rights as defined in article 6 of the eu treaty and, if so, on what grounds? if not, does it intend to implement the procedures laid down in article 7?
counsel. - (pt) mr president, this question has already been raised more than once today. we must understand that the austrian question in particular, and the question concerning italy and belgium, are different from what is provided for in articles 6 and 7 of the treaty of amsterdam. article 6 of the treaty of amsterdam - and this is important because these are new questions in relation to the content of the treaties - provides that the union is based on the principles of liberty, democracy and respect for human rights, fundamental freedoms and the rule of law. although, as we all know, the european union is not a signatory to the european convention on human rights, the same article refers to it by saying that the union respects fundamental rights, as guaranteed by the european convention on human rights and fundamental freedoms. as for article 7, which stems from a portuguese proposal which i had the opportunity to present to the reflection group of the previous intergovernmental conference, it created a specific mechanism, and this is the point to which the question refers, of sanction against any member state in the event of serious and persistent violation of certain principles set out in the previous article, article 6. this penalty may result in the suspension of certain of the rights of that member state as a member of the union. this mechanism goes back to something that was already proposed in the spinelli project in 1984, which concerns the need to prevent any violation of democratic principles within a member state and, in particular, forms that could undermine the principles of the rule of law. the facts to which mr dupuis refers in his question are not - it must be said - a violation of a principle mentioned in article 6 of the treaty. this article shall not be invoked to interfere with the administration of the internal affairs of the member states, in particular in the field of justice. the existence of a breach of a principle laid down in article 6 must be - this is also an important point and this is why no mechanism has been triggered - verified by the council on the proposal of one third of the member states or on the initiative of the european commission after parliament has given its assent. however, no entity with this power of initiative initiated the procedure. we do not see anything in the situation that could fall under article 7. as regards the council statement of 2 march last, since i myself made that statement to parliament, a statement by the presidency of the council but made on behalf of the 14 member states, i repeat that of course the effects of that statement and its elements in relation to relations with austria concern each member state bilaterally. they do not bind the council and do not affect the free and normal functioning of the community institutions, in which austria continues to take part in full.
- (pt) mr paulo casaca, i would like to say that despite all this i am not as pessimistic about the evolution of the european union in terms of the ethical dimension and, in particular, in terms of the legal mechanisms that enable it to deal with new situations, in particular those you have mentioned. i think it is important to take into account that in the course of the evolution of the amsterdam treaty there have been transfers of powers and there will have to be a process of transfers of powers in the next five years from what was the third pillar to the first pillar of the union, especially in the areas of visas, judicial cooperation in civil matters and customs cooperation. we are keeping within the third pillar the questions of judicial cooperation in criminal matters and police cooperation, but we are currently working towards the creation of a european area of freedom, justice and security, to which we hope that the commission will be able to provide a response by presenting a scoreboard which will provide us with a catalogue of ad hoc measures. i would also like to stress that the european charter of fundamental rights under consideration could very likely be a means of strengthening these new dimensions and that it will certainly help to provide the european union with a more solid body of principles which can be legally invoked, as some of us - in particular the council - wish. as regards the question on austria, i repeat what i said about austria's compliance with articles 6 and 7 so far. as the honourable member has rightly said, this is an 'ad hoc decision': it is obviously an ad hoc decision, and an ad hoc decision taken by 14 member states concerning their relationship with a government, knowing that what is at issue is not the behaviour of that government but its type of political formation. i said in a previous debate that we are all austrians in the european union. i repeat. we are all austrians because the union is a space of law, of citizenship. i want to have the same rights in austria as austrian citizens should have in my country. i therefore do not like to be represented by a party which has racist and xenophobic attitudes and statements which may legitimately cause us some concern. these concerns are now being expressed in a bilateral political dimension, not in terms of the european union; the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial interests are not undermined. in future, mr president, we will have to assess the extent to which the behaviour of the fpo deviates from the ideological matrix of its past, because this is a fundamental element. it is important that the fpo clarifies whether it remains bound by the principles of its previous declarations, in particular by the type of individuals who have endorsed such declarations, because in that case i see no other solution for the other member states than to maintain, in relation to this austrian government, the same type of reluctance with the consequences that this entails in the exclusively bilateral field, as i have said. the austrians have every right to have the government they want. we have every right to have our own opinion of the austrian government.
- (pt) the honourable member must have misunderstood what i said or there must have been a mistake of interpretation. i never said the austrian government was a racist government. let me make that very clear. i know members of this austrian government, i have worked with them in the past and i hope to continue to do so in the future. they are miles from any affinity with racist ideology. what i am saying is that this government is welcoming a party whose leaders have not only made extremely serious statements about racism and xenophobia, but have even gone so far as to propose legislation (at the domestic level) which clearly denotes a racist ideology. to date, the fpö has not yet made a statement completely denying its links to these types of ideologies. the answer to the second question is yes. any country can discharge its commitments under the 14th framework programme. these are 14 free countries which have freely decided to express their dissatisfaction with the formula adopted for their government to austria on a bilateral basis, but each of these countries can at any time dissociate itself from the others. the same freedom that brought them together can be used to distance them from this issue, if they have a different reading of the developments in austria. the honourable member also asks me when the council will allow the austrian people to get rid of this pressure. firstly, there is no council decision. as i said, there's pressure from 14 countries. this is not a question within the framework of the european union. i would like to make it clear that austria has participated fully and completely in the formal functioning of the institutions of the european union and will continue to do so. members of the governments of the european union cannot be expected to be satisfied with sitting next to individuals whom they regard as adherents of ideologies which clearly recall a historical past and revive old european ghosts. this is a matter of personal sensitivity. i don't like sitting next to fascists.

- question no 4 by rosa m. díez gonzález (h-0155/00) subject: census of european union citizens sentenced to death in the absence of a reply from the council to question p-2697/99 within the time limit laid down by the european parliament's regulation, could the council state the number, identity, legal status, conditions of detention and personal and family situation of nationals of the member states of the european union sentenced to death in other countries? has it made a census of this and, if so, could it forward it to the author of this question? if the council cannot provide this information, does it not consider that action should be taken to establish systematic control in this respect? what action does it consider should be taken to remedy this lack of information?
counsel. - (pt) the question asked by the honourable member is an important one, but i must confess that the council does not have the information requested in respect of the census of european union nationals sentenced to death in third countries. i would like to make it clear, however, that work is being done on consular cooperation between the member states to assist and protect the interests and rights of nationals of the member states in third countries, particularly when they face the death penalty. to this end, and in so far as a national of a member state is threatened with the death penalty in a third country, there is currently a coordination mechanism which makes it possible to approach the governments of those countries, jointly and conjointly, through the missions of the european union in those countries. this cooperation between member states' missions also includes the sharing of information on nationals facing the death penalty. i think that we will eventually be able to give a concrete answer to this question and that we will in particular have concrete and up-to-date information, but that will naturally depend on the degree of development of this consular cooperation which the european union is seeking to consolidate.

- (pt) madam president, you have asked two questions: the first concerns the council's reply and the time limit for its reply. as you know, there is a procedural issue in this area which is linked to the deadlines set unilaterally by the european parliament. the council did not participate in the approval of the deadlines and never accepted them. the council's position is therefore to recall this point systematically. as regards the point you have raised, i would say that you are quite right and that this is one of the issues which must be quickly included in the agenda for work in this area. what you're saying is entirely reasonable. it is important that the european union, which is, as you say, a power which creates various instruments and mechanisms to strengthen itself, should be able to protect the rights of its citizens abroad. you will also understand that consular cooperation within the framework of the european union is a recent practice. systematic models for the articulation of consular cooperation and common models for the combination of consular activities have been developed in recent years. i guess they're running late. i think you are quite right in reality and i think that pressure on the council is welcome in this matter.

question no 7 by ewa hedkvist petersen (h-0162/00) subject: subsidies to the european film industry the importance of european film productions is considerable in terms of the cultural diversity and heritage of the countries, but also of europe. however, 80 to 90 per cent of the films shown in sweden are american. at present, the eu accepts subsidisation of national film production up to 50%. according to our information, the commission is considering lowering the ceiling for national subsidies to 30%, which would threaten european film production, especially since film production is a costly exercise with significant commercial risks, especially for small countries. does the council consider that national aids are important in the service of european culture? does the council consider it important to promote a diversified european film production?
counsel. - (pt) mr president, on the question raised by the honourable member, which is of the utmost importance, we have not been informed of the commission's intention to reduce state aid in this area. the council is aware that the commission is discussing this matter with the member states as part of its work. i would like to say that this type of aid is the competence and responsibility of the member states, within the framework of national actions, within the legal limits, provided for by the treaty. in addition, it is envisaged that the current media-ii programme and the future media-plus programme will provide additional financial support measures to strengthen the presence of european cinema; this is a key line of action pursued by the european union to maintain and protect its cultural diversity, which is also part of the guidelines set out in its own position in the world trade organisation negotiations, particularly with regard to audiovisual matters.
- (pt) madam member, as regards the situation you mention in relation to the small states of the union, you will understand that i am particularly sensitive to this. this is a matter of concern to us too. it is clear that all member states of the union have been allowed in the past, precisely because of the specific nature of cultural diversity within the framework of the european union and the need to ensure that this specificity can go beyond the mere economic reading of the film industry, to maintain aid specifically intended for the film industries. we hope that this aid can be maintained and we hope that it can even be fully compatible with the new rules of the world trade organisation, particularly in the new cycle which we hope will start sooner or later. at present, the financial assistance is maintained at 50%, as the limit of community financing in relation to the overall cost of each project, but this percentage may reach 60% in cases expressly provided for in the programme. there is no indication at this stage that the commission is considering a reduction, much less the amount and percentage mentioned by the honourable member.

- the next item is the report (a5-0066/2000) by mrs ferrer, on behalf of the committee on industry, foreign trade, research and energy, on the proposal for a council decision on the position to be taken by the community within the ec-mexico joint council on the implementation of articles 3, 4, 5, 6 and 12 of the interim agreement on trade and trade-related matters (com (2000) 5965 - c5-0076/2000 - 2000/0024 (cns)).
the rapporteur. - (es) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, the debate i am opening on this very long title which you have just announced is the last part of a work which parliament, in close collaboration with the commission, has carried out in order to strengthen relations with mexico on the basis of the principles and values which are the foundation of the democratic system. in may 1999 parliament gave its assent to the economic partnership, political coordination and cooperation agreement signed in 1997 by the european community and its member states, on the one hand, and mexico, on the other. once ratified by all member states, it will replace the cooperation agreement signed in 1991 by the community and mexico. the 1997 agreement was accompanied by an interim agreement on trade and trade-related matters, which was provisionally approved by the european parliament in may 1998, and which was intended to allow negotiations on the liberalization of the trade aspects of community competition contained in the global agreement to begin as soon as possible, without having to wait for the fifteen member states to ratify it. once these negotiations were concluded and the council had decided on their content, it was then for parliament, in response to the formal consultation by the council, to deliver an opinion on the results of these negotiations. i would therefore like to thank the commission for making this consultation possible by the council in collaboration with parliament - which i welcome and which i hope will set a precedent - although i must regret that it did not take up the commitment of the previous commission to inform us of the progress of the negotiations, given the importance of the issues raised. as regards the content of my report, the first thing i would like to stress is that we are dealing with an agreement applying to content which is exclusively commercial but has a political dimension, which we must also bear in mind when we give our opinion. this is because the economic partnership, political coordination and cooperation agreement, within the framework of which we must situate the text of my report, is the result of the desire to promote a genuinely democratic political system which respects human rights, social and environmental rights and a fairer social balance, through greater economic development which will be generated by the liberalization of trade. article 1 of the agreement states that respect for democratic principles and human rights, in their most advanced form, is an essential element and the basis of the agreement. in turn, the introduction of a compliance clause, which allows for the suspension of the implementation of the agreement in the event of non-compliance with article 1, also guarantees the commitment of the parties to democracy and respect for fundamental rights. on the other hand, by institutionalising cooperation between the european union and mexico, particularly in the fields of human rights, social affairs and the fight against poverty, an instrument is being created which can be of great use in reducing the social inequalities which persist in mexico and improving the living conditions of the most disadvantaged sections of the population. as regards the content of the negotiations on the implementation of articles 3, 4, 5, 6 and 12 of the interim agreement on trade in goods, public procurement, competition, the consultation mechanism on intellectual property and dispute settlement, it should be stressed that the package of measures agreed is a good agreement, even if there are areas of uncertainty in certain sectors - i am thinking specifically of the textile sector, which is very concerned in particular about standards of origin - the effects of which will prove to be beneficial for both the european union and mexico. the european union, because the creation of a free trade area will return the member states to the level of presence they had on mexican markets before the entry into force of nafta, which means new opportunities for european companies to expand; the commission has already taken a number of measures to improve the situation of the small and mediumsized enterprises in the community, such as the creation of a european company for the processing of agricultural products. it is true that during the transitional period and until the complete liberalization of all products is achieved, the agreement we have reached will be more advantageous for mexico than for the european union, but this asymmetry also exists with regard to the levels of development and competitiveness of the european economy in relation to mexican levels. however, it must be acknowledged that despite this asymmetry, community producers will be in a much better position than before to compete on the mexican market. for all these reasons, ladies and gentlemen, the committee on industry, foreign trade, research and energy, by an overwhelming majority, recommends a vote in favour of the council's decision on the outcome of the negotiations, the benefits of which we must ensure that they really contribute to promoting a more democratic political system which respects human rights and social justice.
- (es) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, the economic partnership, political coordination and cooperation agreement signed with mexico in december 1997 is being referred back to this house for analysis of the trade measures negotiated under the interim agreement. a few weeks ago i went to mexico for various reasons, including to find out what the mexicans thought of the new framework for relations between their country and the european union, which was announced with great fanfare in many media outlets. after analysing what i saw, read and heard during my stay in the united mexican republic, i have come to the same conclusion as mrs ferrer, who drew up the report under discussion today and whom i publicly congratulate: this is the best agreement signed by the european union to promote the development of trade and investment and which will prove beneficial to both sides. some things have changed recently in mexico, since the announcement and approval of the agreement, generally for the better. i therefore support the rapporteur's conclusions, although i am concerned about the impact of customs liberalization on cut flowers, as it could have negative repercussions in certain european regions specialising in this type of agriculture, such as the outermost regions. it is gratifying for this member of parliament, who comes from a region like the canary islands, in the north-east of the african continent, and whose political soul is divided between europe and america, to be a witness to the debate on mrs ferrer's report, which contains parliament's opinion on the partnership agreement, not only for its commercial background but also for what it means from a political point of view, in a situation as unique as the one we are experiencing because of globalisation. with the launch of this agreement, the european union and mexico will, in my view, undoubtedly inspire hope for the improvement of income levels and the quality of life of the communities that make up the agreement, in circumstances that evoke, overcoming distances, the legendary meeting between suchil and quetzalcoatl, immortalized in salvador de madariaga's work "the heart of green stone". however, we add a few constructive remarks to the proposal for support for this report, which refer to the following: first, the need to provide more human resources to the responsible community departments and services, to enable trade actions to be more effective; the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. if that were not the case, this important agreement would be in danger of becoming a dead letter.
- mr president, the conclusion of the trade negotiations between the european union and mexico, viewed in a positive light, could mean the establishment of a new and lasting framework for institutionalising political dialogue and cooperation, provided that this trade agreement works in the interests of both parties. unfortunately, the experience of nafta has taught us that such a result is not automatic: the facts are there that free trade has had a negative impact on the lives of many people, has worsened environmental damage and has marginalized large segments of the mexican population, not to mention reports from mexican human rights ngos that indicate a deterioration in the human rights situation since the interim agreement came into force in 1998. so, all things considered, the current agreement has failed to protect mexico's vulnerable workforce, preserve intensive sectors and guarantee minimum environmental standards. this is not a cause for optimism, because the procedure followed in the recent negotiations, without any effective control by this house or the mexican senate, clearly shows that the agreement does not contain the mechanisms that are absolutely necessary to ensure that the damage done today will not be repeated tomorrow.
president of the committee on industry, foreign trade, research and energy. - (es) mr president, commissioner, we are going to vote on what is another step on the new path which was opened in the middle of 1995 and for which, as for everything new, there was then much criticism and reluctance. today, fortunately, these criticisms and reservations have been left behind; but unfortunately some of them are still being heard, such as those which were expressed in this parliament a moment ago. i think we must be aware that what we are doing is precisely cutting short the fears expressed here, with an agreement which has a purely commercial aspect in this case. we therefore reject the fears that europe is losing ground to the export power of the united states in mexico. on the other hand, we are also strengthening the process of democratization in that country with this agreement. the result of the meeting of two civilizations 500 years ago, mexico is a country culturally and politically linked to europe. however, the united states, its powerful neighbour to the north, remains in the lead in the political and geopolitical arena. until these agreements began to be prepared, the dominance of the united states in the economic, commercial and investment fields was practically absolute. but mexico has made a lot of progress in the area of human rights. he joined the oecd as a permanent observer and completed a constitutional reform in 1999, making his national human rights commission an autonomous body. for these reasons, for economic reasons and also for political reasons, we strongly recommend that this agreement be approved.

commission - mr president, first of all, let me thank mrs ferrer for her report and parliament for its very constructive contribution to the outcome of the trade negotiations with mexico. these trade negotiations are based on the ec-mexico agreement, which was given the green light by the european parliament on 6 may last year. one of the foundations of this agreement is the promotion of human rights and democratic principles. it covers all our relations with mexico, in particular cooperation and political dialogue. the results of the negotiations are balanced, ambitious and open up opportunities for both sides. all major sectors are covered, namely trade in goods, services, public procurement, intellectual property, competition, capital movements, investment and dispute settlement. european operators will very soon be able to compete on equal terms with their foreign competitors, particularly those from the united states, on the mexican market. as in any negotiation, compromises had to be found for certain sectors, but the result is a balanced package that guarantees market access while preserving specific sensitivities. last but not least, i would like to say how much the commission appreciates the speed with which parliament will deliver its opinion: it will take only one month. this is very important because it will enable us to organise a meeting of the ec-mexico joint council on the sidelines of the lisbon council next week. the assent will also allow the results of the negotiations to be implemented quickly, which, as you acknowledge, are in our interest as well as in mexico's.

the commission has examined with great interest the resolution on the threat posed by the development of illegal activities by criminal organizations operating in several countries of south-eastern europe. we share the concerns expressed in the resolution that international criminal networks, whose main activities are trafficking in human beings, drugs and arms, and smuggling of various goods, will end up undermining the reconstruction and development efforts undertaken under the stability pact. there is no doubt that many of these criminal activities have serious negative consequences for the community and its member states. as you know, the european council expressed its firm determination to fight organised crime and demonstrated the need for a coherent and coordinated approach by adopting, in june 1997, an action plan on the fight against organised crime. although many of the actions envisaged are aimed at encouraging cooperation between the 15 member states, the plan does not overlook the need to develop wider forms of international cooperation as well. a tangible result was the conclusion by the council in 1998 of a preaccession pact on organised crime with the candidate countries. as regards the more specific question raised in the resolution concerning the situation in the balkans, the commission recognises that the danger of a massive development of organised crime activities is very real if we do not take coherent and coordinated action in this region, involving the various donors and international and regional actors. the commission considers that member states can play a key role by putting their know-how and human resources to work on projects specifically designed to combat criminal activities in the balkan region, including corruption. the commission considers that a useful contribution to the implementation of the stability pact can be made by combining the know-how of the member states and community funds to create projects and actions that target criminal activities very precisely. in this context, the commission is fully prepared to play the role of coordinator and to work in close consultation with the special coordinator of the stability pact. i would also like to stress that the commission is preparing a proposal for a new specific financial instrument which will provide a general legal basis for community aid to the whole of this region. a formal proposal is due to be submitted to the council at the end of this month. we hope that a new regulation can come into force as soon as possible, perhaps just after the summer holidays. the commission remains convinced of the crucial need to do all it can to support the measures taken to combat organised crime and is determined to develop, within this new framework, regional projects covering the area of justice and home affairs. the commission is also already in a position to announce that, in the context of the programming of assistance for regional programmes for the financial year 2000, some eur 2 million has been allocated to projects in the field of justice and home affairs. in addition, as regards the smuggling of certain products such as cigarettes, and in so far as the territory of the community and its financial interests are affected, olaf has set up multidisciplinary working groups in which several nationalities are represented. these groups are responsible for combating organised crime, whose transnational dimension has been demonstrated on several occasions. they were created for the purpose of support and operational assistance; their investigations target the sectors and products most prone to fraud, such as cigarettes. the report on the activities of these working parties in recent years is particularly telling. in 1996, for example, the smuggling of cigarettes, mainly goods in transit, amounted to ecu 800 million. the overall financial impact of fraud detected in this sector in 1997 was estimated at ecu 1.6 billion, both for the community's own resources and for the member states' revenue. the number of cigarette smuggling investigations increased again in 1998, although the financial impact was less than in previous years. this can be explained by the conduct of large-scale international investigations and the success of the fight against cigarette smuggling from the principality of andorra, as well as the fight against the black market in spain. in short, we take these threats to the community very seriously and we will continue to fight them with all our might.

the rapporteur. - (es) mr president, i am presenting a report by the committee on agriculture and rural development on the proposal for a council regulation amending regulation (ec) no 1577/96 introducing a specific measure in favour of certain leguminous crops. after examining this proposal as early as october 1999, parliament unanimously approved the draft legislative resolution on 23 february 2000. i would like to stress the following aspects of the amendments proposed by the european parliament. first, amendment no 1 on recital 2a. this amendment supplements the council's purely commercial vision and opts for a more ambitious proposal in the economic, human and food quality sense. where the council speaks only of the market, the european parliament draws attention to the community's economic interest in these legume-grain products. in view of the protein deficit in the european union, parliament considered that it was necessary to improve this scheme without reducing the level of aid. secondly, parliament's amendment no 2 proposes that aid may also be granted for the production of seed potatoes. this aid already exists for rice, chickpeas and lentils. we are proposing it because, as we all know, this production is subject to additional technical conditions and quality controls, so that if their cultivation were not supported by aid, the abandonment could have very harmful consequences for the quality of the production of these seeds. thirdly, amendment no 3 indicates that in our view the commission should present proposals for the 2000/2003 marketing year as soon as possible. before concluding, mr president, i would like to recall that in 1993 - that was a long time ago - the council had indicated that it intended to gradually strengthen the current aid scheme for pulses. but this has not yet been done. secondly, the successive campaigns indicate that we are facing a chronic imbalance in this regime. the maximum guaranteed area is systematically reduced, thus penalising farmers once again who see their aid reduced by up to 20%. so, mr president, the committee on agriculture and rural development would really like to improve the system. but we are aware of what the commission is telling us, that we are living in a period of great budgetary restrictions, that we could not put them into practice without reducing aid. that is why we are putting forward this proposal, which is really a proposal for maintenance, and what we want to say to the commission is that it must as soon as possible, for the 2000/2003 marketing year, draw up proposals to improve this scheme without reducing aid. i welcome the cooperation and support of all the members of the committee on agriculture and rural development and the opinion of the committee on budgets. i also thank the commission for its openness to dialogue and i hope that it will also be open to our proposals.

- (es) mr president, i am going to address a subject which has not been addressed by any previous speaker. i am referring to the court of auditors' report on the principle of additionality. this is a report which was published in the official journal of the european communities on 9 march. the report includes a very interesting paragraph - paragraph 62 - on privatisation. in recent years, several governments in the european union have enthusiastically embarked on a policy of privatisation which has placed the heritage that previously belonged to the community in very few hands. for example, in spain, in the last four years, public enterprises worth 4 billion have been privatised - with b as barcelona or brussels - public enterprises that have passed into private hands. mr liikanen is an expert in accounting terms and knows that privatisation is a form of public divestment and, in practice, can be a form of regional divestment. if, for example, an airline providing regional services is privatised, there may be a regional divestment, which would be contrary to the principle of additionality. the court of auditors has addressed this issue by saying that when expenditure, because of privatisation, tends to decline, the member state, already knowing the results, wishes to abolish it. given the importance of the categories of expenditure involved - telecommunications, energy, etc. - this simple operation can result in a considerable change in the final result. we also have the commission's reply, which must be very recent and which mr liikanen, as a member of the college, must remember perfectly well. the commission responds here with a system which, in spanish terminology, is called the 'olendorf method'; a method of language learning where the teacher would ask the student, "are you wearing my uncle's panties?" to which the student would reply, "no, but i'm wearing my grandmother's glasses". and the commission's answer to paragraph 62 is very succinct. the court of justice has held that the principle of subsidiarity is not applicable to the assessment of the existence of an additionality of a measure, but that it is applicable to the assessment of the existence of an additionality of a measure. in short, the commission responds by applying the 'olendorf method'. commissioner liikanen is here; he knows the subject very well and perhaps he could give us a more precise answer, because i think it affects the essence of additionality considerably. secondly, the financial forecasts in berlin foresee a considerable reduction in the structural funds. this year we have €29 430 million, in 2006 we will have €26 600 million in nominal terms, a decrease of around 14% in seven years. given inflation, i can calculate that there will be a 20% decrease. in short, by 2006, the structural funds will have lost more than 20% of their present amount, which means that we cannot meet current needs and, from what we have heard, many regions in the community are still facing many problems. there is another problem, which the commissioner and the members of this house are also aware of: we are talking about the immediate accession to the european union of thirteen states, most of which have an average income below the poorest regions of the community and nothing is provided to support cohesion policies with these candidates. i know the commissioner will not be able to answer me, but i would like to draw the attention of the house and the commissioner to the problem this will pose for community cohesion policies.
