which is a national model - and we are transforming the economic structure of this society. in doing so, we fear that the liberalisation drive will fail to transform the essence of the current european social model. this is evident in such seemingly mundane matters as city transportation. if urban transport is not subject to political considerations and intervention by authorities, for example local authorities, a simple liberalisation can make it almost impossible to commute to work. for example, in venezuela, the total privatization of transport has led the country into a deep social and political crisis. liberalisation presents other difficulties. for example, when public services and public enterprises are privatised and these public enterprises are brought under the control of the private sector which in reality only replaces the state monopoly with a private monopoly, there may be no real liberalisation. liberalisation through the privatisation of public enterprises can lead to the consolidation of dominant positions and private monopolies which are - in my view - more harmful than monopoly designed to benefit the general interest. another aspect - to which we referred in the recent debate on the kuckelkorn report - is the need to coordinate social protection. social protection in a unified internal market cannot be reduced to a mere subsidiarity. finally, i think that cohesion policies are also important. without economic and social cohesion, without a balance in the standard of living in the different regions of the community, the european union risks becoming an unjust european union in which some regions can make more progress and others remain behind. that is the basis of the amendments tabled by mrs berger and myself, which represent the views of the committee on employment and social affairs.

national quotas. it also sets out restrictions on the exercise of activity in certain areas known as 'boxes'. these restrictions on freedom of action, which were provisionally provided for, have been extended and will remain in force until 1 january 2003 as a mechanism to enable the fishing industry in certain member states to adapt to the rules of free competition in an increasingly open and globalised market. after more than 20 years and on the eve of a general review of all aspects of the common fisheries policy, which, due to legal imperatives, is due to take place in 2002, i believe applied to fisheries. in short, the framework of the common fisheries policy must be adapted to the general legal framework of community regulation.

the rapporteur. - (es) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, we are dealing here today with a highly technical subject, one which, at first sight, seems to concern, without any other consideration, questions of adoption or translation of procedures or terminology within the framework of the european union, a political framework within which they are trying to adapt, as is the case with certain instruments in the field of statistics. i think we are all aware, at least, of the importance of statistical data being not only reliable, that is to say, scientifically and rigorously obtained, but above all comparable. this is particularly important in tasks relating to the european single market, where we need comparable and homogeneous statistical data between the different member states. i would even say that this statement is even more forceful, if possible, if we take account of the enlargement of the european union, a process for which it is absolutely crucial that information is available and comparable, especially in the statistical and economic fields. i do not wish to repeat the merits of the esa 95 - european system of integrated economic accounts - or the progress it represented compared with the previous system of 1979, a subject on which i have already spoken in this house in my report on the proposal for a council regulation amending the regulation on the application of the protocol on the excessive deficit procedure. i think that we really need to stress the need to give strong support to a commission proposal which, first and foremost, in a field as serious as the member states' budgets, tends to give priority to the income actually received over criteria such as the rights recognized in the field of taxes and social contributions. it is clear, and it should be clear, that sometimes an administration recognizes a right which it will never receive, even if it carries out the most thorough analysis of its ability to recover it, and the consequence is that this administration then implicitly falsifies its deficit. this is a serious matter which has been the subject of debate. it should be recalled that a major debate was held in the parliament of a member state of the union between one of the candidates for the presidency of the government and his opponent, the current president of the government, during which the candidate, mr borrell, rightly denounced the widespread use of the generating factor criterion which, if not properly corrected, will become a cover-up of the public deficit. to put an end to this kind of practice, we need to establish clear criteria, such as the one proposed by the commission. the proposal also, and i think it is right, presents two options for the recognition of income, namely receipts and amounts materialised by a roll or a declaration. this approach of the commission, which some criticise and which ultimately opposes the end of the practice of concealing the deficit once and for all, is not intended to introduce a distortion in the assessment of these amounts but, on the contrary, to arrive at the same figure in two different ways. the most correct, or at least the most orthodox, solution, in my view, is the one based on the criterion of the event giving rise to the damage, with the corresponding coefficient of recovery, as set out in article 3 (a) proposed by the commission; the other, described in point (b) of this article, is that based on the cashing-in criterion, corrected by the inclusion, in the form of an adjustment, of the balance of actual recovery at the end of the financial year. these two methods of calculation must necessarily lead to the same figure, which corresponds to the amount of tax for the financial year. i would add that there is no other method of correctly recording revenue in a budget. it is also clear that the possibility of using either of these accounting methods has the great advantage of quicker adaptation for those who use either system. i therefore believe that the commission's proposal for the registration of taxes and social security contributions is the most correct, but also the most valid in all respects because of its immediate applicability. nevertheless, we believe that in order to ensure that member states have statistical data, even aggregated, for the taxation of products, article 3 of the commission's proposal should deal with this issue by introducing a similar mechanism for the recording and adaptation of the taxation of products. i therefore welcome the proposal and congratulate the commission on its action. the proposal, i repeat, stresses that priority must be given to income actually received rather than to recognized rights in the case of taxes and social contributions in the member states, and it offers the possibility of choosing between two methods of calculation which allow the adaptation of the systems implemented by the member states. once the commission's proposal has been examined, the accounting of taxes and social contributions can no longer be carried out by any other method than the two proposed. in conclusion, and in line with our view that this commission proposal is more of a modification than a clarification and that it also affects the basic concepts, i would also like to stress that the procedure for amending annex a to the above-mentioned regulation should be followed instead of the method referred to in article 2 (2) of council regulation (ec) no 2223/96 of 25 june 1996 on the adoption of changes to the methodology for clarifying and improving the content of esa 95.
- (es) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the commission's initiative in presenting this regulation, which aims to harmonize the principles of taxation and social security contributions, must be described as very timely. as the rapporteur himself has acknowledged, if the accounts of the various member states are to be homogeneous, they must follow the same principles. it is true that in accounting terms both the cashing criterion and the generating factor criterion can be accepted, but it can also be said that the former makes it less possible to manipulate the figures to distort the real situation of a country's accounts. the cashing criterion ultimately makes it more difficult to use these accounting devices, which at one time were euphemistically called "creative accounting". it is true that the use of these systems has, for example, enabled some countries to meet the maastricht criteria, but it can also be said that their abuse can distort the reality of a country's accounts. as you know, accounting that does not give a true picture can be called anything but accounting. the criterion of the generating factor, if it is not corrected by requiring, for example, the preparation of forecasts for the unpaid, is an inadequate criterion. the rapporteur mentioned a debate in spain which was ultimately due to the fact that in 1997 the government charged the social security revenue with 750 000 million pesetas which were being spent and which the state, as everyone knew, was not going to be able to collect. thanks to these accounting maneuvers, to this 'creative accounting', spain fulfilled the deficit criterion for accessing the first phase of economic and monetary union. of course, these accounting games will no longer be possible if the commission's proposal is approved. perhaps that is why the spanish members of the epp group have tabled certain amendments and tried to delay the adoption of this report. it is not a question of revising what has been done in the past. ladies and gentlemen, what's done is done. it is a question of demanding, starting today, greater rigor, it is a question of demanding that accounting accurately reflects the image of a country's accounts. we therefore approve the commission's proposal and we do not approve either the epp proposal, which seeks to delay the entry into force of this regulation, or the amendments by the committee on economic and monetary affairs which, considering that the regulation contains an amendment and not a simple clarification, in fact delay its entry into force. ladies and gentlemen, if accounting rigor is required, it has been required from the outset.

the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i would like to begin by emphasizing that the commission is in favour of the principles on which many of the amendments are based, for example the system of managing quotas on the basis of historical references. i mean that they correspond to the development of our talks with the complaining parties in the wto and the acp producers. but in the present delicate phase of the negotiations, the commission feels that we should not change its proposal now. i therefore feel obliged to reject your amendments. i would like to give reasons for this refusal on a theme-by-theme basis. the first question concerns the abolition of references to a tariff-only system and the automatic transition to such a system after a given transitional period. to be clear, our proposal is primarily aimed at bringing the banana cmo into line with wto rules. the most important element of the proposal is the introduction of the tariff system after a given transitional period. to this end, however, it is necessary to reach an agreement with the interested parties on the management of the tariff quotas during the transitional period. the commission is of the firm opinion that your desire to replace the tariff regime with a system of sustainable tariff quotas will only lead to further attacks within the wto. i would also like to point out that the proposal already contains a request to the council that the commission be authorized to open negotiations under article 28 of gatt. a reference in the regulation is therefore not necessary. the second important issue concerns the management of tariff quotas. the commission is trying to negotiate with the main producers on the determination of tariff quotas on the basis of historical references. until these discussions are concluded, it would not be wise to further define individual options. in addition, as regards the request that the way in which a tariff quota system is administered should not have an adverse effect on operators already present on the market, it should be noted that if we have to change the whole organization of the markets, there can be no guarantee that everything will remain exactly as it is. that would really be the square of the circle. in the course of our discussions, other alternatives for the management of the so-called c quota were also discussed. however, the commission considers that it would not be appropriate at this stage to amend its proposal for the auctioning of the c quota. this auction system is in any event an authorised method for the granting of licences. the third point on the quota concerns the extension of the period of application of the quota system to at least 10 years. the commission believes that such an extension would undermine the credibility of the leitmotif of our proposal, which is to bring the banana cmo into line with wto rules as soon as possible. as we have explained in the explanatory memorandum, the best way to achieve this objective is through the tariff system. the commission has therefore proposed the transitional period, as this would give producers in the community and the acp states time to prepare for the new rules. moreover, if there is to be an automatic switch to a tariff-only regime, an interim balance sheet or an audit at the end of the transitional period would be meaningless. as regards the preference for the acp states, the commission considers that eur 275 per tonne is sufficient to guarantee these countries access to the community market. a higher preference would also lead to further attacks within the wto. a higher preference limiting access for latin american countries under the c quota could be interpreted as a de facto desire to reintroduce a special acp quota. i now turn to the additional support measures for our own producers in the european union. as i have already explained, the commission's main objective in its proposal is to bring the market organization into line with the wto's condemnation. this condemnation does not concern the community's internal support system. i would like to stress once again that this system works like a differential payment system. this means that a guarantee has been put in place: when prices fall, aid automatically increases. the last point is the measures to promote organic bananas and fair trade. i would point out that there are already horizontal measures to ensure that organic bananas from third countries are assimilated to those from the community. in addition, the european union may grant subsidies for the production of organic bananas in the framework of the agri-environmental measures provided for in the provisions for the promotion of rural development. measures to promote sales of organic bananas may be financed by national and regional programmes. fair trade bananas would also be covered by the horizontal fair trade measures which, i hope, will be adopted shortly on the basis of a corresponding commission communication. as we know, this communication on bananas is not just about fair trade, but fair trade in general. in addition to the possibilities mentioned, the development of organic banana production as well as the development of fair trade banana production in the acp states can be supported under the regulation on aid to traditional acp states. the commission welcomes the in-depth discussions we have had here today. even if, in the current international circumstances, it is not possible for it to accept parliament's amendments, it must be remembered that the whole dossier was dealt with in a very constructive and thorough manner, both in the various committees which contributed to the dary report and during the recent hearing in the committee on agriculture and rural development.

commission - mr president, allow me to thank members from all sides of this house for their constructive contribution to the debate. perhaps i should venture a few superficial comments, because of the time involved, in trying to answer the specific questions asked. first, mr harbour asks us, as he always does in his insightful and constructive way, to what extent we think the commitment to developing managerial skills and culture has been fulfilled. i will mention only one or two points which show the progress made. i wouldn't say they're perfect, and this list is not exhaustive. as regards training, which is, as mr harbour knows, fundamental to the kind of change we want to achieve, the comprehensive training programme for all directors, which is expected to last two years, starts this month. secondly, we are already collecting mission statements from all the directorates-general. most of them have introduced their own. we will also be establishing the evaluation of tasks through a series of pilot projects which will affect about a quarter of the directorates-general, initially, and then we will proceed to compile the job descriptions which will be carried out until the end of july this year. the staff evaluation process, which of course includes managers at all levels, is being refined and will be implemented. as mr harbour says, the role and actions of the secretary-general in all these and many other activities are crucial. i believe that mr o'sullivan is very firmly committed to the direction set out in the white paper and will prove to be a remarkable successor to his extremely talented and committed predecessor, mr trojan, who will take up a new post from the end of this month. as regards the delegation of power to the directors, the best example i can give you is that on 1 may we inaugurated the new internal audit service, the central financial service, and we will soon be holding the first meeting of the audit committee. these are the first steps in decentralising financial control, which is of course crucial for delegating management at all levels in an institution managing appropriations. mr harbour knows my view that making this central and measurable change, subject to continuous scrutiny, will have the effect of changing the culture of the management style, broadly speaking, and the way the house operates. in conclusion, it rightly states that team leadership, teamwork and team building are crucial elements for the effective implementation of modern management skills. we are contributing to this through a combination of structural changes, additional training, evaluations and the appointment system. it is equally clear that the inclusion of probationary periods in contracts for directors will make a significant contribution to the direction we want to take. however, to achieve this will require amendments to the staff regulations and i am pleased that parliament and the council will work together to achieve the necessary legislative changes to continue this process. mr van der berg was right to reiterate in a kind and benevolent way that the commission must be responsible for its appointments and its personnel policies. i suppose he will continue to inquire as to why this question was asked. i can only say that i welcome the opportunity to provide detailed information. i am reminded that during the hearings several members of this house rightly and forcefully raised the issue of the removal of the national character of senior civil servants' posts, the complete abandonment of formal or informal quotas and the rotation of civil servants in a1 and a2 posts. in fact, they had even made very specific demands on this matter. i not only accepted these principles at the time, together with my colleagues in the commission, but i have since then been actively trying to implement them. let me turn to the point concerning the new standards and external posts, which was also raised, quite correctly, by mr dell'alba, who has a question on this subject. i am happy to answer that and i would draw the house's attention to the fact that in dealing with a specific case, in this case the departure of my own chief of staff, mr andrew cahn, it has become very clear to me that the current arrangements for allowing permanent and official officials to travel to outside jobs lack the clarity and the coherence that is required. in practice, the procedure and the rigorous examination i have asked to be implemented in respect of mr cahn means that his case has been dealt with thoroughly and quite appropriately. however, i do not believe that the commission, or other institutions, should rely on individual motivations expressed by officials or commissioners and rely on ad hoc means of applying principles which are, to say the least, rather generalised. i have therefore asked the director-general for administration and personnel to produce a draft regulation which would take into account best practice within member states' administrations and other international public bodies and make procedures more precise. having such rules would clearly be the best way to ensure transparency, consistency and practical direction, in the interests of all parties, particularly, as some members have pointed out during the debate, when member states and institutions are increasingly willing to encourage increased exchanges between national and eu administrations, as well as between the public and private sectors. naturally, as soon as i have a proposal for new and more appropriate provisions, i will present it to my colleagues in the commission and then to this house and the other institutions for consideration. let me take the opportunity of mr sterckx's speech to emphasize the point i made earlier, a point he shares - a wise one - that no one, given the broad geographical balance to which the commission is bound, should try to take a snapshot of the staff profile within the commission and present it, in any way, as a permanent state of affairs. only a moving picture represents reality and the commission is fully committed to ensuring that merit is given priority and that geographical balance is duly taken into account, which is essential in a multinational institution such as the commission. as regards mrs hautala's remark, i would simply say that none of the appointments announced today have been subject to a panel and there is a very obvious legal reason for this. mr david o'sullivan, for example, will take up his post on a rotation basis, as provided for in the staff regulations, and under the staff regulations mr ricardo levi is a temporary official who changes jobs but not posts. therefore, in terms of legal, procedural and employment policy, the use of the panel system for promotion and appointment purposes was not required by existing legislation in the case of such appointments. i think that also answers the question mrs morgan asked on this subject. the question of appointments of women was also raised. of the 25 appointments to very senior posts made by the commission since september, four were female officials. - the next item is the recommendation for second reading (a5-0106/2000) on behalf of the committee on legal affairs and the internal market, on the common position adopted by the council with a view to adopting a directive of the european parliament and of the council on certain legal aspects of information society services, in particular electronic commerce in the internal market (directive on electronic commerce) [14263/1/1999 - c5-0099/2000 - 1998/0325 (cod)) (rapporteur: mrs palacio valleundilers).
the rapporteur. - (es) mr president, the recommendation i have the honour to make on behalf of the committee on legal affairs and citizens' rights calls on the house to approve the common position without amendments. i should add that this is the attitude adopted by the various political groups. i would like to stress, mr president, that by approving tomorrow the council's common position on electronic commerce, this house will be exercising a responsibility of very high political content and of great institutional significance. in addition, by adopting this directive, parliament will take a decisive step towards the competitiveness of european businesses in the online economy and will set a milestone for consumers and businesses to act in an internal market with the same guarantees and ease as in their national market. the directive guarantees businesses and citizens the possibility of providing and receiving information society services throughout the european union, thus making it a truly borderless area. european companies will be able to supply goods, services or information within the union in accordance with the standards of the member state in which they are established and thus, in ordinary circumstances, without being bound by 14 different legal orders. to achieve these results, the directive harmonises certain areas, including - to mention the main ones - the place of establishment of operators, their transparency obligations, the rules on transparency for commercial communications, the conditions required for the conclusion and validity of online contracts, the liability of internet intermediaries, the settlement of disputes and the competences of national authorities. in other areas, the directive builds on existing instruments aimed at promoting the harmonisation and mutual recognition of national regulations. the directive covers - and this is an important point - all information society services, both business-to-business and business-to-user, such as services enabling electronic transactions to be carried out - interactive telemarketing of goods and services, e-commerce, for example - services provided free of charge, for example, services financed by advertising or sponsorship, online press, online databases, online financial services, professional online services - lawyers, doctors or other professionals - legal services such as video on demand, direct marketing and all network access services. the directive also provides - as i have already said - a splendid example of interinstitutional cooperation. it is the result of an exceptional teamwork between parliament, the commission and the council. the position of parliament at first reading, in particular the strong support for the principle of the country of origin, was crucial for the council to ensure that the balance of the text was not jeopardised. in general, the common position follows the lines of parliament and, except in exceptional cases, does not entail significant changes to the annex, which provides for derogations from the principle mentioned, and also maintains the balance as regards the provisions on consumer protection and the liability of intermediaries. i would like to thank my colleagues in the legal affairs committee, and in particular all the political groups, for their cooperation. i would like to thank mrs berger and mr harbour - from my group - and the other institutions for their support. the common position therefore maintains the balance between the various general objectives and the various interests, which is why we have not tabled amendments. although it is not perfect, we believe that it is reasonable and acceptable and that it is urgent to approve it. i will not repeat - even if it is true - that the time on the internet is much shorter than the time we have had so far. we must also understand that this directive is a priority if we want to ensure the development of electronic commerce. we must take account of the globalisation of the economy and the competition of american companies, the legal framework of the internal market which, like the internet, aims to establish an area without internal frontiers... all these elements are assets of the community in terms of the competitiveness of european enterprises. finally, in view of the development of new technologies and market-related innovations, it is essential to establish a legal framework for the development of trade, while allowing, as this directive does, self-regulation and the development of specific codes of conduct in certain areas. in addition, this directive will provide a significant incentive for small and mediumsized enterprises to move as quickly as possible to trade without frontiers, which they are not doing at present because of the legal uncertainty caused by the multiplicity of regimes in the european framework. finally, some member states are already legislating in this area, and without this directive we risk a real fragmentation of the internal market. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the directive is implemented. the legal framework established in this directive will facilitate the adoption of other community directives, such as those on copyright, the distance marketing of financial services or the controversial adoption of the brussels convention on jurisdiction; the commission has already taken a number of initiatives in this area, including the introduction of a new system of national accounts. parliament intends to follow closely the transposition and implementation of the directive into national legislation, and i have therefore taken the liberty of introducing two recommendations, two warnings to the commission, which i hope will be adopted tomorrow, not in the framework of the directive but in that of the legislative resolution; the commission has also adopted a number of proposals for the development of a european content management system. finally, mr president, and i will end on this point, the adoption by parliament of this directive on the eve of the 50th anniversary of robert schuman's declaration that europe would not be made in one go, but would be made by concrete achievements that would forge de facto solidarity between citizens and businesses, is quite symbolic. fifty years ago, the concrete achievements concerned the european coal and steel community, and today, as this directive points out, they concern the information society. i therefore believe, mr president, that tomorrow parliament will be able to radiate joy, joy which will be able to spread to the other community institutions.
- (es) mr president, i too would like to thank and congratulate mrs palacio and all those who have worked in the council and the commission for the work they have done. it is essential to establish a regulatory framework as soon as possible. i would like to make a few comments, however, which may be useful for this second phase, which is so necessary. the internet is global, we cannot forget that. we are talking about a directive for the internal market, but as its constituent name - the world wide web - well indicates, the internet is global and it is essential that we take this into account. the internet will determine europe's economic position in the future, as well as its political position and its ability to exert influence on the world, social and cultural level. so i think it is essential that we think that a lot of this success is due to the creation of new businesses, the creation of small and mediumsized enterprises. if we are to make a review, it is therefore essential to remember not only consumers - who must in any case make decisions for themselves, use encryption mechanisms and legal and technological protection of their data - but also smes, because otherwise, tomorrow, e-commerce in europe will be of little importance. it therefore seems essential to make a real effort to harmonize the rules of the internal market and, at the same time, to work vigorously towards the unification of the criteria governing electronic commerce at world level. it is useless to adopt good standards for our internal market if we lose sight of the general framework within which they are to be found. to achieve this, it also seems important to take into account that the regulation of the country of origin is fundamental, because otherwise the preparation of small and medium-sized enterprises will not be sufficient and they, not having access to the same means as large enterprises, will encounter obstacles in pursuing their objectives.

- doc. a5-0105/2000 by mrs schierhuber, on behalf of the committee on development and cooperation, on the proposal for a council decision on the conclusion on behalf of the european community of the 1999 food aid convention (com (99) 308 - c5-0148/1999 - 1999/0131 (cns))
commission - (de) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by warmly thanking the rapporteur, mrs schierhuber, for her report and her proposal to approve the council decision on the food aid convention. as you know, the international wheat agreement is made up of two separate legal documents, namely the grains trade convention and the food aid convention. the grains trade convention was already substantially amended in 1995 and no amendments were therefore to be made to the new convention. the commission therefore also requests that the validity of the convention be extended until 30 june 2001. the same cannot be said of the food aid convention, which the food aid committee has decided to renegotiate and to follow in doing so the recommendations of the singapore conference. the aim of the new 1999 food aid convention is to contribute to global food security and to strengthen the capacity of the international community to respond better to acute food crises and the food needs of developing countries. the following points have been given special weight in the new convention. first, more consideration should be given to the local food habits of the beneficiary countries. secondly, donor countries can now express their commitments in terms of tonnage, value or a combination of both. thirdly, in the provision of food aid, the members of the convention must give priority to the least developed and low-income countries. fourthly, there are more specific provisions for the promotion of agricultural development on the spot and possible triangular transactions and local purchases are envisaged. more than half of the resources available to the commission in this field are earmarked for such transactions. fifthly, food aid to the least developed countries is provided exclusively in the form of donations. in total, at least 80% of food aid must be provided through such donations and members are working to increase this percentage. sixth, in determining whether and to what extent the provision of food aid on preferential credit terms should continue to be covered by the food aid convention, the members of the convention shall take into account the outcome of the relevant multilateral negotiations. in this regard, the european union and some other members expressed their conviction that humanitarian aid provided through such appropriations should no longer be included in the list of aid measures. our position is that food aid must be clearly separated from regulations on commercial transactions. seventhly, the new food aid convention should allow for better monitoring of the effectiveness and impact of food aid measures and improve cooperation between donors, beneficiaries and other relevant parties. eighth, the provision of food aid under the convention will not be linked in any way to commercial exports of goods or services. in conclusion, since this point has been raised by several members in the debate, i would like to draw attention to the amounts of aid we currently have available to ethiopia. the commission and the community are able to mobilise 542 526 tonnes of cereals between april 2000 and march 2001, i.e. immediately. i would also like to point out that during the negotiations we were in constant contact with the countries receiving food aid, so that we were always informed of their position.
- thank you very much, mr fischler. the debate is closed. the vote will take place tomorrow at 11 a.m.

the rapporteur. - (es) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the committee on development and cooperation unanimously approved a few days ago the recommendation which we are submitting to parliament today. a considerable effort had previously been made to speed up and streamline the procedure in this respect, considering it particularly important and urgent to vote on the new parliament and council regulation on development cooperation with south africa. this was important because south africa is one of the countries that receives the most development aid from the european union. it was urgent because the regulation governing this cooperation since 1995 expired on 31 december 1999, so that there is now no legal basis for this important instrument. it's disturbing that we've come to this. in the first half of 1999, parliament examined the commission's proposal at first reading and adopted six amendments to it which were submitted to the council for its consideration, adoption or rejection. that is where there has been a delay, for the simple reason that the council took no less than eight months to react. the expiry date was thus exceeded, hence the legal vacuum i have just mentioned. finally, the council presented its proposal. it adopted most of the amendments tabled by parliament at first reading and placed greater emphasis on the fight against poverty and the achievement of the development objectives set at international level on the basis of un conventions and resolutions. the committee on development and cooperation, when considering the council's proposal, felt that it was necessary to try to avoid the procedure being prolonged by a third reading. in other words, we have decided to take on all that we consider reasonable and to limit our amendments to what is necessary, but with great restraint. there were two points which were translated into amendments which our committee is submitting to the plenary for approval by way of a recommendation. the first amendment concerns comitology. the council wanted the committee of experts to monitor all cooperation projects with south africa with a budget exceeding eur 3 million. we thought that this committee should be more responsible for guiding and monitoring the broad lines of development cooperation with south africa and for directly monitoring only the most important projects, leaving the less important ones to the ordinary procedures, which are the responsibility of the commission. after considering all the points, our amendment, the one we are putting to parliament today, raises the council's proposal from 3 to 5 million, which means that the committee on the regions will have to deal with far fewer projects and will thus be able to devote more time to all this very important work. the second amendment concerns the budgetary envelope for development cooperation between the european union and south africa for the seven-year period, including the year 2000, covered by the regulation under discussion. over the last five years, this budget has been €125 million per year. the council, in its budgetary restraint policy, reduced this allocation in its budget and set it at eur 112.5 million per year. we say that it is politically unacceptable to send a signal of restraint when at the same time a major cooperation, trade and development agreement is being signed with south africa. on the contrary, it was necessary to maintain this envelope and, if possible, to increase it, even if only symbolically, even if we share the concern about the resources available. finally, the proposal approved by the committee on development, on whose behalf i am speaking, was extraordinarily reasonable: the 123.5 million already allocated for the year 2000 and 127 million for each of the following six years, to arrive at a total amount for the budget of 885.5 million for the seven years for which the regulation is provided. both amendments seem to us to be balanced. the aim is to avoid a third reading, to end the current intolerable legal vacuum and to give a significant political impetus to our development cooperation with south africa. in asking you today to support our proposals, we hope that the common sense and moderation of parliament will be understood by the council. we also hope that the commission will be able to accept these proposals, even though its own proposals, 25 million for comitology and 850.5 million for the budgetary envelope, differ slightly from those which we are presenting to you. without this understanding, the council or the commission will be solely responsible for launching the third reading procedure, with the consequences that the lack of legal coverage could have for the projects under way in our development cooperation with south africa. the amount of the budgetary envelope suggested by the commission, which is very close to our own proposal, should in any case reach the committee on development in time for possible consideration by parliament and, above all, should certainly be approved by the council if we accept it.

commission - (de) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, in february the commission discussed the priorities for the european budget for the coming year and also had the opportunity to discuss these priorities in depth with the european parliament - here in plenary, but also and above all with the committee on budgets - and at the various meetings of the trilogue, which brings together the commission, the european parliament and the council, which have taken place in the meantime. the commission has drawn up the preliminary draft budget for 2001 on the basis of these discussions and it is the preliminary draft adopted by the commission which is now before you. since this is the first preliminary draft budget i have had the opportunity to present to you, let me say a few words about the method and timing of its presentation. i think it is extremely sensible that there should be intensive debate on priorities before we get down to the actual figures and i think it is particularly useful to present the preliminary draft early enough so that the debate can be intensive. as regards the structure of the budget, it is the case that, as with any european national budget, the bulk of the budget figures in the european budget for a given year are defined by conventions, decisions of previous years, legal bases of previous years. this applies in particular to agricultural expenditure in the field of market organization, the largest budgetary item in terms of expenditure, including for the financial year 2001, and to the structural funds but also to multiannual programmes, whether in the field of research, youth aid or foreign policy. despite what has been established in previous years, the 2001 budget also sets out - and unequivocally - political priorities and i think i can say, after the discussions of the last few months, that there is a very high degree of agreement between the priorities set out in the commission's preliminary draft budget and those of parliament. first of all, the priority given to the second pillar of the agricultural policy, the commission's preliminary draft budget allocating the highest rate of growth to the promotion of rural development, and i think that this really underlines that, in the commission's view, the emphasis should be placed on this second pillar of the agricultural policy. the second concerns the priority given to economic policy and the need to develop and promote a knowledge society in europe. that is why the commission's preliminary draft proposes a substantial increase in research expenditure and a re-design of the programme to help small and mediumsized enterprises and, above all, a proposal linking these with technological promotion, which was also a request made by your rapporteur, mrs haug. access to new technologies is not very high among small and medium-sized enterprises. it is obvious that if we want an economic structure strongly supported by smes and if we also want to push europe forward, to push the development of europe in the field of information and communication technologies, it is both wise and necessary to combine these two aspects. the preliminary draft budget also contains a new emphasis on foreign policy. we have already had the opportunity to discuss this in great depth during the debate on aid to the balkans. i would also like to mention the additional priority of the need to apply budgetary discipline to the european budget as well, and this is an objective pursued by the preliminary draft budget. i would therefore like to quote a few figures on the overall budget. excluding agricultural expenditure, the preliminary draft budget provides for an increase of 1% in commitment appropriations, i.e. the financial commitments which can be made, compared with the previous year. i think that this figure clearly shows that this preliminary draft budget fits into the general political landscape of budgetary discipline: for all payments, excluding agricultural expenditure, the rate of increase is 3%. i would point out that the average growth estimate for the budgets of the member states is 3.1%. i am mentioning this because it will certainly play a major role in the debate with the council. however, we have also anchored in the preliminary draft budget a significant increase in agricultural expenditure, since it is 7.6%, or in absolute terms, eur 3.12 billion. this is essentially the result of the decisions taken last year at the berlin summit by the heads of state and government and the financial forecasts agreed are an integral part of the interinstitutional agreement concluded last year between parliament, the council and the commission. i would point out that the figure quoted for the agricultural policy also provides that the draft budget for this area remains below the ceiling set in berlin and that the commission's proposal therefore provides for the reallocation of 300 million from the agricultural budget to the field of foreign policy: and yet there is a high rate of increase for the agricultural policy. summa summarum, this means that the preliminary draft provides, if we take the figures as a whole, for an increase of 3.9% in commitment appropriations and 5% in payments. the rate of increase is higher for payments: this is due to the fact that we are faced with a large number of commitments and that the commission is currently of the opinion that this mass cannot continue to grow and that it is, on the contrary, a matter of absorbing it: therefore, the rate of increase must be higher in payments. what does this mean for the states' share? i mean by this: what share of the total gross national product of the european community is absorbed by the european union? what is the share of the member states, given the substantial growth in gross national product which we can expect in the european community countries next year? the growth prospects are very positive. will this share of gross national product in the european budget fall from 1.11% in 2000 to 1.07% in 2001? i would like to stress this point in particular to show - while we are also witnessing very the commission's white paper on the reform strategy fulfils the promises made to parliament and the council last year to look without delay at how the institution as an organisation is currently performing its functions. any delay in the development of a practical strategy and in the implementation of a necessary modernisation process would have been unacceptable to the commission, the council, parliament and the public - i am sure the honourable member will agree. one of the stated aims of this comprehensive reform is to enhance administrative performance, which will, among other things, enable the commission to deal more effectively with changes affecting the union in its present and future form, and the world at large. it is clear that the challenges posed by future enlargement differ in nature and scale from those arising from previous enlargements. the commission must therefore be able to discharge its powers and obligations with the optimum executive and administrative efficiency in order to facilitate and accommodate this great change. as the college of commissioners clearly stated in the preface to the white paper and elsewhere in the document, i quote: 'the challenges of globalisation and future enlargement require better governance at all levels, including that of the european union'. all political institutions, including the commission, must be up to the task. reform is therefore an essential condition for the realisation of our vision of europe. the current administrative reform is not a limited initiative, it is an evolving process, as we have clearly stated, which will be monitored on an ongoing basis and the results of which will be evaluated in order to make the necessary adjustments. any specific requirements arising from the enlargement process will be duly taken into account and, of course, this will apply to the impact of the changes under way on human resources. particular attention will be paid to certain issues such as the management of the growing cultural diversity within the commission and an early retirement scheme directly linked to enlargement. as with other enlargements, specific measures on the appointment and integration of officials from the new member states will be adopted in due course.

commission. - thank you, mr president. as the honourable member who raised the question is certainly aware, under the northwest atlantic fisheries organisation (nafo) joint international inspection contracting party. nafo inspectors shall be required to carry out their duties in accordance with the rules laid down in the nafo agreement and shall remain under the operational control of and be carried out under his authority. the commission inspectors, informed by the canadians, went on board the santa mafalda to verify the grounds for the serious infringement established by the canadian inspectors. during that verification, the commission inspectors ensured that the evidence on board was kept intact and forwarded their report to the portuguese authorities. the portuguese authorities, in turn, ordered the santa mafalda to sail to the port of aveiro, portugal, for a detailed inspection. the santa mafalda docked in aveiro on 10 may 2000 and two commission inspectors participated in the thorough inspection of the vessel. the commission drew the attention of the canadian authorities to the procedures used by the canadian inspectors, namely the seizure of documents and their continued presence on board the santa mafalda. the commission considers that the canadian nafo inspectors in question acted in breach of the nafo agreement by seizing documents on board without asking the master's permission and by remaining on board permanently. however, it should be noted that in this case the master of the vessel and the portuguese authorities did not object to the prolonged stay on board of the canadian inspectors and that the fishing activities of the santa mafalda were not obstructed.

commission. - (es) i do not see any excessive correlation between the two questions, but i do see that the euro is taken seriously. what happened to the euro? there are many technical explanations for this situation. we would enter into a wider debate that would have a lot to do with the starting point; the evolution of economic forecasts and real economies in each zone; with the evolution, of course, of interest rates; and other technical elements, such as expiry dates for certain types of emissions, etc. the reality is that when we analyse the euro by taking the exchange rate as a fundamental axis, we are not correctly assessing the introduction of the euro. the euro is already a great success in terms of its introduction, the emissions it produces, the consolidation of an excellent economic situation in europe and the prospects for the future. it is true that the exchange rate is not what we would have liked. we believe that a strong economy must be matched by a strong euro. we believe, however, that growth in europe will be strong in the year 2000 and that we will therefore reach the us level by the end of the year. in these circumstances, we believe that the euro's margin of manoeuvre will be upwards in the coming months. therefore, even if there is still some concern - because there is public concern - about the evolution of the euro, we believe that this situation will be corrected and that it should be seen as transitional and not as permanent.
the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. firstly, i believe that closer cooperation on economic policy coordination is both necessary and positive and that this is an element that emerges from the current crisis. the french president has stressed this and it will logically be a key point of the next presidency. i do not agree with your theory that the evolution of the euro means a decline in employment in europe and an increase in employment in the united states. capital transfers may generate additional activity in the us, but positive export developments are creating activity in europe. we should enter into a much more complex and profound debate to develop this point. in any case, i think - as i said earlier - that the euro currently has an exchange rate which, if we analyse it in relation to its components and its historical situation, is not very far removed from situations which have existed in other times. i am convinced that this is a transitional situation which will improve during the year.
question no 38 by mr pedro marset campos (h-0419/00) subject: precarious employment and rates of accidents at work in spain and the region of murcia the lisbon summit committed to full and quality employment in the eu. in the face of the french government's proposal to reduce the working day in order to create stable and quality jobs, the formula agreed by the spanish and british governments was adopted, namely to increase deregulation of working conditions in order to increase employment. the spanish experience of the last four years has shown that this formula does indeed create employment, but it is mainly temporary and precarious in nature and is associated with a high rate of accidents at work, the highest being in the region of murcia. does the commission not consider that the conditions under which jobs are created in the various countries and regions of the union should be closely monitored in order to prevent job creation from being carried out at the expense of the stability and dignity of workers, and in particular of young people entering the labour market for the first time? questions to mr verheugen
commission - (es) mr president, although i was born near the region of murcia, it is difficult for me to analyse the problems of precarious employment in the region of murcia in community terms. so let me just think a little bit more broadly. the evaluation of labour market reforms through the processes we have established in the union - the luxembourg process and the broad economic policy guidelines - shows us that the labour market regulatory reforms carried out in different countries are making a positive and significant contribution to greater economic growth, greater job creation and greater participation of men and women in the labour market. the broad economic policy guidelines and the employment recommendations have never advocated mere deregulation of the labour market, as is claimed in the question. in parallel with the reform of various labour market regulations, we are also always taking into account, for example, the need to adopt measures to encourage entrepreneurship or active labour market policies - and we say this clearly - in order to improve employment opportunities. the measures to be adopted in each member state must be adapted to the problems and realities of each of them. it is also right that the commission should stress the need to carry out discussions and agreements with the social partners so that they can take an active part in the changes in the labour market in each country. just as a significant and sustainable increase in the level of employment is one of the key priorities of the employment strategy, so too is the quality of jobs. at the recent lisbon summit, the union's economic and social agenda was given new impetus and we also stressed this point by talking about more and better jobs. i would also point out, as a fundamental contribution to consolidating the progress achieved to date, the promotion and maintenance of high standards of health and safety at work, which has been a central part of the debate in our college in favour of improving the quality of workplaces in europe. labour market reforms aimed at improving employment opportunities and the adaptability of workers to these new job offers are in some ways an attempt to tackle unhealthy or unsafe working conditions. the commission, in accordance with the legal powers conferred on it by the treaty, has made the necessary efforts to develop and propose various legal instruments and to monitor the integration of the community acquis in this field. as regards your question and the spanish case, it is the responsibility of spain, like the other member states, to apply the commission's directives. it is also the responsibility of the member states to monitor their application in each of their territories. the commission must ensure that these directives are correctly transposed into national legislation and, of course, that all the questions relating to their application are followed up, which is the responsibility of the national authorities.
- (es) i thank mr solbes for his reply and for his intention to look after the workers' situation and to take care of them. however, the political analysis of the lisbon summit reveals that there were two proposals: one more social, more committed, put forward by the french prime minister, mr jospin, and another, the subject of an earlier compromise between mr blair and mr aznar, favouring the flexibilization of work and deregulation, a proposal which was accepted. if we take spain as an example, it is clear that precariousness, temporary employment and the rate of accidents are increasing. in view of this, do you not think that it would be appropriate, when the amsterdam treaty is revised, to incorporate the social charter with concrete instruments and measures, as was done with the five classic points of the maastricht treaty, in order to guarantee full employment, its quality and therefore not to leave it to the fate of each country? the accident rate in the region of murcia was cited as an example because in spain it is in this region that it is highest; that's why you're worried.
commission. - (es) i had a feeling that the reference to the region of murcia was not connected with the fact that i was born near it. as regards the substantive issue, i would make a different comment. we have always been concerned not only with more jobs but also with better quality jobs. in the broad economic policy guidelines for this year and in the specific recommendation for spain, we make explicit reference to the need to analyse the problems, including the cost of redundancy, which may have an impact on temporary work, because we believe that flexibility is one thing but that precariousness is another. these are radically different elements. however, you introduce a second element in your supplementary question which i think is of great interest: why do we not set a target of full employment as we did the maastricht treaty objectives? basically because the nature of the two numbers is radically different. what we set in motion in maastricht was the respect of obligations which depend on voluntary decisions taken by the member states which are part of the european union. in the case of full employment, the figure is derived from measures which attempt to achieve a goal but which in no way have a causal link to guarantee its achievement. we can look at what is being done in the various employment programmes: implementing certain elements to move towards full employment. when we talk about full employment in the commission document which was the starting point for the lisbon debate, we have made it clear that we will achieve full employment if the economic developments we forecast, in the light of the figures we have at present, are combined with the different conditions and policies proposed by the commission. but full employment must not be a political objective, as in maastricht, because it does not depend on the will of the various governments, on a specific decision by each of them.
- (es) i would like to say that in order to be able to judge from a distance, it is often essential to know the reality. in the southern mediterranean countries, and particularly in the region of murcia, we have in recent years moved from managing unemployment to managing employment. from the exorbitant and appalling unemployment that resulted from large state-owned industries whose economic model could no longer continue, we have moved, after a crisis, to a situation of small enterprise (sme) growth and economic incentives that have generated a new vibrant and active model. however, it is clear that the accident rate - to which i now refer - is a matter of education and mutual responsibility on the part of business leaders, the state, public administrations and, of course, trade unions. we can't achieve our goal unless they all work together. in spain, a law on this subject was passed in 1995, and we are trying to implement it, but it cannot be done in one day. so, commissioner, first of all, what active policies and economic sectors do you think you can mobilise to achieve better education in this particular area, for the development of responsibility? secondly, and very concretely: is there a programme for education in the language of the emigrant, so that we can teach them and they understand the minimum standards of safety in a region which is hosting a huge number of emigrants who do not know our language?
commission. - thank you for your consideration. as regards your questions, i will say, as i have done before, that in the scheme of the distribution of responsibilities between the commission and the member states, these questions are the responsibility of the member states. therefore, both the funding of these immigrant education programmes and the active policies are decisions that logically depend on what the spanish government accepts or decides in social matters.
- question no 39 by mr jens-peter bonde (h-0352/00) subject: adaptation of the applicant countries could the commission indicate the total number of documents sent to the applicant countries and the volume of the community acquis as a whole and consider forms of cooperation which give the applicant countries the possibility of not accepting all the rules?
commission - (de) madam member, the debate you wish to open is hypothetical. this debate was held in the first half of the 1990s and was concluded by the decisions which you know, which have been the subject of many discussions in this parliament and which we cannot go back on: these are the decisions taken by the european councils in copenhagen, essen and luxembourg and which were aimed at preparing the countries of central and eastern europe as well as cyprus and malta for accession. it is no use asking today if there would have been an alternative. as i recall, at any rate, the candidates would not have settled for less than that. they would not have accepted anything less, they would have felt it was discrimination, so that no other decision than the one taken in luxembourg in 1997 would have been realistically possible. no country in the process believes that we should deviate from this objective of full membership. if it was, i'd know. but it's not. the 12 candidate countries with which we are negotiating are preparing carefully for membership and i therefore dissuade you from discussing the modification of the basic objectives of enlargement after the opening of the process. the candidates could only feel it as a very serious breach of trust.
- question no 40 by mr wuermeling (h-0388/00), substituted by mrs müller: subject: eastern enlargement - transitional provisions in the field of the free movement of services the negotiations on the free movement of services with the first group of candidate countries (the luxembourg group) are provisionally concluded. could the commission state what transitional measures have been adopted so far? what impact does it think these provisions will have on small businesses and craft industries, particularly in regions bordering the applicant countries? questions to mr monti
commission - (de) madam president, i assume that you are aware that the accession negotiations are a conference bringing together states, that it is not the commission but the member states that negotiate, and that i am therefore not entitled to inform you about the content of negotiations which have not yet been concluded. i'd love to, but i can't. i can nevertheless answer your question because the commission naturally has an opinion on the various points you have raised. firstly, the commission is of the opinion that transitional periods should only be envisaged in the context of this enlargement process if the objective of enlargement cannot otherwise be achieved within the time limits or in a timely manner. the transitional periods must be very, very limited in scope and duration, especially when it comes to the internal market. you should know that any transitional period, regardless of the country with which it is concluded, hinders the internal market. and if we agree on a large number of transitional periods, we can forget about the internal market as a whole for many years. this cannot be the direction of enlargement. the question you would really like to have answered is how we are preparing for the problems that will arise in certain border regions after enlargement. the region you come from and the region i come from are part of it. as you know, i have spoken on this subject on many occasions, including in your area, so i can be brief now. as regards the free movement of workers, which is a very difficult issue, i think there will probably be transitional periods after all. but we are not there yet. in the area of freedom to provide services, which will indeed lead to increased competition in border regions, i believe that it is necessary to prepare an action programme now which will enable small and mediumsized enterprises in particular in border regions to prepare for and face this new competition.

question no 43 by mr david w. martin (h-0354/00) subject: requests from member states for public aid is the commission satisfied with the time taken to reply to requests from member states for the granting of public aid?
commission. - as you know, mr martin, our work on state aid is moving in several directions and we are seeking to strengthen control in this area. as regards the deadlines, no change is planned in the near future. the deadlines are laid down in a council regulation which, for the first time, codifies the procedures for state aid. and since the adoption of the regulation dates back only to 1999, it should not be amended any time soon. however, we are ready and fully willing to speed up certain aspects of the decision-making process, where possible, including the development of standard notification forms. you mentioned the problem of resources. of course, this issue is important for all competition policy activities, and this includes state aid. the higher the quality of the information provided, starting with the information contained in the notifications from the member states, the more likely it is that the procedures will run smoothly and in a relatively short time.
question no 44 by mr claude turmes (h-0355/00) subject: state aid to nuclear energy given that the rules of the common market in electricity which came into force last february have the effect of subjecting the production of electricity as a whole to the rules of the internal market and that, under article 92 of the eaec treaty, electricity is not among the products to which the provisions relating to the nuclear common market apply, does the commission agree that electricity produced from nuclear energy is now subject to the same rules as all other forms of electricity? does the commission therefore consider that any state aid to the nuclear industry is prohibited by the ec treaty, since no derogation is specified, and since article 98 of the eaec treaty does not provide for a subsidised accident insurance scheme for the coverage of atomic risk? in this context, has the commission made any proposals to the uk government regarding the nffo (non-fossil fuel obligation) scheme in accordance with article 87 of the ec treaty and, if so, what are they? can it now confirm that it is carrying out investigations into the granting of state aid to the nuclear industry, as requested by the greens/efa group in its letter of 10 march to commissioner monti?
the commission is not prepared to accept the amendments tabled by the committee on budgets. i'm very sensitive to environmental requirements. i was already a member of the previous commission when i proposed the directive on the taxation of energy products, and i am trying to do the same in the prodi commission. i understand your concern, but let me make a few comments. the draft new framework for state aid for the environment is very flexible as regards the granting of aid to renewable energy. it allows for aid of at least 40% of eligible costs in the case of investments, and for operating aid member states may choose a system which allows for aid of up to 100% of eligible costs. i think that it cannot therefore be said that the commission is prohibiting aid for renewable energy. there is competition, let me say again, not only between renewable energy on the one hand and conventional energy on the other, but also within renewable energy itself in its various forms. the support for these sources of energy may also differ from one member state to another. the commission considers that the aid is compatible with the internal market if it is granted through state resources. the commission recognises that renewables may need support to develop, but at the same time it is also important that renewables gradually adapt to competitive markets to ensure their long-term development.

the rapporteur. - (es) mr president, there are not many of us here at this time of the evening, but it is also true that this is the third time that this report has been debated in the european parliament. the report on the reduction of co2 emissions from new passenger cars was approved at first reading with 48 amendments at the first debate in december 1998. the council and the commission accepted some of them in their entirety and others in part. the report was then returned for a second reading. it is true that the council accepted some amendments which we considered important, but certain aspects of the report and the amendments unanimously approved by the committee on the environment, public health and consumer protection - and by a large majority in parliament's plenary - also seemed to us to be essential and were not taken up. the main aim was to include in this plan the reduction of co2 emissions from new vehicles to light commercial vehicles, which are widely used in cities and whose co2 emissions also pollute. we also felt that the data quality guarantee had been left in the past. for a plan like this, the accuracy of the data collected by governments, and a certain equality between them, is fundamental. it was also important to preserve something that was now traditional in the position of the environment committee of the european parliament: a certain distrust of voluntary agreements. since community law - directives and regulations - is often not respected, we believe that it is even more difficult to enforce voluntary agreements. the committee on the environment was wary of such voluntary agreements and in another amendment it was asked to draw up a clear legal framework to be used in case the voluntary agreements did not work. our wish to have a paragraph on stabilising and reducing emissions has finally been fulfilled. another amendment which we considered essential was the one concerning the dimensions of vehicles. finally, mr president, the amendments which were approved by a qualified majority in this parliament and which were not accepted by the council numbered ten, so that the conciliation procedure had to be used, which was neither very contentious nor very difficult. as the name suggests, conciliation procedures involve each party making sacrifices in order to reach a final agreement. our main concerns are reflected in this final agreement. it includes a study to introduce light commercial vehicles in the future and mentions the possibility of presenting a proposal for a legal framework shortly and reviewing the data so that they are rigorous and more or less equal in each country. in conclusion, parliament's fundamental concerns are incorporated, if not radically and immediately, with a commitment to adopt decisions on this subject in the future. the only amendment which was not included was the one on the dimensions of the vehicle. parliament went on to stress that this was very important because the larger and more powerful a vehicle is, the higher the level of emissions, and we felt it was essential to recognise this in one of the annexes; but given that six other elements on the capacity and conditions of the vehicles are present, it seemed to us that we could no longer extend the conciliation procedure. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the new car industry is not affected by the introduction of new technologies. finally, i think we have reached a reasonable agreement, which is neither the one originally proposed by parliament nor the one originally proposed by the council. i think, mr president, that we shall have no difficulty in getting this agreement approved.

the rapporteur. -es) mr president, commissioner, i am glad to take up your last words in the debate on subsidiarity or coordination. i agree with you, commissioner, that there is no contradiction between these two terms, but we must be able to accept them. perhaps it is time - on the occasion of the debate on the 11 stability plans presented by the euro countries and the four convergence plans - to review the harmonisation between the subsidiarity and coordination required for the introduction and future of the single currency. it is therefore the reverse of the debate we have just had on the report by my colleague mr katiforis, and we must begin to think, first of all, about the instrument. this is the first time that this house has debated the 15 plans submitted by the member states. i think that in future the report should not be a single document, but a detailed study of the solutions, the strengths and weaknesses, which this parliament detects in the economic policies proposed by the member states. we will therefore ask for more details on the submitted plans, on the cost structure and on the revenue structure, with particular attention to investments. we will also ask that the medium and longterm forecasts take into account different scenarios for interest rate developments, demographic developments and other variables affecting the stability of our long-term accounts. we also ask - and i return to the debate on subsidiarity - for a better political compromise between the 15 national parliaments. we believe that this is a task that should be shared by all, and not just by the european parliament. some member states have submitted their stability and convergence plans to internal debate in order to give political support to this idea of jointly building an economic unit, and we should ask those member states which have not done so to debate these programmes in their parliaments in order to try, first, to involve the states and parliaments in this joint task and, secondly, to give political support to the compromises agreed in the framework of the necessary coordination of economic policies. as regards the points proposed in the report to the house, i can only note with satisfaction that all the budgetary objectives set in previous programmes have been achieved, even beyond the forecasts. but this satisfaction has its downside, because while one may criticize the fact that the objectives may not have been sufficiently rigorous or demanding, we find that the objectives were achieved not because of the interest and effort of the member states, but simply because of factors such as the favourable development of interest rates or the fact that tax revenues were higher than forecast. we therefore consider that while fiscal consolidation should remain a priority, the economic environment - which has improved considerably - should allow us to accelerate consolidation and, at the same time, to undertake structural reforms in the medium term. it is unacceptable that this relative improvement in the economy should encourage member states to stop taking decisions - sometimes difficult - on structural reforms. the first of these is the labour reform, which we have already discussed. it is clear that not all states have undertaken the labour reforms we believe are appropriate. the improvement in the labour market is, of course, the result of satisfactory economic growth, and not all member states have undertaken the necessary rigorous reforms, the more radical reforms which would solve the unacceptably high unemployment rate in european countries compared with other countries, which is an economic, but above all a personal and family scourge which we cannot afford in the 20th century in a modern europe. there is also an urgent need to liberalise telecommunications and energy markets, and not all countries are doing so in the same way. as for tax reforms, we should welcome the reduction in the high level of taxation in france, germany, the netherlands and spain, and we should take into account the fact that the high unemployment rate is often due to the fact that our tax levels are high. the serious demographic problem should also be included in the long-term reforms. in the programmes presented to us, we see that special attention is paid to the ageing of the population. perhaps the time has come to ask the member states to tackle the demographic problem at its root, by targeting tax revenue and social cost policies appropriately, protecting families with children. this is how the root of the problem must be tackled and not just its effects. only in this way will we prevent the old europe from becoming a decrepit europe.
