- (es) mr president, i listened to the council and the commission with great interest. the socialist group considers that the debt which is detrimental to the development of the world's poorest countries cannot be treated in isolation as a purely financial problem, but must be part of a broad and coherent strategy which, by eradicating poverty, would lead to development. to do this, first of all, debt relief must not lead to the elimination of other sources of financing but must be part of a coherent development policy. secondly, the funds released by the rebate must be transformed into funds for human development, in particular investments in health and education. i do not agree with the council that this may be a new form of settlement. i think it is not. to be effective in terms of development, debt relief also needs, as we call for in the resolution, a global strategy conducted in unison in and by the international financial institutions. the european union, as the largest donor of development aid, must coordinate its action with the poorest countries and set poverty eradication as a common objective of its member states, one aspect of which is the debt relief for the poorest countries. we are therefore faced with a case of coherence and coordination between community policies. the common foreign and security policy, which is too often regarded as a mere security policy, must take this aspect into account in the same way as trade and development policies. as for the heavily indebted poor countries, beneficiaries of this debt relief strategy already undertaken counsel. - (pt) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, it seems clear today that the situation in question is a matter of concern and that it has attracted the attention of the council. this is essentially a relatively consensual issue, particularly within the european union. the portuguese presidency of the european union was prudent in including this issue in its work programme and making it a key issue on the agenda of the euro-africa summit in cairo. but this question must be viewed in a calm and balanced way, regardless of the dramatic nature of the serious situation affecting the populations of heavily indebted countries. the essential question of debt is not the crucial question for the countries concerned, the crucial question is their development. development is the fundamental issue underlying it. we must all be aware that what is at stake at the moment is the overall reflection on general development policy and, in particular, on how the european union and its member states are situated in the global context of the definition of this policy, which is currently at stake. this is the fundamental question: the symptom is debt and the disease is underdevelopment. there are problems of inequality and problems of unequal distribution of wealth in these countries, but these problems must be overcome through solutions of a political nature. i have spoken before of neo-colonial temptations or drift, but i did not mean to say that the forms of conditionality associated with the granting of aid - which derive from the current philosophy underlying acp-eu cooperation - are not perfectly legitimate and normal. we cannot forget that there is a policy on the internal management of the allocation of resources, in particular the resources released for these countries under debt relief. we must be careful to respect the way in which the governments of these countries manage these funds. we must know that we must make efforts to ensure that political conditionality and the strengthening of democracy in these countries are the fundamental elements underlying our action. work to promote good governance, work to strengthen democratic structures and political participation are fundamental elements for the creation of liberated societies which allow for better management of domestic resources and a more appropriate management of the distribution of wealth and, in particular, which do not encourage corruption and embezzlement. we believe that these are basic questions of development. as i said, i think the debt issue is a symptom of something much more global: development. i believe that the european union and the member states have shown that they are attentive and have concrete measures to propose.
commission. - mr president, i would like to begin by addressing the need for conditionality. i agree with a number of the points made here. i would also say that what we are facing is not a stricter conditionality than that applied by the member states in bilateral development cooperation, because at the moment it is necessary to ensure that the use of resources corresponds to the objectives that are set. if we look at the substance of the matter, there is also a link with a greater focus on social aspects within the ldcs - this is the key to what we are proposing to do. it would appear that the world bank and the imf are in favour of this approach and that these institutions are determined to give priority to these aspects. in a way, we could say that we are witnessing a transition from the washington consensus to the copenhagen consensus. the positive aspect is that with the poverty reduction strategy papers, the imf is aligning itself with the objectives set by the world bank a few years ago. all this shows that the fight against poverty is at the heart of this effort. maintaining the focus on ldcs whose definition may be narrow and examining the social consequences within these countries is therefore a fairly reasonable combination. i come to the question of whether too few countries are involved in the initiative. it would be wrong to think that we can simply extend its scope to include all developing countries. to do so would have many negative effects. first, the cost of the lfp initiative would increase enormously because the more prosperous these countries are, the less poor they are, the more debt they have incurred. the aim is to help the poorest countries to determine in what areas they can manage the remaining debt. the idea has never been to cancel the entire debt of the third world countries because it is a totally unworkable idea. official development aid is at 0.22%, or 0.23%, which is far from the 0.7% target, the principle of which was unanimously agreed but which few countries have actually achieved. the figure of 350 billion would be unmanageable; similarly, the value of the initiative for the poorest countries would be diluted if it were distributed among the least poor, middle-income countries. i would say to mrs schörling that almost all the money for the pple initiative comes from existing development budgets. the same applies to the billion we are reallocating from the edf. the good thing is that the acp countries have accepted it and that it is a reallocation that transfers money from the relatively prosperous countries to the poorer countries of the acp group. the commission's proposal is to be adopted by the council at the next meeting of the european council in brussels. that is a very welcome aspect. the positive aspect is that we had the money and were therefore the only donors who could act in a really effective way, with the exception of a few "elite donors" - the usual gang - who try to shame others by putting themselves forward and setting a good example. the european union is the only donor capable of taking effective action. finally, i am pleased with the way this debate has unfolded. the interest shown by parliament is an important asset for the european union.

- question no 2 by mrs marie anne isler béguin (h-0361/00) is hereby referred to as: subject: armenia-turkey dispute on 11 december, the council accepted turkey's application for membership of the european union. in its article 3, the ep resolution of 18 june 1987 'calls on the council to obtain from the present turkish government recognition of the genocide committed against the armenians in 1915-17 and to encourage the establishment of a political dialogue between turkey and the armenian representative delegates' a2-0033/87, oj c 190, 20.7.1987, p. 95. turkey does not recognise the genocide in question and still imposes an economic blockade on armenia. what action has the council taken to develop political relations between armenia and turkey? does the council consider the lifting of the embargo to be one of the essential conditions for turkey's accession to the european union?
- (pt) the honourable member raises two questions: the first concerns the 1987 resolution on the recognition of the genocide of 1915-1917; the second concerns, in essence, the political relations between armenia and turkey. as for the first point, it is clear that this type of question is a political one, although it is based on a historical premise which we all recognise and which is of the utmost importance, but which does not represent a precondition for the resumption of dialogue with turkey. as regards the relations between armenia and turkey, which we hope will be positive in the future, the european union has simply tried to bring turkey into line with the normal framework of the european union's external relations. this framework includes a dimension of good relations with armenia, particularly in the commercial field. these good relations, and the whole framework of cooperation associated with them, are part of the acquis which turkey must accept. however, we cannot impose good relations between countries at the international level, this is not decreed, but it is required by political decision. turkey must show in practice that, regardless of the interpretation of the situation in armenia, if it wants to enter into negotiations with the european union and become a member of the european union, it will of course be obliged to respect the whole framework of good relations which the european union has with armenia. this is a matter which has hitherto been purely bilateral and the european union cannot intervene in this context.
- question no 3 by mr john purvis (h-0365/00) subject: association agreement between the european union and jordan would the council indicate the member states which have yet to ratify the association agreement between the european union and jordan and indicate to what extent it considers it a priority to encourage them to speed up the ratification process?
- (pt) mr president, with regard to the last part of the honourable member's question, i would like to say that the importance of the actions undertaken in the mediterranean region is one of the priorities which we have maintained during the portuguese presidency. we intend to continue to work on the establishment of a common strategy for the mediterranean, and various initiatives have been taken in this area. in concrete terms, as regards the agreement with jordan, apart from the recognition and regret that this agreement has not yet entered into force, past practice has shown that these agreements take about three years to be ratified. the agreement with tunisia was the one ratified the fastest; the agreement was signed in july 1995 and entered into force in march 1998, i.e. after just under three years. experience with all the other agreements indicates a delay of about three years, and i think that the agreement with jordan is at present in line with the average. this depends very much on the national parliaments; however, the portuguese presidency will certainly raise awareness of this problem among the various governments.

counsel. - (pt) mr president, in accordance with article 13 of the treaty establishing the european community, the commission has timely presented three proposals currently under discussion in the social affairs working party: a proposal for a directive establishing a general framework for equal treatment in employment and occupation, a proposal for a directive on the principle of equal treatment between persons irrespective of race or ethnic origin and a proposal for a council decision establishing a programme of community action to combat discrimination for 2000-06. the three proposals put forward by the commission set out different ways of combating discrimination. the first proposal prohibits discrimination in employment on the grounds of race or ethnic origin, religion or belief, disability, age or sexual orientation. the second proposal for a directive prohibits discrimination on grounds of racial or ethnic origin in the fields of employment, education, access to goods and services and social protection. the proposal for a decision, which establishes an action programme to combat discrimination and which aims to support and complement the application of the directives through an exchange of information and experience, is implemented by means of the dissemination of good practice in legislative or other fields. the fight against discrimination on the basis of disability is also covered by the first proposal for a directive aimed at applying the principle of equal treatment in matters of employment and occupation. this proposal covers an area which is fundamental to the exercise of citizens' rights, since it covers an area where discrimination is most visible and produces the greatest negative effects on the integration of people into society. as the european parliament knows, the power of legislative initiative is vested in the commission and not in the council, and the proposals which will be adopted by the council will therefore be based on what the commission proposes to us.

the rapporteur. - (es) mr president, commissioner, before i begin, i would like to point out that the house voted unanimously on the previous report, so that the commission can consider the amendments we have tabled. i hope that this unanimity will encourage you to reconsider your position on these two amendments which you did not wish to support. however, as regards the report under consideration, i would point out that these technical measures are precisely aimed at protecting juveniles of marine organisms in order to reduce the threat to future yields. we are therefore working with the commission to protect fisheries resources. these measures include, as we know, rules on the size of fishing gear - and more specifically, nets - minimum sizes for fishing, specific areas of closure, protection of endangered species, etc. regulation 850/98 entered into force on 1 january last but it is clear that it will need to be periodically adapted in the light of evolving scientific data and developments. in the case before us today, the commission, in its fifth amendment to the regulation, adds several new elements which we consider to be fully justified. the proposals concern shrimp nets, closed areas for spear fishing and the revision of the minimum sizes for a number of bivalve molluscs and crustaceans. the revisions and additions to annex xii proposed by the commission appear reasonable. however, in the case of the recently introduced pink shrimp, the shell length of 24 mm seems excessive and could cause problems for fishermen; the rapporteur has therefore proposed an amendment, which has already been approved by the committee on fisheries, to the compromise figure of 22 mm. the compromise has already been adopted by the member states, who consider it more appropriate. the reduction in the size of the cloves from 40 to 38 mm, which is widely requested by the industry, also seems appropriate to us. the aim is therefore to adapt measures that will have a positive impact on the economic and social environment in strict compliance with scientific advice. it is therefore essential that this regulation be fully updated and based on the best available scientific advice. this will not be the last change, as there is a constant need to adapt to new circumstances and scientific advice. in view of this amendment - which i think may be taken into consideration - we accept the commission's general proposal and hope that the commission will also accept our amendment.
- (es) mr president, today we are discussing the fifth amendment, within two years, to the regulation on technical measures for the protection of juveniles of marine organisms. this is a technical report which, for the majority of our colleagues, is of no interest. however, their attitude might change if we explained to them what it is and how such a report can affect the lives of european citizens. to illustrate this point, commissioner, i will take the example of clove - mentioned in paragraph 4 - and welcome the fact that the commission in its proposal reduces the minimum size required for marketing from 40 to 38 mm. two millimeters of clove, ladies and gentlemen. the increase to 40 mm has caused serious damage to the women in my region, galicia, who fish for this shellfish, as well as to the marketing sector and to the consumers themselves. in galicia, shellfish fishing with their feet - this is how the clove is extracted - is a women's job. it would be too long and complicated to explain the reasons. the men, however, fish for shellfish using basic technological means, while the women fish for shellfish on foot, using a hook. in galicia, nearly 10 000 women are employed in the extraction of clove, since the shells are not fished but extracted. these women work selflessly, sweeping acres of beaches all day long in very difficult conditions for a small income, burdened by social security contributions that can represent more than half of their annual income. the evidence seems to contradict a study which the commission used to raise the minimum size of these molluscs. the cloves are mature and can lay eggs from 30-32 mm. the environmental conditions in the densely populated regions where this cloves, the galicia rias, are reared and bred do not allow it to reach the 40 mm required by the regulation we are going to amend today. the fact is that 80% of the natural production of clove is below the size required at present. if the fishermen wait for the cloves to reach this size, the mortality rate will be enormous, and it will not be their fault, but environmental conditions. in the areas of abundance - i am thinking of the rias of ferrol and arosa - the clove does not exceed 36 to 38 mm. 40 mm nails are not produced, marketed or consumed simply because they do not exist. one of the tasks of this parliament and of any other parliament is to adapt the rule to reality if we do not want to encourage, in the case of shellfish fishing, poaching and the development of a parallel market free of any health controls. this parliament must know that we are trying to protect juveniles through technical measures by allowing them to reach a certain size and reproductive age while ensuring that bycatch is reduced. for a regulation to make sense, it must be adapted to reality. in this way we will protect not only these courageous galician fishermen but also consumers who will have a product subject to all health checks and traders who will no longer feel threatened by a regulation leaving the market completely out of stock. the socialist group, which i represent, therefore supports the proposal to amend this regulation and the amendment by the committee on fisheries concerning the size of the pink shrimp. we hope, commissioner, that we will not have to revise the regulation in a year's time, in which case the european commission and ourselves would have made a mistake in our calculations. however, if that were the case, we would be here to amend it again.

question no 32 by mr jan andersson (h-0444/00) is now closed. subject: concerted efforts in the field of industrial restructuring the globalisation of the economy is accelerating the restructuring of european industry, which is necessary to respond to the changing competitive situation. in some cases, however - such as the measures taken by renault in belgium or, more recently, the measures taken by abb alsthom powers - we can see that restructuring is carried out without regard to the right of workers to participate in decision-making. this situation highlights not only the shortcomings of the common rules on information and consultation of workers but also the weakness of the european union strategy for preventing and managing the consequences of industrial restructuring. would the commission state its position on the establishment of a 'code of conduct' for the management of industrial restructuring, in the light of the gyllenhammar report, and on the establishment of a european observatory of industrial change, as proposed by the federation of european metallurgists?
commission - (el) mr president, according to the gyllenhammar report on industrial restructuring, there are two separate proposals: the first concerns the action of companies with more than a thousand employees to draw up, on a voluntary basis and at regular intervals, a basic report on how they will carry out restructuring; the second concerns the european observatory on industrial change. as regards the first, we are already in contact with the european employers' organisation to promote this project in all companies at european level, as part of the social agenda. as regards the observatory, the commission has understood its importance and emphasizes it, particularly at a time when we are experiencing concentrations, continuous mergers, but also structural reforms in entire sectors. the question has already been included in the social dialogue and we are awaiting the common position of the social partners on 15 june. i should like to say that the commission's approach is not to set up a new structure, a new centre or institute, but to create, within existing structures such as those in dublin, bilbao or seville, a department devoted to industrial restructuring. finally, as regards mergers and acquisitions, which are usually accompanied by problems and a large number of redundancies, there is already written and verbal contact with the competent commissioner, mr monti, and with the relevant directorate-general, so that the commission monitors, as far as possible, the application of the legislation on the works council and checks whether all the provisions laid down by law have been observed before the mergers take place and before major decisions are taken. as you know, competition law in particular does not take into account the impact unless it is measurable, but we are making sure - and the commission has always been the provider of workers and employers - that the best possible preparation takes place, so that we do not end up with thousands of employees being laid off without any provision being made.
commission - (el) mr president, the gyllenhammar report is of course well known and can also be used by the commission, and that is our objective in the context of the social agenda. first of all, i should like to say that, as one of the main points of the report relates to the operation of companies with more than a thousand employees, it is not easy for the commission to get in direct contact with industries and companies throughout europe. these are subsidiarity issues, issues which concern the national employers' organisations, and that is why the dialogue took a considerable amount of time. but i think that in the context of the social agenda we can use some of the very important points of the gyllenhammar report. i must stress, mrs andersson, that these measures are mainly aimed at preparing workers or firms for large-scale structural reforms, so that there are no job losses and, at the same time, no serious social problems. the commission's important task is to complete and implement the employment strategy, which aims to direct all this workforce towards new jobs. in other words, how are we going to tackle structural unemployment and how can people who are suffering mainly from the effects of industrial restructuring find jobs in the new fields that are emerging, which, as you know, are primarily services and the information society?

commission. - (el) it is clear that the european commission has taken a position on the need for a balance between competition and social cohesion. but i would remind you that even in countries with very high growth rates and a very competitive environment, such as the united states of america or some european countries like britain, we have high rates of poverty, a large number of excluded people and very acute social problems. it is clear, therefore, that competitiveness alone, or growth alone, cannot solve social problems, which are particularly complex since the poorest people cannot always reap the benefits of growth. this is why social policy is essential if wealth is to be redistributed and the weakest groups are to be able to adapt. and that is what we are constantly striving to achieve: not to lose our competitiveness while preserving social cohesion.

the rapporteur. - (es) madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the dismantling of obsolete nuclear installations and the appropriate treatment and final disposal of the corresponding radioactive waste is a matter of great importance from the industrial and environmental point of view in the debate on the future of the energy supply needed for sustainable development throughout the world. fortunately, the scientific and technological knowledge is now available to ensure that these operations are carried out safely for the workers concerned and the public at large, and it is up to the public authorities to provide the appropriate resources and to ensure that the relevant legislation is complied with. in this connection, the commission's document on the impact of the nuclear past on the centres linked to the joint research centre, which lays the financial and technical foundations for the dismantling of obsolete nuclear installations and the closure of those still in operation, as well as for the final storage of the radioactive waste already generated and that resulting from the proposed process, should be welcomed. the commission document has been substantially improved and supplemented after its passage by the industry committee of this parliament, and thanks to the rigorous reports for opinion by the budgets and environment committees. i would like to mention six points in particular on which our work in parliament has been particularly significant. firstly, parliament believes that a long-term programme of this magnitude cannot depend on the chance of the budgetary quota each year. it therefore called on the commission and the council to launch a trilogue on the matter immediately in order to enable the three institutions to establish a specific, stable and sufficient budgetary line of action. it is clear that the costs incurred cannot in any way affect the funds earmarked for research in successive framework programmes. i am aware, commissioner, that in the present budgetary context it is not easy to solve this problem, and i would ask you to make your views clear on this in your speech. secondly, the member states concerned must be fully involved in the development of the programme, as it will be conducted in accordance with their respective standards of nuclear safety and radiation protection. thirdly, all operations must be carried out in full transparency, so that the workers involved and the people living in the surrounding areas are informed and, of course, listened to in a timely and comprehensive manner. fourthly, the experience gained and the technological progress derived from this work must be used in similar situations in the enlargement candidate countries, whose participation must be encouraged through the phare and tacis programmes. fifthly, parliament will monitor the programme in detail by receiving a detailed and precise annual report. sixthly, a committee of independent external experts will assist the joint research centre in its task and will assess the technical quality and safety guarantees of the programme throughout its development. i should like to conclude my speech without installations which have reached the end of their useful life.

the rapporteur. - (es) madam president, it is necessary to take account of the fact that the means of research and control available to the supervisory authorities in the financial field are much greater than those in other fields. in the financial sector (and largely through a public call for credit and savings, thus including companies that use the stock market), there is a public interest in protecting the interests of a multitude of third-party savers who place their trust in companies that will manage foreign money without the real owners of that money having the possibility of intervening in the management. the protection of the interests of third parties justifies greater intervention by the public authorities, which is reflected in particular in exorbitant means enabling the authorities to know the internal functioning of enterprises. it is clear that if the data obtained through the exercise of those powers were to become known to third parties, this could not only cause irreparable damage to the audited entities but also cause significant market fluctuations and, ultimately, market distortions. to counterbalance such extensive surveillance powers, therefore, the authorities are required to maintain confidentiality. if this were to be pursued to its ultimate consequences, it could impede some of the objectives pursued by the supervisory authorities, which are ultimately intended to ensure the proper functioning of the market. it is clear that one of the sectors in which the phenomenon of globalisation is most evident is the financial sector, where large companies use the stock market. today, large companies are active in many countries, but there are no supranational supervisory authorities and, moreover, the eu authorities have difficulty carrying out their duties outside their own borders. ultimately, these are sovereignty issues: the problem may be that an authority which supervises the activities of a company in a given country cannot itself access information on the activities of that company, its parent company or its subsidiaries in other countries because its supervisory powers do not extend beyond the borders of the country to which it belongs. to solve this problem, cooperation with the authorities of the various countries is needed, and this cooperation must include the exchange of information collected. the problem is that the implementation of this exchange usually involves a breach of the duty of confidentiality. it is therefore necessary that the standards provide for the way to resolve this conflict between the duty of confidentiality and the exchange of information, by providing balanced solutions. as regards european legislation, after the fluctuating and, moreover, different regulations for the different sectors, the first banking sector directive was amended in 1998 to allow member states to conclude information exchange agreements with third countries, provided that the information communicated benefits from guarantees of professional secrecy at least equivalent to those in force in the european union. this directive now introduces the corresponding amendments in the other financial sector directives, in the same sense as the banking sector directive. as we agreed with the 1998 amendment at the time, and for the same reasons, we will support these amendments in the terms proposed by the commission. one last thought. a report by the european parliament on the review of the slim initiative to simplify internal market legislation is currently pending. what has happened in this sector can be very significant and could have very beneficial consequences. simplifying legislation will also require reducing the number of standards and streamlining initiatives. it is therefore necessary to ask why, when the banking directive was amended in 1998, the directives relating to the insurance sector and to collective investment undertakings were not amended at the same time, and these directives are now being amended. perhaps this is what simplified and coherent legislation would have done.

commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i shall therefore reply to this series of questions which all go in the same direction or more or less in the same direction, to question or question the european commission. on the initiative of the chairmen of the main political groups in your assembly, mr poettering, mr barón crespo, mr cox, mrs hautala and mr lannoye, you have asked the commission to give its opinion on an important and topical question, the status of political parties in europe. we have therefore decided to work on this matter and i am able to give you the position of the european commission, after discussing it yesterday at its weekly meeting. ladies and gentlemen, we are aware of the many reports that have been produced by your assembly - and many of you have referred to them - on this subject over the last ten years: the reports by professor tsatsos and mr ferber, and more recently, on 13 april, that of your two colleagues, mr dimitrakopoulos and mr leinen. we know the problem and we know the proposals of your assembly; we share your interest in a development which would consolidate european democracy, which would consolidate the extremely important process of european integration. president poetterring recalled what is currently written in the treaty. i am referring to the former article 138a, now article 191, which states that: 'political parties at european level are important as a factor of integration within the union. they contribute to the formation of a european conscience and to the expression of the political will of the citizens of the union.' indeed, mrs hautala, it is clear from this text, which is only declaratory but has the merit of being there, that the european political parties are in no way replacing national parties. you have to say it over and over. nor, mrs muscardini, does european citizenship, which is also enshrined in the texts, replace national citizenship. she adds to it. and that's what this is about today. however, as i have just said, this text, important as it is, is merely declaratory. it is not accompanied by any operational mechanism, which is clearly visible in the absence of such a mechanism and in the need for it, particularly to respond - as president barón crespo has mentioned - to the court of auditors' requests or requests. i will therefore reply by telling you what the european commission intends to do, but i will also stress the twofold concern and the twofold demand that we must make, or more precisely, that you and we must make. first, the need for speed: perhaps things have gone on for too long in the last 10 years without a solution being found. but this speed must be accompanied by another requirement: that of legal security and stability. in the light of this double requirement, ladies and gentlemen, two possibilities must be considered. the first, as called for in the ferber report, would be to draw up a legislative proposal on the basis of the present treaty. in this context, article 308 could be an operational provision, at least in a transitional phase, in connection with article 191 as regards the substance. but - and this is not a restrictive but: it is simply an expression of the concern for legal certainty that i was raising - you know as we do that the use of article 308 is subject, in general, to certain reservations and that it requires, in any case, unanimous agreement after consultation of the european parliament. the status of european political parties, it seems to us, requires an unassailable legal basis. the second possibility, as recommended in the dimitrakopoulos-leinen report and also desired in the letter we received yesterday from the president of the commission, mrs schreyer, the leaders of the five major european parties and myself, would be to amend article 191 in the context of the intergovernmental conference, which would probably offer greater legal certainty. ladies and gentlemen, mr president, having said all that, i would like to confirm, in order to answer your question precisely, that the commission is ready to act. she'll take responsibility. so she's going to take the initiative. we shall do so immediately, taking the opportunity of the first trilogue to come to discuss and find the best approach which will actually bring the three institutions together. we shall do so in the light of the discussion which will take place in july, working and exploiting the best possible legal combination of articles 308 and 191.

- question no 11 by mrs maría izquierdo rojo (h-0462/00) subject: effective action against the death boats in the strait of gibraltar the policy of curbing immigration and closing the strait of gibraltar area, financed with european aid, is grossly misguided, as the andalusian government and the ombudsman have publicly pointed out. does the council not think that, in order to make this action effective, an agreement should be concluded with morocco to combat the mafias operating in the region and that effective surveillance measures should be adopted, for example the use of observation boats, to prevent those who swim across the strait from dying in the attempt and to ensure that the planned investments in northern morocco are carried out?
counsel. - (pt) the question put by the honourable member relates to the council's action: firstly, with regard to the controls carried out by the member states at the external maritime borders and, secondly, with regard to the measures which can be taken in the country of origin to prevent illegal immigration and to combat the activities of smugglers. measures to strengthen the effectiveness of controls carried out by member states at external, air and sea borders have been applied mainly in the schengen framework; they are now part of the acquis of the european union, since the entry into force of the treaty of amsterdam. although these measures are taken by the member states, the council, through its competent bodies, monitors their effective application. for example, on the basis of the decision of the schengen executive committee of 18 december 1998 on the coordinated use of document consultants, measures to combat illegal emigration by air and sea are being implemented in collaboration with the various african countries. in addition, a 1999 decision of the schengen executive committee approves a mutual assistance project concerning the exchange of liaison officers for assistance and advice in the performance of security and control missions at the external borders. beyond the schengen acquis, similar practical measures are also taken on behalf of the european union, broadly based on the previous acquis of the european union, in particular the common position of 25 october 1996, from which the assistance and information missions upstream of the border derive. however, these measures will be coordinated within the relevant council bodies and do not currently cover any african country. as regards the root causes of flight and emigration in certain african countries, we refer to the action plan for morocco, approved by the council in october 1999. this action plan is part of a set of five action plans, each covering a comprehensive and coherent approach focusing on the situation in a country of origin or transit of asylum seekers, which has been identified as significant. for each selected country, the action plans present a balanced combination of the different opportunities offered by the european union in the fields of foreign affairs, development, humanitarian and economic aid. in the action plan for morocco, which specifically concerns the situation referred to by the honourable member, morocco was considered as a country of origin and transit for economic migration to european countries. the measures in this action plan include recommendations to build on existing channels and improve data collection, disseminate accurate information on immigration, develop strategies to combat illicit trafficking and promote measures to implement readmission agreements. it also recommends promoting foreign direct investment and vocational training, including for small businesses, and encouraging the voluntary return and reintegration of moroccans living in eu countries. in signing the action plans drawn up by the high level group, the tampere european council of 15 october 1999 recognised that the european union - this is an important point - does not yet have a comprehensive approach to the phenomenon of immigration, covering political issues, human rights and the development of countries and regions of origin and transit. this will require fighting poverty and improving living conditions and employment opportunities, preventing conflict and strengthening democratic states. we therefore call for greater coherence between the union's internal and external policies within the respective competences of both the union and the member states. partnership with third countries is also an essential element of the success of this policy. the union is well aware that the implementation of the morocco action plan will require partnership and cooperation with the moroccan authorities. to this end, a mission visited morocco in june last year, before the action plan was finalised, to establish a dialogue with the moroccan authorities. it is now planned to carry out another mission of the same type at the end of this month to engage in concrete discussions with the moroccan partners. as i said, the european union's policy also covers development as well as humanitarian and economic aid in morocco. the implementation of the action plan for morocco is obviously a long-term strategy, but it is on the basis of the dialogue initiated in this context and also in that of the association council that progress can be made in this area.
- (es) i understand, after this long reply, which i have not fully understood, that the council is maintaining a goodwill attitude towards this extremely serious problem. given the inconsistency of the european union in devoting more resources, for example, to the control of driftnets or the control of fisheries and paying more attention to their efficiency than to the control of vessels, i would like to ask the president-in-office of the council whether he does not think that there should be a regular assessment of the situation in the strait of gibraltar and a report on any progress in this area. i think you've been very clear. your answer was long, but it hid the cruel lack of efficiency. by using means of controlling vessels in the strait, the european union, together with morocco, would put an end to this loss of human life, which already amounts to over a thousand and for which we are responsible. the immigration observatory is just a media thing, an anecdote. mr president-in-office of the council, would you not be in favour of having a regular evaluation?
- (pt) madam president, first of all i would like to say that i agree with your reading: this is a very serious situation, a human tragedy of every day to which we must pay attention. the spanish authorities have been in contact with the moroccan authorities on this matter and the prime minister, mr aznar, recently had a meeting with the moroccan prime minister on this matter. the development of the north zone is being considered as a way of mitigating this situation and the deterioration of the economic conditions which favour these flows. as regards the possibility of having a periodic quantitative assessment of incidents, i believe that the spanish authorities will be able to provide the necessary information in this respect. i also believe that, in the spanish domestic context, this information is known and that the spanish authorities have this type of information. what i wanted to explain to the honourable member - and that is why i went into detail in my explanation - is that the measures taken by the european union in this area, or indeed those it is taking, are long-term measures which obviously do not provide immediate answers to a specific situation, but are measures which act upstream of the situation, that is to say on the creation of the conditions necessary for the fixing and retention of moroccan citizens on their territory. these are development measures which are in keeping with the spirit of the euro-mediterranean partnership. i understand that the honourable member feels that the practical effect of such measures is limited in the short term. we should all know that the european union has a set of policies which it wants to put into practice and which reflect strategic options. these options cannot be systematically penalized by some careful action, whatever the humanitarian repercussions of such situations may be. we must know that it is now up to the spanish authorities, in their bilateral relations with morocco, to solve part of the problem. the european union is involved in a whole range of projects in its relations with the countries of the southern mediterranean concerned by development projects, projects to settle populations and to guarantee better economic conditions. we cannot make the european union into a kind of technical mechanism responsible for finding practical solutions to specific situations.
- question no 12 by mr per gahrton (h-0466/00) subject: decision on the use of the edu military force in the context of the decision to strengthen the eu's capacity to manage crises, the question of the legal basis for the use of the eu military force arose. the swedish government's interpretation of the decisions taken in cologne in 1999 requires a decision by the un security council to this effect. in these circumstances, would the council indicate where and when it took a formal decision that eu military forces can only be called upon on the basis of a decision by the un security council?
- (pt) i would simply say this: these military capabilities, this capacity for intervention by the european union and this extension of the framework for action are provided for by the treaty of amsterdam, which entered into force in may last year. these questions have been raised only since then.
the forthcoming export of p-90 revolvers to mexico proves, once again, that belgium does not look too closely at this when it comes to human rights. gross violations of human rights continue to be observed in mexico after the chiapas revolt: torture, arbitrary arrests, "disappearances", etc. the european code of conduct on arms exports, adopted on 8 june 1998, prohibits the export of arms to countries where such weapons are likely to be used in internal conflict. does the council consider that this arms supply to mexico is in accordance with the european code of conduct? if so, should this code of conduct not be strengthened? if not, what action does the council intend to take in this case with regard to the member state concerned, namely belgium?

- doc. a5-0133/2000 by mr marset campos, on behalf of the committee on foreign affairs, human rights, common security and defence policy, on the communication from the commission to the council and the european parliament on a community action plan for the reconstruction of central america (com (1999) 201 - c5-0111/99 - 1999/2114 (cos))
the rapporteur. - (es) mr president, hurricane mitch devastated central america (honduras, nicaragua, el salvador and guatemala) in 1998, killing nearly 20 000 people and causing losses of over 5 billion euros (10% of the gdp of these countries, which are themselves faced with the perennial problem of external debt). it has destroyed crops, housing and infrastructure of all kinds, mortgaging the future of their populations. the response of european solidarity, linked to the stockholm conference, was immediate and important and is reinforced by the proposal of the european parliament, on the initiative of the commission, which we are now examining. i would like to emphasize four points. the first is that we are partly responsible for these disasters. the link between our economic activity and the increase in pollution, the greenhouse effect and the initiation of climate change, calls for us to ratify immediately the kyoto protocols on the reduction of emissions of the gases which cause this effect. in addition, our uneven development model is plunging these countries into poverty and debt. it is paradoxical to advise the reconstruction of central america in an environmentally friendly manner, according to the model of sustainable development, without changing the economic relations with these countries. the second point concerns the overall objective of our solidarity action. the commission's proposal to concentrate its action on two areas, namely health and education, is a sensible one. but it needs to be given more ambition, to allow for the coordination and integration of all the different initiatives in the region. this will require a substantial increase in our staff, a measure which parliament supports. this action will allow for synergy between the various forms of aid and ensure that the effort made is not limited to reconstruction - otherwise nothing would change - but that it is transformed into an opportunity for regional integration, harmonious and sustainable development, thus creating wealth and general welfare, and for the consolidation of the democratization of those countries which have just ended years of violence and conflict. in this connection, two facts raise our concern. the threat of hostilities between nicaragua and honduras due to border disputes would call into question the purpose of our aid, and we therefore believe that both countries should submit to the decisions of the international court of justice. in addition, the recent resurgence in guatemala of political kidnappings, such as that of professor mayra angelina gutiérrez, political assassinations, such as that of community leader josé amancio mendoza, or threats against journalists (the prosecutor in charge of the gerardi case or nobel prize winner rigoberta menchú) is a cause for concern. reconstruction assistance must be accompanied by firm and verifiable commitments to guarantee human rights by the guatemalan government. the third point concerns the way in which aid is to be implemented and regional coordination and integration. we believe it is vital that the most dynamic and responsible part of society, the indigenous peoples, be included, that women be fully involved, that social organizations be characterized by their efficiency and solidarity and, finally, that there be no partisan use or fraud in the management of our aid. improving the efficiency of the european union also means our official participation in the stockholm monitoring group. the fourth and last point is the most important at the moment: the amount of aid. although it is considerable, we believe that the amount indicated by the commission, namely eur 250 million, is insufficient, in view of the scale of the disaster and the slow pace of recovery. the european parliament is therefore calling for a substantial increase. the news that has appeared in the press today indicating that the commission intends to reduce all european union aid, including aid to latin america, in order to meet its commitments in kosovo is worrying. we believe that such a foolishness cannot be committed, since europe represents an important hope for latin america to overcome its underdevelopment and free itself from the heavy yoke imposed on it by the north. the european parliament had already agreed that no action could be taken to reduce aid to the rest of the world. we therefore continue to regard this as a crucial point. our conduct would make the rest of the arrangements, both with the european investment bank and with other financial institutions, important and would encourage the immediate implementation of the approved programmes, all with the presentation of regular reports to the european parliament on the progress and the evaluation of the results achieved. finally, i would like to thank all the members of the committee on foreign affairs, human rights, common security and defence policy and its secretariat, as well as the committee on budgets, the committee on industry, foreign trade, research and energy and the committee on development and cooperation for their valuable and warm collaboration.
the commission has already submitted a proposal for a regulation to the council. - (es) mr president, as the rapporteur, mr marset, has said, and we support his words and report, hurricane mitch is the worst natural disaster in the history of central america. the death toll stands at over 10,000, the number of missing is also close to 10,000 and the number of affected is over two million. the damage to property is estimated at more than 5 billion euros, or 10% of the gross domestic product of central america. a significant part of the socioeconomic infrastructure has been destroyed and production and export capacity has been greatly reduced in the short and medium term. the worst-affected countries, honduras and nicaragua, are the poorest in the region. the devastating impact of the hurricane was fuelled by deforestation and the lack of adequate flood control systems, which once again shows that environmental degradation hits the poorest hardest and highlights the intrinsic link between poverty and environmental degradation. as the commission has pointed out, hurricane mitch will have the effect of substantially reducing the results of the economic recovery effort and investment that the european union has made in this area over the last decade. in april 1999 the commission approved a special action plan with a budget of eur 250 million, which parliament fully supports as it was drafted when it was approved. as regards the model for implementing this programme, the committee on development and cooperation supports the first option proposed by the commission. only if such an option could not be carried out due to lack of human resources could the second option be considered viable, subject to the involvement of highly qualified european experts. as rapporteur for the committee on development and cooperation, i cannot end my speech without once again calling for the cancellation of the external debt of the countries of central america, an initiative which should be tackled by the european union as a whole and in a coordinated manner, and not by some of its member states in individual and specific initiatives. finally, i think it is also necessary to ask that the strategic reconstruction plan include measures to increase the european investment bank's lending to the region.
- (es) mr president, i should like to begin by congratulating the rapporteur, mr marset campos, on his excellent report. this report - and it could not be otherwise - is influenced by the tragic consequences of hurricane mitch. the european parliament, it seems to me that it should be recalled, reacted immediately to the organization of an extraordinary meeting on 4 november 1998, in which the commissioners responsible at the time took part. in its resolution of 19 november, the european parliament set out the terms in which the european union's response to the situation created by hurricane mitch should be expressed. the answer had to be given as quickly as possible, by adopting a strategic plan for the region as soon as possible. i remember the date: 18-19 november 1998. it must be said that this request from the european parliament, at least as regards speed, has not been met, and that is regrettable. the lack of human resources, while an administrative excuse, cannot be used as a pretext for implementing political priorities, especially in the case of the basic needs of the populations of countries that have experienced large-scale disasters. it is not fair to put the responsibility on the budgetary authority. the commission must in any case ensure that resources are appropriately allocated in accordance with the priorities defined. this morning, commissioner, in the debate on the common security and defence policy, i had the opportunity to tell your colleague, mr patten, that i have never hesitated, never have and never will hesitate, far from it, to firmly support the commission in its objective of clarifying and extending its powers. but as other colleagues have pointed out in this debate and as i also had the opportunity to say to mr patten in the budget debate, it is difficult for me to understand how it is that the commission has no difficulty in managing the eur 800 million that the preliminary draft budget for 2001 proposes for the balkans when it has difficulties in managing the eur 250 million that this plan for the reconstruction of central america provides for, spread not over one year but over four. in any case, commissioner, the countries of central america have not pursued a policy of genocide and ethnic cleansing. unlike other regions, they have included a democratic clause in their agreement with the european union as an essential element of the relationship. the countries of central america have embarked on very painful processes of structural adjustment, which have imposed great sacrifices on their societies. they have done their homework in relation to the multilateral institutions and have done what the european union expected of them. mr president, european civil society has already shown how sensitive it is to the tragedy experienced by the peoples of central america. it is time that, in the face of such a catastrophe, our institutions lived up to the expectations of civil society and the circumstances.
- (es) mr president, at this stage of the debate and especially after the excellent report by our friend mr marset, which i fully endorse, i cannot say much more. i would like to stress some of his remarks, however. it is very important to talk about solidarity intervention - we have talked about sensible intervention - concentrated on education and health programmes mainly, as the report itself states, and he also spoke about coordination and the need for staff. for those of you who, like me, were in kosovo just a few days ago, it is necessary to emphasize something that many of the delegation's visitors have said: unlike other interventions, what is most characteristic of the intervention in kosovo is that it was implemented by an integrated and perfectly coordinated management, which improves the effectiveness of our action. i am also, like mr salafranca, strongly opposed to budgetary restrictions and find it difficult to understand how it is that obstacles are imposed on countries like those in central america whose agreements include certain clauses, while they are not imposed in other latitudes. for those of us who, like myself, make solidarity the leitmotif of our political action, solidarity is important, but also the effectiveness, sustainability of programmes and the implementation of policies where we act, because they help latin american friendly societies to achieve higher levels of development and social justice. i would like to conclude, mr president, by quoting the following words: 'we must be rebellious but also competent'. i transpose it to other concepts: let us be solidarity but effective.
the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i am also grateful for the support and confidence which parliament has shown in the commission in implementing this important community action plan. the eur 250 million regional programme for the reconstruction of central america, spread over a period of four years, will contribute to the reconstruction and transformation of the four countries most devastated by hurricane mitch - honduras, nicaragua, el salvador and guatemala. the programme is based on the principle of sustainable development, as was emphasised by several speakers. it provides assistance in education, vocational training, public health and social housing. the first beneficiaries will be those living in the most deprived rural areas where the consequences of the disaster are most acute. particular attention will be paid to indigenous peoples and to reducing vulnerability to such disasters in the future. the commission is aware that the success of such an ambitious and complex programme also depends on the degree of coordination between the various actors involved. a coordination group between the commission and the member states is being set up. another important element will be the stockholm follow-up group. the commission has always been involved in an informal way in the activities of this group. in order to ensure maximum transparency, the commission will submit an annual report on the progress of the central american reconstruction plan to the member states and to parliament. a first report on the commission's activities was distributed to the parliamentary committee on industry, foreign trade, research and energy. after the first-minute emergency and other aid after mitch's passing, we are now preparing to implement this rebuilding programme. the mobilisation of statutory staff required for the decentralised management and implementation of the programme has certainly delayed the rapid launch of the programme, as has been emphasised by several speakers. those problems have now been solved. the first official will arrive in managua on july 17, the others will arrive in the following weeks. no further delay is to be expected at this stage. the commission shall take all necessary measures to ensure that the programme is in place and operational within three months. i understand the arguments mr salafranca has raised about human resources. as you know, this is not a specific question for this debate. however, you should bear in mind that for the kosovo programme we have set up a special agency. in this programme we have had to make do with the available staff, given the constraints on human resources. let me stress - and i share the view of mr salafranca and other speakers - that the time it has taken to come to the aid of this region is absolutely unacceptable. we have cited this as an example in our proposals for a general reform of our foreign aid programmes. this is one more reason why the commission, and commissioner patten in particular, is determined to push these reforms forward so that we will stop disappointing, and disappointing ourselves, in this way. since this issue has been raised by several speakers, i would like to take this opportunity to ensure that funding for kosovo does not come at the expense of funds for latin america, and certainly not for this programme. additional measures were adopted by the commission as part of the community action plan. these include the european community's contribution to the hipc initiative (for heavily indebted poor countries) and the approval of an improved system of generalised preferences for central america and the council regulation of 21 december 1998 applying a multiannual scheme of generalised tariff preferences, extended until 31 december 2001. in addition, the commission is participating in the hipc initiative, contributing eur 50 million to honduras and nicaragua.

- the next item is the report (a5-0123/2000) by mr schmitt, on behalf of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs, on the commission working document 'towards common standards in asylum procedures' (sec (1999) 271 - c5-0157/1999 - 1999/2148 (cos))
- (es) if i may, mr president, commissioner, rapporteur, i would first like to thank mr schulz. mr schulz, i will tell you from the bottom of my heart what i would like to hear: you have been a good opponent, that is to say a tough opponent, always clear, firm, very often uncomfortable, and there is no doubt that we will miss you. if i may, mr president, i will now get to the heart of the matter. i think this commission document is important because it really opens up a debate, which was envisaged in many previous documents, in particular in the tampere conclusions, but whose content needed to be clarified. there is no doubt that we need to clarify the differences between the asylum procedure, the reception conditions, the interpretation of the definition of the term 'refugee', the links between this asylum procedure and the procedures of the 'dublin mechanism' and other forms of protection, and in this sense the document is perfectly central to the debate. i shall not repeat all the points that have been made by other speakers, but i would like to stress two in particular. firstly, i think the commission is right to link the issues of asylum procedures, which are the subject of a future directive, to the dublin procedure and the notion of safe third countries. i have to say that i was the lead rapporteur on an amendment against the list system. there's a problem with the methodology. fiji was once a safe country, but overnight it was not. if we stick to a closed list system, the difficulties of updating lists will cause great harm. the other amendment i signed is about burden-sharing. we are all aware that the principle of solidarity requires a distribution of the consequences of the current asymmetry in the asylum application. firstly, it must be said on this point that if we achieve a harmonization of asylum procedures, the applications will tend to become homogenized. secondly, i would like to highlight one of the qualities of this report among others - although i was critical on some points, i did in fact put a lot of emphasis on legal certainty, on procedural guarantees, on the right of defence of the asylum seeker and in particular on everything that is set out in point 4 and, of course, everything that concerns access to legal counsel and the possibility of contacting ngos or unhcr. of course, this is not compatible with certain quota measures, which have an image very closely linked to deportation. that is why, mr president, i hope that certain groups, and in particular the ppe group, will reconsider this amendment, which is a literal copy of an amendment by the green group. this amendment is therefore not of a conservative or other origin, it is not of a geographical origin. it takes up an amendment by the green group which was not approved in committee and which i think should be supported by the house.
the commission is aware of the difficulties facing the community in the field of the internal market. i would like to congratulate the two rapporteurs, mr schmitt and mrs echerer, on their excellent reports. i would ask you to convey my best wishes to mr schulz, who is no longer here. i am sure he will return to this debate, if not out of duty, at least out of enthusiasm. the commission has already received feedback on this working document from several member states, many ngos, and will be in a position, with parliament's report, to fulfil one of the commitments of the scoreboard, which is to present a directive on minimum standards for asylum procedures. i intend to present a proposal for a directive in the autumn of 2000. i would remind parliament that the commission proposed to the tampere european council that a common european asylum system be adopted. but the tampere european council opted for an approach based on common minimum standards. the directive is therefore, in my view, the most useful instrument for addressing the issue of minimum standards for asylum procedures which should reflect the pillars of the european union's asylum policy as defined by the tampere european council: absolute respect for the right to seek asylum, full application of the provisions of the geneva convention on the status of refugees and the maintenance of the principle of non-refoulement. the commission welcomes the european parliament's approach to many parts of the motion for a resolution. the commission agrees with the recital calling for the conduct of asylum policy to be as fact-based as possible. we fully agree with parliament that common standards for asylum procedures should not only be based on the principle that administrative and judicial activities should be speeded up, but should also be based on the need to preserve the dignity of asylum seekers. we must recognize that finding a balanced solution between simplifying procedures on the one hand and guaranteeing legal certainty and respect for the rights of asylum seekers on the other is not an easy task. but we are determined to find a solution that can be widely regarded as balanced. the commission shares the view of the european parliament that the issues of entry of asylum seekers, immigration for economic or other reasons and the temporary admission of displaced persons and refugees in the event of a large influx must be dealt with quite separately. the resolution calls for temporary protection within three years. on 24 may 2000, the commission adopted a council directive on minimum standards for the provision of temporary protection in the event of a mass influx of displaced persons and on measures to ensure a balance between the efforts of member states to receive such persons and the consequences of such reception. we have already sent such a proposal to the european parliament for consultation. i would say that this proposal on temporary protection explicitly addresses the issue raised by several speakers on burden sharing, as we have taken an approach to this problem in the proposal for a european refugee fund which we have already submitted to the council. i would therefore like to stress that this proposal cannot be considered separately from the other proposals already on the table which take into account the sensitive issue of solidarity between member states. i would remind parliament that as far as asylum is concerned, the scoreboard that has been presented reflects the conclusions of the tampere summit where a two-step approach was adopted by the heads of state and government. the first step is to harmonize the standards for asylum and protection, the second step is to introduce a common asylum procedure as such. in order to complete the first stage, the commission will not only present a proposal for a directive on common standards for fair and efficient asylum procedures, which we are now discussing, but will also, among other things and as soon as possible, table proposals on the determination of the state responsible for examining an asylum application and on common minimum conditions for the reception of asylum seekers. i would remind parliament that, as i have already said, we have already submitted a working document for consultation by the member states, the aim of which is to replace the dublin convention by a community regulation, bearing in mind the practical experience of the application of the dublin convention with all its shortcomings and imperfections. as regards the second stage, the tampere conclusions called on the commission to present a communication on a common asylum procedure and a uniform status for those granted asylum, valid throughout the union. i intend to present this communication by the end of the year 2000. the commission notes - as has been pointed out by several speakers - that in this resolution the european parliament has opted for a general position on the rationalisation of community law on asylum matters. the commission will not only study the resolution very carefully in preparation for its proposal for a directive on common standards for asylum procedures - which, i repeat, will be presented in the autumn of this year - but will also reflect on them in preparing the communication it will present by the end of the year on a long-term common asylum procedure. i am encouraged that this communication has such broad support in this parliament. with such a commitment from the commission and parliament, i sincerely hope that we will succeed.

commission. - mr president, i should like to start by referring to the speech by mrs cederschiöld. traditionally, victim protection has been seen as primarily concerned with compensation for victims. approach considers that the issue of victims also involves work on prevention, information, assistance and the status of victims in criminal proceedings. i would like to stress that the tampere european council endorsed this broad approach. it therefore said that it was in the union's interest to adopt minimum standards for the protection of victims of crime, in particular as regards access to justice for victims and their right to redress, including reimbursement of legal costs. it is not just a question of addressing this issue at european level, but the tampere council also advocates the establishment of national programmes to finance both public and non-governmental measures to assist and protect victims. the commission therefore welcomes the excellent report by mrs sörensen, whom i congratulate. we are fully prepared to work along the broad lines set out in this report. the commission fully agrees with the approach concerning the need to develop networks of assistance to victims, and in particular linguistic assistance. we also share the rapporteur's concern about the special attention that certain categories of victims deserve, such as foreigners, minors, victims of sexual assault or trafficking in human beings and victims of terrorist acts. it is also important to improve the training of staff who may be in contact with 'these' victims. finally, parliament provides for the development of all the mechanisms for assisting victims, for facilitating the participation in criminal proceedings of victims who are geographically distant by the implementation of systems of written and video testimony and for the development of separate waiting rooms for victims to enable them to avoid encounters with the offender as much as possible. but we are already working beyond this framework decision. as mrs sörensen has also pointed out, the commission is keen to use all the instruments available under the treaty to strengthen the protection of victims, and i am referring to articles 65 and 66 of the ec treaty and article 31 (e) of the treaty on european union. the commission considers that measures concerning the provision of assistance to victims, i.e. the standards to which assistance services may be subject, the setting up of victim support hotlines, all matters relating to information and linguistic support for victims of crime, should be regulated by instruments falling within the first pillar. the same applies to the mechanisms for the intervention of any compensation funds as regards common rules, eligibility conditions for the funds, the possibility of advances, the link with insurance systems and cooperation between national victims' compensation funds. we are already developing contacts with the future swedish presidency, which will organise, with the support of the grotius programme, a specific seminar on the question of compensation mechanisms in the autumn of this year. the commission has also decided to examine the feasibility of setting up a european victim support system in the form of a multilingual free-of-charge telephone service. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of the health of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos at work is a welcome step towards the creation of a european health insurance system. as i have already explained on several occasions, 2004 is the deadline imposed on us by the vienna action plan of 1998. nevertheless, as you can see, the commission is already working on this important subject for the citizens of europe and i hope that we will have concrete conclusions even before 2004.

the rapporteur. - (es) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, as you all know, the cohesion fund was set up to contribute to economic and social cohesion and at the same time to reduce regional and social disparities, within the framework of solidarity between the member states. the fund has enabled many countries in the european union to try to close the gap between them and the richer countries, and they have achieved results that can be described as spectacular but also insufficient. per capita income has risen from two thirds to three quarters of the community average and the contribution of european funds to growth in each of these four countries has been on average 0.5% per annum. however, two problems which are likely to arise in the future can be mentioned at present. firstly, with the integration of new countries, the current beneficiaries of the cohesion fund, who have not achieved the objectives of real convergence, may no longer be eligible for the fund. here we must have a series of programmes to help the new members to achieve convergence with the european union and at the same time the four beneficiary countries must continue to have these funds at their disposal if they are to achieve the objectives of real convergence, growth and full employment. the second problem is the temptation of some of the richest countries to penalize those countries which, receiving aid from the cohesion fund, have achieved nominal convergence through serious, responsible, solidary and rigorous structural and economic policies, but of course without yet achieving real convergence, by removing them from the cohesion fund, which could lead to two scenarios for these four countries. the first is the encouragement of lax and inflationary policies in order not to lose these funds, the second is the suspension by some of them of growth and convergence with the other countries of the union. that is why, commissioner, we should distinguish between real convergence and nominal convergence. finally, i would like to make a number of recommendations concerning the cohesion fund. first, it would be good to invest more in railways, ports and maritime transport. secondly, priority should be given to transport to integrate peripheral territories, islands and isolated regions. thirdly, greater attention must be paid to sustainable transport. fourthly, more action is needed in the field of reforestation and soil restoration. fifthly, the problem of waste and solid waste management must be tackled. sixthly, as we have said before, more investment in urban centres is needed. i would add that four amendments will be tabled tomorrow in plenary, two approved in committee and two new ones. i think - and i have explained the reasons in committee - that they should not be accepted, because in the main they simply set new criteria. we are talking about the cohesion fund and the 1998 balance sheet, on which there is a regulation and criteria already approved for the period 2000-06, and we do not think that the time has come to change the criteria concerning the eligibility and distribution of these funds.
