make available to the commission data on the transactions constituting payments and receipts under the eaggf guarantee section. however, it only requires that such information be transmitted to the commission on request and exclusively in the context of the clearance of accounts for the preparation of on-the-spot checks. this situation creates various constraints for control. effective management must enable the institutions responsible to provide analysis and decision-making tools, in particular the cost-effectiveness index. this approach must be applied systematically and must be based on an analysis of the payments corresponding to each regulation. the fact that this information is currently linked to the clearance of accounts process places a time constraint on the availability of information essential for management and control. once the clearance of accounts for the preparation of on-the-spot checks is completed, any possibility of management analysis or control action is lost. but in addition to these checks linked to the clearance of accounts, effective control requires other types of checks, for example, by cross-checking the different information available. to overcome these shortcomings, it has been proposed to use the information available under regulation (ec) no 2390/1999 in the integrated management system mentioned above, which mr casaca - oral question (b5-0491/2000) by mr graefe zu baringdorf, on behalf of the committee on agriculture and rural development, on support measures for nuts and apricots.
- (es) mr president, in the absence of mr graefe zu baringdorf and at his request, i am speaking on behalf of the committee on agriculture and rural development. within the european union, dried fruit production is mainly carried out in arid areas and on steep slopes under dry growing conditions. these productions provide protection against erosion and desertification and act as fire barriers. they are of fundamental importance as a supplementary source of income, essential for the maintenance of a good number of farms in rural areas of disadvantaged areas. moreover, this production forms the basis of a large primary and secondary processing industry, which is essential for the economic diversification of rural areas experiencing difficult conditions. the community's level of self-sufficiency is between 50 and 60%. community production is faced with competition from third country producers, whose costs are much lower, and with very limited customs protection. for example, in the case of hazelnuts, the production costs in the european union are three times higher than in turkey because of differences in labour costs. in the case of almonds, the difference in cost is due to the fact that production within the european union is carried out in areas with very difficult climatic and soil conditions. customs protection is very low and is being phased out as a result of negotiations within the world trade organisation and other preferential agreements. it is clear that the commission cannot ignore that when it enters into trade negotiations, its concessions have consequences which sometimes end up being negative. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the effects of the trade concessions granted by the commission are not unduly damaged. although the measures laid down in regulation (eec) no 789/89 have had positive results, they have not succeeded in balancing production costs against prices in a market subject to extremely high pressure from low-priced imports. the problem is that the aid granted to these productions is coming to an end, while the harsh production conditions have not changed and competition from third country productions has increased. on the contrary, the customs duties on almonds, for example, will be reduced again next month, as they will be raised from 4.1% to 3.5%, and there is a quota of 90 000 tonnes at 2%. in addition, us exports to certain third countries enjoy preferential agreements which the european union does not have. in fact, over the past ten years, the price has remained the same. the customs duty on hazelnuts is 3.3%. however, a reduced rate of 3% is applied to goods from turkey. the pressure of imports is such that the price difference between the superior and the ordinary varieties is getting smaller every day, which has a devastating effect. the difficult growing conditions in the european union prevent our products from competing with those of third countries and it is impossible to improve competitiveness unless we abandon the current production areas and choose others. this would entail significant environmental damage, serious risks of depopulation and serious problems in terms of land management. that is why, commissioner, the committee on agriculture has tabled the oral question which has given rise to this debate. the diagnosis of the problem in the area of community dried fruit production needs is fairly well known, as is shown by the agreement of all the political groups in this house on the resolution they have tabled. import pressure and difficult climatic and soil conditions therefore require aid for community dried fruit production. the committee on agriculture, in the resolutions tabled unanimously by the political groups, echoes the conclusions of the recent hearing of the dried fruit sector before the committee on agriculture and, in a way, takes up and accepts the demands made today by the sector, with great concern and great anxiety, as the commissioner knows. these concerns and demands, which we have echoed in the committee on agriculture and the political groups in the european parliament, are aimed at finding a solution providing for direct income support for producers in order to prevent environmental damage through the conservation of crops, to avoid depopulation and to preserve primary and secondary processing industries in less-favoured areas. but on the other hand, and this is the element which is causing great concern in the sector at the moment - the measures foreseen for this sector are coming to an end in the next few days - it is absolutely necessary that the aid be extended until a new system or a new support scheme is put in place.

- question no 3 by roy perry (h-0525/00) subject: digital radio does the council agree that political support for digital radio, similar to that enjoyed by mobile phone technology and digital television, could help to build confidence in the future of radio?
council. - i would remind you that digital audio broadcasting has been in existence since 1989 and that the main problem still to be solved is that the receivers are still expensive. one of the main issues which the council, which has an open mind, will have to examine in due course is the definition of certain principles designed to enhance the readability and efficiency of this area of electronic communications. the issue of convergence between telecommunications, media and information technology was raised at a council meeting at the end of 1999 and in a public debate on 2 may 2000. the council emphasised the following principles: regulation should be based on clearly defined policy objectives, stimulate economic growth and competitiveness and ensure general interest objectives. the regulation should also aim at technological neutrality, with rules on communication services being as independent as possible of the technology used to provide these services. on 2 may 2000, the council stressed the importance of striking a balance between legal certainty, mainly guaranteed by binding provisions, and the ability to react quickly to technological and market developments, through flexible measures. i repeat, the council's attitude is open-minded.
- question no 4 by john walls cushnahan (h-0531/00) subject: agreement between the european union and china in connection with the wto is the council aware that china has ordered state television, newspapers and billboard owners to stop running the sprite advertisement featuring the popular young star sherry chang huei-mei, who sang at the inauguration of president chen shui-bain? is the council also aware that the chinese authorities have recently asked companies in hong kong and mainland china not to do business with taiwanese companies which they consider to be pro-independence? given the recent agreement with china for its accession to the wto, how does the council intend to react to the use of this type of political blackmail, which is contrary to the principles of free trade?
council. - the council has long been committed to improving the human rights situation in china, including civil and political rights, which are seriously affected by events such as those reported by the honourable member. the most significant aspect of this commitment is the dialogue that the european union has initiated with china on human rights. despite some progress towards improving the legal system of economic and social rights, little progress has been made on the ground, particularly with regard to civil and political rights. the council is therefore deeply concerned at the persistent and widespread restriction of fundamental freedoms, including freedom of assembly, expression and association. it was agreed that the european union would continue to express publicly its concern about the human rights situation in china and raise this issue in meetings with china at all levels. in these circumstances, the council agreed that the european union would take a firm position on the draft resolution on the human rights situation in china, presented by the united states at the 56th session of the united nations commission on human rights. the council agreed that if the draft resolution on china were put to the vote, the member states in this committee would vote in favour. finally, the draft resolution was not put to the vote, following the adoption of a non-intervention motion, initiated by china. the council further agreed that its approach at the next session of the hrc would be based on the results of the dialogue on the human rights situation in china. with regard to the process leading to china's accession to the wto, the council considers that it is not the appropriate forum for addressing human rights issues and, in this regard, also considers that increased trade would support the european union's efforts to ensure respect for human rights, democracy and the rule of law, all of which are founding values of europe.

not use five languages. i will reply that the community patent is designed in such a way that it is the european patent office which will grant the patent valid throughout the community. the commission has therefore decided not to change the procedure. the community patent is distinctive from the european patent in that it will be valid throughout the community and will have its own court to settle disputes concerning it. but the european patent office will continue to work as it does now, until the patent is granted. let me stress that the european patent office is not a community agency. there is a european patent convention to which 15 member states and a number of other states have subscribed. the commission cannot therefore dictate to the european patent office its policy on language matters. i would therefore respond to mr de clercq's suggestion that the office should become an agency of the european union by saying that the european union should become a signatory to the convention and negotiate this possibility, but it is no longer realistic to expect the european patent office to become an agency of the union. the penultimate point raised by mr de clercq concerned the codecision procedure. nothing changes at this level. the european parliament will therefore continue to play its role when it comes to examining the commission's tasks and objectives at the time of the final decision this autumn. finally, the enlargement. after enlargement, the union will be larger, this is not a scoop, and the community patent will apply to the new countries that have become members of the european union. this is the only way to keep a community patent. i repeat, the other two possibilities will continue to coexist. there will therefore always be a polish national patent and a european patent which may concern poland, if the applicant so wishes. i hope that a large number of experts in the business and research world in europe will encourage the transition from the european patent to the community patent in order to improve the competitiveness of the european union as much as possible.
thank you very much, mr bolkestein, for your answers. the commission communication and the debate are closed.

commission. - i share your view that the question of having an encryption strategy at community level is crucial to strengthening the security of internet use. but, as you can imagine, in this area we must respect the principle of subsidiarity, in the sense that we must recognize that each member state has the power to adopt its own national legislation to ensure that the legislation is complied with at national level. the commission's role is to coordinate at community level the efforts made to ensure the application of the law. the aim is to guarantee a common minimum level of enforcement, but member states remain free to introduce stricter legislation or national legislation. in doing so, the comparison of national legislation would be useful to us when the time comes to adopt common rules at community level. it is not possible to do so at the moment because some member states, including the united kingdom, have not yet completed the compilation of their legislation. the national parliaments have therefore not yet been able to adopt it.

the 'petersberg principles' as defined in the amsterdam treaty. as was the case with the incorporation of these principles into the treaty a few years ago, the recent development has been possible only with the full and active support of all member states. at this stage it is too early to say whether further adjustments will be necessary in this area. so far there has been no formal debate on the defence dimension of the european union. according to the presidency report submitted to feira, it would be possible to implement the cologne and helsinki conclusions without the legal need to question no 35 by mr camilo nogueira román (h-0523/00) subject: principle of additionality on 12 april 2000, the european parliament adopted a resolution on the principle of additionality as an essential element in the implementation of the structural funds. is the commission aware of any situation where this principle has been applied by a member state?
mr president, i would like to ask the commissioner whether he has not already made a statement on the question of the financial impact of the structural funds on the community's economy. mr nogueira román, i am very attentive to the information we ask for and receive from the member states on this matter. i should like to say that so far the commission has not found that a member state has failed to comply with the principle of additionality in the implementation of the structural funds, as defined in the general regulation, particularly since berlin. i do not think that the commission has any right to interfere in the work of the council, but i do think that it is important that the council should be able to intervene in the work of the council. in view of these difficulties, and in order to resolve them, the council, on a proposal from the commission, wanted to simplify the control and exercise of additionality, both in terms of certain methodological rules and in terms of the timetable for monitoring additionality for the new programming which starts this year and continues until 2006. mr nogueira román, the verification of additionality is thus carried out only three times during the period, instead of once a year. it is also in this spirit that a certain flexibility is left to each member state to set the starting point for average expenditure between 1994 and 1999. at this stage, the ex ante verification of additionality, which is prior to the adoption of the programming documents for 2000-06, seems to me, i can tell you objectively, satisfactory. but that does not prevent us from being vigilant, from asking questions and from recalling, as i have done in the case of several governments, the attention i continue to pay to the reality of this additionality. most member states have submitted the appropriate information, including information on financing. the latter generally indicate not only the maintenance of their own public structural expenditure, but in the majority of cases an average and significant increase in this expenditure between 2000 and 2006.
- (pt) mr commissioner, thank you for your reply. as you have understood, my question, in so far as it was based on the moral conviction that many states - and very concretely, i am sure the spanish state is one of them - do not respect the principle of additionality, contained a rhetorical part intended to motivate your answer. in any event, since it is obvious that failure to respect the principle of additionality has very serious negative consequences for countries with low economic development and high unemployment, i would like to ask whether you are prepared to put into practice the new conceptual and political-administrative instruments which are necessary to prevent, with all the force of law, a practice which actually undermines the application of community funds and the very objectives of social and territorial cohesion of the european union which are your responsibility as a member of the college of commissioners?
commission - mr nogueira román, you are targeting your question specifically at the countries or regions which are experiencing the greatest difficulties. i would also like to point out that many of the countries with the greatest development delays benefit not only from regional policy funds but also from the cohesion funds. the fact is, mr nogueira román, and i have a text to respect, that the cohesion fund is not subject to the provisions on additionality. it is not subject to this principle because i think it is necessary to recall that the cohesion fund was and remains to help the least developed member states to reduce their deficits and, in many cases, to facilitate their accession to monetary union. that's part of the answer. now you ask me to ask me, with the general rules i have at my disposal, to actually enforce this principle of additionality. i must admit that there is a weak point in the regulation concerning possible sanctions for a country which does not respect this principle. that is why i put so much energy, in a preventive way, when we approve the community support frameworks, when we approve the spds, when i meet the ministers who come to see me, or i will see them on the ground, almost every week in a region of europe, to say my commitment to a few principles. the question of additionality, the question of partnership, the respect of the major policies - we shall discuss this with mrs frassoni later - the respect of the major european policies, particularly in the field of the environment. what is true is that the general regulation on the structural funds does not provide for specific sanctions for member states which do not respect this additionality. however, the commission, in accordance with article 11 of the general regulation, makes and will make the approval of the community support frameworks, the spds 2000-06 and the approval of the mid-term reprogramming conditional on the transmission to our services of information on this additionality and on compliance by the member states. i'm telling you straight up. i have recognized a certain weakness in terms of sanctions for those who do not respect additionality. i am particularly pedagogical, vigilant, at the moment, and everyone will have an extremely precise meeting halfway through, i can assure you.
commission - mr. maccormick, i appreciate your insistence on this point. ladies and gentlemen, what you should expect from a commissioner is that he should implement the policy you want and that he should respect the texts and regulations which have been laid down by you and the council. in this particular case, i said "a weakness". when i say "weaknesses", mr. nogueira, mr. maccormick, i don't mean to see them and sit back and say, "that's the way it is, there's nothing to be done". i'm not a fatalist. i shall therefore endeavour, when we begin to prepare the new regional policy for 2006 and 2013, to take account of these weaknesses and to make proposals. there is probably something else to be reviewed, which mr maccormick has pointed out: that is that, both for objective 1 and for objective 2, we must verify, and we can only verify, the reality of this principle of additionality at national level. and that's where the problem lies. it is possible to see that the principle is respected at national level and, at the same time, to see that it is not respected in a region which needs it. that is what mr maccormick has emphasized. i am again showing vigilance, as i have done in particular with regard to the united kingdom: i ask questions, i draw attention to this or that case which has been brought to my attention, as you have done, mr president. however, i must also say that the rules do not allow me to give instructions on this particular point. i can only demonstrate this concern for dialogue and i am available, in the case you have indicated to me as in others, to demonstrate it as actively as possible, while respecting the general regulation on the structural funds.

the commission is not prepared to accept the amendments tabled by the committee on economic and monetary affairs and industrial policy, which are not in line with the commission's proposals. this would require considerable financial resources. it is quite clear that the problem must be addressed at national, regional and local level. however, if the member states were to express the wish to do so, we would clearly have no objection to doing this work. i think we are already doing that when we see the need. at the moment, for example, following the accident at baia mare, we are trying to identify hot spots and see which dangerous sites really need to be monitored to prevent further accidents. but as far as the clean-up itself is concerned, i think the principle of subsidiarity should be applied.

the rapporteur. - (es) mr president, commissioner wallström, we thank you for being here at this hour, ladies and gentlemen. of all the environmental issues, the system of co-management and environmental audits is not exactly a very popular topic, but it is a fantastic tool for making progress in the integration of economic activities and environmental protection. by adopting an environmental management system, companies - whether industrial or service - learn to integrate the environmental factor into the ordinary management of society, discovering the many and important benefits, not only environmental but also economic, that this brings them, among other things, because they improve their competitive position. i therefore believe that the current revision of this regulation and the incorporation of new elements which are extremely useful for the environmental improvement of processes, services and products is very important. the main objectives of the amendments, which i took over from parliament's first reading and which were unanimously approved in the environment committee, are to create more incentives for european companies to access the system, to involve stakeholders - particularly workers - to increase reliability vis-à-vis third parties and to improve the transparency of information. however, the committee also approved certain amendments contrary to the rapporteur's opinion, on which i continued to maintain a negative position. i am referring to amendments nos 5, 6, 10 and 17, which deal with a controversial issue, namely the use of the best available technology as an instrument for improving the environment required of companies wishing to register with emas. it should be recalled that emas is a voluntary market instrument; recall also that one of the fundamental objectives of the current revision of this regulation is to make the system more accessible to small and medium-sized enterprises and also to the service sector; the commission has also been asked to provide a report on the implementation of the new emas standard, which is being prepared by the european commission. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's environmental policy is not distorted by the introduction of new technologies. so i think you will agree with me that, whilst i am absolutely in favour of the development and progress of the integrated pollution control (ippc) directive, this is not the right time and emas is not the right instrument to require the application of the best available technologies for companies wishing to join the system. in fact, large installations, as stipulated in the ippc directive, will have to be registered in the emas register, because they will have to comply with the existing environmental legislation - amendment no 12 - which logically includes compliance with the ippc directive in the case where this affects companies. i would also like to stress amendments nos 41 and 50, which my group would be prepared to accept on condition that it is clear that the word 'representatives' refers to the persons elected as such in each undertaking and in no case to the organisations, whose participation would complicate and delay the process of adopting the system. i hope that tomorrow other groups will be able to table an oral amendment to that effect. there are two other amendments on which i would like to comment: amendment no 19, for which i have asked for a split vote down to the paragraph on 'public structures and public contracts', leaving the commission's text until then. i think that the commission is preparing - and in this respect a comment from mrs wallström would be welcome - a proposal on the inclusion of the environmental criterion as an objective condition as a selection criterion for public contracts, so i think that it is appropriate to wait for the adoption of the proposal. as regards amendment no 22, concerning the inclusion of the commission, the council and parliament within four years in the emas system, i have consulted the commission in writing and i would like the commissioner to reply. finally, amendment no 25 concerns the harmonisation of emas with the iso standard, a very important aspect for the dissemination of the two tools, the harmonisation agreement of which we welcome.

the agenda calls for the report (a5-0139/2000) by mrs peijs, on behalf of the committee on regional policy, transport and tourism, on the communication from the commission to the council, the european parliament, the economic and social committee and the committee of the regions on the development of short sea shipping in europe: a dynamic alternative in a sustainable transport chain - second biennial progress report (com (99) 317 - c5-0206/1999 - 1999/2164 (cos)). i give the floor to mrs peijs, the rapporteur.
- (es) mr president, on behalf of my colleagues, mr ripoll and mr pérez álvarez, who worked on this report - but who had to be absent - i would like to congratulate the rapporteur, mrs peijs, on her excellent report, especially because it tackles an important problem in a very real and practical way. i would also like to say that i regret two things at the moment: firstly, that i cannot hear what our friend mr fatuzzo thinks about how short sea shipping affects the interests of european pensioners and, secondly, that there are so few members because, thinking about the selfish interests of this house, they will probably regret one day not having heard about the short sea shipping problem, because perhaps we will have to use it one day for our comings and goings in strasbourg. to get to the heart of the matter, i should like to tell mrs peijs that we have followed with great interest the actions and developments which have been undertaken in the european union in recent years, particularly following the establishment of the maritime industries forum, with a view to promoting short sea shipping as an alternative to land transport. the commission report and the rapporteur's report highlight various comparative advantages between the two modes of transport, among which i would highlight, as far as maritime transport is concerned, the reduction in congestion of infrastructure, their lower cost, the reduction in their energy consumption, which implies a reduction in pollutant emissions in, and the improvement of communications with, the peripheral regions of the european union. we believe - and i think we all agree - that the shift of burdens from land to sea should be considered a priority objective of transport policies in the european union. i would like to stress that a series of actions taken in the last two years have had a positive impact on short sea shipping. as the commission report indicates, this has allowed intra-community shipping to grow by 23% between 1990 and 1997. nevertheless, its growth rate is objectively modest - the cumulative annual growth rate is only 3%, and lower than that of land transport, i.e. 26%. as a result, instead of these relative positions between sea and land transport being brought closer together, the difference between the two has continued to increase. there is therefore every indication that more vigorous quantitative measures are needed and that the problem should probably be viewed from a different qualitative perspective. we think mrs peijs' report is very balanced, but we would like to draw attention to one of the key objectives for promoting short sea shipping: the simultaneous reduction of the time and direct cost of port operations of vessels providing this type of service. in many cases, port services - concerning the ship and the goods - are provided without any real competition or with very limited competition, which often leads to abuses of dominant positions, such as the imposition of unnecessary and even unused compulsory services such as pilotage, towing, mooring or port handling, and the payment of very high tariffs. in any event, with a few exceptions, trans-oceanic maritime services do not face competition from road transport and, in most cases, air transport is not a real competitor either. we therefore believe that if we are to promote short sea shipping in a realistic and effective way, it is essential to maintain the current type of provision of port services, improving their efficiency and reducing their costs. nor should we forget their importance for the economy of regions where there is a shipbuilding industry. this implies a revitalization of the whole region, as those who live in these towns and regions know very well, where the shipbuilding industry is a very active part of the local economy.
- (es) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, at a time when we are trying to correct regional disparities, mrs peijs' report, which deals with the problem of short sea shipping and calls on the member states and the commission to adopt measures to promote this type of transport, is very timely. as always, i would like to point out that the union's regional and structural policy is primarily a response to the specific constraints faced by certain european regions, such as the so-called outermost regions. the commission presented a report last march setting out a strategy for their sustainable development, which contains several main aspects, among which it is important to highlight the relations of these regions with their geographical environment, which to a certain extent determines their development. we therefore consider that mrs peijs' report is relevant, especially if it is strengthened by the adoption of my amendment on the inclusion of maritime transport between ports in the outermost regions and the countries in their geographical environment. we could thus correct the mistake made by the commission when it drew up the biennial report on the development of this type of transport on the basis of an incomplete definition of short sea shipping.
commission - mr president, allow me to thank mrs peijs for her excellent report and for the work she has done. the report shows that short sea shipping is a subject on which there is broad agreement between you, the member states and the commission. the commission and this agreement go further. i do not know of anyone or any organisation which does not want to see the development of short sea shipping. in the past we have made the mistake of denigrating short sea shipping. we were talking about its potential, and so we were implying that this sector was not doing well. but he's doing well. although it has been little discussed, short sea shipping is the mode of transport which, in the 1990s, has best withstood the development of road transport. we must therefore recognize the merits of short sea shipping. however, there is always room for improvement, and the shipping industry is the first to recognise this. let me mention a few of the key points in mrs peijs' report. we need a holistic approach to a true door-to-door service concept. it must be fully integrated into the transport chain and offered through one-stop shops. several bottlenecks are hampering the development of short sea shipping. the commission services, the new member states and industry are currently working to identify them and to find potential solutions. one point already identified is the diversity of documents required for short sea shipping. in the interests of uniformity, the commission intends to present, by the end of the year, a proposal to harmonize certain documents required for the departure and arrival of certain vessels. the efficiency of ports is essential for short sea shipping, and the commission will therefore also present by the end of the year a package of measures to increase their efficiency through liberalisation. in addition, it is necessary to renew the outdated image of short sea shipping, which i am very pleased to have already mentioned in the debate. the national offices for the promotion of short sea shipping must play a key role in the implementation of this policy. some promotion offices already exist and the commission encourages the establishment of others in order to create a european promotion network. the question of community subsidies was raised during the debate. i'd like to answer that question. the pact programme - a programme of pilot actions in favour of combined transport - has historically been the main source of community subsidies for short sea shipping. last year, 40% of the pact programme budget, or eur 2.3 million, was allocated to promoting short sea combined transport. this amount will be even higher in 2000, reaching 50% of the total budget of the pact programme. the responsible dg wishes to continue along this path so that a large part of the pact programme budget is again allocated to short sea shipping. it may even be possible that this principle will be an integral part of the legal text in the next revision of the pact. mr. purvis has asked me to convey an invitation to my colleague mrs. de palacio. i won't miss it, and i'm sure mrs. de palacio will enjoy this romantic cruise to scotland. i think the crossing would be even more romantic if you invited me to go with him. mrs peijs, thank you for your work. thank you for making sure we're all moving in the same direction. let us join forces in this effort. i can assure you that the commission will do its best.

- the next item is the report (a5-0178/2000) by mr di lello finuoli, on behalf of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs, on the initiative of the kingdom of denmark with a view to adopting a council framework decision on the fight against serious crime against the environment (5343/2000 - c5-0078/2000 - 2000/0801 (cns)).
- (es) mr president, i would first of all like to congratulate the danish government on taking the initiative to propose the council framework decision we are now discussing, which aims to give us more effective instruments to combat serious environmental offences. we also congratulate the rapporteur, mr di lello finuoli, who, throughout the whole procedure of this initiative, has acted with great clarity and firmness on the principles and values we share, but also with caution and flexibility, which has allowed for a large number of amendments, which bring different nuances. we have therefore come to a final proposal which we consider to be reasonable and ambitious. we were pleased that with this framework decision the european union is supporting the convention on the protection of the environment through criminal law, which was approved by the council of europe in 1998 and has not yet been sufficiently ratified to enter into force. to date, only nine member states have signed it and none have ratified it, which is quite scandalous. my colleague and compatriot carmen cerdeira has put forward ideas and amendments which are now incorporated in the text we are about to vote on. i would like to stress that i agree with it and would like to highlight four aspects which, in my view, have improved the original proposal during the parliamentary process. first, it is recognised that a country may act against offenders when the environmental offence has been committed on its own territory, but also in another country if the latter suffers the consequences. secondly, the same possibility of action is extended to cover offences committed but also attempts which for one reason or another would have had no consequences but which could have led to them. thirdly, this proposal identifies legal persons as responsible, the vast majority of serious environmental offences being committed by legal persons rather than natural persons. fourthly, i would like to stress that the economic and other sanctions imposed for these offences should always be far greater than the profits which these acts may bring to their perpetrators. this will put an end to the fact that, in many cases, crime is not only cheap but also quite simply profitable. this is a document which we hope will have an impact. that is what our commitment must be.
- (es) mr president, i too would like to begin by congratulating the rapporteur, mr di lello finuoli, on his work. i welcome the danish government's initiative, based on the new procedure recognised in the treaty of amsterdam, to examine a matter aimed at improving and strengthening environmental protection at community level, protection which of course cannot have any frontiers within the union. my colleague, mrs thors, has already expressed her favourable opinion on the report and the amendments tabled by the respective committees, so i shall focus on three points. for a while, my task was to ensure that the commission gave proper treatment to european forests, and i saw the difficulties in giving a precise environmental dimension to the diversity of treatments. the first difficulty in actually implementing this proposal is to classify environmental offences in the light of the diversity of the union's territory. the second point is the need to consider the international dimension of the infringement. we have seen that it is difficult to find the real perpetrators of many large-scale environmental attacks, but, in addition, the interplay of legal responsibilities of the entities which, in the end, may appear to be responsible makes the actual criminal prosecution of these attacks extremely difficult. i think this will be a very important mission for the commission. we must avoid diluting the criminal liability. thirdly, mr president, i would just like to say that the community framework for the internal market and justice must be community-oriented and this proposal is proof of that.
- (es) mr president, yesterday we discussed and voted on a report by the committee on petitions. the committee dealt with a thousand complaints from citizens this year. of these one thousand complaints, 40% concern breaches of community environmental law. in analysing these complaints, we have seen the need for the proposal we are considering, the council proposal at the request of the kingdom of denmark, and for the approval of the report by mr di lello finuoli and mrs schörling of the committee on the environment. i think there are three important aspects to this report. first, the request for the signature of the council of europe convention on the protection of the environment, but also for its ratification. no state has ratified the convention to date, and this is not inconsistent with the approval of this report in this house. the report perfectly reproduces the definition of the parameters useful in defining the infringement: repeated breaches of community law, seriousness of the damage and sometimes priority of economic benefits over any other consideration. it seems to us that there is often clear premeditation. in any case, mr president, it exists, even in the context of offences against the environment which appear to be accidental. i remember very well the cases of doñana in spain, or the danube. it was obvious that a body of water containing so many dangerous products near a natural park like doñana could cause an accident at any time. secondly, mr president, i believe that sanctions are essential. there is no doubt about that. other colleagues questioned the need for sanctions. i do not, i even think that the polluter pays principle is biased. sometimes people prefer to pollute and pay a small fine, which is far less than the profits that can be made from these offences. sanctions are therefore essential, they must be dissuasive and proportionate to the damage caused to the lives of citizens. thirdly, we must restore the environment. mr president, in the case of doñana it is inconceivable that the public authorities should be responsible for cleaning up the area and that the company responsible for the damage should have a minimal involvement. the rehabilitation of the affected area is essential. the responsibility of legal persons must be recognised. standards for the recognition of the liability of legal persons exist only in the united kingdom, finland and denmark. finally, mr president, i should like to speak about the cooperation between the states, which is indispensable. the members of the committee on petitions are aware of the terrible frustration of citizens who take the trouble to report environmental crime and who find that in europe we are unable to help them improve the environment in which they live and prevent such crime.
commission - (de) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, with regard to your last request, i can say that i am happy to take note of your appeal to this effect. the commission considers that the kingdom of denmark's initiative for a council framework decision consists essentially of two parts. the first part aims to ensure that any serious and damaging breach of environmental law throughout the community is followed by effective and dissuasive penalties. it sets a minimum standard for the length of sentences. this part, which corresponds in the main to the provisions of a convention voted by the council of europe in november 1998, constitutes the basic demand of this initiative. unfortunately - as has been pointed out on many occasions - this convention has not yet been ratified by any member state, so i can only understand the danish initiative to bring this subject back under community competence. the second part contains regulations to improve cooperation and the exchange of information between the law enforcement agencies and the courts of the member states. there are a number of arguments for dealing with issues of mutual legal assistance and improving cooperation in the field of justice in a comprehensive approach that goes beyond environmental law. the council's working party is therefore currently examining the first part of the initiative - a speaker has already mentioned this - in other words the part concerning substantive criminal law. improving cooperation in criminal matters is already the subject of several initiatives and proposals which go beyond criminal law in environmental matters. the promotion of mutual legal assistance, the exchange of information and other forms of cooperation between the courts and public prosecutor's offices of the member states with a view to creating a genuine area of freedom, security and justice is an essential requirement of the treaty of amsterdam and a general task of the communities. we therefore need very clear, orderly and easy to implement regulations which can be used quickly by anyone involved at legal level. in order to achieve this objective and to avoid legal fragmentation, the commission believes that the rules on mutual legal assistance should be universally recognised. specific regulations, such as those in environmental law, should be the exception only when necessary. it is in this spirit that joint action in 1998 led to the creation of the european judicial network, which has begun its work and is carrying out various activities to facilitate mutual legal assistance and the exchange of information. the commission believes that this type of initiative should of course be further developed. in addition to the existing convention on international law to promote mutual legal assistance and the mutual recognition of judgments, the community must provide for further action in this field. the commission welcomes the first part of the danish initiative. as a legal asset, the environment is not yet protected by criminal law in all member states. while some member states have incorporated certain environmental offences into their criminal law, this is not the case in other member states. a serious breach of environmental law is therefore not punishable in every member state. this is of course an encouragement to cross-border environmental crime. the criminal deficit in the field of environmental protection cannot of course be eliminated by criminal measures alone, but even on this point the framework decision could well give a new impetus. the question of whether the existing community law at the level of the first pillar already contains sufficient obligations has already been addressed in the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy and in the committee on civil liberties and internal affairs. in this respect, it should be noted that the instruments of the first pillar often provide for penalties, even though they do not necessarily have to be of a criminal nature. under the first pillar, it is mainly up to the member states to decide whether they consider administrative sanctions to be sufficient or whether they have to resort to criminal law. i now come to a point which still remains problematic for the commission and which has been raised in various contributions to the debate, namely the question of the penalty for legal persons. the danish initiative provides that legal persons must be held responsible for serious environmental crimes. the commission considers that the growing legal rules in some member states should be taken into account, while excluding any punishment of legal persons. comparable provisions of community law only provide that sanctions must be imposed on legal persons, which may then be entirely administrative in nature and that - as has rightly been said - the material damage caused must then be subject to financial sanctions. this is also taken. as regards financial sanctions, i would like to stress once again the importance of the green paper on environmental responsibility published by the commission a few months ago, in which the environmental damage caused is finally identified. in order to have a chance of success, the initiative should be advised to proceed with caution and to speak of the liability of legal persons without using the word 'criminal'. regardless of this, those responsible for environmental crimes should naturally be subject to criminal law. this was also a point on which there was a clear consensus during this very interesting debate. in conclusion, i can say on behalf of the commission that we unfortunately have to introduce infringement procedures in environmental law against member states once again and that a very large number of these infringement procedures are pending in this sector. unfortunately, this gives the impression that many member states do not take environmental protection and environmental law very seriously. in this context, the danish initiative is very important and remarkable in the commission's eyes.

the rapporteur. mr president, various circumstances could have justified the postponement of this report until everything was ready, including the amendments. but in any case, i think that we as members of parliament must carry on the work so that the meda report is not delayed at any time, with the consequent damage that this may cause to the countries concerned. after making these reservations, i shall now make a summary of the meda programme. i shall now give my opinion on the proposal for a regulation and on the report as a whole. as you know, the meda programme is part of the euro-mediterranean partnership which was founded following the barcelona declaration in november 1995. the meeting was attended by the foreign ministers of the european union. this is an initiative involving 27 countries on both sides of the mediterranean. the 15 member states of the union on the one hand and algeria, cyprus, egypt, israel, jordan, lebanon, malta, morocco, syria, tunisia, turkey and the palestinian territories on the other. as for libya, for obvious reasons, it has only observer status. our main objective in this cooperation is to forge links, especially in the many areas of common interest that we share with our mediterranean neighbours. to this end, some eur 3.5 billion has been invested over the past five years, spread over two major forms of cooperation: bilateral and regional. in particular, this economic and financial support should make it possible to achieve a free trade area by 2010, for which projects have been launched to assist both macroeconomic reforms and sectoral reforms and structural adjustment. it should be remembered that the ratio of per capita income between the european union and the meda countries is 1 to 10, that is, really significant. i therefore think it is logical that sustainable economic development for the area should be our main objective. i should add that the trade balance between the two blocs is positive for the european union by eur 21 billion. measures are also planned to facilitate private investment in these 12 countries, which in 1994 amounted to eur 3.5 billion, in particular by adapting legislation and administration and by bringing together companies from the meda countries and the european union. it is also worth remembering that we are dealing with a particularly war-torn part of the world. it is not worthwhile to enumerate the different wars waged by many of the countries that enjoy this partnership. the meda programme seeks to pave the way towards a definitive and lasting peace in that part of the world through, among other things, economic stability. this is a population of some 230 million human beings, and at the present rate of growth, in 10 or 12 years it will be 300 million. the diversity of religions and customs in all these countries is noteworthy. this is one of the pillars on which the european union is working hard. as you know, meda also includes a short- and medium-term action programme for the environment, which seeks to reverse the trend towards environmental degradation in the area. the commission's proposal, which is partly the result of criticism of the implementation of this programme, is, in my view, insufficient as a whole. the institution defines three main initiatives to achieve greater effectiveness: on the one hand, a dynamisation of the decision-making process, focusing the activity of the med committee on strategic planning and programming. national and regional financing plans shall be adopted annually on the basis of indicative programmes. it also calls for an increase in planning and implementation capacities, for which a greater provision of human resources is essential. finally, the commission intends to reduce the procedures for more effective implementation in order to increase the rate of implementation of the programmes. in particular, it is intended to develop harmonised procedures common to all assistance programmes. finally, i would like to say that i think this report is important because anything that helps the countries to our south helps us ourselves.

mr president, as a person who lives in the mediterranean, under the mediterranean sun and enjoying the mediterranean tradition and culture, i would like to make a plea for the countries around you. the meda programme, which largely failed in its first phase, may not have understood that the situation of the mediterranean countries, as european policy is being conducted, is extremely difficult. the mediterranean countries are in many cases still less developed than other countries and are faced with the threat of a single agricultural market which they cannot afford. i refer to the splendid article by mr riccardi two or three months ago, in which he said that the mediterranean countries are not attractive for investment because of their scale. it is extremely difficult for these countries to change their agricultural system, and yet they have to share their products with other countries in north africa, the mare nostrum, which belongs to all of us at the same time. and it's from these countries that the greatest migration impact comes. we must therefore pursue a fair policy, and in this respect the meda programme can be a start, although i believe that in many cases it is based on the criteria of the northern countries. first of all, it is not possible to do a project without highlighting the major weaknesses of these countries, such as water scarcity and desertification. what are the european policies against desertification? none of them clear. secondly, in culture, intermediaries are being given more importance than the recipients and producers of culture themselves. and so it is with many other industrial projects. there are many ngos that have sprung up, forming networks that i do not know who can benefit, when what southern europe really needs to do is to wake up. i therefore support a process of industrialisation based on innovation - we do not have to go to the old industry, but to the innovation industry - and support technological innovation and training projects. and in that sense, i think it's a mistake to go for the big projects. with them we will make a few rich, but what mediterranean europe needs is to wake up, to get out of its narrow-mindedness, to take advantage of human resources. and that will only happen if we support multiple initiatives that together create awareness, critical mass and the foundation system so that from there, many more initiatives and small businesses of all kinds can emerge. some will succeed, others will be left behind, but if we do not have a policy of multiple initiatives of many types, allowing society to express itself and to draw on its resources, we will achieve nothing.
the rapporteur. - mr president, i think we can all agree that in the year 2000 the community obviously already has a number of fundamental powers in the external sphere. the maastricht reform responds to the aspiration, so often expressed in this house, that europe should speak with one voice on the international stage. the cfsp gives a new dimension to the union's external action, moving beyond the economic sphere to become an active participant in foreign policy. the european union is, however, constantly lamenting - and we are experiencing this in our own days - that it is not up to the challenge of external action. that said, i should like to begin by pointing out that the purpose of this report is not to call for a further extension of the union's powers in external affairs. those who wish to do so have other debates, in the field of institutional reform, to give their aspirations a chance. we are simply proposing that measures be taken to streamline and improve the way in which the community institutions carry out this enormous external activity. we propose, in short, to make decisive progress in three areas. first, to improve the training of community officials who are to be engaged in the exercise of external activity. the many officials in the commission who are responsible for external relations, assuming responsibilities of fundamental importance, are technical specialists but, in general, lack the diplomatic training necessary to perform their duties. we therefore believe that it is necessary to set up a community diplomatic school which would provide commission officials for external action with a proper diplomatic and international training. we believe that the european union should be able to provide a framework for cooperation between the member states and the community, and that the community should be able to provide a framework for cooperation between the member states and the community. secondly, it is a question of clarifying and developing the legal status of the commission's current external delegations, their role and their relationship with the various community institutions. the commission delegations have experienced a dramatic quantitative and qualitative expansion over the last few years. however, they operate unevenly and their relationship with the other institutions is imprecise as it is not regulated. we therefore propose that the commission's delegations be transformed into community delegations, so that they have closer relations with the council, through the high representative for the cfsp, and with the european parliament and its members, thus ensuring greater efficiency and political control of their activities. thirdly and lastly, we want to improve coordination between the delegations and the external services of the member states. we must encourage such coordination by avoiding confusion and lack of coherence, as well as other shortcomings, as was shown at the informal general affairs council in evian this past weekend. we are proposing various mechanisms for this purpose, including the possibility of grouping missions from member states, if they so decide, with the commission's existing delegations where appropriate. this would also lead to a substantial reduction in costs. ladies and gentlemen, mr president, none of the proposals announced involves institutional reforms, much less the surrender of sovereignty by the member states. we are simply seeking to exercise more effectively the powers that have already been conferred. it is not a question here of confronting different models of europeanism, but simply of being more effective. the rapporteur cannot therefore support amendments which would involve profound structural changes in the institutional architecture of the union. i am particularly grateful for the other contributions which, in committee and with the vote tomorrow in the plenary, add a very considerable amount to the initial proposal. i ask the various groups to vote in favour and the european commission to echo the sentiments of this house.

mr president, i would like to congratulate the rapporteur on the report. as mrs carrillo has said, this is the first own-initiative report that parliament has adopted in the field of foreign policy in this parliament. it is curious to hear the comments of some members who say that they think the report is too timid, and others who think it will end the last stronghold of the sovereignty of the member states. i think this report is heading in the right direction. i think it merely follows the community method in a pragmatic sense and makes it clear that common diplomacy is one of the fundamental aspects of the visibility of the european union's external action. i do not know whether we can say today that the european union is the first economic power, the first industrial power or the first financial power on the planet. what we can say, without fear of being wrong, is that the european union is today the leading donor of development aid, and that means that the delegates of the european commission have a very important role in representing the community institutions, and in particular the commission. this means that their specific weight is in many cases, given the large amounts they have to distribute, higher than the role of ambassadors and member states. it is therefore clear, mr president, that anything which improves the preparation and knowledge of commission officials will be a useful element in the european union's external action. the rapporteur has explained the main initiatives in his report: the creation of a common diplomatic school, the holding of hearings of commission delegates in third countries - - mr president, commissioner, the report by mr dell'alba concerns the winding-up of one of the largest financial instruments of the european community to assist the private sector. the socialist group supports all cooperation measures such as this one which encourage the dynamisation of enterprises and of economies in general through private initiative. in particular, ecip, whose projects are now being closed, has been particularly successful as already mentioned. the external evaluation of the project has shown that it has had a significant multiplier effect, creating jobs and joint ventures. we now hope, commissioner, that the future programme to replace it will add to these positive effects by better management. we must say, however, that we welcome the successes of this programme, but the socialist members of the committee on development have also considered the need for any aid instrument, including those in the private sector, to have as its primary objective the reduction of poverty among the population, which is the ultimate aim of these instruments. wealth creation and job creation through community-funded enterprises must be reversed in these populations. the application of these instruments must take account of the achievement of labour, social and environmental standards, or else we can say that these instruments do not help development but are subsidies to individuals. we cannot always say that the evaluations have checked the quality of the aid through ecip. for example, when ecip funds are used to set up a bank in one of the beneficiary countries, how can we ensure that these funds are channelled to attract investment and not just to subsidize the bank's presence in this country? as the rapporteur has said, this is a matter of putting community aid within the framework of a comprehensive strategy involving the private sector, which the commission does not mention in its plan for aid policy reform, even though the attraction of private funds is a necessity for the development of many countries. in this connection, we would like to repeat the question that mr dell'alba asked the commission about its plans for extending this instrument to countries in sub-saharan africa, whose need for funds is also urgent. we hope, in short, that the ecip experience, which has been very important for latin america, will serve to improve the programme which will replace it, whose role we have not seen clearly defined in the commission's reform plan. coordination within the commission is essential to improve aid effectiveness and this requires that the various instruments be put to use in the service of a broad objective and an overall strategy.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat fraud. for those of us who have followed closely the evolution and development of the ecip instrument throughout its short but intense history, it seems to us that the best way to sum up mr dell'alba's report is to highlight the message contained in the amendments of the committee on development and cooperation, since they recommend the continuation of this financial instrument as having been the best vehicle for establishing and strengthening the european business fabric in those countries concerned and, consequently, for creating employment. now that the agreement on free trade, political consultation and cooperation between the european union and mexico has just entered into force, it is appropriate to recall the desirability of continuing with this type of financial instrument which, in some cases, such as mexico's, has been used intensively and positively, and is the ideal one for strengthening trade ties between unique blocs such as the european union and the countries involved. otherwise, the european union would not be consistent with its commitment to cooperation and development, not only in the case of the countries of latin america but also in those of asia, the mediterranean and south africa. finally, we strongly support the report by mr dell'alba, whom we congratulate for his clarity of thought in addressing the need to continue in the future the application of the ecips, in my view as a single instrument, and which we hope will, after more than ten years of positive experience, be geared towards making the administrative burdens more flexible and faster in their processing to allow for more efficient action. and that, in my view, requires a strengthening of the human resources of the commission's offices in the countries concerned.

mr president, commissioner, first of all i would like to congratulate mr imbeni because i think he has produced a splendid report and we were in full agreement with his proposals when we discussed it in committee. the socialist group believes that aid policy should be the flagship of the european union's external activities insofar as it reflects the ideas which should inspire the building of the have seen and evaluated what echo has done, believe that its work has been very positive. this report therefore serves to reaffirm the principle of humanitarian aid as a right of the people in the midst of disasters and an obligation of the international community, of which the european union is the principal actor, both quantitatively and qualitatively. however, with a view to the future, some progress is needed. firstly, the so-called 'grey area' mentioned earlier, i.e. the interregnum between the end of emergency aid and the start of rehabilitation and development measures. as long as of staff involved in humanitarian aid activities. the importance of echo's work is not proportional to the number of its staff. thirdly - and this is closely linked to the previous point - the budget - question no 5 by mrs cristina gutiérrez cortines (h-0597/00) subject: request for a documented assessment of the schooling of children and young people in the countries applying for eu membership in view of the economic crisis and the profound structural changes in most of the countries applying for enlargement, are all children and young people in these countries in school, up to what age is schooling compulsory and is it possible to guarantee, to some extent, that all future european citizens will be in school?
counsel. - the council has the latest statistics from eurostat which i have here and i am prepared to hand them over to the honourable member. these data refer to the 1997/98 school year, which is already old, and show that in 11 candidate countries the duration of compulsory schooling is nine or ten years, i.e. up to the age of 15 or 16, as the case may be. so we can estimate that about 90% of 16-year-olds and 60% of 18-year-olds are in school. reliable statistics are not yet available for cyprus and malta and eurostat's collaboration with turkey in the field of education statistics has not yet started, but it is understood that this is not easy for the retrospective material. for further information, the honourable member may also consult a collection entitled 'the key figures for education in europe' produced by euridice in collaboration with eurostat and published by the commission in german, english and french. i'm going to do a little publicity by saying that the 1999-2000 edition is available. finally, as regards the education of all european citizens, it is recalled that it is up to each member state and each candidate country to ensure that this objective is achieved. i would like to make the statistics available to mrs gutiérrez cortines again, as they are.

- question no 6 by mrs maría rodríguez ramos, substituted by mr medina ortega (h-0605/00): subject: negotiating directives for the agricultural chapter of the free trade agreement with the maghreb the commission presented its proposal for negotiating directives for a free trade agreement with morocco, tunisia and israel to the council's maghreb group. the proposal includes all the liberalization measures that are theoretically possible, from the increase of quotas to the reduction of customs duties and various formulas for managing entry prices. can the council indicate the scope and content of this mandate?
the council. - morocco, tunisia and israel are the three mediterranean partners of the european union whose euro-mediterranean association agreement has entered into force. these agreements contain an agricultural rendezvous clause whereby the parties commit themselves to considering further liberalisation of their agricultural trade and this process is complementary to the gradual tariff dismantling aimed at preparing the establishment of the industrial free trade area by 2010. it is strictly limited to agriculture. it does not therefore concern, for example, fishery products which are the subject of negotiations in another context. the association agreements with morocco, tunisia and israel provide that as from 1 january 2000 the situation of agricultural trade will be examined with a view to establishing measures for progressive liberalisation, as from 1 january 2001. the negotiations which are about to begin must therefore make it possible to strengthen this euro-mediterranean partnership. they also aim to achieve a better balance in agricultural trade with the three countries concerned with which the union has a structural deficit. the european union is the main market for the agricultural products of its partners and absorbs two thirds of their exports. at present, 95% of exports of agricultural products from morocco, tunisia and israel to the union are exempt from customs duties. on 20 july 2000, the council approved the commission's negotiating mandate, which contains general guidelines. the aim is to promote better market access for community products in partner countries and a better balance of reciprocal preferences, including by exempting new products from customs duties. it also sets out the margin of manoeuvre given to the commission to achieve trade rebalancing and to conclude negotiations. at the request of the member states, the measures which may give rise to concessions shall be clearly delimited. the mandate therefore authorizes the community negotiator to provide for the possible granting of tariff preferences for new products or the improvement of existing concessions, but taking into account the sensitivity of certain products and the mechanisms of the common agricultural policy. the commission will, in collaboration with the member states, carry out an assessment of the possible impact of the concessions on the economic and commercial interests of the union and it is clear that the council will take a decision only in the light of the results of this assessment.
- mr president, i am reassured that the council is also taking into account in these negotiations the sensitivity of certain regions and certain products, particularly in the agricultural sector. at the moment there are agricultural sectors in the mediterranean basin, and also in the outermost regions of the community, which could be threatened as a result of the very generous concessions proposed by the commission. i would simply like to stress and encourage the council to continue in this line of maintaining the utmost vigilance so that these sectors are not fundamentally harmed by too generous concessions.
counsel. - i think that's the philosophy we're going with in this negotiation. so i can only approve what is not a question but a complementary intervention.

counsel. - the us has not yet notified the wto of the measures referred to by the honourable member which could be subject to review under article 18 of the agreement on agriculture in the wto framework. it should also be recalled that agricultural subsidies were among the subjects discussed in the wto negotiations which began in june 2000. the negotiations, which are based on the principles set out in article 20 of the agreement on agriculture, are also to examine the implementation of the reduction commitments agreed in the marrakesh agreements in 1994. the relevant council bodies are regularly informed by the commission of the progress of these negotiations and of other activities undertaken at the level of the wto agricultural bodies and, if the commission deems it appropriate, it will refer to the council the question of the compliance of the us subsidy policy with the commitments made in the uruguay round and any measures to be taken in this regard.
counsel. - i will not go into detail, but it is precisely on the basis of these considerations that we reject the aggressions that have been committed against the common agricultural policy and our own system, and it is also for this reason that the european union has adopted, with a view to the wto, a comprehensive negotiating mandate, which aims to protect the social and agricultural model, not to mention the european cultural model. you can be sure that this mandate will remain the basis for future negotiations.

- question no 10 by mrs maría izquierdo rojo (h-0617/00) subject: cost of enlargement and mediterranean agriculture in view of the forecasts and the latest legislative proposals concerning mediterranean agriculture, in particular in relation to products such as cotton, rice, fruit and vegetables, tomatoes, nuts and olive oil, which will have a very serious negative impact on employment and social progress in the poor areas of europe concerned, and bearing in mind the budgetary plans for the enlargement of the european union, how does the council intend to avoid mediterranean agriculture becoming the practical cost of the next enlargement?
council. - i understand the concerns underlying the honourable member's question. however, it seems to me that your question has a different meaning. i would like to return to your opening statement: the reforms under way in the common organization of the markets for products mainly from the mediterranean are designed to adapt these markets to the often very tough competition from outside europe and to stabilise these products within the union. the aim is therefore to maintain employment in areas where there are generally few opportunities for conversion to other cultures. it is in this spirit that the council will, in due course, take a decision on legislative proposals put forward by the commission. the union's agriculture ministers, who have been meeting informally in biarritz since saturday, have just reiterated their desire to orient agricultural policies more clearly than in the past towards improving the quality and diversity of products. secondly, you mention the budgetary impact of the enlargement of the union, which in my view has no direct link with the adoption of the reforms of the cmos i have just mentioned. the budgetary impact of enlargement was the subject of intense discussions at the berlin european council in march 1999, at which the financial perspective for the period 2000-06 was drawn up. the financial perspective indicates, for each year of the period, for each heading, the amounts of expenditure in commitment appropriations and these commitment appropriations provided for under the various headings of the financial perspective are not fungible. the expenditure linked to enlargement cannot therefore be financed at the expense of agricultural expenditure under heading 1 of the financial perspective. i therefore do not think that mediterranean agriculture can bear the cost of future enlargement, in the context of the financial perspective for 2000-06. of course, we will have to find, when the time comes, in any event by 2005 at the latest, a new institutional agreement on the next financial perspective, but that deadline, you will agree, seems too far away for us to be able to deal with it today.
in order to avoid the negative impact of enlargement on the mediterranean, would you be prepared to make any recommendations in this regard? indeed, with his actions and proposals, commissioner fischler has made this anti-mediterranean impact of enlargement a reality. the fears of this are a fact throughout the mediterranean area. since i see that the council is firm in its political will, and in order to prevent - as you say - something of this kind from happening, not with intentions but with facts, i would like to ask you whether the french presidency, before it concludes, would be prepared to formulate, in the way it deems appropriate, some kind of recommendation that dispels these fears, namely that in no way will the cost of enlargement be paid by mediterranean productions.
counsel. - i shall not here be improvising any particular recommendations on this subject. the only thing i can assure you, madam president, is that the financial perspective, which was negotiated with great difficulty in berlin, is a framework which will be extremely difficult for us to change. we do not wish that. so, once again, we'll talk about it in 2005.

counsel. - i share your sentiment, madam president, that the incidents referred to seem, a priori, to be a matter of general security and public order in albania rather than a malicious action directed against the greek minority. there is a general problem here, and it must be treated as such. the action plan for albania to which you refer is an action plan for albania and the region bordering it drawn up by the high level working group on asylum and migration and adopted by the general affairs council on 13 and 14 june. the aim of the report is to define and coordinate the european union's response to the problems of asylum and migration in albania and neighbouring countries, and it is not intended to promote the rights of any particular minority. however, among the suggested actions are projects or programmes aimed at strengthening democracy, respect for human rights and minorities in general. the council working parties are currently examining the various measures proposed in order to identify those which could be implemented within a short time. a progress report is expected for the december european council in nice.
