mr president, i believe that the work done by the commission and also by the rapporteur, mr veltroni, has many important aspects. it is clear that a great deal of effort has been made to introduce new topics and take new steps in european audiovisual policy. however, i think that on certain points we still have a lot to do, both in the commission and in parliament. we are far behind the big changes taking place in the audiovisual sector, especially as a result of digitisation. if we do not act, we will be like the ostrich that puts its head under the ground. i'm sure that's not what we want. we all know that digitisation started about five years ago and therefore these works on audiovisual policy are more than timely. there are five points i would like to stress because i think that sooner or later they will have to be revised: the first is the definition of public service. this is important if we want to have a public service in europe in a frankly competitive environment - and we are seeing this from the audience of publicly owned services - and also for the sake of the private audiovisual service. there are many issues to be resolved, one of which is the separation of the requirements for both. the second point, which i think is fundamental, is the revision of the directive on television without frontiers. in this, we are like the ostrich i was talking about earlier. thirdly, there must be some definition - and i think this document does not cover this sufficiently - of what happens to interactive services on television, what happens to the internet on television. the fourth point concerns the transition from analogue to digital television and its consequences for users in the use or acquisition of new terminals. and finally, the implications of competition and concentration laws. audiovisual policy should address these points and also delve into the area of competition.

the rapporteur. - mr president, two new international fisheries protocols between the european union and third countries call for our attention today: guinea and mauritius, the atlantic ocean and the indian ocean. two agreements which differ in their geographical location, size, fishing opportunities and financial compensation, but which are also important agreements, adding to the already extensive network of international fisheries agreements between the european union and third countries, a fundamental pillar of the common fisheries policy, since it is essential to meet our supply needs, both for the european consumer and for our industry, and it is also essential to be able to do so with our own fleet. fisheries agreements with third countries thus cover a crucial objective of the common fisheries policy, to which must be added their contribution to employment, in most cases also in european regions heavily dependent on this activity. the commission has also proposed that the community should be able to provide a financial contribution to the fisheries sector. that is why, this afternoon, our committee approved in its opinion on the budget for the coming year, 2001, the proposal put forward by our vice-president, mrs miguélez, to increase line b7-8000 (international fisheries agreements) by eur 7 million, thus restoring the amounts in the preliminary draft budget presented at the time by the european commission. morocco, mauritania and greenland are major negotiating challenges for the european commission, which we all hope will be successfully concluded soon. for the moment, we welcome today the agreements with guinea and mauritius, which are meeting the important needs of different fleets, of different european union states in the atlantic and indian oceans. in both cases, the constant and worrying increase in ship owners' payments is striking, whereas, curiously, these provisions are not covered by other agreements, such as the well-known greenland agreement. for example, in the case of mauritius, the licence fees payable by shipowners are increased by eur 5 per tonne of fish, i.e. from eur 20 to eur 25, and the equivalent in catches per vessel is also increased. the european union contribution is reduced by 29%, to be borne by the shipowners who, in the event of full exploitation of the fishing opportunities, would contribute 23,5% of the total cost. in the previous protocol, the figure was 7%, i.e. from 7% to 23.5% of the total cost would be borne by the shipowners themselves. we also want to highlight in this context the imbalances in the internal allocation of these fishing opportunities, carried out by the european commission itself between the member states, as was the case for cephalopods in the agreement with guinea. both agreements provide important support to local authorities for the conservation of their own fisheries resources and also advocate agreements between states as opposed to private agreements - which is of great importance in agreements such as the one in morocco, which we are trying to negotiate - as well as the european union's contribution to the establishment of modern control systems, which contributes to the european union's conservationist position in all the seas of the planet, in line with its internal position in its own community waters. there is also a direct link between the financial compensation and the objectives and cooperation measures agreed. in the case of the agreement with mauritius, it is 50%, compared with 30% in the previous agreement. as is often the case, more documentation is needed to compare figures and data between protocols, although in this case the european commission should be thanked for including the minutes of the negotiations, in the case of guinea, which allows for more data and, in short, greater transparency, which is welcome and which the european parliament is grateful for. the european parliament's committee on fisheries has voted in favour of these agreements, as is now the custom, considering that both are highly beneficial for the parties, that is, the european union and third states. the liberal group has now tabled an amendment in the plenary with similar content to each of the reports so that - in the rapporteur's view - the common fisheries policy ceases to be common and the important pillar of foreign policy is separated from it, so that only the agreement negotiated by the european commission, and therefore, on behalf of the 15 member states of the european union, the direct beneficiaries of the agreement, pay for it. the rapporteur is against this amendment, because if only those who directly benefit from community policies paid for them, we would simply be breaking up the internal market and dismantling the european union itself. we are therefore in favour of both fisheries agreements, which we hope will continue in the future, and we look forward, commissioner, to being able to discuss in our committee on fisheries soon and to say the same thing we are saying now about the very important fisheries agreement with morocco. i am sure that you are working hard, as i understand from the conversation we had this afternoon, and i encourage you to take this important negotiation forward.
mr president, the socialist group supports the proposals for council regulations on the european community's fisheries agreements with mauritius and the republic of guinea. both agreements are part of a general policy of the european community based on our presence in the rest of the world. the fisheries sector is part of the community economy and, in order for the community fleet to be able to work and develop its activity, the community needs to conclude agreements with third countries and international organizations so that our fishermen have fishing opportunities. both agreements are followed regularly. in the case of guinea, we have had an agreement since 1983, and in the case of mauritius, since 1989. there is no doubt about the profitability of these agreements for the european union, as demonstrated by the study on cost-benefit ratio commissioned by the commission itself. nor can the beneficial effects for the other contracting parties, in this case mauritius and the republic of guinea, be doubted. both countries are getting valuable resources for their development in exchange for the fishing opportunities they give to our fleet. these are mutually beneficial agreements which have been modified over time to meet the requirements of sustainable exploitation of the resource and to support the efforts of the third country authorities to develop their own fisheries sector. the protocols which periodically renew the agreements have been adjusted to reality, to the quantities actually caught and to the state of the resources in those fisheries. despite the reduction in the amount of catches in the agreement with guinea, the economic compensation to be received by the african country will be maintained, as the new protocol increases the amount of fees and licences to be paid by community shipowners. the contrast with other agreements - i would like to emphasize, for example, the agreement with greenland, where shipowners do not contribute to the cost of the agreement - is therefore even more striking. in the case of mauritius, the volume of authorised catches is also reduced and the number of vessels authorised to fish is specified. the european parliament's approval of these two fisheries agreements is a political signal of our support for the conclusion and renewal of other agreements which are of far greater importance to our sector, because of the number of vessels and fishermen who depend on them. i am referring in particular to the agreement with morocco. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. let each one shoulder his responsibility and fulfill his obligation. the commission has done so by approving today, at a special meeting of its committee on fisheries, the quantities proposed by the european commission in chapter b7-800 on fisheries agreements with third countries. it is now up to the european commission to negotiate with a weighty argument to reach a reasonable agreement with morocco. we're still waiting for him.
mr president, i think it is convenient for the commission to continue ignoring the requests of the council and of this parliament - the first of which were already clearly expressed at the october 1997 council of ministers - and to delay work on the guidelines for the negotiation of fisheries agreements. the protocol with guinea-conakry is a good example. we had already expected an increase in the share of the payment to be made to shipowners, but i think it is intolerable that the commission should be allowed to call such an increase in the council working parties a slight increase when it means an increasing sacrifice for the fleet and when, i repeat, in the northern agreements the shipowners do not pay a cent. the commission has also had the luxury of flouting the principle of relative stability by graciously withdrawing from a community fleet fishing rights acquired under that principle. either the principle of relative stability is sacred or it is not, but it cannot be untouchable in community waters and quite the opposite in the fisheries agreements of the south. the commission says that it has taken away the fishing opportunities for cephalopods from spain because it did not fully exploit them under the previous protocol, and it is giving them to countries which have never fished there. i have always advocated the full exploitation of the fishing opportunities granted, but in all waters, not just in the southern agreements. i repeat, the agreements in the north are totally wasted and there is no way for the fleets that are very interested to fish. why these differences? let's get this straight. what is the commission's reason for assuming that, since it did not exhaust the fishing opportunities under the previous protocol, it will not do so under this one, when for nine months it has tied up the cephalopod fishing fleet in morocco, with no sign of a solution? mr president, all this is indicative of the mental and material chaos in our community fisheries authorities, which will only be resolved when the guidelines to which i referred in the beginning are clearly established and agreed.

question no 41 by mrs ilka schröder (h-0613/00) subject: cooperation with drug prevention networks already since 1998 cooperation between the commission and the networks it supports has deteriorated considerably: contracts between the networks and the commission are finalised while the subsidised projects have been on the rails for several months. the commission insists, however, that projects should only be implemented after receipt of a provisional written certificate. the commission's delays in paying the advance sometimes amount to several years. the networks as a whole are faced with an ever-increasing administrative workload and, above all, with the lack of payments from the commission, which considerably limits their work. these delays in payment by the commission have even led some associations to cease their activities. why has the commission not been able in recent years to sign contracts and pay grants for the networks it supports in a timely manner and in real time with the projects?
commission. – the commission shares the concerns of the honourable member about the problems relating to contracts and payments for the drug prevention networks subsidised by the community action programme on prevention of drug dependence. these problems have several causes. firstly, it is clear that there has been a human resources problem in the public health directorate in luxembourg, which deals with this work. in short, the staff complement has been insufficient to deal with complex procedures and often inexperienced beneficiaries proposing too many small projects. this situation was aggravated last summer when a decision was taken in the light of the report of the committee of independent experts to end the contract with the technical assistance office which helped in the implementation of this programme. secondly, a large number of small projects are implemented under the anti-drugs programme, placing additional strain on the already limited human resources at our disposal. during the last five years, the average size of projects in terms of co-financing granted by the commission has been eur 180,000. thirdly, experience shows that participants in the network have had little understanding of the commission's contract and payment procedures. in many cases, therefore, the commission has had to make repeated requests to the drug prevention networks for missing documentation needed to finalise contracts or produce payments. fourthly, in the light of experience with subsidies from the community budget and the criticisms of the court of auditors, greater rigour may have been brought to bear on the documentation relating to contract costs, resulting in knock-on effects on the timing of payments. in responding to these problems, i am taking a number of steps. the commission's proposal for a new public health framework and strategy highlights the need for clearer objectives and more efficient management with a greater impact on key priorities. therefore, fewer but bigger projects will be co-financed in future, making for more efficient use of the human resources needed to manage implementation of the programme. as the budgetary authority repeatedly stresses, we must match resources and priorities more realistically in the future. in addition, as you are aware, following the commission's recent review of its staffing needs, a request for additional posts is being put forward to the budgetary authority, including a significant increase in posts for the health and consumer protection dg. if the budgetary authority agrees, a number of these posts could be allocated to tackle the kind of problems which we are discussing today. the inexperience of contractors regarding financial control requirements will continue to necessitate significant advice and other inputs from already limited staff resources. the public health directorate intends to carry out an information campaign to help contractors to understand the commission's procedures and requirements more clearly. on the issue of red tape, the departments concerned are currently reviewing their documentary requirements with the aim of simplifying and speeding up payment procedures without neglecting the necessary financial control measures. as a result of the measures already taken, the situation has been improving, and i expect it to improve further so that contracts can be agreed more quickly and payments made in accordance with the commission's 60-day rule. should you have any specific points to make, perhaps you could provide me with the relevant information in writing, and i will certainly raise them with my staff.
commission. – in relation to the first issue raised, i do not suggest that the problem lies wholly with, as you say, incompetent project partners. what i am saying is that is the reason for some of the problems that have arisen. it is something i am concerned about and am seeking to address by making sure that there are clear guidelines, as you suggest, so you and i are fully in agreement on that point. with regard to the size of projects, since 1996 a total of 149 projects have been selected for over eur 25 million, with an average amount of eur 180 000 per project. under the new health strategy we will reduce the number of projects and increase their value and impact, thereby using our limited human resources more effectively. it does not always follow that smaller projects are better than bigger projects, but if human resources are applied efficiently it will be for the betterment of the projects concerned.

question no 47 by mr lennart sacrédeus (h-0606/00) subject: abolition of border controls in the schengen area what is the commission's view on the application of the abolition of border controls in the schengen area at the european football championship in the light of the mass arrests that took place in brussels and charleroi?
commission. - first of all, i think it should be noted that many of the people involved in the incidents in brussels and charleroi are from a member state of the union, the united kingdom, which is not part of the schengen area. these are therefore persons who, when travelling to attend football matches in the context of euro 2000, have been subject to the checks on persons carried out at the external borders of the schengen area. it should also be recalled that the belgian and dutch governments have invoked, for the duration of euro 2000, a safeguard clause referred to in article 2 (2) of the schengen convention, which provides that, where public policy or national security is threatened - and, in my view, the fear of hooliganism probably meets this criterion - a member state may decide that, for a limited period, national border controls, adapted to the situation, will be carried out, even at the internal borders of the schengen area. the belgian and dutch governments have followed the prior consultation procedure required by the schengen agreement. the controls referred to here have been temporarily reintroduced at internal borders but have not been systematically carried out. the controls were targeted, in particular on the basis of information provided by the member states, in the context of police cooperation, concerning supporters who could constitute a threat to public order. the implementation of external border controls and, temporarily, internal border controls in the schengen area does not mean closing a border or systematically turning back people who want to enter the territory to watch a football match. in accordance with the treaty establishing the european community, citizens of the union have a fundamental right to move freely within the territory of the member states, but restrictions may be imposed on grounds of public policy only in individual cases, namely where the person concerned constitutes a genuine and sufficiently serious threat affecting a fundamental interest of society. that is why i say that collective restraint is not permitted under community law. it is not enough to have the nationality of a particular member state and to want to attend a football match to be turned back at the border. i therefore believe that an evaluation of the measures of cooperation between the authorities of the member states concerned is already under way and that this joint exercise is intended to draw lessons from euro 2000 to see how it will be possible in the future to improve legislative and police cooperation in the fight against hooliganism.
commission - i don't think there's any direct or indirect connection between portugal's defeat and hooliganism. that was the truth of the game, but sometimes you don't get lucky. in any case, yes, portugal is indeed hosting euro 2004, and that is why the commission has supported, in the context of euro 2000, several concrete initiatives on police cooperation to experiment with new methods of cooperation and to learn from them. we are in the process of evaluating these measures. as soon as the report is available, it will be considered and legislative action will be taken at european level. the aim is to adopt legislation at european level to support police cooperation in the fight against hooliganism. at the moment, i'm waiting for the report. as soon as it is ready, it will probably be made public, and the debate on the initiatives to be taken can begin.
commission. - i would say, mr president, that this question is put in another perspective, namely the creation of common standards for travel documents, whether passports or identity cards. the existence of such common standards is provided for in the treaty and the commission is in the early stages of preparing a proposal for the adoption of common standards for the instruments concerned. i cannot give you a fixed timetable, that is, i cannot guarantee that these documents will be adopted before the date set for the integration of the nordic passport union into the schengen free movement. what i can assure you is that we are actively working on the formulation of uniform standard forms of documents which solve problems such as the one the honourable member has just indicated.

counsel. - mr president, madam commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by thanking you for devoting this morning to sport. in eight days, the olympic games will open in sydney; athletes from all over the world will be there. the outcome is not written, it is planned; everything is uncertain. it's the sport. the champions and champions who are about to make you dream have their own itineraries. many of them are involved in professional sports, but, you know, all of them have at least two things in common: their selection is the result of many years of hard work, of meticulous training. volunteers, educators, public and private resources have been mobilized around them. but most importantly, they started their sports in a club or a school. in order to defend sport, we must therefore, at the same time, and in the same way, defend the local amateur club, high-level sport, in its amateur or professional dimension. high-level sport is a dream; it contributes to the development of mass sport with an educational social role. today, top-level sports, both amateur and professional, are the subject of worldwide media coverage. more and more men and women of all ages and circumstances are taking up sports. sport has acquired a social dimension. so it is no surprise to anyone here that this human activity is sometimes marred by acts of violence or racism, or that it arouses financial appetites. i'm not one to demonize economics in sports. sport needs resources, and those resources cannot be public. the question is not to distinguish between a sport without money, which is pure, and a sport with money, which is lost. no, the real question is something else; it is expressed in the following way: will the sporting movement have the means to preserve the ethics of sport by controlling the money that benefits the sport, by preventing that money from dictating its law to the sport. let us be clear: this problem will not arise in twenty years' time, it arises today. sports have become so attractive that some financial interests want to exploit them for profit, even if it means sacrificing ethics and treating athletes as commodities. who has not witnessed the buying and selling of sportsmen, sometimes very young? who has not been shocked by the amount of certain audiovisual contracts or transfers? who hasn't been alerted by the sports calendars that are overloaded? who has not been concerned about the plans of certain private groups to create, outside the national and international sports federations, private sports competitions based on a single criterion, namely the budget of the clubs, as we have recently seen in football and then in basketball? what kind of sport do we want for the 21st century? the answer to this global, fundamental question depends on the answers we give to it every day. there are two possible choices: either, based on the observation of its deviations, we consider that sport is no longer dependent on the market; sportsmen, on their added value. in this case, the rules of competition must be applied, deregulation must be added to the current follies, and in the name of free movement, young people aged 18 to 20 must be bought and sold. so, starting from the construction of modern sport in europe, with its humanistic values and associative structures, we decide, in the present context, with the economic and social issues at stake, to give the sports movement the legal and institutional means to protect sports practices in their diversity within the federations. the latter option, that of the french presidency, does not mean the status quo, but on the contrary, it presupposes innovative proposals from the sports movement - and i welcome the fact that this is now the case on the question of transfers - and from the states to combat the drift in sport and develop practices, protect the associative structures in the cohesion of each sport. ladies and gentlemen, the european parliament has already done a great deal of work on this option and we are beginning to make progress at council level. in june 1997 sports ministers met at the stade de france, then in germany, finland and portugal. there was the annex to the amsterdam treaty, the conclusions of the vienna council, the helsinki report on sport last december. then, at the council meeting in feira, portugal, in june 2000, a clear call was made for the specific characteristics of sport to be taken into account in the implementation of community policies. the french presidency hopes that we will be able to identify in concrete terms what the specificities of sport are and what their recognition implies. it is therefore necessary to recognize that sport is first and foremost the daily practice of millions of men, women and young people, and the commitment of hundreds of thousands of volunteers. it is an irreplaceable tool for informal education, integration and access to citizenship. the commission has already taken a number of initiatives in this area, including the creation of a european sports federation. sport is a whole. we need federal cohesion. i am glad that the report drawn up by mr mennea and adopted by the commission emphasizes this. it is in the name of this approach that my colleagues from the fifteen and i have worked closely with commissioner viviane reding. after two meetings of the working groups set up by the portuguese presidency, a meeting of the troika and a great many bilateral contacts with my colleagues from the fifteen, these are some of the objectives which seem to us to be the most widely shared within the council. the first concerns the protection of underage sportsmen. we must put an end to the commercial exploitation of underage sportsmen. specific actions should be taken to protect the health of young athletes, in particular to prevent the use of doping substances and to ensure their education and vocational training. to directive on the protection of young people at work, we will be able to make specific recommendations on this point. secondly, i also want to see measures taken to preserve the training policies of sports clubs. sports federations and states should be able to take appropriate measures to protect training clubs if they so wish. it should be possible to introduce clauses such as the obligation to the rapporteur. - mr president, doping is not a new problem, it did not even start in this century but comes from the last century. in fact, the first death from doping occurred in 1896, when a cyclist ingested narcotics. the first anti-doping measures, however, were taken after the olympic games in helsinki in 1952; but it was at the 1998 tour that the glass was overflowed and the problem began to be fought seriously. in fact, we have heard this morning that this is a priority for the french presidency, the council and the commission as well. we need to analyse why it exists and why doping has increased so much in recent years. on the one hand, there is the over-commercialization of sport, the saturation of sporting calendars and the increased physical and mental demands on athletes. and it's that before, the motto of sport was that of pierre de coubertin, "the important thing is to participate". now, however, it seems that the first one wins, the second one loses, and the others simply participate. on the other hand, we must not forget that more and more tests are being carried out lately, many of them outside competition, and this also leads, logically, to more doping cases being discovered. however, it is very important to distinguish between two types of doping: on the one hand, there is intentional or planned doping, that is, a team plans which substances the athlete should take and when, to improve their physical performance. logically, it's more common in sports with greater financial resources. on the other hand, there is accidental doping, which often does not even improve the athlete's physical performance. it is more common in sports with few resources, so that the public often does not even know what happened. obviously, both must be fought, although each must be approached in a very different way. fighting intentional or planned doping is much more difficult. police cooperation plays a very important role, because we must not forget that the trafficking of doping substances amounts to one billion euros a year. it is also important to listen to the athlete when making sports calendars or planning a competition or a test: sometimes we demand more from the body than it can give without having to resort to external aids. above all, we must fight against doping globally. it is not an isolated problem of a member state and therefore the presence of the european union in the world anti-doping agency is absolutely essential. fighting accidental doping is much easier. the report proposes that the boxes of pharmaceutical products should bear an indicator consisting of five olympic rings and a traffic light. thus, when buying a drug, athletes will be able to clearly see the red traffic light indicating the risk of a positive test, or the green light indicating that they are not at risk, or the orange light indicating that they may be at risk and should call their doctor or a specialist for advice. this is very important, because we now have 15 member states with 15 lists of prohibited substances, and in each country you can change the trade name of the same medicine. in this respect, the european medicines agency is requested to intervene. however, although the types of doping are different, athletes are treated the same and, from the moment the result is positive, they are considered guilty, without the right to prove their innocence and without assessing whether or not there has been intentionality in this doping, as happens in other facts of life. we also call on the european commission to request that the fifth framework programme investigate doping substances and their impact on the health of athletes, on detection methods and the natural limits of the hormones that the human body can produce. as regards laboratories, it is very important that they comply with iso standards on uniformity in the collection and analysis of samples and that there is protection and confidentiality, both in the collection and in the processing of the file, in order to preserve the right to the honour and privacy of athletes. finally, i would like to refer to the sanctions. when someone other than the athlete has intervened, such as a club, an association, a federation, a doctor, a coach, etc., he must also be subject to a sanction, just as the athlete, because let us not forget that the shortest active life will always be that of the athlete.

commission. – the commission shares the deep regrets expressed in the resolutions on the accident involving the russian submarine the kursk in the arctic bering sea on 12 august and the loss of the lives of 118 seamen. we were particularly concerned about the policy of the russian authorities in the first days after the accident on foreign assistance and information provided to the russian population and the wider public. russia is ultimately responsible for devising and implementing a plan to manage its nuclear waste and spent fuel, and the resolutions, therefore, quite rightly call upon russia to use all available resources, including its own specialists. the commission considers that the international community should offer the necessary assistance to russia. it has already launched a number of assistance projects under various community programmes. improved radioactive waste management in north-west russia is one of the explicit priorities included in the new tacis regulation covering the next seven years. the commission welcomes any action that would increase the budget funding to be used to reduce the ideological threat in north-west russia and in particular to enable laid-up nuclear submarines to be dismantled more quickly than 10 of the north fleet's 100 disused nuclear submarines moored at various based in north-west russia have been dismantled so far. besides the submarines, spent fuel from a number of nuclear-powered icebreakers also adds to the ecological risk. the lack of storage capacity for spent nuclear fuel remains one of the major bottlenecks in dismantling operations as a whole. community-backed activities are studies to design and cost a storage facility in north-west russia or in the southern urals. in the light of these studies, the international community, perhaps including the european community, might later finance the construction of such a storage facility. to speed up dismantling, the community is supporting the design, construction, and licensing of a transport and storage tank for damaged spent fuel produced in the operation of nuclear submarines and icebreakers and currently stored under primitive conditions. the commission is also involved in a number of studies aiming to improve radioactive-waste management in north-west russia. before concluding, i would like to stress the importance of international coordination in this immense task. to give two examples, the commission is serving in the iaea-sponsored contact expert group. the group's work might eventually make it possible to draw up a comprehensive strategy and key investment projects that should be supported by the international community and, together with a number of donor countries, the commission is currently negotiating an agreement with the russians. this agreement, known as the 'multilateral nuclear environmental programme', is intended to overcome obstacles to international aid stemming, for instance, from tax exemptions and nuclear liability. the commission hopes that the kursk accident will bring about real progress in these negotiations and, in particular, strengthen the resolve of the russian authorities to conclude the agreement.

the report on the european year of lifelong learning is a document of apparently little importance, but it has revealed deep gaps and deep black spots in the european system. it was a year of dissemination and promotion, in response to the luxembourg summit and other summits which have attached great importance to training as a means of integrating europeans into the world of work, regardless of age. well, the report has shown, first of all, that when you give money to education, the money multiplies. countries eager to participate have quadrupled their budgets. i mean, the money invested in education is the one that gives the best results because it multiplies and does not produce cases of fraud or anything like that. secondly, the european year of lifelong learning has shown the commission's difficulties in providing information, in giving answers and in being transparent. it has been virtually impossible to gather all the required documentation, partly because countries do not seem to provide it and partly because there are no procedures in place to collect it with the required ease and agility. we have therefore turned the report into a response and a series of recommendations on the criteria which, in our view, must be met by continuing training. we have encountered a great confusion of criteria, partly introduced by the council, because the document published by the commission, the proposal for the year of continuing training, was of much higher quality. clearly there needs to be much more clarity for training. however, integration training, language training and training for the entertainment of the elderly are mixed with training for employment, so that the result is a confusing magma in which it is impossible to make an assessment, to know the quality and to know what the criteria for good practice are. we therefore call for the objectives of education to be regulated and clearly defined. education for the the rapporteur. - mr president, i have no doubt that in the era of new communication technologies, in the era of the internet in which we have been immersed since the beginning of this new century, legislators have a very exciting challenge: to protect people from intrusion and attacks on their privacy, their dignity or their reputation. the protection of these rights is recognised in numerous legislative texts, whether universal in nature, such as the universal declaration of human rights, transnational in nature, such as the european convention for the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms, or national, such as the constitutions of the states, but the dispersion of legislation in this area requires an effort to harmonise and unify criteria. most countries are now starting a legislative process to prevent violations of fundamental rights of individuals, such as the right to privacy, and the draft charter of fundamental rights also expressly includes this right in its eighth article. we are therefore faced with a legislative challenge of undoubted importance which must regulate respect for this right and the exceptions which in a democratic society are necessary to ensure public security, the defence of public order or the prevention of crime, as the convention for the protection of human rights says. the report i am submitting to this house is intended to analyse one of the many aspects of this legislative task. the creation of a single secretariat for the three data protection supervisory authorities of europol, schengen and customs information, within the framework of the third pillar and in the field of police and judicial cooperation in criminal matters under title vi of the treaty. the council's proposal for a decision is a good one, but in my view it is timid and lacks the necessary wording. in this sensitive area of data protection, we must achieve two fundamental objectives: the transparency of the role to be played by the future secretary and the independence of his task. i think that neither of these is fully guaranteed by the council's proposal, hence the content of the amendments i am proposing, which have been accepted almost unanimously in the committee on civil liberties. i wonder whether the existence of three common data protection authorities in the third pillar is a positive factor for transparency. i don't think it is. i therefore believe that the ultimate objective must be the creation of a single authority which responds to a single legal framework within the european union and that this single authority is provided with its own budget and staff, even by going beyond the distribution of pillars, taking advantage of the possibility offered by article 42 of the treaty on european union. this parliament, ladies and gentlemen, is currently examining and debating the consequences for the personal and economic relations of the european union of the discovery of a possible spy network called the echelon system, and is also studying a regulation on the protection of individuals in the processing of data by the community institutions. we are also now examining this proposal for the third pillar. as you will see, they are different aspects of the same problem. that is why i think that this parliament must go beyond the council's decision, which falls short, as i have said, in such matters as the election and appointment of the secretary, his dismissal or the guarantee of professional secrecy in his function. independence is the other basic element which the council's proposal does not sufficiently guarantee. the institution which must guarantee its independence is parliament through the democratic control which is its legitimate prerogative. the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for adoption, and the council will be able to accept it. let's not kid ourselves, financial independence is fundamental to ensuring functional independence. ladies and gentlemen, we are legislating on a matter which is fundamental to the future of our interpersonal, economic and commercial relations. our challenge is to balance and make compatible the right to privacy with the right to free information. the introduction of new technologies, computers and telecommunications has broken down barriers and crossed borders. we can already speak of a genuine revolution in commercial, social or personal relations which actually affect the daily life of citizens: health, advertising, banking operations, or even aspects relating to the security and defence of citizens and of the states themselves, can be disturbed if there are no rules to guarantee the correct use of the transmission, storage and storage of data which today circulate in complete freedom and which are not exempt from the serious danger posed by the indiscriminate use of them.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would first of all like to congratulate mr evans on his excellent report and once again point out the high degree of agreement we have had in analysing the whole of the reforms of community competition law and the social consequences of competition. it is true that, as a result of a proper competition policy, the greatest beneficiaries are consumers, all citizens. let us not look at this regulation as something which concerns only companies; it concerns all citizens. we also agree to assess positively the commission's attempts to modernise and reform community competition law. we must congratulate mr monti and the commission as a whole for their courage and bravery in carrying out a reform which the commission is committed to and which was initiated years ago. i have already had occasion to comment on this in other speeches, and i believe that it is not only necessary but also in the right direction. the commission's approach is a good one. after almost 40 years of application, community competition law had begun to show signs of exhaustion. there is no doubt that the competition rules contained in the treaty and secondary legislation have made a decisive contribution to the spread of a culture of competition and have been fundamental to the completion of the single market. the commission's decisions and the case law of the court of justice have also enjoyed a well-earned reputation for achieving this aim. but we must not forget that these rules were, at the outset, foreign rules in european law. the european legal tradition, especially the continental one, was more focused on aspects of unfair competition; aspects of free competition were imported from the united states. a master spanish mercantilist, professor garrigues, said very graphically that the american soldiers who came to fight in europe in the second world war brought with them in their backpacks the legislation on "antitrust". these positive aspects could not, however, hide some of the shortcomings that had traditionally been highlighted by experts. perhaps the most well-founded criticism was that the rules were too rigid. it is true that it may have been necessary to apply the rules with such rigidity in the beginning, because new rules had to be applied, imported from the united states, in accordance with the continental legal tradition. i would like to make a point of saying that it is not surprising that mr evans' assessment and concern do not exactly coincide with those of his fellow member of parliament, mr karas. mr evans acts more like an anglo-saxon jurist, whereas mr karas has shown the normal preoccupations of continental jurists. i think that this reform is more in line with anglo-saxon law and i, despite being a continental jurist, agree with it. i don't have as much concern for legal certainty as some. it is true, however, that what was acceptable twenty or thirty years ago need not be acceptable today. the internal market is now a reality and the culture of competition is widespread enough. change was therefore necessary. it is no longer possible to apply competition rules which do not take account of economic analysis and consideration of market power. the new block exemption regulations and the guidelines for their application have already been adopted in the field of vertical restraints. the time has now come to introduce the reform of horizontal restraints. in this field, the commission is now presenting us with two proposals for regulations, one on research and development agreements and the other on the regulation of specialisation agreements, together with guidelines. it should be noted, as the report does, that there is now a difference in the treatment of vertical and horizontal restrictions, since in the case of vertical restrictions there was a single regulation and guidelines covering all the possibilities covered by that regulation. in the case of horizontal restrictions, however, there are guidelines which are to a large extent broader than the two specific aspects covered by the two proposals for regulations. the group of the party of european socialists has tabled five amendments to this house which express some of our concerns. among them, i would draw attention to our concern at the lack of treatment of the crisis cartels which were included in the previous regulation and which have disappeared here without sufficient justification. i therefore ask for a vote in favour of these amendments. in short, ladies and gentlemen, as a result of the reform, the commission will be able to focus on prosecuting the behaviour of those who have market power, because it is that behaviour which is really anti-competitive and harmful to the market. we are in agreement on that point. it seems that we can finally say goodbye to the rigorousness and formalism and welcome the economic analysis in european competition law.
the commission mr president, i would first like to congratulate mr evans on the quality and importance of his report. i would also like to express the commission's appreciation for the constructive attention which parliament always pays to competition issues, which we see as an important instrument in the context of the social market economy, to which mr karas referred, and whose ultimate aim, as mr berenguer fuster has stressed, is consumer protection. mr berenguer himself has perfectly grasped the approach which the european commission intends to adopt, namely to give greater attention to economic analysis in the conduct of competition policy, but we are trying to reconcile this aspect, as requested by mr karas, mr evans and others, with the greatest possible degree of legal certainty for companies. the debate today concerns an important aspect of our attempts to modernise competition policy. the commission has drawn up, on the one hand, a review of the block exemption regulations on research and development agreements and specialisation agreements and, on the other hand, a draft guidelines on the applicability of article 81 to horizontal cooperation agreements. the commission thus sought to codify the case law and practice in this field as they have developed in the assessment of individual cases over the years, without thereby radically changing the criteria for assessing horizontal cooperation agreements under community law. the purpose of these texts is therefore to clarify the criteria for applying competition policy in this field, not to change them. i would like to stress this point because of some criticisms of the commission's proposal, which would conceal a thorough review of the approach to horizontal cooperation agreements. these are arguments that are completely unfounded. it is generally accepted that agreements between competitors are likely to restrict competition to a far greater extent than other forms of agreement. this is certainly the case with agreements between competitors to fix prices, share the market or limit production. we do not want to suggest that horizontal agreements, which have serious negative effects on competition, will be treated less strictly in the future. in the absence of fundamental restrictions, however, it is necessary to examine the agreements in their economic context in order to ascertain whether they have adverse effects on the market. what is needed is to update and clarify the rules governing horizontal agreements, for two main reasons: first, as these regulations are a response to the current economic reality, firms must react to increasing competitive pressure and adapt to a constantly changing market. cooperation can often be a way of sharing risks, making savings, sharing know-how and bringing innovations to market more quickly. cooperation is an important tool, especially for small and mediumsized enterprises. consumers will be able to benefit from these economic advantages provided that effective competition is maintained on the market. the second reason why we have revised the legislation in this area is that clarification of the rules is fundamental to our commitment to modernise competition policy, a commitment which the rapporteur, mr evans, has understood to its full extent: i am grateful to him for this, as well as for the reference to state aid, another no less important component of competition policy. the approach adopted is similar to that recently adopted in relation to vertical agreements and is mainly geared to two objectives: the commission has not yet decided whether the agreement is compatible with the common market. the commission has not yet decided whether the agreement is compatible with the common market. the motion for a resolution shows that parliament shares the objectives of this reform. the questions raised - by you and others - are extremely valuable suggestions. i can inform you today that i intend to accept most of these suggestions. in particular, i shall recommend to the college of commissioners that they follow your advice on three important points as regards block exemption regulations: first, the maximum duration of the exemption for research and development agreements should be extended beyond the current five years. however, a compromise must be struck between the interests of firms in exploiting the results of their research and the public interest in ensuring competition in new markets. i shall therefore propose that the duration of the exemption be increased from 10 to 7 years. secondly, restrictions on the parties' ability to exploit the results of jointly carried out research and development projects should be as limited as possible in order to encourage the circulation of knowledge, which is itself a function of technical and economic progress. in view of your comments, i will propose, however, that such restrictions should normally only be applied as long as they concern undertakings which are not directly competitors. thirdly, the transitional period should be extended. in this respect, the example of the block exemption regulation on vertical agreements can be followed and an eighteen-month period can be envisaged. as regards the guidelines, we will certainly be able to respond to your request for a clearer distinction between the guidelines on horizontal and vertical agreements and for greater clarity on the treatment of industrial supply agreements. the commission intends to adopt the final version of the block exemption regulations and guidelines by the end of this year. this would not only avoid a legal vacuum after the expiry of the current regulations, but would also make a substantial contribution to keeping community policy up to date. mr president, a number of other important and interesting points have been raised. i do not have time to go over all of them, but i would like to make a few comments. mr theonas, you referred to concentrations. the commission's careful exercise of its powers in merger control is certainly not lost on the commission. we strictly adhere to the rule that mergers are prohibited if they lead to the creation or strengthening of a dominant position. often this is not the case, this danger does not exist, partly because companies, aware of this need, propose remedies which are sometimes very, very effective.

commission. – on behalf of the commission, i wish to congratulate the rapporteur, mr wijkman, and the members of the conciliation delegation on having put together a compromise package which the council has already formally adopted. the commission supports the proposed regulation currently before you. it considers it a valuable instrument for carrying out strategic and pilot activities in the field of the environment. it is, of course, a supplementary instrument to the others at the disposal of the commission. fortunately, our activities in the field of environment and development are not limited to actions funded under this regulation. we are mainstreaming the environment in everything we do. hence, we intend to use it in a strategic fashion focusing, in particular, on support for the various international environmental conventions. plans to finance projects which will meet the objectives of the regulation are already advanced. once it has been formally adopted and funds made available we will proceed to finalise agreements for their implementation. however, time will be against us since we are fast approaching the end of the financial year. once more, i wish to thank parliament for their work in ensuring the passage of this regulation and the interest that many members have shown. i am confident that the regulation will provide us with a useful tool for ensuring that the environmental dimension is fully taken into account in our development cooperation.
the rapporteur. mr president, with this report on the regulation on the conservation and sustainable management of tropical and other forests in developing countries, as with the previous report by mr wijkman, parliament is today, and tomorrow with the corresponding vote, completing the exercise, for the first time, of its new powers of codecision in the field of cooperation and development. the procedure is coming to an end after a long period of time, as we have spent almost three years on first and second readings and on conciliation. as rapporteur i wish to express my satisfaction because i believe that such a long period has been fruitful, allowing us to reach agreement on the text of the regulation for which i ask the house today to vote in favour. we started from very distant positions. the main differences between parliament and the council concerned the budgetary financing of the programme, the timetable and the comitology. parliament had already proposed, in previous proceedings, a number of amendments which the council and the commission had endorsed and i must say - and it is fair to say - that the management of the previous programme by the commission, its high level of implementation and its good results have enabled the rapporteur, with the support of the committee on development, to persuade the council of the need to maintain the programme with a sufficient level of funding to ensure its success. tropical forests and their various functions and benefits for humanity can make a significant contribution to the achievement of the union's objectives, not only in terms of development and the environment, but also in its objectives of combating poverty and sustainable economic and social development. this regulation provides for the provision by the european union of appropriate financial and technical assistance to promote the conservation and sustainable management of tropical and other forests in developing countries, so that forests can fulfil their functions as generators of wealth and social development with the sustainable environmental criteria expected of them at local, national and global levels. the regulation states that sustainable forest management must seek to improve the living conditions and well-being of populations within the limits of the ecosystems' capacity, while maintaining the natural heritage and its biological diversity. this should be done by encouraging the active participation of forest-dependent populations and local communities in national policy-making and development planning. this requires better coordination and better information flow between the commission's projects - which the commission will present in the coming years - and those of the member states, so as to achieve more coherent action and thus better use of resources. in the budgetary field, we should be pleased that, after the restrictions imposed by the general plans for the reconstruction of kosovo, we can now count on an allocation of eur 249 million, based, as it were, on an initial proposal from the council of eur 9 million for a period of six years, from now until 2006. this will allow for sufficient funding to meet the objectives at least as effectively as they have been met in the period ending now. however, the different position of parliament, and especially the committee on development, with regard to the council's position on comitology is well known. we are more inclined to give the commission greater powers in this area. we have not been able to reach an agreement, because this agreement is waiting for a global approach to the problem. but at least the committee on development can be satisfied that, on this question of comitology, an agreement has been reached which makes it possible to establish the necessary budgetary forecasts and a precise timetable for keeping timely information on the strategic guidelines and priorities for the implementation of the actions for the coming years. it is, in short, a good agreement, mr president, for a good programme for the conservation of tropical forests.
commission. – on behalf of the commission, i wish to congratulate the rapporteur for his work on this regulation. i congratulate mr fernández martín and the other members of the conciliation delegation for their efforts to achieve a satisfactory conclusion on the tropical forests regulation. the commission supports the proposed text before you. as with the environment budget heading we intend to use the tropical forests budget heading strategically and in coordination with actions funded under the other instruments at the disposal of the commission. at international level i envisage this regulation to be an important tool for the community to promote the conclusions of the un intergovernmental forum on forests. this area, as has been clearly expressed in these contributions, is crucial for biodiversity, for climate, and for our conscience in handing over an earth that has these qualities to future generations. anybody who has had the thrill of being in a real tropical forest will never forget the experience and we should certainly not deny our children that. once more, i offer my congratulations to parliament for this successful conclusion and i also wish to express my appreciation for the input it has made during the first and second readings of the regulation.
the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the increase in poverty, despite the gradual growth of world gross domestic product over the last few decades, the current tendency of the member states to reduce the funds allocated to official development assistance in favour of direct investment, of which only 1% is allocated to the least developed countries - which increases the gap between these countries and the rich or developing countries - and the conviction that the process of globalisation can increase the difficulties of the poor countries, are all factors which highlight the urgent need to improve the effectiveness of development cooperation policies. we are also far from achieving the desirable standards in terms of democracy and respect for human rights: coups d'état, violence, wars and violations of human rights are still part of the reality of the least developed countries and we must therefore help to correct them. in this context, it is essential to strengthen the complementarity of the development cooperation policies pursued by the community and the member states. firstly, because complementarity allows the synergy resulting from a coordinated approach to the actions to be carried out, not only by the european union but by all international donors, to be exploited, which will improve the impact of these actions. secondly, because it allows an added value to be added to the member states' interventions, which will help to optimise the resources allocated to development aid and to achieve better results. thirdly, because it makes the european union more visible and its development policy more credible, which will help it to exercise the political influence that it deserves as the main donor - let us remember that between half and two thirds of development aid comes from the european union - an influence that both non-governmental organisations and the beneficiary countries would like to see more emphasized given the european union's greater sensitivity to social justice and human development. finally, the reinforcement of complementarity is important because the treaty on european union clearly states that the member states and the community must coordinate their development cooperation policies and agree on their aid programmes. the commission's communication on the complementarity of community and member states' policies in the field of development cooperation should therefore be welcomed, since the measures proposed therein can help to remove the obstacles to significant progress in this field. in general terms, the committee on development and i myself agree with the main lines of the document and with the measures proposed in it. however, i would like to make a few clarifications: firstly, i think that the commission should have taken into account that complementarity is not an isolated element, but must be considered in the context of an overall strategy which also covers the issue of coordination and coherence, since coherence is inseparable from coordination and complementarity, and without coordination there is no possible complementarity. i therefore believe that, in order to really improve the impact of european development policies and to ensure the credibility of the union, it would have been much more appropriate and enlightening to have dealt with these aspects together in the framework of the communication on development policy, as this would have made it possible to highlight more clearly the inseparable and essential nature of these elements for the formulation of a development policy in line with the objectives of the union. the second point concerns the very concept of complementarity, which should not be understood as a precautionary principle to preserve the competence of the member states in this field, but as the manifestation of a political will to join efforts to improve and better contribute to the achievement of the objectives of development cooperation policy. the need to ensure the unity, consistency and effectiveness of the union's external action, which is also laid down in the treaty, must also be extended to development policies, since they form an integral part of the union's external action. the commission should therefore take the initiative and make a qualitative leap in this direction in order to enable the european union to design the strategic priorities of the european union in the field of development aid. thirdly, i must say that measures to strengthen complementarity alone will hardly produce the desired results. this requires, as a precondition, the political will of the council to move towards greater integration in cooperation, because what has prevented progress in the field of complementarity has been above all the fact that member states define their development cooperation policies more in terms of their geostrategic and economic interests and their colonial past than in terms of the union's development objectives. finally, it must be stressed that, beyond the operational measures to improve the management of the programmes, with which - as i have already said - the committee on development agrees in principle, we believe that the commission should assume the responsibility for reflection and proposals, an indispensable requirement to enable the union to direct aid not only to promote the economic growth of the beneficiary countries but also to ensure that this growth reaches all sections of the population, thus assuming its commitment to the development of peoples and, consequently, its commitment to peace, since without development peace will always be a precarious good. in any case, and as a summary, i would like to stress the timeliness of this communication - although we would have liked it to be part of an overall package - and to indicate the appropriateness of the measures which, together with the measures also proposed by the committee on development in my report, we hope will help to steer action towards better operational management. in any case, it should be stressed once again that the council must show political will, without which we will hardly be able to put the principle of complementarity into practice.

mr president, the good report presented to us today by my compatriot mrs ferrer responds to a problem which has been discussed on numerous occasions and at the same time to the urgent need to solve it and to open up new perspectives in the relations between a united europe and the third world. the problem i am referring to is the one which represents the marked lack of synchronisation and coordination in policy and action in the field of development cooperation between the european union and its member states on the one hand, and between each of those same states on the other. what has been described and denounced by many authoritative voices and, in particular, by organizations working in this field - but also by our own parliament - is that over the years the various member states have been acting, in the field of cooperation, each in its own way, often responding to their own national visions and interests, sometimes more confessional and sometimes less, but in any case without any significant effort, not even mutual information and even less coordination, coherence, distribution of roles. in short, there has been no effort to rationalize and to make it more efficient so that the limited resources available are not wasted but are used to the best possible effect. nor has there been until very recently the effort required to ensure that community policy in this area is reasonably coordinated with that which has been pursued by each of the 15 member states, although this is certainly not exclusive to the field in question. it was quite regrettable to see how community action was being taken here, which sometimes did not even take into account the knowledge of what was being done in each of the member states for each of the countries or sectors concerned. the result was and largely still is the dispersion of performances, the overlap of many of them, if not the duplication and even the contradiction of what we did to each other. a nonsense, then, and a disaster. this situation was naturally unsustainable and a further problem to be solved, but the need for it has become even more evident and more urgent when the very process of european construction, reforms and progress of the union itself make it essential to act on the international scene with one voice, as one country, when the implementation of a common foreign and security policy appears as an unassailable priority for the viability of our very project. in our view, what we can do from europe in the field of development cooperation is only a substantial part of this common foreign and security policy. this is what mrs ferrer has said, whose report already emphasizes the key concept of complementarity in the title. of course, this is not the first time we have commission nor the council has dared to do: to engage in a realistic debate on the substance, on consumer protection in the 21st century, not consumer protection in the 19th century, nor in the 20th century, with all the interested parties and taking into account all the interests involved. when we look at the history of this dossier, we see that the commission, in making its proposal, has simply taken up a draft revision of the brussels convention drawn up - before the entry into force of the treaty of amsterdam, that is to say, when this was an intergovernmental matter, very close to public international law - by a committee of experts. moreover, mr president, this committee has worked alone, without any transparency, without interministerial consultations and without consulting the media concerned. it is clear that the council of justice expected, in view of the weak institutional powers of this parliament in this area, even after amsterdam, that the final adoption of the regulation by the council would be a mere formality. the council's apparent refusal to open a debate on this question explains why parliament has been under all kinds of pressure in recent times. after more than a year of discussion in the committee on legal affairs i can simply say that the arguments against your report are unfounded and are the result of intimidation or demagogy rather than substantive reasoning. let's look at it briefly. some are trying to politicize the debate, hoping that this will lead to a right-left split, and to take the consumer hostage, saying that the report would be against consumer protection. it is an argument as demagogic as it is unjustified, which is based in the end on an outdated, ineffective protection, which is also based on a nationalist perspective and is contrary to the construction of europe. the solutions adopted are much more protective than those proposed by the commission or - i disagree with mrs wallis - than those presented to the house, which in reality limit protection only to consumers targeted or targeted by a website, by a company. pseudo-legal arguments have also been put forward, such as an alleged incompatibility with the unfair terms directive or with the case law of the court of justice. there is no incompatibility with either of them and let me quote the report which was distributed by the directorate-general sanco on 20 september 1999, which states, and i quote in french because it is the only original that exists: 'les clauses attributives sont donc possibles et licites, au titre de cette proposition, pour autant que certaines conditions soient garanties. it is therefore important that the consumer be clearly informed before the contract is concluded. 'that is precisely why, mr president, the committee on legal affairs has laid down strict requirements for transparency. it is therefore not true that this report goes against a purported community achievement. finally, and perhaps the most cynical of the arguments, it says: 'well, this puts small and mediumsized businesses in a difficult position, but they must be sure.' it is as if we said: "there are no firemen in the villages or in the towns. we must make good legislation that is balanced for all. finally, i disagree with mrs wallis, despite having shared this adventure with her, on her solution, because i think that in the end her solution is no more consumer-friendly, since it is limited to protecting the consumer to whom a company has addressed itself. between an active or passive site, between a directed and an undirected activity, a lawyer could be "paddling the partridge" for years and years with whatever jurisdiction might be applicable. in conclusion, mr president, i think that in this area of judicial cooperation parliament must send a clear signal to the council and the commission that it will not allow itself to be discarded or manipulated by dogmatic arguments which represent purely nationalist interests. on the contrary, parliament, thanks to its in-depth work, has a great opportunity here to show that pragmatic and reasonable solutions can be found to rebalance this proposal, and that is, whatever the outcome of the plenary session tomorrow.
