the rapporteur. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, two dangers threaten the health of members of the european parliament: heart attacks and attacks of modesty. i hope, therefore, that you will forgive me if i omit the second and call my brief report very important and congratulate myself on the success achieved, almost unexpectedly, with the commission and the council. the report was unanimously adopted by the committee on budgets a few weeks ago and no amendments have been tabled to date. so it is to be expected that thursday will, in principle, pass with ease. however, let me explain some of its basic elements. the proposal i ask you to sign by voting in favour of the report is the culmination of a long process and satisfies an almost age-old aspiration of parliament. since 1985 - i say 1985 - parliament's committee on budgets has been working to ensure that the european parliament's procedures take account of the financial impact of resolutions voted by the house. and already, on that distant date, 15 years ago, a working group was set up for that purpose. we also ask the council - we do not know how successful it will be - to adopt a similar approach. although the council, in its decision of 24 june 1988 on budgetary discipline, established a link between legislation and financing which was later incorporated into the ec treaty as article 270, i will admit that even the council itself has not been diligent in complying with that decision. what's the matter, gentlemen? i think it can be said that the fundamental problem is the enormous growth of the legislative work of the union as a whole, above all the exponential growth of legislative co-decision, the multiplicity of legislative decisions taken in parallel. so far, in accordance with the rules in force, the commission has sent us a financial statement with its own-initiative proposals, which basically includes a multiannual proposal for the budgetary programming corresponding to the proposal. however, as is well known, the human race is divided into two classes: the budgetary and the rest. that is why, when the foreign ministers meet and take any laudable decision, such as helping kosovo or serbia, the last of their concerns is whether there is money to finance that decision and whether it should be taken from another heading, such as development aid in africa, meda or the promotion of human rights in the former soviet union. it is the problem of the cars proposal, for example, which is on the table these days. and when there is a legislative consultation on social, cultural or environmental matters - the commissioner will admit that i am right - we, the budget commissioner, the finance ministers and the members of the budget committee, come together to pray together so that no financial misconduct is committed. the agreement reached in july extends the information contained in the financial statement. from now on, any new proposal must be accompanied by an estimate of its compatibility with the financial perspective and its organisational needs. the commission is implicitly required to consider at the start of the legislative procedure whether it has the required manpower and whether the proposal may need a revision of the financial perspective or a redeployment of programmes already approved. in short, a cost-opportunity analysis. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. and the poor execution of some of them is due to or justified by insufficient staffing. commissioner patten proposes to reduce the amount of meda and at the same time increase its staffing by 25 posts. it is the paradigmatic example of what we are trying to avoid a priori. we shall therefore also be amending our rules of procedure to take account of this agreement. we believe that this declaration should be included in the interinstitutional agreement, but i would point out to the honourable members that it only makes sense in the context of an interinstitutional agreement with financial perspectives. i would like to thank the other institutions for their diligence in the preparation of this joint declaration. parliament reiterated its suggestion in a tripartite dialogue held in the middle of the portuguese presidency and culminating in an agreement at the first conciliation meeting chaired by france in july. this is a real record, and i hope that it will now be translated into a better forecast of the financial framework for our legislative activity. - doc. a5-0279/2000 by mrs paciotti, on behalf of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs, on the proposal for a european parliament and council regulation on the protection of individuals with regard to the processing of personal data by the community institutions and bodies and on the free movement of such data (com (99) 337 - c5-0149/1999 - 1999/0153 (cod))
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial interests are protected. - mr president, the rapporteur, mrs sudre, has done a good job in her report on the outermost regions. on behalf of the committee on legal affairs and the internal market, i should like to thank you for the way in which you have incorporated our amendments and views in the spirit and in the concrete text. the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for adoption. the attempt to establish a completely uniform legal order for these outermost regions, which are separated from the rest of the community territory, from the mainland, by thousands of kilometres and which are divided into small island regions with very difficult conditions for capital formation and transport, prevents the application of the general rules of competition. i therefore draw attention to paragraph 21 of mrs sudre's report, which states that, with regard to state aid, the application of article 87 (3) (a) of the ec treaty should be automatic, because the reason for the differences in that paragraph is the aim of achieving equality in the competition regime. only a general derogation for the outermost regions would put them on an equal footing with the companies in the continental core. i should also point out that the report by mrs sudre refers to the need for special tax and customs arrangements for the same reasons. when regions are so far from the mainland, to seek automatic application of the tax rules, customs rules and rules which apply in the mainland would put these outermost regions at a disadvantage. for example, in the field of transport, in paragraph 26, the application of the state aid rules to the ports and airports regime in a free competition system would mean depriving these regions of an essential public service such as ports and airports, which in the outermost regions would never be a normal private activity but an essential public service activity. the commission has sent a communication, which is a programme, a kind of timetable of what is to be done. we expect the commission to develop this calendar or programme and, above all, we expect that the great institution which the commission has at the moment, the inter-services group, will continue to be in contact with the outermost regions, informing the central authorities of our specific needs and problems. i therefore congratulate mrs sudre and look forward with great interest to the normative development of the commission's proposals so that the specificities can soon be taken into account, as provided for in article 299 (2) of the treaty of amsterdam.
mr president, for the european union this is one more debate than the many we have. for the outermost regions, this is the most important debate that the european parliament can have on them. in fact, what we say here today and vote tomorrow will be front page news in the press of the seven outermost regions and the news on regional television will broadly report on what we say and decide here. for many europeans, some of the outermost regions are just a tourist destination on the map. even for some of our colleagues in the european parliament, this may be their idea of the outermost regions. for those of us who are speaking here tonight on behalf of our home regions, this idea is very negative and, of course, profoundly wrong. the idea behind this, beyond our landscape and exceptional climate, is the social and economic reality of some of the least developed regions in the union, with the highest unemployment rates, with enormous structural difficulties that hamper our development. for more than a decade, the european commission has been sensitive to our problems and our particularities. this is the first debate on our regions in the european parliament's plenary after the treaty of amsterdam introduced a new article on our regions. the commission's proposal for a regulation on the establishment of a european agency for the evaluation of medicinal products for human use is a very good one. the commission's document on the implementation of article 299 (2) of the ec treaty is a good document and our rapporteur, mrs sudre, has done well in presenting an excellent report today. with this article and the rules which are being drawn up to develop it, we have a legal basis which we have not had until now and a good instrument for our development. mrs sudre has succeeded in producing a balanced report which incorporates many of the more than 100 amendments which were tabled to her initial draft report. one of those amendments proposes the development and implementation of the policies of the financial instrument for fisheries guidance. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial instruments are used to the full, and i am sure that the commission will take the necessary steps to ensure that the community's financial instruments are used to the full. the internal market and the rules governing it do not benefit the outermost regions as much as the mainland europeans. the natural limitations of our island markets, thousands of miles apart, make it difficult for our companies to be competitive: problems of transport, communications, supplies, operating costs. that is why we have such difficulty in generating wealth and creating jobs. our unemployment rates are among the highest in the union. it is therefore necessary to develop a series of measures which are detailed in the margie sudre report. we believe that these measures must go beyond regional development policies because our deficits and handicaps are structural and not cyclical. we will always be far away and we will always have difficulties arising from our insularity, from our beautiful but hard and difficult geography. we're not asking for grants. we want to have tools that allow us to develop. the outermost regions give europe an atlantic, american and african dimension, enriching our cultural, political and economic diversity, of which we are all rightly proud.
the commission has already done so. it is not disputed that, as mrs sudre rightly points out in her very good and detailed report, the outermost regions have five characteristics which will lead to a permanent or very long-term disadvantage. firstly, the geographical proximity to non-eu countries while at the same time belonging to the european union. secondly, the relative isolation due to the great distance from europe. thirdly, the small size of the local internal market. fourthly, geographical and climatic conditions which are very much in opposition to the development of endogenous potentials. fifthly, the economic dependence on a few products in the economy. this inevitably means that these objective disadvantages are only to be compensated for in the longer term in the interests of cohesion if the necessary financial resources are provided for this purpose on the basis of article 299 (2). this article should enable the outermost regions to avoid being subject to permanent budget cuts in the budget debate. as you, mrs sudre, as the representative of the outermost regions, rightly call for solidarity, i also ask for your solidarity with the interests of the objective 1 regions in the sense that no cuts in funding should be made as long as disadvantages in comparison with the developed european regions persist. the test is whether we want to meet new political needs not with fresh money but at the expense of policies which have not yet been worked out, contrary to the approval of the procedure expressed by most of the groups in the budget debate today. this question is becoming more relevant as the eu's enlargement to the east gets closer. i am convinced that it is already clear today that this problem cannot be solved without a change in the financial perspective. let us simply follow the saying: "don't put off until tomorrow what you can do today".

make a major contribution to the health protection of our citizens as well as to the restoration and maintenance of consumer confidence in food safety. european consumers have every right to expect the highest achievable food safety standards and our ambition is to develop systems that deliver this. a food safety chain from farm to fork, correctly regulated and effectively controlled, is the road to building high levels of confidence in the european food supply. in this respect the commission is already hard at work on its programme of legislative reform set out in the white paper. authority is conceived as a point of scientific excellence at the service of the community in its broadest sense: consumers, the institutions and member states alike. the food authority will also need to be visible to the general public and be the authoritative voice in matters relating to the scientific aspects of food safety in europe. the commission intends to adopt a proposal for a regulation establishing the overarching principles and objectives of food law, which will provide the framework for future health protection measures relating to food. this proposal will put forward the establishment of a european food safety agency which will provide the community with advice on scientific and technical issues and thereby enable the commission to give effect to the general principles of food law. our intention is to adopt this proposal in the commission on 8 november 2000. this schedule continues to reflect the importance the commission attaches to the matter and is - doc. a5-286/2000 by mrs bonino, on behalf of the committee on foreign affairs, human rights, common security and defence policy, on the proposal for a european parliament and council regulation on the control of anti-personnel mines (com (2000) 111 - c5-0158/2000 - 2000/0062 (cod)); and the following oral questions :- b5-0544/2000 by mr miranda, on behalf of the committee on development and cooperation, to the commission, on anti-personnel mines; - b5-0545/2000 by mr brok, on behalf of the committee on foreign affairs, human rights, common security and defence policy, to the commission, on anti-personnel mines.
- mr president, i am glad that there is finally european legislation, in the form of a regulation, on anti-personnel mines and that we have a good report from mrs bonino on it today. as has been said, in the previous parliament the european parliament endorsed the european union's commitment to combat one of the most cruel, deadly and cowardly weapons in existence. the committee on development and cooperation introduced in 1996 - as mr patten has said - a budget line devoted to demining. but unfortunately, that line is shrinking in inverse proportion to the emphasis we are putting on this issue here. since we are now approving the budget, i shall dwell for a moment on the figures which concern me. this year we have counted on 8,100,000 euros. for next year the council and the commission agree to reduce the amount to 7.4 million and parliament proposes an increase of 3 million compared with 2000. these numbers are not much to solve a problem that affects 110 million people in 64 countries, 26,000 victims of mutilation a year, and, fundamentally, many children who are known in countries like el salvador as broken children, because they are children who are torn apart, without hands, without arms, without legs. i therefore ask that the council, which is not here, and the commission be made aware of the importance of increasing this quantity, since for every mine removed, unfortunately, between 20 and 50 new mines are planted. at the rate of elimination we are doing, it would take - as has been said before - well over 100 years to clear the planet of antipersonnel mines. i therefore ask that the amount proposed by parliament be taken into account, even if it is insufficient, and that this should contribute to respect for the ottawa convention and i ask those countries which have not signed or ratified it to do so.

mr president, the new cooperation agreement signed in cotonou is an ideal opportunity to correct the shortcomings of the previous phase and to clarify concepts and rules of action in specific situations of our cooperation with the acp states, for example in the situation which gave rise to the commission communication in this case and to the reports by mr van hecke and mr maes, that is to say, what must happen when an associated country is involved in an armed conflict. in line with what the rapporteurs have said, we feel that the union must review its programmes of assistance to countries at war, among other reasons, to prevent the funds allocated from being diverted to military activities. even as a matter of principle, support for countries or regimes that are responsible for armed adventures in neighbouring states or that spend disproportionate resources on armaments, when not on operations to suppress the rights of individuals or minorities within their own population, must be reconsidered. we must bear in mind article 11 of the new treaty, which affirms europe's commitment to policies for peacebuilding and the prevention and settlement of armed conflicts. dialogue between the parties to the conflict and the union's dialogue with those parties should be the key mechanism for such action. we are also concerned about the paradoxical behaviour of the union in approving aid worth millions of euros to countries which are clearly engaged in military occupation of one of their neighbours. in this respect, the double standards with which aid policy is sometimes applied are unacceptable and we are also concerned about the contradictions that may arise in the actions of member states, or some of them, and the union itself. i think that parliament should have more transparency, more coherence, more information and more control over these policies. finally, let us remember that often the reduction or freezing of our development aid to a particular country at war would require an additional effort in humanitarian aid to the populations of the country itself, the main victims of such conflicts. here again, the intervention of solvent ngos will be essential, through which such programmes could be carried out with guarantees of success and effectiveness.

line will, in any case, be defined by the real political will of member states to stick to a common line. the commission cannot promise parliament miracles in this field. we are prepared to broaden deliberations to other countries involved in armed conflicts. violent conflict is not a phenomenon limited to acp countries. the european union must be prepared to react to violence in an efficient and coherent manner in other regions of the globe too. the communication is an invitation to engage in a debate about eu relations with countries for which the traditional form of development cooperation has become questionable or obsolete. this is a difficult debate. we would prefer to devote all our efforts to assisting the acp countries in the difficult task of overcoming poverty and of integrating into a rapidly changing global economy. however, for a considerable number of our acp partners, the major challenge is the restoration of peace, or the containment of regional destabilisation. peace is an indispensable precondition to development, and countries that remain entangled in violent conflict exclude themselves from the potential benefits of the new cooperation relationship the eu is offering them. they are also depriving themselves of the opportunities of the ongoing transformation of the global economy. they contaminate the prospect of foreign investment, not only in these countries, but also in their regions. in less unstable countries, our efforts to fight poverty and provide debt relief are contributing to conflict prevention in the longer term. the commission has not been idle since submitting the communication. it has already taken numerous initiatives aimed at strengthening its capacities for effectively addressing the problem of violent conflicts in acp countries. support is given to the oau and sub-regional organisations such as ecowas and igadd in the areas of conflict prevention and management. it is remarkable how much funding is committed for the management of crises or for post-conflict reconstruction. we are committed to stepping up our efforts for effectively preventing violence and for resolving crises peacefully. the community has a great number of instruments available for conflict prevention and resolution, ranging from trade and cooperation agreements to support for institutional capacity building, for strengthening respect for human and minority rights or for demobilisation and rehabilitation. we are committed to making even more effective and targeted use of these instruments. in this context we are aiming in particular to introduce conflict prevention objectives into the programming of economic and development assistance programmes. the problem is, however, that the rigid character of these instruments is in itself a limitation to what we can do and how we can use them. budget line limitations and comitology-based decision-making procedures limit our options for flexible and quick reaction. all this looks very different from the toolbox concept, which is what i think of when we talk about the numerous instruments that are available. the toolbox concept provides a good image of the ideal situation and a satisfactory way of making use of the diversity of instruments. however, we find ourselves in a different situation even though we are making determined reform efforts. i would add that the basic value of development cooperation in relation to the issue of conflicts is the preventive effect. our hands are not so strong once conflict has actually broken out; we can make more meaningful efforts beforehand. there is no doubt whatsoever that the hipc initiative, funded by the eu but not yet funded by the us, is making the biggest contribution to conflict prevention in the world right now. there is little doubt that the very poor, highly indebted countries will plunge into instability and conflict if the rich world does not deliver on hipc. also the creation of regional economic cooperation, as provided for in the cotonou agreement makes a basic contribution to stability in africa. in the next few years we will give top priority to the creation of regional stability and cooperation structures as a major contribution to the promotion of peace and progress in africa. i should say a few words on the situation in the ivory coast, in view of what has been said in this debate. unfortunately there has been a rapid deterioration in the situation since the elections on sunday. it is changing almost from hour to hour, but we are of course following events very closely. we anticipate that we will have to reopen the article 96 consultations if a situation of stability and clarity is not established following the election. this is really a situation that is highly regrettable and we fear there will be even more violence if things are not brought under control quite rapidly.
commission. – this parliament and, for what it is worth, this commissioner, have been long-standing opponents of the death penalty. speaking for myself, i voted consistently against it when i was a member of another parliament. one of the first decisions that i took when i was governor of hong kong, with the support of organisations like amnesty and human rights watch, was to take the death penalty off the statute book of hong kong and i am delighted that it remains off the statute book. parliament has declared in the past that it considers capital punishment an inhuman, medieval form of punishment and unworthy of modern societies. i know that many people would echo that sentiment. i am pleased that all central and eastern european countries which are candidates for membership of the union have abolished the death penalty. we are moving towards a europe in which the death penalty is outlawed continent-wide. the european union is opposed to the death penalty in all circumstances and has agreed to campaign for its universal abolition. that stance is rooted in our belief in the inherent dignity of all human beings and in the inviolability of the human person. in my case, my opposition to the death penalty is also rooted in my belief in the sanctity of human life. some 87 states retain the death penalty and about 30 carry out executions in any given year. one or two states carry out executions in industrial quantities. the european union has been for some time now actively seeking a global moratorium. the union has defined a set of guidelines for identifying circumstances in which the european union can take specific, targeted action. these guidelines specify that the european union will encourage states to accede to the second optional protocol of the convention on civil and political rights and comparable regional mechanisms aimed at the abolition of the death penalty. we will also raise the issue of the death penalty in multilateral forums. the european union shares the deep concern of all those opposed to the death penalty, that it is impossible to reduce to zero the risk of applying the penalty in error. that risk, the risk of taking innocent life, is reason enough in the view of many of us to outlaw it as a punishment. nor do we accept the argument that the death penalty is a deterrent to violent crime since in our countries the evidence simply does not support that claim. in countries which maintain the death penalty, the european union aims at the progressive restriction of its scope and respect for the strict conditions set out in several international human rights instruments under which capital punishment may be used, as well as at the establishment of a moratorium on executions, so as to eliminate completely the death penalty. during the presidencies of finland and portugal, the european union raised the issue of the death penalty with a host of countries including the authorities in antigua and barbuda, burundi, the bahamas, china, guyana, india, iran, kyrgyzstan, the palestinian authority, pakistan, the philippines, tajikistan, thailand, trinidad and tobago, turkey, the united arab emirates, the united states, uzbekistan, the yemen and zimbabwe. in the case of china, we used the forum of our dialogue on human rights to press the issue time and again. i regret that china continues to make almost daily use of the death penalty. the european union is especially concerned about the imposition of the death penalty on young people below 18 years of age at the time of the commission of the crime. the european approach to juvenile justice is consistent with internationally recognised juvenile justice standards as enshrined in the international human rights instruments. i said at the outset that the european union had decided to raise the issue of the death penalty in multilateral fora. this has not always been simple. the house will recall that following intensive negotiation, we decided at last year's un general assembly in november that no resolution was better than a fatally flawed text and that therefore the european union should not pursue its initiative in the united nations general assembly. this april's un commission on human rights resolution was, however, adopted with a clear majority, i am extremely pleased to say. it would seem that while the hard-line retentionists are resigned to further commission on human rights texts on this issue, they will continue to resist strongly any efforts to secure a general assembly resolution. this would lead to further divisive debate. as a result the european union has decided that it would not be either advisable or timely to table a resolution on the death penalty at unga 55. in the meantime we continue to support campaigns designed to achieve a moratorium on the death penalty and executions, and eventually the abolition of capital punishment throughout the world. we do so under the budget lines that fall under the chapter "european initiative for democracy and human rights". in particular under budget line b7-704 we are pursuing a number of initiatives throughout the world designed to mobilise public opinion against the death penalty. in 1999 a joint programme was established between the commission and the council of europe to raise public awareness about various themes related to the abolition of the death penalty in russia, turkey, albania and ukraine. the programme, worth over eur 670 000 over two years, will provide information to parliamentarians, to legal experts and to the general public on the penal policy arguments against capital punishment. let me repeat, this is a subject we take seriously. it is a subject which i personally take extremely seriously. we speak on it as a union with a degree of moral authority. we are making progress. but it will take time and persistence as well as the continued advocacy of this parliament if we are to attain one day our goal, which is to see the death penalty consigned to the history books as a form of punishment which has absolutely no place in the modern world. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, first of all i would like to add my congratulations to those which the rapporteur has received for these two excellent reports. i would like to make a few comments on the report by mr de gucht, which i think is very important. with regard to the second report, i believe that emissions trading should be approached as an instrument to facilitate compliance with the obligations of the kyoto protocol. this flexibility mechanism can be approached in a variety of ways: expectant, reactive or active. i think that from both an economic and an environmental point of view we must take an active approach. the reasons for this include the realistic view that this will allow the achievement of short-term environmental objectives by setting concrete reduction levels as well as compliance timetables. it is also an opportunity to encourage research and development of new technologies in pollution control, contrary to the opinion of those who believe that this mechanism is a way to perpetuate the interests of large polluting companies. if this tool is applied correctly, pollution will become more and more expensive, and the market will take care of leaving out products obtained in the least clean way. the fact that emissions are traded also gives greater control over emissions and documentation. this will encourage the development of activities with a lower environmental impact. it is essential to develop this mechanism in a transparent manner and as an indivisible part of the package of measures to be taken by the member states within the european strategy to combat climate change. in this connection, all member states should make a great effort to communicate with the public so that from the outset it is clear what objectives are pursued by this mechanism and what its benefits are, which are always partial and complementary to other types of measures. this way there will be no misinterpretations.
- mr president, as some speakers have already pointed out, in the tragic coincidence of this debate - and i congratulate the rapporteur, mr moreira da silva, on his report - nature was reminding us of the consequences of climate change. in northern italy and also in the area where i live - the mediterranean coast of spain - nature was once again unleashing its wrath and causing loss of human life, loss of property, of farms, of factories, etc. on our coast, on the mediterranean coast of spain, this is the product of a phenomenon called the cold drop, caused by the warming of the waters of the mediterranean, which produces a rise in water vapor which, when colliding with the cold layers of the stratosphere, produces these large precipitations. it is true that it usually takes place in the autumn months, but it is also true that these series previously occurred every 15 or 20 years, whereas today they occur practically every year and at least every three or four years with tragic consequences. is this a consequence of the greenhouse effect and climate change or not? although experts cannot guarantee it with all the scientific evidence, i believe it is a reality. so we have to remedy this situation. it is true that the measures contained in the kyoto protocol, to which the report we are discussing today refers, are not going to produce results in the short term, but it is also true that men must try to solve the problems they are causing. other causes - also caused by human greed - such as the construction of streams and torrents, which further exacerbate the damaging effects of these natural disasters, are also linked to this greenhouse effect. that is why i am also one of the signatories of a motion for a resolution which proposes not only the rapid implementation of the measures contained in the kyoto protocol to combat climate change, but also other types of preventive measures, the continuation and deepening of infrastructure construction, for example, by preventing the effects of floods and, finally, also aid for all those affected, since they are not responsible for the short- or long-term damage caused by human speculation and greed.
commission. – first i would like to express my appreciation for the parliament response to the commission communication on a community strategy for endocrine disrupters and for the work of the rapporteur, mr lund. there is hardly any conference on the topic of chemicals that does not touch on the subject of endocrine disrupters. one of the reasons for this is the significant potential damage that such substances can cause to animals and human beings and, most importantly, to the unborn foetus and our reproductive capacity. it is difficult to imagine a more unsustainable trend than one that would lead to deterioration in our capacity to reproduce. the area of endocrine disrupters is a complex one where there are still many questions to be answered. there are certain things we know. for some we can make predictions with confidence and others where we are faced with considerable uncertainty. what we do know is that a number of man-made chemicals that have been released into the environment, as well as a few natural ones, have the potential to disrupt the endocrine system of animals, including humans. among these are persistent bio-accumulative compounds that include some pesticides and industrial chemicals as well as other synthetic products. many wildlife populations are already affected by these compounds. there are adequate quantitative data showing a causal link between exposure to these substances and a reduction in reproductive success in wildlife. there are also some general conclusions that have been drawn by the research community such as the fact that the chemicals concerned have entirely different effects, as mr arvidsson said, on embryos, foetuses and perinatal organisms than on adults and that effects are more often manifested in offspring, rather than in a parent that has suffered exposure. however, there are also many uncertainties since the nature and extent of the effects of exposure on humans are not well established. information is limited, especially on concentrations of contamination in embryos. the need for further examination of the potential risks of such substances to fill the knowledge gaps so we can take appropriate action is the very reason why i presented the proposal for a community strategy for endocrine disrupters. all of us have the right to know and the obligation to learn. let me turn to the key elements of the strategy. the basis for it is the precautionary principle. i am pleased that parliament supports the commission objective to identify appropriate policy action on the basis of the precautionary principle in order to respond quickly and effectively to the problem of endocrine disruption. this principle and the need to develop quick and effective risk management strategies in relation to endocrine disrupters was also stressed by the environmental council in its conclusions of 30 march. at the same time, parliament perceives a lack of ambition in the commission strategy concerning the need to reduce human exposure to endocrine disrupters and protect wildlife. this i would like to address at the outset with a number of comments. there are two core components of the commission strategy. one is further research and development and the other is the development of agreed test methods. regarding research and development, the commission's main instrument is the fifth framework programme on research and development. i am pleased to inform you that endocrine disruption has been highlighted as a priority research topic in the latest revision of the relevant programmes concerning human health and the environment. the commission is also planning a dedicated call for proposals on endocrine disruption which will serve to further reinforce endocrine disruption research. the recommendations in the parliament motion for a resolution will be taken into account. regarding the development of agreed test methods, this will require a two-to-four year horizon. agreement on test methods aims to ensure that everyone involved agrees that the tests designed to detect the right elements and the test results can be interpreted in a uniform way. without such agreement we will constantly be faced, not just with scientific uncertainty but with opposing views on the science. for this reason we believe that legislative action to reduce exposure in a comprehensive manner, on the basis of the precautionary principle, can be considered only when agreed test methods are available. agreed test methods are also necessary to launch a comprehensive exercise in the search for substitutes. otherwise, possible substitutes may be open to the same suspicion as the substances they replace. at the same time we need to take into account existing scientific evidence. that is why we make provision in the short term to act without agreed test methods on the basis of the precautionary principle and on a case-by-case basis. parliament supports the commission objective to identify a first set of endocrine disrupting substances by the end of this year and to identify specific cases of consumer use and eco-system exposure for special action without awaiting further tests. an analysis of existing legal instruments relating to endocrine disrupters will also be part of this exercise. let me make two comments on this. first, the commission objective of the end of 2000 is based on a two-step process: firstly a candidate list compiled by consultants and secondly prioritisation. commission adoption of a proposal for prioritisation will follow. so far, only the candidate list has been completed. the second step of this exercise involves consultation with stakeholders in which we aim to achieve as wide a consensus as possible on priority substances. i cannot give a commitment now that all 553 candidate substances will be on the priority list without pre-empting the outcome of the stakeholders' discussions, which are under way. the scientific committee as well as industry have been critical of the candidate list, the bkh report. in contrast, initial comments received from member states and ngos indicate support for the report as a valid starting point. the scientific committee's criticisms of the scientific shortcomings of the report will be addressed in the next stages of prioritisation and further evaluation. i would like to add here that some of the criticisms are based on the false assumption that a group of 60 substances identified in this report will be the priority substances. these substances are in fact part of a candidate list of 553 substances on which discussions on priorities are still under way. it is also important to bear in mind that the list to be established must be a dynamic one. new substances can be added or indeed initial substances removed as new evidence comes to light. my second comment in relation to the priority list of substances concerns the request in the motion for a resolution for a decision on intervention on specific cases by mid-2001. in order to identify specific cases for special action from the priority list, a more in-depth evaluation will be required on consumer uses and eco-system exposure. in addition, the role of the scientific committees in providing independent scientific advice will be crucial in these specific cases. it is ambitious to expect to achieve these goals in six months. however, we will use our best endeavours to work as quickly as possible. finally, as you are aware, the commission intends to present a white paper on the overall chemicals policy by the end of this year. we are working on that right now and i have seen the first drafts. one of the fundamental principles for this policy is to ensure a high level of protection. clearly the endocrine disrupting strategy must be consistent with the overall policy on chemicals. a number of specific elements in parliament's motion for a resolution, such as the shifting of the burden of proof, a redefinition of the responsibility of manufacturers, a review of labelling legislation and grouping of chemicals for screening and testing, must be and are being addressed in the context of this overall chemicals policy. the views of parliament expressed in the motion for a resolution will be taken into account in the white paper under preparation. finally, regarding international cooperation and information exchange, the commission is organising a workshop on endocrine disrupters in the first half of 2001 with the sponsorship of the world health organisation among others. this workshop will convene all stakeholders to take stock of progress and make further recommendations on the development of test methods and testing strategy, research and the establishment of monitoring programmes. i should again like to thank parliament for its support in addressing this issue and i would like to underline the commission's commitment to implementation of its strategy and to taking on board the elements of the parliament motion for a resolution in a comprehensive way.
the rapporteur. madam president, the commission has put forward a proposal which, under the guise of technical adjustment, conceals new budgetary restrictions for a sector which is already discriminated against within the common agricultural policy. in recent years, the evolution of the euro-dollar parity and other circumstances have brought the level of aid down to half of the level it was four years ago. the commission's proposal is to stabilise aid at the reduced level and to grant aid directly to producer organizations, thus abolishing the minimum price system. the commission should present a report on the operation of the fruit and vegetables cmo before the end of the year, accompanied, if necessary, by further reform proposals. the commission justifies the proposal under consideration on the grounds of urgency. the commission's proposal for a regulation on the common organization of the market in cereals, which is to be adopted by the council on 1 january, is a very important one. the committee on agriculture has highlighted the need to strengthen producer organisations as a matter of urgency. the problem is that, after the reform of the 1996 cmo, producer organisations became its main instrument. however, only 40% of fruit and vegetable production is currently grouped in producer organisations. a com covering only 40% of production does not deserve that name. if there is any urgency, it is to encourage the pooling of supply in producer groups. since it is an exception in the common agricultural policy and the producers themselves are obliged to co-finance the operational funds, it is clear that the increase in community funding is the most obvious instrument to achieve this objective. for this reason, the committee on agriculture has proposed increasing the percentage of community funding for certain joint actions of several producer organizations and under certain conditions, mainly in the regions most dependent on fruit and vegetable production or for associations or mergers of producer organizations. the quantitative differences between the commission proposal and the proposal of the committee on agriculture, which was approved almost unanimously, are mainly concentrated on the level of aid and the processing thresholds. the aid requested by the committee on agriculture may seem excessive, but let us not be fooled. the aid proposed by the commission is excessively low and is intended to make a short-term situation permanent, thereby eroding farmers' incomes. this cyclical situation is defined by the evolution of the euro-dollar parity and special events on the markets. in fact, the line of the committee on agriculture is limited to the reimbursement of aid existing before 1996. in addition, with regard to the question of aid, the disappearance of the minimum price and direct payment through producer organisations may cause problems, particularly in countries with a stronger fruit and vegetable vocation. a reasonable level of aid would make it possible to maintain the income of producers in a particularly difficult situation. to avoid absurd situations of systematic penalisation, the committee on agriculture has decided to propose that it be fixed at the level of what has been produced in recent years. we are trying to adjust aid to the production structure and the possibilities of absorption by the market without running the risk of creating surpluses. the question that some might raise is how to finance the amendments. you see, at the moment fruit and vegetables receive 445 million euros less than the ceiling set in the financial perspective. it is true that budget neutrality must be respected, but we must agree on its meaning. in my view, budget neutrality means remaining within the limits set when the financial perspective was adopted. the commission is, however, seeking to reduce expenditure below historical lows. i think the discussion should focus primarily on how to achieve the objectives entrusted to the cmo and, from there, establish budgetary commitments. it seems that the institutions are often asked to be less rigorous, as long as they merely propose budgetary savings. the commission's proposal for a regulation on the common organization of the market in fruit and vegetables is a very important one, and it is a very important one, and i would like to thank the rapporteur for the work he has done in this area. i would like to end by thanking my colleagues on the committee on agriculture. their understanding and effort has been of great help in arriving at the final transactions that have allowed the preparation of a frankly not easy report.

- mr president, i would first like to recall the kind reference made by mr maccormick to my speech to the committee on legal affairs and the internal market. mr maccormick says - and it is true - that i said that the principle of subsidiarity was not a legal principle but a political one. after having studied the report very carefully, i have come to the conclusion that it is not even a political principle: it is a theological principle. mr maccormick himself has just pointed out that the principle was stated by a pope, and it is clear that he is imbued with theological considerations. i would remind you that in the 17th century a great dutch jurist, hugo groot, better known as grotius or grocio, one of the founders of international law, warned theologians to stay out of the legal sphere with that famous phrase: "silete, theologi, in munere alieno". i would like to express my sympathy, my admiration and my pity for the commission at this time for having to live by these kinds of principles. the second paragraph of article 5 of the treaty establishing the european economic community is not understood by anyone. this definition is a circular definition, not a legal definition. it states that 'in areas not falling within its exclusive competence, the community shall intervene, in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity, only to the extent that the objectives of the proposed action cannot be sufficiently achieved by the member states and can therefore, by reason of the scale or effects of the action, be better achieved at community level'. no one understands this. and no one understands the protocol annexed to the treaty of amsterdam to define subsidiarity, and no one understands declaration no 30. the poor commission has made a very worthwhile effort with the documents 'better legislation 1998' and 'better legislation 1999', in which it tries to keep up with these trinkets that governments approve in the treaty on european union and in the additional protocol. the report of the committee on legal affairs and the internal market was not received with enthusiasm by its members. the proof is that of the 17 members of the committee, 8 voted in favour and 9 abstained. i mean, there were more abstentions than votes in favour. the reason why there was so much abstention is that the socialist members of the committee - and other members - expressed our scepticism about the overvaluation of the concept of subsidiarity in the report. the concept of subsidiarity, as set out in the report of the committee on legal affairs and the internal market, is a concept that is exalted to heavenly heights and, therefore, as a theological principle, it goes beyond the community. we have tabled 12 amendments to the report of the committee on legal affairs. we also support amendment no 13 by the group of the european liberal, democratic and reformist party. we hope that the house will be able to accept our amendments and if so, we would vote in favour. otherwise we would be forced to vote against.

instead of coordination, common action is spoken of; a step is taken. mr president, we are back to the previous debate: if we are to build this area we must establish, we must strengthen the mutual trust between the states, which led to the establishment of common rules in the internal market. now that mutual trust has to take a leap and we understand that it is a qualitative leap from the point of view of national cultures. that mutual trust has to go into that space of justice and from there go into mutual recognition. there can be no mutual recognition if there is no mutual trust between the founding states. in the previous debate, commissioner vitorino emphasized this very well by calling it by its name: the raison d'état. cooperation within the european union cannot be excluded on the grounds of state power; they must be treated equally. that is the meaning of extrapolating the principles which have served to build the internal market: non-discrimination on grounds of nationality. if we, in agreement with the state of which we are nationals, give certain information to a national judge, then obviously, if we want to be consistent with the idea of building that area of freedom, security and justice, we have to give it to a judge of the european union when he asks us for it, because that is the only way we are going to express that mutual trust between the states in a way that reaches the citizens. i think, mr president, and i conclude with this, that this is a step, a timid step, which we hope will soon be consolidated in this eurojust network, which will no longer be provisional but will become a definitive network.
commission - mr president, i should like to begin by very briefly congratulating mrs gebhardt on her excellent report and to say that the commission can agree with almost all the points which have informed its considerations. i shall take this opportunity - since several members have raised very delicate issues - to say quite frankly, as mr coelho has just said, that this initiative seems to us above all to be a first initiative which demonstrates the political will of the council to make up the backlog which exists in the field of judicial cooperation, as compared with police cooperation. and i can tell you quite frankly that i cannot understand how this initiative for judicial cooperation at eurojust level can be accused of being an infringement or a threat to the guarantee and protection of fundamental rights. it must be said. or we can subscribe to the model of democracy we know, which is based on the separation of powers, which recognizes that the supreme bodies for guaranteeing individual rights are the courts, and we recognize that european judicial cooperation at the criminal level consists precisely in strengthening the coordination of the european courts in their role of protecting fundamental rights. that's the model i subscribe to. or we do not subscribe to it, and in that case i do not understand how this initiative to develop a common judicial area can be seen as a threat to the guarantee of fundamental rights. let's be very clear about this. we are not in the process of harmonizing european criminal law in a brutal way. what tampere has asked us to do is to adopt transnational rules to combat transnational crime, where we recognise that transnationality, or if you want supranationality, legal instruments are an added value to combat illegal and criminal activities which are, by their nature, supranational. criminals must not have any doubts about their supranational nature. that is why, when we are asked in tampere for common rules on prosecution and sanctions for crimes against the environment, drug trafficking, human trafficking, child pornography, terrorism or cybercrime, it is because we recognise that this is a supranational criminal activity that must be addressed with supranational instruments. but since eurojust is concerned with the coordination of national prosecutors and magistrates in the fight against all forms of serious crime - and i agree with the rapporteur's approach - the concept is being broadened: we are no longer talking about cooperation for purely transnational crimes, but also about cooperation in the repression of criminal activities. this is the case, for example, of a criminal who commits a crime in one member state and flees to another member state, provided that the crime is serious. this is a step towards combating insecurity in a global sense, but it is done in compliance not only with substantive laws but also with national procedural laws. this means that the action of each magistrate is in accordance with its national legislation and that the powers to act and to combat this type of crime fall within the framework of the national legislation of each member state. that is why i do not see where the birth of a european judicial big brother lies here. i do not even see the birth of a european prosecutor, and i might add unfortunately. because, as you know, the commission has proposed the creation of a european public prosecutor, but not in this context, not on these issues. the commission's proposal is very specific and has been submitted to the rightful authority: the intergovernmental conference. what has the commission proposed? to create a european prosecutor to ensure the protection of the financial interests of the european community. and now, yes, we can speak of a european prosecutor. but as far as eurojust is concerned, it is a network for coordinating the action of national magistrates and prosecutors with the aim of improving the capacity to combat forms of serious crime at european level. and that is why i also see it as an important instrument for ensuring judicial control of europol. tampere was clear in saying that eurojust would be the judicial counterpart of europol. this means that criminal investigations and prosecutions which can rely on the participation of europol must be accompanied and monitored by eurojust as a network of magistrates and prosecutors at european level. the mutual relations between eurojust, europol, olaf, as the body specialised in the fight against fraud, and the existing european judicial network must therefore be clearly defined. the commission welcomes your report, mrs gebhardt. i hope that parliament will approve it. we will have the opportunity to engage ourselves in this provisional unit as from 1 january 2001, but the commission wants to support the debate on what the final eurojust unit should be. that is why we will be submitting to the council and the european parliament a proposal for a communication on the final unit of judicial cooperation, so that we can have as soon as possible a picture, a vision of what the final version of this eurojust network will be.

at the same time be vigilant, because there is no such thing as perfection. the report highlights a number of areas where improvements are needed, as you have pointed out. i will take up a few of them to tell you how we feel about this. as regards the annual monitoring of research programmes, which provides independent advice on the state and quality of implementation of our programmes, we have put in place several types of actions to improve them: an analysis of research management practices in the framework of national and european union programmes, with a view to exchanging good practices and facilitating mutual learning; the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. like the commission, parliament is of the opinion that joint responsibility for the implementation of projects is very close to joint financial responsibility. but i would like to emphasize one point: joint financial responsibility is not conceivable in the strict sense in the context of the framework programme, which aims to create consortia of different entities, universities, smes, large companies, public or private research institutes. these entities will not be able to provide sufficient financial guarantees to each other and, in the case of smes, will not necessarily be liable for the insolvency of the other members of the consortium. it is clear that this consortium work does not establish a duality in joint financial responsibility. it's a more complicated problem. this is one of the points where we obviously have to find methods that give greater security, but we must avoid excluding smes or public institutions from the framework programme for fear that they will be faced with responsibilities that they cannot assume. we must therefore strike the right balance between joint financial responsibility and, on the other hand, not frighten the partners in a consortium, because in that case only the strongest will participate, whereas we want to encourage the participation of small and mediumsized enterprises. i do, however, share your view that the risks of double financing must be reduced as much as possible. in this connection, you should know that, under action 74 of the white paper on reform, the commission services are already preparing the introduction of a central register of contracts concluded by the commission, which will in future be linked to all the commission's financial information systems. you have obviously raised other issues, including the problem raised by mrs langenhagen in her introduction: the time elapsed between the sector letters and the discussion of the report in parliament, which is a function of the relationship between the commission and the court of auditors. this happened, as you pointed out, a few years ago, but it is clear that lessons must be learned from this exercise. since then, measures have been taken at the level of the internal organisation of our departments to speed up, as far as possible, the court's sector letters. it is quite clear that these dialogues are necessary. of course, the responsibility is shared; it is also up to the court to establish these dialogues, but i can assure you that there is a constructive will, which is also that of parliament, between the court and the commission services to solve these problems. i come now to the question mrs morgan asked about the recovery of sums. there is an amount of €3.4 million, which can be considered as a large amount, but which in fact represents only 0.3% of the programme. of course, just because it's 0.3% doesn't mean we shouldn't recover it, and we should try to find it. in this connection, you should know that the commission departments have done everything in their power to recover the amounts in question. but the relevant services forwarded the case to the legal proceedings two years ago. two of the three cases examined by the commission's legal service have now reached the stage of legal proceedings, since they are subject to the national legislation in force. so the procedure is in place, but we are entering the jurisdiction of the member states and we are not always in control of the time limits. but i would point out that the three cases i have just mentioned accounted for 92% of the total. so we really worked on getting the 3.4 million back, and we can say that we achieved it by more than 90 percent. then there was a question about fishing and the person who was doing the checking. i just got the answer. it has been upgraded to the most appropriate level. and as far as dg agriculture is concerned, the problem has been solved by transferring the team responsible to the directorate-general for research. this transfer has led to better policy coordination. so these are the elements that i can give in answer to your questions. there are still new applications to be implemented, and i take this opportunity to tell you what guidelines for community research we want to develop for the future framework programme and which the itre committee has already examined, since i tabled a note of orientation to the parliament's committee on 4 october and a report is going to be drawn up. the main elements of these guidelines are: the shift from a project-based approach to a programme-based approach; the introduction of a minimum size of projects; the outsourcing of a number of activities, such as exploratory awards for small and medium-sized enterprises and mobility grants; and the general simplification of these procedures. i think that substantial changes must also be introduced in the future framework programme. we shall see what the effects of the changes to the fifth framework programme have been and i would like to thank you for your desire to improve. this is also the commission's intention, and i hope that we will be able to work under the best possible conditions to carry out this research programme, which is indispensable at european level, but which must be carried out in accordance with the best possible rules of efficiency and financial control.

- madam president, mr president-in-office of the council, mr commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, in the history of european integration there are certain moments which can be regarded as historic turning points, and this is one of them, because the adoption of the charter by parliament will be a further step towards the realization of the dreams and projects of the founding fathers. i would remind you that the declaration of rights was first discussed at the congress of the european movement in the hague in 1948; it is the origin of the european convention on human rights of the council of europe. we have given real substance to european citizenship, as recognised in the treaty on european union, and we have consolidated our area, not only as an internal market, but as a legal area in which the fundamental rights of individuals are recognised. for socialists and social democrats throughout europe, the adoption of the charter also represents the fulfilment of a commitment to our electors; we went to the elections with a manifesto containing twenty-one priorities, one of which was to promote a european charter of rights to enshrine the fundamental civil, economic, social and cultural rights of the citizens of the union. the european summit in cologne, under the german presidency of chancellor schröeder, proposed the premises that became the convention and the drafting of this charter, gave the mandate and appointed a former president of the republic, roman herzog, as president of this body. i think we should stress this today because the work we have done is not the exclusive heritage of any political family and this gesture honours the german presidency at the time and shows that we must all together move forward in the realisation of the fundamental values. i think we have done that in the european parliament too. i have had the opportunity to express my admiration for the work carried out by mr íñigo méndez de vigo, as president of the european parliament delegation. i would also like to highlight the essential role played by my colleague, mrs pervenche berès, when she led the socialist group delegation. i think we can all be proud of this success, which is a shared success. today europe is more than a common market and we also have a fundamental part of what a future constitution should be; however, despite all the efforts made, there is still a fundamental step to be taken before we can be satisfied - and i say this with the nice summit in mind - which is the last point mentioned by the president of the council: the inclusion of the charter in article 6 of the treaty. i think that, apart from the repeated personal support of the president-in-office of the council, there are a number of elements in favour; at present most heads of state and government belong to our political family; others do not, but they are in favour of this inclusion and of a reformed and democratic europe. the charter gives the union a fundamental legitimacy as a community of values, and this must be underlined. because we have also seen events which show that article 7 must have much stronger support. our governments need to get concrete results in nice to offer to the citizens - institutional issues are important, but, as the president of the council and the commissioner know, they are difficult to sell to public opinion. the charter also gives substance to the copenhagen criteria, which we consider to be fundamental in the accession negotiations; and i would go further, thinking of the countries that are negotiating with us, it also offers them guarantees vis-à-vis us; in other words, it is not a mere declaration, but an element that fits perfectly into the negotiation process. my group therefore still thinks that it is absolutely essential to include a reference to the charter in article 6 (2) of the treaty. as i think the president-in-office of the council will be very busy this weekend with the next conclave, i ask him to send a message to the conclave, so that the foreign ministers can convey it to the heads of government. it is this: if the european council in nice fails to include the charter in this way, i fear that the european parliament will have difficulty in approving the reform of the treaties. i think that is a positive message that the president-in-office of the council should send to his colleagues, because we are still in time to include the charter in article 6 of the treaties. after nice we can start talking about the european constitution. the key now is to consolidate this stage. this is our proposal.

has been used. however, this is not enough. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos is a good example of the need to ensure that the safety of workers is not compromised. the second is a policy on the human aspect of managing migration flows, essentially. the third is to reflect on and seek aggregation and consensus - mr president, since the barcelona conference and now, as has been said, at the very doorstep of the marseille conference, much has changed in the mediterranean region. it is true that this conference is being held in a context of violence and a crisis of peace as a result of the middle east conflict, but it is also true that its holding will help to keep the flame of the euro-mediterranean process burning and to ensure that it is not tainted by the tragic conflict. there are many common problems affecting the euro-mediterranean area today: illegal immigration, poverty, external debt, human rights, drought and terrorism, which mercilessly destroys the lives of innocent people and families, as we are tragically experiencing in spain, algeria or the next middle east. today more than ever we must proclaim that only regional cooperation, dialogue with civil society, economic and cultural exchanges, solidarity and mutual understanding can make the two shores of the mediterranean a prosperous and peaceful area. the commission and the council must urgently implement the agreements reached in feira and make a common policy for the development of the mediterranean region viable. we cannot and must not waste our human resources, our agricultural, industrial and craft resources, which, together with products as vital as oil, gas and new technologies, must be the basic instruments for the development of a mediterranean society that is much more balanced, fair and competitive than the present one. mr president, i would like to return to the middle east conflict. not two months ago, the president of the israeli parliament and the president of the palestinian assembly joined hands with the president of the european parliament in this house in an appeal for peace and harmony, and all the members of this house joined in a loud applause for that gesture. when weapons replace words, dialogue and understanding, the basis and substance of democracy, which is parliament, fails; that is also our failure. it is a wake-up call for the european union to play a much more active role in the mediterranean area, which has historically and culturally enriched and enlarged our european continent. it would be a mistake not to take the lead that history demands of us. i also believe, mr commissioner, that the geopolitical boundaries must be such that those who make organized crime, arms, drugs or human trafficking, and especially terrorism, a form of life condemnable by all civilized countries, cannot move freely. let us make borders a real filter for crime and criminals and not a barrier to development, culture or the prosperity of peoples. the european union needs a new culture of immigration and better management of migration flows. the european union shares responsibility with the countries of origin for immigration and for managing these migratory flows, which are so necessary for the development of the region.
mr president, europe is sometimes in a hurry, and sometimes those in a hurry leave things behind. and i note that in all these documents on the strengthening of the barcelona agreement we have forgotten some things. one of them is that liberalization, the single market cannot be done without addressing some important aspects, such as people and culture or education. if we liberalize markets and encourage a drive to integrate them, forgetting the above, we run the risk that in the end what we achieve instead of cooperation is colonization. europe must think outside the subsidiarity principle or go beyond it and realise that it must provide very important help in raising the level of the receiving countries, both for men and women, not only in basic education but even in a minimum education which in europe is considered to be for all citizens. we cannot therefore talk only about products and the organization of markets and not think about these citizens. secondly, i think we are also forgetting another important issue, which is the environment. europe has not pursued a policy on desertification or water that benefits the mediterranean countries, and we must think about pursuing a mediterranean environmental policy that takes account of the coordinates, the logics and even the climatic diversity of the mediterranean. the policy as it is now set out could not be transferred to many countries in the southern mediterranean. in this connection, it must be borne in mind that in europe there is a serious pressure from the citizens of the north to the south of the mediterranean, through tourism. with the rise of oil there will be even more pressure on the mediterranean. this is a waste of land and a policy of environmental dumping which is totally unacceptable. nor can we expect european citizens to be good at their environmental policy and not apply this policy to other countries.

- doc. a5-0324/2000 by mr lagendijk, on behalf of the committee on foreign affairs, human rights, common security and defence policy, on the amended proposal for a council regulation on the european agency for reconstruction (com (2000) 628 - c5-0526/2000 - 2000/0112 (cns));
the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner, i am aware that the balkans are not the most fertile ground for optimism. however, i am not optimistic when i say that the european union is reaping the rewards of concerted and persistent action. and those fruits, after the tragedy in the balkans, have already appeared a few months ago in croatia with free elections, with a system willing to respect human rights, and they have just been shown in belgrade, where citizens have confirmed their will to live in peace and freedom among themselves and to integrate into the european family. we must not disappoint their expectations and now more than ever all these countries need our help. it is necessary to continue this process of stabilising the region and to prepare them for a longer-term perspective of integration into the european institutions. it is clear that we are risking our credibility and our own stability. if we want to help them, we must do so more effectively than we have done so far and in a more coordinated way; otherwise we would lose the visibility of the european union, which is the one with the biggest financial burden in the balkans, but which is much less visible than countries such as the united states, which can react in real time to virtually any need that arises in the country. so when i was in bosnia-herzegovina and visited some villages, they welcomed me with great enthusiasm and said: 'how good it is that you americans are here to help us.' the european union's action had thus far lost its visibility. in the report i have prepared on aid to the western balkans, in close collaboration with mr lagendijk, on the two subjects we are dealing with today and which is an example of cooperation between two committees, we have noted a number of limitations: on the one hand, geographical; this implies that the agency's action must be extended not only to kosovo, but also to yugoslavia. we also found some functional limitations. firstly, that the international organisations carrying out these operations, such as unmik in kosovo or the office of the high representative in sarajevo, also need to benefit from this aid. on the other hand, there are a number of actions - i am referring specifically to the cards programme - which must go beyond reconstruction and extend to training, education and the reconstruction of civil society in close cooperation with ngos. it is very important that ngos should work together on this, but also that they should have some coordination between them, if we really want their action to be more effective and to reach all parts of those regions. the media also need to be emphasized. the media in that region have been responsible many times for the tragedy that has occurred and we need a media that is totally free and that operates according to the rules that govern our democracies. it is also very important to ensure that the judiciary is really independent. we have also encountered some operational limitations, which are one of the causes of the lack of visibility. operational limitations referring to the aid management system. sometimes there is too much red tape, too much red-typing and too much hesitation when granting aid. it is therefore important that, as far as the cards programme is concerned, the management committee should be a committee which is limited to the broad lines of multiannual programming, but which does not make too detailed day-to-day 'micro-management', otherwise we could have the same problems as in the past. it is also important that the work of the cards management committee and the work of the kosovo reconstruction agency should not be confused with each other and that there should be no duplication or overlap, but a perfect division of functions. it is also important to strengthen the role of the european parliament and i believe that with the amendments, which are expected to be voted on tomorrow, the european parliament will be able to have a greater consultative role in an interinstitutional collaboration process. finally, i would like to refer to the financial package. the president knows very well that it is very difficult to repeat the miracle of the loaves and fishes today, and with the few loaves and fish we have now it will be virtually impossible for us to meet all the external obligations of the european union. we must make aid more effective and more coordinated, by gathering all the scattered elements. i would like to conclude by saying - and i repeat the commission's words - that these two proposals are the cornerstone of a process which must lead to the full integration of these countries, which have had and have so many problems, into european structures. i am firmly convinced that the balkans have a solution, that the balkan curse can be cast aside, but for that they need all our support and these two programmes are going in that direction.
