counsel. - mr commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, we are all aware that the western balkans constitute a major challenge for the european union and the credibility of its foreign policy, both because of the scale of our human, political and financial commitment to the region, but also because of our desire to promote stabilisation through construction, development and ultimately the reintegration of the balkans into the european family. this year has fortunately opened with democratic change in croatia, following parliamentary and presidential elections. it was followed by another major event, the victory of the democratic forces in the federal republic of yugoslavia and the fall of milosevic. we hope that it will culminate in the consolidation of democracy on 23 december next, on the occasion of the parliamentary elections in serbia. the european union - as you know - has been determined to contribute to these historic changes. the commission has reacted immediately to the new situation in croatia by initiating the process which will lead to the opening of negotiations on a stabilisation and association agreement with that country at the zagreb summit on 24 november, i.e. in ten days' time. as it had committed itself to the serbian people, it has taken the necessary measures since the election of president kostunica, which you will receive tomorrow: the lifting of sanctions against the federal republic of yugoslavia, emergency aid of 200 million euros decided by the european council in biarritz and the integration of the federal republic of yugoslavia into the international community, in order to support the process of consolidating democracy. i would like to return to the presidency's priorities for the western balkans. in preparation for the zagreb summit, we wanted to focus the union's action on consolidating democracy and enhancing the stabilisation and association process. we are pursuing two objectives: firstly, the development of regional cooperation, and secondly, the implementation of a genuine policy of rapprochement between these countries and the european union. the european council in cologne had offered the prospect of accession to the union. at feira, he recognised the potential of the countries participating in the stabilisation and association process as candidates for membership. we want to confirm this offer at the zagreb summit, but we also want to go further by defining for each country the steps to be taken and the reforms to be carried out along this road. finally, we want to see the community provide vital support to support this process. at the initiative of france, the zagreb summit will bring together for the first time the heads of state or government of the european union and the western balkan countries participating in the stabilisation and association process: albania, bosnia and herzegovina, croatia, the former yugoslav republic of macedonia and the federal republic of yugoslavia. the summit will therefore be an opportunity to draw the consequences of the decisive democratic changes in the region at the highest level and, therefore, to reaffirm that the way is now open for all the countries of the region to move closer to the union in the framework of the stabilisation and association process. we want to make this process more valuable, in particular by marking the conclusion of the negotiations on the first stabilisation and association agreement with the former yugoslav republic of macedonia in zagreb, or by confirming an individual approach adapted to the situation of each country, and, as i have already indicated, by drawing up the prospects for each of us. the summit will also aim to consolidate democracy in the fry, support the process of reconciliation between the fry and its neighbours and encourage the development of trusting cooperation between the countries of the region. the union will therefore, without waiting for the entry into force of the stabilisation and association agreements, reiterate its expectation that the five countries concerned will commit themselves to establishing regional cooperation agreements between themselves as from now. these regional cooperation agreements, provided for in the stabilisation and association agreements, should, in our view, include the establishment of a political dialogue, a regional free trade area and close cooperation in the field of justice and home affairs, in particular with a view to strengthening the judiciary and its independence in the fight against organised crime, corruption, money laundering and other criminal trafficking. the council considers that rapprochement with the european union is closely linked to the development of regional cooperation. the westendorp and lagendijk reports on the proposals for regulations, one on the framework programme and the other on the european agency for reconstruction, give us an opportunity to review the extent of the support that the union intends to provide to the western balkans in order to support the stabilisation and association process. both reports are heading in the right direction. the presidency shares your concern that the framework programme should implement the principles of the reform of the management of the union's external aid: fewer procedures, more coordination on the ground, fewer backlogs of commitments. we also support the extension to the whole of the federal republic of yugoslavia of the scope of the european agency for reconstruction, which has proved its worth in kosovo. we want it to be more efficient and faster in implementing the programmes which the commission will delegate to it. the presidency's objective is to reach agreement on the proposals for regulations on the cards programme and the agency for reconstruction at the general affairs council at the end of november, which is next week, and to announce them in zagreb on 24 november. i would like to recall the main priorities assigned to the cards programme: institutional strengthening in the sense of democracy and the rule of law, economic development and reconstruction, and regional cooperation. cards should thus bring more coherence, more efficiency, more visibility to the union's aid in the region. the member states unanimously, particularly at the budget council on 20 july, wanted to place the debate on the amount of the financial envelope foreseen for cards for the period 2000-06 in the context of respecting the ceiling of heading 4 of the financial perspective adopted at the berlin european council. this amount, which will include aid to the federal republic of yugoslavia, will be the result of an overall arbitration on the distribution of the 10 billion euro available within the ceiling of heading 4 between the two aid programmes, meda ii and cards, the adoption of which is one of our priorities. finally, at the general affairs council on 18 september, the presidency had asymmetric trade preferences adopted for the countries participating in the stabilisation and association process. these measures grant preferential access to the community market for agricultural and industrial products from these countries. the union has thus made an exceptional gesture, since this liberalization, especially for agricultural products, is almost entirely offered without quotas and at zero duties. these measures entered into force on 1 november. the council is currently working on extending them to the federal republic of yugoslavia. the french presidency set itself ambitious objectives for the western balkans, which are now being achieved: the development of the stabilisation and association process, the adoption of the cards programme, the adoption of asymmetric trade preferences, to mention only the most important community measures. the long-awaited victory of democracy in croatia and then in the federal republic of yugoslavia requires, as we know, that the european union go much further. the european union must not be afraid to say to these countries: yes, your place, your future, is within the european family.

- question no 8 by maj britt theorin (h-0836/00) is replaced by the following: subject: honor killings in turkeyevery year, dozens of women are victims of "honour killings" in turkey. although turkish law provides for equal rights for women and men, in practice many men continue to sentence women to death for rape, adultery or simply for meeting other men. men who commit such a crime are rarely sentenced to long prison terms, sometimes not exceeding two years. while the new legislation being drafted in turkey to prohibit the reduction of sentences is essential, it is above all important that muslim officials officially distance themselves from the honor killing which is totally contrary to islam. both legislative measures and actions to increase debate and raise awareness are needed. what steps does the council intend to take to ensure that turkey takes effective measures to combat honour killing?
council. - the honourable member has drawn the council's attention to the question of honour killings in turkey. these practices seem to be in sharp decline and are said to be only residual in rural areas. the council remains concerned, however, about these crimes, which often take place in intolerable conditions. the turkish government has undertaken important reforms to better combat such acts, which are naturally prohibited by national law. in the report adopted by the turkish council of ministers on 21 september as a reform programme, the legislative amendments include several proposals: to incorporate in the civil code measures to strengthen effective equality between men and women in the social and educational fields; to better combat domestic violence; to better condemn such violence by creating specialised family judges; and finally to prohibit the possibility of a reduction in the sentence for crimes of honour. the council will be particularly vigilant in implementing these measures, which help to ensure that the copenhagen criteria, which were mentioned at length earlier, are met. in any case, honor killings are not a problem specific to turkey, as they affect a large number of countries around the world. the council therefore supported the dutch initiative to introduce this year, in the third committee of the united nations general assembly, a draft resolution against these crimes, which is still under consideration. the council notes that turkey has also supported this initiative.
counsel. - i believe that these crimes must be fought with all means, absolutely all means, and i see that both the council of the union and the united nations general assembly and, i think, the turkish government are prepared to do so. we must put an end to this kind of regressive practice from another age.

the rapporteur. - commissioner, regional fisheries organisations are becoming increasingly important, particularly in fisheries of shared sovereignty or for the management of migratory or trans-zonal stocks. they are particularly suited to the specific characteristics of their fisheries and are therefore a suitable instrument for the rational management of resources. it is therefore essential that the european union should have the necessary mechanisms to ensure full and dignified participation. the commission's communication is limited to the aspects of the community's and the member states' responsibilities in the tasks arising from participation in them. this approach is necessary but not sufficient, since a clear, uniform and homogeneous framework for the participation of the european union in regional fisheries organisations should be adopted; taking into account the diversity of existing regional organisations, the participation of the community in each of them should be appropriate to its particularities. however, it must be based on the same basic principles from a legal and institutional point of view. for this reason, the draft report by the committee on fisheries of the european parliament calls for a uniform division of responsibilities between the community and the member states for all regional fisheries organisations. the commission, as the guardian of the community's interests, has a leading role in community action. the commission's services will not be able to limit themselves to a frontal role in future; they will have to take over in a clear and precise manner all aspects of community participation in these regional organizations, both in the field of representation, control of the transmission and verification of data and participation in scientific forums: in general, the direction of community action, including the control of fisheries carried out within the framework of these organizations. the control of fisheries affects the jurisdictional powers of the member states and therefore, to a certain extent, affects the core of their sovereignty. this control must be transferred to a purely community body in order to make the common fisheries policy applicable to all member states and to all vessels and operators, irrespective of their nationality, avoiding any risk of breaching the principle of equal treatment. the management of the control and, progressively, its practical implementation should therefore be entrusted to the commission services and, consequently, its cost should be borne by the community budget. the existing mechanisms for transposing community law need to be improved in order to increase legal certainty and overcome their current slowness. however, the acceleration of the transposition into community law of the rules adopted within the framework of regional organizations does not preclude the council and parliament from fulfilling their responsibilities in the direction of the community's fisheries policy. the growing importance of regional fisheries organisations (rfos) means that the european union must assume its full responsibilities in fisheries matters. this poses a problem, first and foremost, of human and material resources. the commission, perhaps to avoid the problem of resources, has decided to propose a reformulation of the roles to be played by the community and the member states, without changing the respective powers. this approach, which could be acceptable on a transitional basis, could present serious problems of rigor and, above all, institutional problems if it were to be made permanent. the division of responsibilities proposed by the commission would reserve for the community representation, which could be described as high level, and would delegate to the member states representation on the scientific and technical committees; the contribution to the work of regional fisheries organizations would also be entrusted to the member states as well as inspection and control missions. in other words, the community's status as a contracting party would be reduced to that of a mere front. the european construction cannot be confined to empty declarations of substance. as long as there is a common fisheries policy and the community has powers in the fisheries sector, it must have the human and material resources to meet its obligations, as required by the principle of the sufficiency of resources of the common fisheries policy. similarly, if the community is a contracting party to the rdps, it must behave as such and play the role required of it. the application of this principle has financial implications and requires legal developments and perhaps the transfer of sovereignty; but if a particular model of political construction is chosen, it is necessary to provide the means for that model to be put into practice.

disappearance of family farms, whose only way out is to close down or to enter what is called integrated production, that is to say, where the producer loses his autonomy as a livestock farmer and is mr president, those of us who have devoted our lives to the study of social questions remember that the old handbooks used to include a definition of social protection as a set of state protection measures for the care of economically evaluable risks, of individual or family concern and to which individuals - the family unit - could not attend on their own. of course, health is one of those things that we value most, although it is true that very often we lose it or we are in danger of losing it. it is also true that social systems and protection systems have been affected and affected by economic, demographic, health and other factors. it is also true that economic recession, unemployment, social exclusion, the emergence of new diseases, population ageing - as well as the progress of research, the improvement of therapies, the development of new diagnostic and treatment techniques - have had a profound impact on the levels of compulsory social health coverage. it is a well-established fact that the protection of europeans against the risks arising from illness, maternity or old age - this is in a new form today, because of the ageing of the population - is not being taken care of solely by the social and state systems, and as such, by the imperative and obligatory social security or social protection systems. our very young charter of fundamental rights of the european union, in articles 34 and 35, recognises and respects the right of access to social security benefits and social services and at the same time proclaims the right of every person, legally residing and moving within the union, to social security benefits and social advantages in accordance with community law and national laws and practices. complementary private health insurance - the commission. - mr president, in my contribution to a secular miracle, i would like to say that the main measures to be taken by the union in the field of asylum policy harmonization are defined not only in the vienna action plan and the tampere european council conclusions, but also in the evaluation panel which the commission has presented to the council and the european parliament, and which will be developed in two essential stages. the first stage - which i hope will be fully completed by june next year - is to define minimum common standards on the essential elements defining an asylum policy. in a subsequent, longer-term phase, the aim is to define a common, globally comprehensive asylum system. and with a view to defining this comprehensive asylum system, the commission will present, by the end of this year, a communication to promote its debate. as regards the specific question of the legal basis, it is article 63 (3) (b) of the treaty on european union which provides for the adoption of measures relating to illegal immigration and irregular stay in the territory of the countries of the union, including measures on the repatriation of persons in an irregular situation. the council is currently considering a first initiative by the french presidency to adopt a directive on the mutual recognition of decisions on the expulsion of thirdcountry nationals, a draft directive which is also being discussed in this parliament. the public perception in the member states is that the existing return policies are poorly coordinated and largely ineffective. the commission considers that readmission agreements play an important role in clarifying and coordinating these policies, and the first community readmission agreements with russia, sri lanka, pakistan and morocco are currently being negotiated. the commission expects the 2001 budget to include a financial instrument for cooperation with countries of origin and transit to improve their capacity for readmission and voluntary return. as regards future policy, the commission is of the opinion that the need for a comprehensive and coherent policy on repatriation must aim above all at giving priority to voluntary repatriation. in view of this voluntary repatriation, would remind the house that the european refugee fund provides for specific measures of a financial nature to support the development of member states' policies on repatriation; i would like to ask the commissioner whether he is aware that the commission has not yet taken a decision on the matter. i am convinced that this will be a good theme for the commission's work programme for 2001.

- question no 22 by mr camilo nogueira román (h-0809/00) subject: monetary policy and the role of the european commission during a debate in the european parliament's constitutional committee, former commission president jacques delors said that it should be the responsibility of the european commission to make public the european policy on the state and development of the single currency's exchange rates. will the commission take any steps to put an end, at any rate, to the current divergences of opinion on this matter, which are so damaging to the health of the euro? questions to mrs wallström
commission. - mr president, i would say to mr nogueira that, of course, in the model we have defined, monetary policy, it is the responsibility of the central bank and it is the european central bank which acts according to the criteria laid down in the treaty. a more important problem is how to make a single monetary policy compatible with economic policies which are national in accordance with the treaty. this is precisely the whole of the coordination of economic policies, which has two fundamental objectives: firstly, that the economic policies of the different member states are not inconsistent and, secondly, that they are not inconsistent with monetary policy either and create a situation which could lead us to an excessively restrictive monetary policy. we are trying to achieve this coordination mainly through the instrument of the broad economic policy guidelines, which are applicable in each of the member states that adopt them and which contain not only broad economic policy guidelines but also specific recommendations for each of the member states. however, we have also put in place, as a consequence of the stability and growth plan, the so-called stability programmes. here we have a much more precise, much more specific approach, because we are introducing only and exclusively the public finance element. the objective during this period has been to reduce the government deficit in order to achieve a more accommodative monetary policy, lower interest rates and higher growth. the objectives set are being achieved satisfactorily. we hope to reach a zero deficit situation next year. in these circumstances, the eurogroup, as the main body responsible for economic policy coordination, is considering going further in terms of our fiscal obligations and, above all, improving the quality and sustainability of public finances, which will undoubtedly mean an improvement in the stability and growth pact and the treatment of more precise and more substantive issues.

commission. - in its decision approving the french scheme to support film production, the commission had laid down four specific compatibility criteria. in the same decision, the commission undertook to review the aid schemes in all member states on the basis of these specific compatibility criteria approved until 2004, when the validity of the authorisation of the french aid scheme expires. the commission's intervention aims to create the legal certainty and regulatory stability needed for the sector to develop and which it has lacked until now, by setting minimum compatibility criteria, but without seeking to harmonise the aid schemes whose diversity reflects the cultural diversity which the commission is seeking to preserve. so, madam member, this bilateral approach is only aimed at examining the conformity of the various existing schemes with the prototype which was established when the french scheme was approved, on the basis of the four specific compatibility criteria.

council. - mr president, i should first like to thank you for your concern about the length of this sitting, but as you know, i have been a member of parliament for 21 years and therefore i am impervious to this kind of nonsense. i would simply add a word to the remarks that have been made about afghanistan, to say that the council's determination is to bring humanitarian aid to the ground as far as the operational conditions allow. i would then like to make a few remarks on a few of the elements of the very rich debate which has just taken place on the reports by mr brok and mrs lalumière, the general meaning of which i believe has been broadly accepted, which of course encourages the governments in the work they are pursuing and which i think the nice council will support. i would like to begin by addressing the question of the place of defence in the european union's policy and practical instruments. many speakers have said that military means must be used as a last resort, within the possibilities available to the european union. i can of course only emphasize this principle, which is that of governments. but let us ask ourselves what "as a last resort" means. in the end, it means that everything else has failed, and it happens. we lived it in europe two years ago, and a year and a half in kosovo. all the political, diplomatic and economic pressure has failed to prevent the outbreak of violence in the heart of europe and an unacceptable challenge to all european values. so military force is only a last resort. but if he's going to prevent the unacceptable, he has to be trustworthy and credible. i also believe that the combination of these different means is a property, a possibility, specific to the european union and that the task before us, if this policy is to progress and consolidate, is to develop a genuine european culture of conflict prevention and management. the experiences we have had and are still having, particularly in the balkans, show us that europeans, through their historical experience, which is rich in conflicts, and through their understanding of the subtleties and sometimes the hardships of confrontations between communities, can develop valuable and respectable know-how and methods of dealing with conflicts. the question of duplication: i would like to emphasize that the resources, the military means, which the nations have freely agreed to offer within this joint force, are the same capabilities that most of these nations put at the disposal of the atlantic alliance. there is no duplication of effort. these are the same forces, with the same level of preparedness and readiness as most of our nations - i am of course speaking for the non-alliance nations - but there is no duplication in the defence effort of the atlantic alliance nations between what provides support for the actions of the atlantic alliance and what could be made available to the european union. the concept has been in place since 1992. these are petersberg's assignments. they are the subject of a strong agreement between european governments and this provides guidelines which are, i believe, tried and tested and very widely approved by european opinion. the actions, if any, will of course be decided by governments by consensus, and as several speakers have said, if we emphasize in the declarations that there is no european army, it is because there is obviously no authority higher than the nations which could impose on them to commit their forces to any operation. so europe is not going to form a new alliance, as i have heard it suggested, i believe, by an incompletely informed development. it will operate on the basis of national decisions, taken in intergovernmental cooperation, under the control of national parliaments, respecting the petersberg mandates and complying, as we have also stated, with the principles of the united nations charter. i believe that one of the developments that will be made in european security and defence policy is to provide additional capacity, practical support, to the united nations' function of settling conflicts, including when it comes to separating the belligerents. i am responding to the comment made by one speaker that an agreement was concluded in saint-malo between britain and france to limit the rights of the european parliament. that's not what this is about. the agreement reached in saint-malo, and above all the agreement between the 15 nations, is that if we want a practical, effective european defence capability, it can only exist on an intergovernmental basis. we must not forget that for 50 years we have hesitated or failed to give the european union the minimum capacity to avoid being a helpless witness in crises where violence is rampant. today, the only possibility is intergovernmental action. it is appropriate for all our democratic nations, because it preserves their ultimate right to decide on the use of force. so parliamentary control, it's true, is essentially because of this intergovernmental choice within nations. i would also point out that there is no, and there will be no, budgetary commitment by the european union to finance any military activity whatsoever in all the positions adopted by the council. does this mean that dialogue between the council, representing the governments, and the european parliament on defence and security matters is impossible? i think that this discussion, which was welcomed by all, is the first demonstration of the contrary. i believe that a positive dialogue will develop. why would you do that ? because if we are consistent with the decisions that have been taken, there will be a gradual increase in the level of responsibility, the level of credibility and the influence of the european union in dealing with crises. we will no longer be mere commentators. therefore, a thorough political reflection will develop in our public opinion, in our parliaments, here too, on what is at stake in this resolution of crises by a full range of means in which military force is only one component. and the value of the principles and reflections in the report by mr brok and mrs lalumière already demonstrate, foreshadow, what the richness of these debates will be. there will still be ways of bringing national parliaments closer together, but what is within our reach and represents a turning point, which i believe we can all welcome, is that the 15 nations that make up this union, which have already built a political reality that has a positive impact on the balance of world influence, have chosen to give themselves the means to act together in cases where violence challenges our values. they do so on the basis of our common values. i think that's good news. the rapporteur. - mr president, mr kinnock, mrs schreyer, ladies and gentlemen, this debate is the culmination of parliament's examination of the white paper on the reform of the commission, an examination which is intended above all to give fresh impetus, new support to the commission after the past crisis, which we all deplore. i would like to thank mrs guy-quint and mr harbour and mr lamassoure for their work. the four rapporteurs have worked in an excellent spirit of cooperation and this will enable this procedure, which is in itself complicated, to produce four coordinated reports tomorrow, without any overlap between them and which will give the encouragement we all want to the commitment and responsibility assumed by president prodi. while each report deals with the issues which concern each committee, there is one thing in common with all four: they all express a general favourable opinion of the reform proposals put forward by the commission in its white paper, although they do so with a vigilant attitude towards their implementation and development. as for the committee on budgetary control, i am pleased to inform you that my report was adopted unanimously, with one abstention, and that we were unanimous in stressing once again the need for a strong, independent, transparent and efficient commission, in short, a true pillar of the european construction. we were also unanimous in finding that many of the deficiencies and irregularities which were denounced during the approval of the 1996 budget were due to the fact that the previous commissions failed to modernise their management and control systems and to apply the existing rules in full. in drafting my report i have been able to study not only the white paper but also the second report of the committee of independent experts and the resolution adopted in this parliament on 19 january, proposed by mr michiel van hulten, on the work of the committee of independent experts. the committee on budgetary control and i are pleased to know that in drawing up the white paper the commission has drawn heavily on the proposals of the independent experts and has taken account of a good number of the comments made by this parliament on 19 january. as the committee responsible for budgetary control, i stress in the report adopted by the committee the relevant aspects of the reform of the powers in this area. and so we have fully supported the establishment of a real sense of responsibility for civil servants. this is the basis of the commission's new management philosophy: each administrative unit will be called upon to assume responsibility for the regularity and legality of all its acts. the directors-general will be responsible for the internal control of their directorate-general, but we do not in any way relieve the respective commissioners of their own political responsibility for the functioning of the services and, where appropriate, the president of the commission. the new internal audit service, under the direct responsibility of you, mr kinnock, vice-president responsible for reform, will have as its main task the analysis of the functions and systems of internal control which exist within the commission. this role is, as the court of auditors points out in its report 4/97, much broader and more general than the current role of general ex ante control. i would remind you that on 5 october our parliament gave the green light to the amendment of article 24 (5) of the current financial regulation. parliament has thus put an end to what the court of auditors has been denouncing since 1981 and repeated in its report 4/97: a latent conflict between the power to grant a visa - and therefore to authorize expenditure - and the burden of evaluating it shortly afterwards according to criteria of sound financial management. this amendment makes sense in the transitional period until the adoption of the new financial regulation which, on the basis of the recommendations of the committee of experts, aims to establish a control system based not on centralised ex ante control but on ex post, ex post auditing. i believe that the new system will prove to be more effective than the present one. the court of auditors, in its report 4/97, reiterates its position on the impact of financial control, which is uneven. the commission's budgetary policy is based on the principle of the budgetary authority's own resources, which are not used for the purposes of the budget. the commission's extremely limited number of visa and authorization refusals is proof of this weakness. the court of auditors states in its report that it does not object to the abolition of prior authorisation provided that it is replaced by other procedures offering at least equivalent guarantees and thus involving other actors than the financial controller. the other factor is precisely the internal audit service which will enjoy complete independence. the court of auditors also says that, on the express condition that the role of the authorizing officer... we're not exactly here to celebrate victories. the support given by this parliament to the reform of the commission must lead it to take its risk, its responsibility, as mr kinnock promised, and also to get it right. you have a duty to get it right and to take risks, not to avoid them.
mr president, commissioners, ladies and gentlemen, we should like to begin by thanking mrs guy-quint in particular for the consensus she sought throughout the drafting of her report. as the committee on budgets, we find that the establishment of the budget by activity causes us problems because of the low visibility of expenditure and our desire to strengthen the powers of the european parliament as budgetary authority. we have just had a budgetary conciliation with the council, as mrs guy-quint knows, where the most difficult part was to determine in a clearer and more precise way where the limits of each other's budgetary powers lie. the committee on budgets believes that parliament should not lose its control over the allocation of administrative appropriations. the fact that when the activity budget is established category 5 of the financial perspective will disappear does not give us much comfort. we are not against these consequences, but we are in favour of safeguarding parliament's budgetary powers. the commission's reform policy, which covertly seeks to alienate parliament from this control of administrative expenditure, would therefore create interinstitutional problems in the short term. an approach which ensures, however, that parliament's powers of control and decision-making over the current category 5 expenditure are maintained will ensure that the reform of the commission is carried out without any major upheavals. as regards the tabs and their transitional period of dismantling, my group insists that the commission should make every effort to limit this transitional period. we therefore ask the commissioner: can the commission guarantee a transitional period that is really limited in time? mr president, every administration needs to be periodically reviewed, adjusted and adapted to the times. the commission's proposals - the white paper - which were put forward by commissioner kinnock, remembered that the crisis in the commission was not caused by any defect in the community administration but by political problems which had little to do with the functioning of the administration, and to link the crisis in the commission to a malfunctioning of its administration would be arbitrary. it should be borne in mind that the community administration is based on certain principles which are well established in the practice of continental administration, such as the principle of career and employment stability. these principles were established after an earlier stage in which public offices were nourished on the basis of the distribution of influence, the system of loot or plunder. and in the face of that the system of stable public administration was the guarantee that political changes would not affect the functioning of the administration. in some countries, such as spain, where we have gone through tumultuous periods in our political life, the administration has been, at particularly to her budget portfolio. i would like to begin by reporting to the house that this morning's meeting of the college as mr van hulten said earlier, adopted a proposal for an interinstitutional agreement establishing an advisory group on standards in public life, as outlined in action 1 of the white paper action programme. it adopted a preliminary strategy for decentralisation and simplification of decision-making procedures – something which eventually will lead to substantial increases in commission productivity and reducing those strata of bureaucracy that everybody rightly talks about. the college also agreed today substantial proposals relating to the reform of human resources policy. those human resources policy documents relate to discipline, to whistle-blowing and to equal opportunities. they will be the formal basis for the legally required consultation between the commission, its staff and staff representatives, which of course will take place over the coming months. our approach on disciplinary procedure proposes several necessary changes, including the improvement and restructuring of the investigative phase of disciplinary proceedings, which would be handled by a specialist service. they include: making the disciplinary board a permanent and more professional body, chaired by a qualified specialist from outside the commission; improving the provisions governing the justified suspension of officials, including those being prosecuted in criminal cases in national courts; consolidating the vital coordination between the commission and olaf whilst not compromising the essential independence of olaf; refining the list of possible sanctions to relate them better to any proven contravention of staff regulations. all these proposals are focused on enabling the commission and the other european institutions, including parliament, to improve the professionalism, the consistency and the reasonable speed of disciplinary procedures and to do so without loss of fairness or rights of the accused. the document on whistle-blowing proposes a system that compares well with the best existing practices in member states. it proposes the integration of the existing olaf regulation reporting obligation into the body of the staff regulations. it sets out the rights of career protection for whistle-blowers who report genuine concerns in a responsible way. it establishes safeguards against frivolous or malicious reporting. it emphasises the responsibility for those receiving reports of possible wrong-doing to act promptly, seriously and effectively. it defines many clear procedures in several channels for reporting alleged wrong-doing inside and outside an official's employing institution. in addition in the right to report to olaf and to the hierarchy of his or her own institution, an official will also be entitled to report suspicions and evidence to the presidents of the council or this parliament or the commission or the court of auditors or the ombudsman. the provision of external channels will be a major and progressive change, which i am certain will work to the benefit of the institutions and their staff, the european union and, of course, the public interest. finally, our equal opportunities document presents specific policy proposals to ensure equality of employment opportunity, so that the evident inequalities, which have been endured by women, by people from ethnic minorities and people with disabilities, can be addressed effectively without compromising standards of merit. in these documents we have again sought to take examples from best practices in member states. to save time and to recognise portfolio relevance, i hope that the house of why the commission has not acted on the proposal made in a number of budgetary control committee reports that there should be a separate chamber for disciplinary hearings for budgetary irregularities, either within the court of auditors or in the court of justice. i think mr van hulten made the point in the course of the debate again. it is a fair question and there are basically two reasons for not taking up proposals that the commission should have recourse to such external institutions. first, the committee of independent experts stipulated, in my view rightly, that any such body should be an internal one, not least because the treaties attribute very specific roles to the other two institutions in controlling the financial implications and the legality of the commission's disciplinary decisions. it would create untenable conflicts of interest, not to say some constitutional gymnastics, if either court were to be directly involved in the commission's internal procedures. in addition, such changes would obviously only be possible with amendment to the treaties. secondly, in practical terms, dividing a disciplinary case up into its financial aspects of the financial regulation. the new draft budgetary regulation is at the heart of the reform. the main objective of the new version is to simplify, increase transparency, strengthen the budgetary principles, which means in concrete terms fewer derogations, less incomprehensible special arrangements, and it means increasing the efficiency and effectiveness of the budgetary procedure. the new rules on contracts and grants are introduced in the financial regulation. the rules for the day-to-day management of the budget will therefore become clearer and more manageable, and we hope that this regulation, but you have also expressed concern that information for parliament could be lost through activity-based budgeting. i think i can allay that concern. the basic idea of activity based budgeting is to make clear in the budget plan how much money is available for each policy area, both operationally and for the necessary administration. we want to show the costs of a policy area, and you are right that this is not a cost-benefit analysis, but a summary of the resources available for a policy area, and this is a new thing for the budget of the european union. the abolition of the division of the budget as we have had it up to now - the division into a part of administrative costs and a part of the costs of political measures - the abolition of this separation is the logical consequence, but this does not mean that the costs of staff and administration are no longer identifiable, no longer shown separately, but they will of course continue to be shown on specific budget lines, but will be assigned to the policy area itself and will no longer disappear anonymously in a general administrative budget for the commission. this activity-based approach aims to better align resources with policy priorities. it is a tool for estimating costs more accurately, for better recording, and it is a management tool which can also help management to set priorities. it was a major concern of parliament to make political priorities more clearly identifiable. so again, transparency is the goal, and i think we're achieving that goal. i would like to say briefly, mr garriga commission. – chairman, this debate is timely as the commission has in fact taken important steps, new steps in the reform of external relations. it agreed today in the creation of the new office responsible for european cooperation from the identification of activities to implementation. the process of implementing the commission’s decision of may on reform of external relations is going well. there are three main elements to the reform: the enhancing of the programming process; the reunification of the management of the project cycle; and the devolution of powers to our delegations, all are making substantial progress. as regards country programmes, the commission has adopted a standard framework for country strategy papers. this was discussed during the recent development council and was positively welcomed by all member states. we now have a harmonised scheme to draft country strategy papers and indicative cooperation programmes in all developing countries. this will put the country concerned at the centre of the process, and it will also provide a basis for close coordination with member states and other donors involved in that country. this is the tool we have missed in the discussion over many years about how to coordinate better. the clear focus of our action on fighting poverty as part of our overhaul of the policy framework and concentration on a limited number of sectors will be key elements in improving the impact of our cooperation. within the commission, the inter-service quality support group has started work under the chairmanship of the development dg. it will ensure that strategy papers follow the agreed framework and methodology and i am confident that this group will bring more quality and consistency to our country strategies. this covers the whole geography and it makes also a big improvement as to the consistency with the policy we are backing. last but not least, i shall with my colleagues, the external relations commissioners, very soon submit to the college legislative proposals to modify the rules relating to the legal basis for all external relations instruments and budget lines. this will allow the management committees to focus their work on strategies and not on individual projects. as regards the reunification of the project cycle, the creation of the new office has now been agreed today formally in the commission. the office will be responsible for the management of all steps of the project cycle. as from the beginning of next year, 250 officials will be transferred from the development dg and the external relations dg to the office and gradually contractual agents will also join the staff of the office while, in parallel, the technical assistance offices will be dismantled. here also, things have moved quite fast with the help and understanding of the budgetary authority. finally, a programme of devolution of powers to the heads of delegations has been set the rapporteur. madam president, mr president-in-office of the council, madam commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the erika accident on 12 december last year and more recently the ievoli sun accident have clearly demonstrated the limits of the action of certain classification and inspection societies in the area of construction control and, above all, the monitoring of the navigability of vessels under their responsibility by delegation from flag states. however, and especially in this area, it is the public institutions which have the inescapable duty to respond to the demands of citizens by developing legislative initiatives to ensure the preservation of the environment and an optimum level of maritime safety, as well as the obligation to ensure that the established rules are properly complied with. in this connection, and in order to address the marked differences between the various classification societies at international level in the competence of their inspectors, the level of development of their computer resources and the degree of technical demands in their inspections, the commission has presented us with a proposal to amend directive 94/57/ec which will apply to all ships, including those carrying petroleum products, and which lays down the rules to be complied with by the member states and the classification societies authorized by them. the proposal has been examined by the committee on regional policy and transport, with the support of the environment and industry committees. interviews were also held with the sectors concerned and numerous contacts were also made with the french presidency with the aim of reaching a consensus text that could be quickly adopted by the two legislative bodies, the council and the european parliament. as a result, we have drawn up a parliamentary report amending the directive, which proposes improvements in various aspects leading to the strengthening of the classification system as a means and a valid instrument for ensuring the safety of maritime traffic. it is thus considered, first, that nothing in this directive should be interpreted as derogating from the absolute and non-delegable duty of the shipowner to maintain and operate ships in seaworthy condition. the commission, assisted by a committee, is responsible for granting and, where appropriate, suspending or withdrawing european recognition, taking account of the accident rates and the results of incidents and accidents recorded for all the vessels classified by each of them. the commission is committed to improving the quality of inspections of ships as a preventive measure against maritime accidents. on the one hand, it provides that classification societies must have their own system of internal audits to measure the quality of their services at all workplaces, as well as clear standards of accountability and control of all their branches and staff. the inspections must be carried out by specialised inspectors who are contracted exclusively, must not be related to or dependent on the shipowner and the shipowner must not control the ship's classification society. in addition, a high level of transparency is introduced in the provision of information on the results of inspections carried out on ships, operating conditions or operating restrictions, and class changes, suspensions and withdrawals. these data shall be made available to the european, state and port authorities and to the public concerned. similarly, the transfer of a ship from one class to another - change of classification society - is conditional upon satisfactory compliance with all deferred recommendations and reservations it may have to comply with, and there are also regular checks and supervision by the commission and the member states to verify compliance with this directive by organisations recognised at european level. finally, the commission should establish strict rules and control measures for the maintenance of ships, with a view to holding all parties concerned accountable. in this area, the commission's initial proposals and parliament's amendments sought to specify the financial responsibility regime for classification and inspection companies. however, the commission has already announced a second package on maritime safety, which will propose a system of liability for all parties involved in accidents: ship owners, cargo owners, classification societies, etc. i therefore believe that the various groups in this parliament should not now lose themselves in a partial, at the same time sterile and delaying debate on the final approval of the financial responsibility of the classification societies, but that we should leave this for the second package and move immediately to reach a consensus at first reading with the french presidency so that at the next council of ministers on 20 december there will already be an agreement with the european parliament and the first package can be finally adopted this year.

- mr president, at the moment, mrs palacio vallelersundi has put the commissioner in the dock and, in this case, speaking of the interinstitutional balance, the commission has only presented a proposal for a directive. it is for parliament and the council to approve this proposal for a directive and to examine, among other things, the appropriate legal basis for this. it is therefore not a question of accusing the commission of any irregularity. and above all, it cannot be accused of any irregularity because the commission, in this case, has only proposed a proposal for a directive which recasts three previous directives on the content of certain tobacco products and on certain warnings on the packaging of these products. so there's nothing really new. the only new thing is a judgment of the court of justice of the european communities of 5 october last, in which the court of justice says that, with regard to another completely different directive, which is the tobacco advertising directive, the legal basis of the current article 95 - which was the old article 100a - was not adequate. the reason why the court of justice declares that this legal basis is not appropriate is that the court of justice considers that, by means of this legal basis, an attempt is made to circumvent an express prohibition of the treaty itself in another article - which has also changed its number from article 129 to article 152 in the current text - which prohibited any harmonisation of national provisions. the court is therefore trying to avoid a ruse by which such a subterfuge could be used. but in this case, that is not the case because the proposal for a directive, like the previous directives already in force, is actually intended to remove existing obstacles to the functioning of the internal market. and they therefore have a correct legal basis on the basis of the old article 100a or the current article 95. the rapporteur, mr maaten, has wisely proposed to strengthen this legal basis by a reference to another article, article 133 on external trade, and has also proposed a number of amendments to some of the articles in order to avoid challenging this directive on the basis of the case law established by the court of justice's judgment. i would point out that the court of justice's judgment has been taken too literally. it is a judgment which is in many respects to be criticised, but if we accept the judgment as such - because we have no other choice, since the court of justice is the highest body for interpreting community law - there is nothing to prevent this parliament from giving a favourable opinion on the proposed legal basis of article 95 with article 133, and introducing the amendments to which i have referred, which are included in the rapporteur's amendments. i have to say, on behalf of the socialist group, and in particular the socialist members of the committee on legal affairs - who voted against the majority opinion to which mrs palacio vallelersundi has just referred - that we believe that to continue down this road, to reject the proposal for a directive, as proposed by two amendments, nos 52 and 53, tabled by mr poettering, on behalf of the group of the european people's party, and by mrs palacio vallelersundi and 32 other members, would be a tremendous limitation of the european parliament's legislative power. my concern at the moment is not so much the health problems, which are of course important and considerable, but the limitation that would be involved if we accepted such a restrictive interpretation of the legislative power of this european parliament. i understand that such a restrictive interpretation would practically lead to the elimination of the legislative power of this institution and of the council. i do not think that such a restricted approach can be taken, that is to say, that regardless of the content - and the substantive content that mr maaten and others have highlighted - there is a danger that if this parliament and the council accept the restrictive interpretation proposed by the leader of the european people's party and mrs palacio vallelersundi, this parliament, the council and the community institutions as a whole would be tied up in the legislative development of the community institutions, which is so important for the development of community law. for this reason, the socialists support the amendments tabled by mr maaten and we reject, of course, amendments nos 52 and 53 by the group of the european people's party.

the rapporteur. - mr president, i should like to begin by congratulating the portuguese presidency on its initiative, which was then followed up - in my view, quite correctly - by the french presidency. ladies and gentlemen, as you know, we live in a society where crossborder movements are increasing, on a truly gigantic scale and absolutely unknown in other eras of humanity. in this connection, it is sufficient to recall, for example, that in 1997, within the territory of the european union, more than 200 million people crossed the borders of their states of residence to go to the territory of other member states. the european union and the creation of a single market also imply the creation of an area without internal frontiers in which the free movement of goods, persons, services and capital must be guaranteed within the territory of the member states, as provided for in article 14 of the treaty establishing the european community. all these factors, acting separately but multiplying their effects when they act together, have caused millions of people to cross the borders of their home countries every day in a natural way, to go to another member state of the european union, whether to live, work or simply travel. this reality, the political and economic consequences of which will be incalculable in the medium and long term, has, however, negative implications for citizens who move. one of these is the risk of becoming a victim of crime, both outside and within the territory of their state of residence, ranging from personal theft to, sometimes, terrorist crimes, the scourge of which still strikes cruel and inhumanely at certain member states of the european union. however, incomprehensibly, the european union has so far been unable to devise adequate formulas to combat this scourge, which knows no national boundaries, because the states remain closed within 15 national borders in the judicial sphere. the european union is currently facing the paradox that the abolition of internal borders for the free movement of goods, persons, services and capital must go hand in hand with the maintenance of 15 borders in the police and criminal justice fields, which member states are having difficulty eliminating. this situation has unjustifiable consequences for european citizens who move freely within the territory of the european union. when the unfortunate circumstance arises of being the victim of a crime in a state other than that of his habitual residence, the citizen has the bad experience of witnessing the unbearable helplessness that results from the inability of states to build a genuine european judicial area. it is therefore necessary that all victims of crime, regardless of their place of residence or nationality, be guaranteed respect for their rights and the assurance that they will receive the same treatment, prompt and secure compensation, as every human being deserves for the simple fact of being a human being. he should be treated in this way in any member state in whose territory he has been the victim of the crime. for this reason, the creation of a genuine statute for victims of crime, a statute common to all the member states, is inexcusable. a key objective of this initiative is to ensure minimum compensation for victims in all member states, by guaranteeing at least a common minimum. i also think it is important to point out that the european criminal legislation of the member states has always paid attention and made efforts to the figure of the criminal, both in terms of the prevention of crime and offences and in terms of programmes and measures for the reintegration and rehabilitation of offenders. this initiative is the first to give special attention and prominence to the figure of the victim. we can call this initiative novel and, in a way, revolutionary in the treatment of victims. it is undoubtedly a new element in the european legal system, in which, for the first time, the victim has a legal status of his own and not, as hitherto, derived from the crime. in many cases, the victim is the object of the crime in the territory of a state other than his habitual residence, so that the problems and sufferings in these cases are aggravated and complicated by the sum of negative circumstances, but habitual and constant, in the treatment given to victims: their isolation due to lack of knowledge of the language, their lack of information, their abandonment, their lack of protection in areas where each state has preserved its own legal system. for this reason, and in order to be able to respond adequately to the needs of this type of victim, rules have also been developed at international level which take into account the defence of the rights and interests of victims. i would like to highlight only two aspects of this initiative at this stage: the council of europe convention no 116 of 24 november 1983 on compensation for victims of violent crime. and i would like to stress that, despite its importance and its status as a mandatory reference point in europe, the convention has not yet been ratified, as of 18 september 2000, by the following member states of the european union: austria, belgium, greece, ireland, italy, portugal and spain. another international initiative is the united nations declaration on the fundamental principles of justice for victims of crime and abuse of power, adopted by general assembly resolution 40/34 on 29 november 1985. in the light of the foregoing and in accordance with the mandates of the fourth indent of article 2 of the treaty on european union, which sets as one of the objectives of the union the maintenance and development of the union as an area of freedom, security and justice in which the free movement of persons is guaranteed, we must ensure that this area of freedom, justice and security ensures genuine access to justice so that citizens can benefit from adequate legal protection anywhere in the territory of the union. for this reason, the citizens' europe will not make sense unless, among other things, the necessary measures are adopted to improve and also take into account the rights of victims of crime, approached from a global perspective which takes into account all their rights and interests, on the one hand, and which, from a community perspective, approximates the legislation of the 15 member states. it is necessary that everyone, including third-country nationals who have been the victims of a crime in the territory of any state of the european union, should receive a similar minimum treatment. the european union cannot accept that people can be treated differently depending on the state in which they were the victims of the crime or their nationality. this discrimination is clearly unacceptable. finally, the initiative represents a major step forward in the creation of a european criminal justice area, which, although partial and limited, meets the real needs of a huge number of european citizens who, up to now, have been virtually helpless when they have been the victims of a crime outside the territory of their habitual residence. as positive elements of this initiative, i would like to highlight the definition of the concept of victim and the adoption of measures which are intrinsically linked to the overall attention to be given to them. the amendments proposed in this report are therefore mainly aimed at ensuring that the rights of victims of crime are respected and their interests and circumstances taken into account. in short, that the person who has been the victim of a crime is guaranteed the same minimum treatment, that his dignity is preserved, that his rights to inform and to be informed, access to justice and that compensation for the damage suffered is immediate, comprehensive and effective.

counsel. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, after the nice european council, where the construction of europe has made significant progress, which the president of the republic will present to you shortly, i have the pleasure today of presenting to you the second reading of the draft budget of the european union, as drawn up by the council on 24 november last. it is a pleasure, but also an honour and a personal emotion to be here in the heart of european democracy. the council's second reading was preceded on 23 november by a conciliation meeting between the european parliament, the council and the commission. the result of this long meeting was, i believe, a double success, a success for europe because we were able to overcome our initial differences, and a political success because this budget reflects not only a compromise but above all priorities. the representatives of the three institutions have indeed spared no effort to reach an overall agreement on the 2001 budget and i would like to take this opportunity to express the council's thanks to both the members of the parliamentary delegation and to mrs schreyer. the council therefore proceeded to its second reading of the budget, taking account of the agreements reached with the parliament's delegation, with the constant aim of voting a budget which would enable all the priorities of the european union to be financed and which would correspond to real needs and the real capacity to implement appropriations. this budget will thus make it possible to implement the reform of the common agricultural policy and to translate the programming of structural actions as adopted in 1999, but also all the major programmes decided jointly by parliament and the council. i am thinking in particular of research, transeuropean networks, culture and audiovisual creation, with the media plus programme, which was agreed on 23 november. let me now turn to the main developments of the council's second reading. the first point on which the council and parliament agreed was external action, namely heading iv of the budget, for which our institutions shared a common objective, namely to provide substantial funding for the balkan regions in 2001, in view of the recent political developments in serbia, without the other geographical priorities of the union's external action having to bear the cost. the agreement reached on 23 november therefore provides for a total allocation for the balkans of eur 839 million, including eur 240 million for serbia. this very large amount, which corresponds to the very high needs in 2001, will be financed in particular by the mobilisation of the flexibility instrument amounting to eur 200 million. parliament thus retains considerable scope for manoeuvre in its second reading to finance all the other geographical priorities, while respecting the ceiling for heading iv, as requested by the council. the second important item on the council's second reading concerns letter of amendment no 2, which allows the new commission forecasts in the agricultural field to be translated. the council adopted this letter of amendment as a whole and, in the same spirit of adapting to the most recent data available, also accepted the european parliament's amendments on rural development expenditure, which reflect the progress made in the adoption and implementation of the national programmes. finally, as agreed at the meeting on 23 november, the council voted to allocate additional appropriations of eur 60 million to finance bse tests. this amount of €60 million is a first budgetary response, very rapid, to the council's decision to extend testing on cattle. it must therefore be considered as a provisional amount. the bse crisis will call for other measures whose budgetary expertise is not yet complete, and when a mechanism is defined more precisely, it will obviously be necessary to take account of its possible budgetary impact and to release the necessary appropriations by studying as a priority the possibilities of redeployment within heading i. the additional financing may then be provided by an amending and supplementary budget, in accordance with the financial perspective. i am pleased that our institutions have been able to agree to adopt in one reading all the elements of this letter of amendment no 2 which concerns not only agricultural expenditure but also fisheries agreements and the entry of an estimated balance for the year 2000 in the initial 2001 budget. the third important element of this second reading by the council concerns the agreement reached on the budget for the 'spirit of enterprise' programme, which continues and complements the 'employment initiative' programme for the years 2001 to 2005. the council and parliament have agreed on a very significant budget of eur 450 million for this period and an allocation of eur 100 million for 2001. this result, which reflects the priority given by the european union to the development of small and mediumsized enterprises and to employment, is to the credit of your rapporteur, jutta haug, who is present here. it also corresponds to a political priority of the council, as expressed at the luxembourg, lisbon and feira summits. finally, on 23 november, agreement was reached on an increase in payment appropriations for the 2001 budget, limited to 3.5% compared with the 2000 budget. you know that this objective is particularly 'important' to the council and i would like to stress that an increase of 3.5% represents a major effort for the member states, since it is considerably higher than the increase in their national budgets, but i am of course aware that this agreement also reflects a major effort on the part of parliament, since it involves on your part sometimes delicate arbitrage compared to your first reading. this agreement on the development of payments was made possible by the commission's proposal to reprogram the commitment appropriations for the community initiative programmes for the financial years 2002 and following at an amount of eur 1600 million. this proposal, which is due to the delays in adopting these programmes, was accepted by the council and parliament. this means that the payment appropriations needed in 2001 are eur 700 million less than in the preliminary draft budget. it was with this new element in mind that the council voted at second reading a budget increase of 2.5%. parliament therefore has a considerable margin of manoeuvre of around eur 1 billion for its second reading to finance its budgetary priorities, while respecting an overall increase of 3.5%. so, of course, the council did not limit its second reading to the four points i have just mentioned. it also accepted several amendments by the european parliament under heading iii on internal policies, in particular to take account of legislative developments. it also accepted certain preparatory actions and pilot projects within the limits of the interinstitutional agreement, after consulting the commission on their feasibility. finally, the list of points of agreement between the council and parliament would not be complete if i did not mention two important texts adopted this year. firstly, a joint declaration on improving the information of parliament and the council on the commission's financial programming, adopted in july on the initiative of mr colom i naval, which i welcome. on the other hand, a joint statement has just been adopted on the progress report on the reform of the commission, on the initiative of mr elles. these two declarations strengthen the transparency of the budgetary procedure and the reforms under way in the commission. i believe that they can improve their efficiency, which i believe is a common objective of our institutions. i'm very attached to it. more generally, i would like to stress that the budgetary procedure which will be concluded in a few days has shown the full value of the interinstitutional agreement of 6 may 1999. it is thanks to the consultation between the three institutions, which is provided for and organised by this agreement, that we have been able to reach agreement on this draft budget for 2001. the mobilisation of the flexibility instrument, one of the key innovations of the 1999 agreement, made it possible to reach agreement on the financing of the european union's external actions in 2001, taking account of the elements that had emerged during the procedure. the additional appropriations will make it possible to accelerate the european union's aid programme for the western balkans in 2001. in accordance with the interinstitutional agreement, the council also left substantial margins below the ceilings of the financial perspective established in 1999, in particular for heading 3 - internal policies - and for heading 4 - external actions. these margins allow the european parliament, at its second reading, to set its own priorities for the various community policies and actions. finally, before you proceed to the final adoption of this budget, i would like to stress the council's commitment to respecting certain basic budgetary rules, in terms of reserving appropriations, legal basis and classification of expenditure. firstly, the budgetary authority may reserve appropriations only if the corresponding legal basis has not yet been adopted in accordance with the provisions of the financial regulation. the council therefore reinstated at second reading all the appropriations which parliament had set aside for reasons other than the absence of a legal basis. i welcome the agreement reached between our two institutions to remove the conditional reservations made by parliament at first reading on heading 4, the performance reserve, and on heading 5 concerning appropriations for the reform of the commission, in the context of letter of amendment no 1. secondly, i would like to stress the need for the institutions to respect the rules governing the classification of appropriations between compulsory and non-compulsory expenditure. your committee on budgets proposes that you amend two lines at second reading, one on the early retirement system and the other on expenditure on fisheries agreements. let me draw the attention of the european parliament to the fact that under the terms of the interinstitutional agreement these budget lines constitute compulsory expenditure, which parliament had also recognised at its first reading. the appropriations entered under these headings must therefore be considered as definitively adopted at the end of the council's second reading, pursuant to article 272 of the treaty, and cannot therefore be amended. at the end of this review, i too would like to stress the excellent atmosphere in which this budgetary procedure took place. the discussions were sometimes close, but they were always relevant and based on continuous exchanges, which allowed us to understand each other better and, therefore, to reach an agreement more easily, which i hope will satisfy everyone. a good budget is a budget that is well discussed. so this one should be born under the best of auspices. i would like to personally thank mr terence wynn, chairman of the committee on budgets, and the three rapporteurs, mr jutta haug, mr markus ferber and mr joan colom i naval, as well as all the members of the committee on budgets whom i have had the pleasure of meeting during the six months i have been president of the council. i can assure you that the council's objective throughout this budgetary procedure has been to arrive at a 2001 budget which will enable the european union to meet the expectations it raises both within itself and beyond its borders. i believe that together, beyond the priorities of each of our institutions, we have built, step by step, a budget for the financial year 2001 which reflects the ambition, which we all defend, of a europe at the service of the citizens. this result must now be approved by you. i hope she can intervene quickly.
