the council has already taken a number of decisions on the basis of the commission's proposals. in fact, the repeated use of the flexibility instrument for two years in a row can be seen, wrongly in my view, as a form of revision of the financial perspective. i do not think that is true either in terms of procedure or, above all, in substance. the procedure for the flexibility instrument was provided for in the interinstitutional agreement and is designed to enable, in exceptional cases, the financing of a particular expenditure to exceed the ceilings agreed in berlin, without jeopardizing the financial perspective. it seems to me that, in substance, there is no contradiction but rather complementarity between the two approaches. as regards the special cases of application we have seen in the last two years, namely kosovo and serbia, the mobilisation of the flexibility instrument has made it possible to finance exceptional expenditure with exceptional effort. in both cases, the flexibility instrument helped to anticipate needs: in the case of kosovo, it was a matter of speeding up the implementation of aid; for serbia, it was a matter of showing a significant amount, even before the needs assessment had been finalised and even before the distribution of roles between the different donors could be decided. the council therefore does not consider that the mobilisation of the flexibility instrument calls into question the viability of the financial perspective agreed in berlin. the council has also defined a multiannual amount for the framework programme for aid for reconstruction in the western balkans, which is, of course, indicative and compatible with the financial perspective. i hope i have answered mr colom i naval's question.

- mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, representative of the council, rapporteurs, the european parliament gains budgetary importance in each budgetary year. we do not get this relevance from the air, but from the treaties, although the council sometimes finds it difficult to recognise this. last year, with the bourlanges report, the flexibility instrument was used for the first time and an institutional declaration was also obtained which acknowledged the possible financial insufficiency of category 4. this year, with the haug report, we have used that institutional declaration of last year to discuss the need to revise the financial perspective. it has been shown that this was not the right time for a review, that there was enough scope to meet the commitments to the balkans and the meda programme without changing the berlin 1999 forecasts, and it has been shown that the compulsion to revise is only in the minds of those who voted against agenda 2000 in the past. however, the european parliament cannot go on indefinitely downsizing its external commitments. this year the flexibility instrument has been used again, but we must not continue down this path. we do not want the colom resolution to include a proposal for revision for next year, because we want to wait for the world bank's assessment, but we share its criticism that this way of resolving the financial shortfall in category 4 distorts the multiannual nature of the union's major external objectives and the very definition of the financial perspectives. this time, more than ever, the secret of success will be in the proper implementation of the budget.

the council. - the council would like to point out that its constant policy is to ensure the highest possible level of consumer protection. in particular, it has ensured, through its recent decisions, that consumers are provided with meat offering the maximum guarantees in this respect, in particular through its decision to ensure better traceability of the origin of meat and the removal from the food chain of a list of specified risk material, to which it has just added bovine intestines. as a precautionary measure and to eliminate the risk of cross-contamination, the council decided to suspend the use of meat meal in feedingstuffs to farmed animals from 1 january 2001. finally, untested animals over 30 months old are no longer allowed to enter the food chain. a buy-to-destroy system will be set up for these untested cattle, to compensate farmers at market price. the council considers that all the measures taken must be such as to avoid the risk denounced by the honourable members. as regards the way in which livestock production is organised and the criteria for developing it, the council recalls that, in its decisions under the agenda 2000 reform, emphasis has already been placed, particularly through bonuses, on greater incentives for extensive production. furthermore, on 4 december 2000 the council took note of the commission's statements on the production of high-protein crops and called on the commission to rapidly deepen its analysis and draw the consequences for the current policy in this sector and for the freezing of land, including, where appropriate, through appropriate proposals. the council, through all these decisions, intends to restore the confidence of consumers in the european union. however, in view of the need to maintain the principles governing the internal market, it intends to give priority to community measures rather than proposing specific measures for certain member states.

trying to reach agreement on the administration of the scheme on the basis of historical reference quantities, but all this effort has been unsuccessful. that is why in our october communication we proposed that the quotas should now be managed under the so-called winddog procedure, which means that all three quotas should now be managed under this procedure. the commission's services must, however, be able to reduce the tariff preferences within the quota, as has already been said, so that in principle all supplier countries have access to all quotas. it would also be impossible to give preferential treatment to acp suppliers under the c quota, because then it would not be a greedy procedure and would not comply with the rules of that procedure and would not be in conformity with the wto. the next question, which is also linked to quotas, is the extension of the period for which the tariff quota system is to apply. the commission considers that the 10 years requested in amendments nos 11 and 13 are too long. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament. i now come to the amendments relating to additional support measures for eu producers and to compensatory aid. the additional support measures proposed include a marketing aid (proposal 24), additional support from the structural funds (proposal 10) and a review of prices and, if fluctuations. that question concerns motions for resolutions 7, 10, 13, 21 to 24. as regards proposals 19 and 32, which concern organic bananas, i would like to point out again that there are already horizontal measures to ensure the equivalence of organic bananas from third countries with those produced in the community. moreover, the production of organic bananas is also eligible under the applicable agri-environmental measures. measures for the marketing of these bananas are also included in the national and regional programmes for the promotion of rural development. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of consumers in the event of the introduction of new technologies is a very good one. it community's agricultural policy is not distorted by the introduction of the single market. and i would also point out that the representatives of the fair trade banana industry have expressly welcomed the regulation we have proposed. i would also add that the development of both organic and fair trade banana production in the acp states is already being financially supported under the regulation on aid to the traditional acp countries. finally, amendments nos 1 to 5, 12 and 36. these essentially only repeat the main principles already contained in the original text of basic regulation 404/93 or - the next item is the joint debate on the following reports: - a5-0362/2000 by mr garcía-margallo y marfil, on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs, on the proposal for a european parliament and council regulation amending regulation (eec) no 218/92 on administrative cooperation in the field of indirect taxation (vat) (com (2000) 349 - c5-0298/2000 - 2000/0147 (cod)) and the proposal for a council directive amending directive 77/388/eec on the value added tax arrangements applicable to certain services supplied by electronic means. the rapporteur. - mr president, in this joint debate we are going to discuss three reports on four commission proposals, which gives me a certain amount of paperwork. i am the rapporteur for two of them, i am the shadow rapporteur for mrs torres marques' report and i am an amendment to the report on aviation fuel, because i do not share some of the theses which were adopted in committee. the second peculiarity, as the honourable member will be able to see, is that i find myself in a unique position within my own group. my military career was neither long nor brilliant, but i did learn that the mission of artillery was to bomb the infantry, if possible the enemy. i'm afraid i'm under fire from my own group right now. i shall begin by arguing for the first of the reports, the one on vat on e-commerce. the proposal which the commission is submitting to this parliament has, in my view, one primary objective: to remedy the discriminatory situation in which european e-commerce companies currently find themselves in relation to companies from third countries. electronic commerce refers to the provision of services downloaded from the internet and to radio or television services provided through subscription or pay-per-view. i stress this because some of the amendments seek to introduce a zero rate of vat for services which, in my view, are not essential or social. the commission also pursues other secondary objectives, in accordance with the traditional science of taxation: to achieve this objective - to put an end to this discrimination - by simplifying taxation, making it remarkably effective in terms of collection and reducing the administrative costs associated with the payment of tax, achieving the objectives of effectiveness and fairness and finally achieving the modernisation of the tax system. these objectives, the main one and the secondary ones, will be the touchstone on which the specific proposals put forward by the commission will have to be judged. but i said, mr president, that the first criterion by which we must judge this proposal is the need to put an end to the discrimination which penalizes european companies in relation to non-community companies. that discrimination arises because article 9 of the sixth directive provides for the presumption that the place where the service is provided is the place where the person providing the service, that is to say the supplier, has his place of business. in other words, at the moment european companies are subject to vat when they provide electronic services, whether inside or outside the union. on the other hand, companies established outside the union never pay vat, they either pay it to european customers or to global customers, thus undermining our competitiveness on foreign markets. in conclusion, and to put it very simply, services provided by european companies are at present subject to a tax burden which is not borne by non-community companies providing services in the territory of the union. the current european legislation therefore encourages european e-commerce companies to set up outside the community. some of the arguments we will hear this afternoon are that taxing foreign companies providing services in the union is a brake on the growth of e-commerce, but it is the opposite, that maintaining this situation is detrimental to the growth of a european e-commerce industry. that is something we all agree on, on this side of the atlantic and on the other. so much so that at the ottawa conference in 1998 three conclusions were reached which i believe are important: firstly, national taxes on consumption should apply to consumption within the national territory. second, the digital product service is a provision of services and not a delivery of goods. thirdly, it is necessary to resort to simple formulas for the collection of the tax and, in particular, to the form of investment of the taxable person. in accordance with this objective, and with this international legal framework agreed by all in ottawa, the commission is proposing to amend the sixth directive to provide that the location of digital services should be where the purchaser, not the supplier, is established. consequently, services provided by european companies to non-european companies would always be exempt from taxation, which would restore our international competitiveness. secondly, services provided by european companies to european customers would be taxed, as is normal. and thirdly, services provided by non-european companies to european companies would also be subject to taxation, which establishes a level playing field, fair play in the international framework. the problem is not with transactions between companies, but when the recipient of the service is a private individual, and the commission is doing the only thing it can do: forcing foreign companies to register in a european union country and then, with a community passport, provide services throughout the union, but paying the same tax as european companies. in my view, this solution solves the problem of eliminating the previous discriminations and achieves the objective of simplification. a company must be registered in only one country of the union. it does not have to register in fifteen countries, it does not have to know fifteen legislations or deal with fifteen administrations. it does not, however, solve the problem of justice. it is well known that such a solution - a facility in one country with the possibility of providing services throughout the union - could enable a flood of those countries with lower taxation. the french presidency therefore proposed that a foreign company providing services in the union should be registered in all 15 countries, which is contrary to the objective of simplification. what does the commission propose? the commission proposes, in keeping with the objective of simplification, that there should be a single place of establishment, but that the tax collected by the treasury should be redistributed to the other countries of the union, depending on relative consumption. it is exactly the formula which will make possible the introduction of vat at source, it is exactly the formula which we have decided for crossborder vat refunds, it is exactly the formula which ecofin has approved, in accordance with the feira conclusions, in the case of withholding tax on direct taxes. is this commission communication complete? it's not a good idea. there are some problems which i highlight in the explanatory statement, such as ensuring that a company which can provide services from outside the union is registered. how can it be ensured that there is no discrimination between like products? the digital service, the consultation or access to a book or a magazine, would be taxed at the normal rate if it is done over the internet, while it would be subject to a reduced rate if it was a physical delivery. how do you solve the problems of customer identification? the answers given in the commission's proposal seem to me to be sufficient, and in any case, mr president, it is clear that these difficulties are not specific to the tax on digital services. vat was a tax intended for the traffic of goods and is ill suited to the provision of services, and even worse to a phenomenon as new as internet services. the second report i am going to refer to deals with the problem of hydrocarbons, and the subject is very simple. the 1992 directive introduced a mandatory exemption for fuels used in international aviation and at the same time provided for the revision of the exemption to take account of environmental costs. the legal difficulties for this revision are the 1944 chicago convention, an international obligation exempting from taxation the fuel on board supplied in aircraft, and bilateral agreements. in this situation, the commission has commissioned a study, which is what we are investigating here, on what can be done. the first conclusion is that little can be done unless that international framework is changed. the second conclusion reached by the commission is that a tax on domestic or intra-community flights would be desirable, subject to amendment of the bilateral agreements, which i do not share. thirdly, and i share this view, the need - in the international framework of icao - to make all the necessary progress towards establishing a worldwide, and therefore non-discriminatory, tax on community transport. mr president, having abused your patience, i look forward to the criticisms and comments of the rest of my colleagues, both from my own group and from others.
- mr president, it is indeed very touching to hear allegedly angelic arguments in favour of promoting electronic commerce, but here the problem we have is that of a real competitive disadvantage for our european companies, and that of correcting this situation by establishing certain rules of the game, so that all services provided to individuals by electronic means in the european union are subject to vat. thus, in order for non-eu operators to be subject to the same tax obligations as domestic operators when providing services to consumers, they must register for vat purposes in a member state of their choice, the vat rate of the chosen state being the one applied to their operations. we discussed this in the committee on economic and monetary affairs and industrial policy and some people spoke in favour of tax exemption for this type of service, arguing that this would eliminate the competitive disadvantage. i think this argument is fallacious. it is an inappropriate argument, not in accordance with european legislation, and it is also harmful compared with services provided by other means. and it is not true that a moratorium on taxation of electronic services has been introduced in the united states. we therefore support the commission's proposal as a whole and the excellent work of mr garcía-margallo and mr ivory. i personally proposed an amendment on the harmonization of vat rates to correct the effects of unfair competition resulting from the freedom of choice for foreign operators when registering, since there is a very wide range - between 15 and 25% - in the vat rate for them, while domestic operators cannot choose. i understand, however, that a better solution has been found to compensate member states for the loss of vat revenue caused by these differences in rates, which i find satisfactory. the group i represent in this house objects to the fact that while newspapers normally enjoy reduced rates of vat, this reduction does not apply to electronic newspapers.

- the next item is the report (b5-0559/2000) by mr de gucht, on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs and industrial policy, on the proposal for a council regulation (ec) on the common organization of the market in bananas (com (2000) 0173 - c4-0535/2000 - syn 30). part one
question no 33 by mr john joseph mccartin (h-0873/00) subject: united kingdom proposal on a tax on foreign lorries is the commission aware that the uk minister for finance announced on 8 november 2000 his intention to introduce a special road tax on foreign lorries using the uk road network? can the commission state whether it has been notified of this proposal and whether this measure would be contrary to the community's free trade policy and would infringe eu law?
commission. – mr president, the commission is aware that one of the plans announced by the uk government on 8 november 2000 was the introduction of some form of road-user charge such as a vignette payable by all road hauliers, british and non-british alike, for their use of the road network in the uk. the commission sees, therefore, no indication that the announced measure introduces direct discrimination on the basis of the nationality of the haulier or the origin or destination of the vehicle. provided that the implementation aspects of the charge in question do not introduce indirect discrimination either and they respect all other relevant specific rules governing the introduction of user charges in the european union, such a charge seems at this stage to be in line with current community law, that is directive 1999/62/ec. this directive, adopted by unanimity in 1993, laid down the conditions under which member states could, if they wanted, apply time-related user charges or motorway tolls. the overall aim of this legislation was the elimination of distortions of competition through the establishment of fair mechanisms for charging infrastructure costs to hauliers and the harmonisation of levy systems within the eu internal market. twelve of the 15 member states have already adjusted their levy systems with more emphasis put on direct charging, user charges or motorway tolls and less on taxes. the commission considers that such adjustments go in the right direction towards the establishment of fairer charging systems which give also an incentive for a more rational and efficient use of the road network. the measures announced by the uk signal such a readjustment of their charging system. the commission is following closely the development of the uk scheme in order to ensure its full compatibility with eu general principles and specific legislation. the uk government has confirmed it is in the process of preparing its reply to the commission's request for detailed information on the entire package of measures planned in the uk. the commission will then analyse and evaluate those measures. depending on the outcome of this analysis, the commission will decide what course of action to take next in view of fulfilling its role to assist member states to take the measures which are right for them and at the same time respect the rights of the others.
commission. – president, the honourable member will understand that it is difficult and probably inappropriate for the commission to speculate on hypotheses and possibilities. i have set out in the commission's response the principles and the criteria and assured parliament that the commission will analyse and follow closely the development of the uk scheme, including its implementation in practice, and of course the absence of any discrimination be it direct or indirect will be a crucial reference point in such an assessment.
commission. – thank you for the supplementary question. i have to stick to the measures as announced and i find it even more difficult to speculate about the ramifications of the subject as i am not the commissioner specifically in charge. i hope you will understand this and i can only refer back to the elements i gave in the reply provided a few minutes ago. in reply to the honourable member who asked how the structure of the charging system in the uk affects competition in the road haulage sector, perhaps i could add that at the moment british hauliers pay road-tolls or user charges – "vignettes" – when travelling in other countries such as france or belgium, while at the same time they pay at home high vehicle taxes through which they contribute towards the infrastructure costs of the road network in britain. on the other hand non-british hauliers pay nothing when travelling in britain. they therefore do not contribute at all towards road infrastructure costs in britain and at the same time pay lower vehicles taxes at home. this imbalance of an economic nature between the charges and taxes imposed on hauliers in different member states distorts the conditions under which hauliers of different nationalities compete in the uk.

question no 44, by mr bernd posselt (h-0872/00) subject: european patent court what is the state of preparation for the creation of a european patent court and what is the commission's view of the proposed seat of this institution (munich)?
- i am aware that important economic activities have developed in munich in the field of patents. the european patent office is therefore located in munich. however, i believe that it is premature at this stage to discuss the location of the future community patent court. at present, the efforts of my services and myself are directed towards reducing the effects of the distance between the parties and the future court. we want to ensure that the centralised judiciary is close to all the people in the community. i would add that it is not possible to have a community patent, a centralised patent, without a centralised judiciary. if that were not the case, it would mean that there would be a court in every member state of the european union to hear infringement cases and that could mean that a german company would be in a court in member state x, far away from the seat of that company and with enlargement that could mean much greater distances. it is essential that there should be a single court, both at first instance and on appeal, to hear and decide patent disputes.
commission. – i am not sure what the honourable member means by the word ‘proliferation’. does he mean a geographical proliferation or a functional proliferation, according to various subject matters? if mr maccormick means a functional proliferation of courts of justice, i can see his point of view. i understand that his concern is that there should not be a proliferation of special tribunals dealing with this, that and the other. that is certainly an understandable point of view, which i share. however, patents, represent very specialised work. just as the law courts in düsseldorf, munich and elsewhere in germany have specialised in the law of patents and there is also a specialised court in london, a community court to sit upon and judge cases concerning community patents would have to be very specialised. it is not work that could be given to a new judge – if i may put it that way – even though that judge might be very experienced in other fields. therefore, the specialised courts which the european commission wants to see come into being, to deal with all possible litigation concerning community patents, would have to consist of specialised judges and would, therefore, perhaps be organisationally a part of the court in luxembourg but, as far as its work is concerned, form a specialised part of that court. having said all that, i agree with mr maccormick that one should be very sparing in erecting special tribunals. we do not want a tribunal for traffic accidents, international agreements, or for maritime law, etc. these matters would continue to be the normal province of the court in luxembourg and certainly the commission would not want any special arrangements for normal cases.

subject: free movement of goods and right to strike following the commission's reply to question p-3079/00, i would also like to put the following question. in its reply, the commission stated that the right to strike must be respected, in accordance with regulation (ec) no 2679/98 oj l 337, 12.12.1998, p. 8. at the same time, it is prepared to intervene against obstacles to free movement, whether or not a trade dispute arises. this is a contradiction which can be illustrated by the following example: as a result of a legitimate labour dispute in swedish ports, all loading and unloading is stopped, as the trade unions have decided to blockade these ports. would this be a situation in which the commission would ask the government of the member state concerned to intervene so that the free movement of goods is not interrupted within the internal market? how long can the strike last before it threatens free movement? what are the measures that the member state in question can impose to restore free movement? can the member state legislatively oblige the social partners to accept an agreement imposed by the government?
commission. - the previous answer given by the commission to question p-3079/00 may have been misinterpreted. i therefore intend to address the following communication to mr sjöstedt on behalf of the commission. all member states are bound by regulation 2679/98, which clearly states that the regulation may not be interpreted as affecting in any way the exercise of fundamental rights as recognised in the member states, including the right to strike or the freedom to strike. the commission obviously respects that principle. nevertheless, that regulation requires member states to take all necessary and proportionate measures to restore the free movement of goods within their territory as soon as possible in order to avoid serious disturbances to the free movement of goods where an obstacle as defined in the regulation has occurred in the context of a strike or similar action. in addition, member states should inform the commission of any obstacles encountered on their territory and of the actions taken by the member states. i would like to draw attention to the fact that it is for the member states themselves to decide what constitutes a legal strike under their legislation. i would like to stress that it is for the member states alone to determine whether, when and to what extent measures are necessary and proportionate to facilitate the free movement of goods within their territory. this is clear from recital 6 of the regulation. the principles i have outlined here apply to all the questions put by mr sjöstedt.
- i can only repeat what i just said. it is up to the member state to decide when a strike is legal. if a physical obstacle to trade flows exists, the commission expects, after having called on the member state concerned, to be informed of the measures to be taken to remove the obstacle. this means that the commission will use the legal remedies at its disposal only in the sense of the regulation. the legal remedies which are used in the territory of the member state itself are reserved to the inhabitants and economic operators of that member state.

commission. – mr president, the situation is as follows if i may address the question directly: if a ferry coming from and going to a member state, for example finland, makes an intermediate call in a third country or a third territory – in this case the åland islands – where the passengers have the opportunity to disembark and to make purchases, then it would be possible to have tax and duty-free sales on board. however, when the vessel returns to community ports, customs provisions including appropriate controls apply and that means that the passengers are allowed to import excisable goods free of taxes and duties up to the limits laid down in the customs provisions governing travellers' allowances.

commission. – mr president, i would like to thank the members of parliament for their support for the commission proposal. this wide participation of parliamentarians in this late debate is further proof of the interest shown in this important proposal. promotion of european digital content is evidently and rightly a subject of interest to many parliamentary committees. the rapporteur, mrs gill, has succeeded in bringing together the different opinions in a balanced manner, with an important contribution from mrs fraisse and the committee on committee on culture, youth, education, the media and sport. let me first say a few words on why we launched this initiative. the key role of content first. in order to exploit the strong european position in mobile telephony and digital tv it is key for a new range of services to emerge. european firms are in the best position to localise services geographically and tailor them culturally and linguistically to users' needs. we have to ensure that there is an environment conducive to these changes in europe. secondly, the internet is going mobile. this means the appearance of personalised and localised services that respond to what consumers want, where they want, but the consumers are probably only willing to pay for this content if it is available in a culturally customised format and in their own language. thus having the right conditions in place for european multilingual digital content production is becoming increasingly important. in response to this challenge, the commission has proposed a five-year programme with the aim of accelerating the process of transformation and filling the gap open in the mobile services: three specific lines with the help of strategic studies and input from market actors who are identified in the areas where impact at european level can be maximised, namely, stimulating the exploitation of public sector information, enhancing linguistic and cultural customisation, and supporting market enablers. the budget proposed by the commission is eur 150 m over five years. this programme has ambitious objectives and has to have appropriate means to achieve them. i would like to thank parliament for its strong support for the budget of the programme. let me comment on some of the amendments proposed by parliament. first, on the social and cultural function of digital content, the commission welcomes the fact that parliament emphasises the social and cultural dimension of digital content. the commission supports these amendments which bring out this dimension even more clearly than in its original formulation. second, on economic dimension content. the idea of e-content is to marry the social and cultural dimension content with its economic value in order to maximise its expected value. in this respect the report stresses the need to invest in the linguistic and cultural customisation part of the proposal. we welcome these elements. thirdly, on the simplification of procedures and payment delays. this is an important point and i agree whole-heartedly with the rapporteur. we have to have put in place fast and simplified procedures for the execution of programmes. in this connection it is worthwhile to notice that as part of the administrative reform, the commission has recently adopted a communication on the simplification of its decision-making procedures. we intend to make maximum use of these measures and reduce as much as possible the time between the presentation of a project proposal and a decision on its financing. in conclusion, out of 49 amendments voted by the committee, let me say that the commission can support 23 as they are, and 15 are acceptable in principle subject to reformulation. the remaining 11 are not directly compatible with the objectives of this specific programme, or would stretch its mandate beyond what can be achieved with the financial means associated with it. some of them are indeed very valuable in themselves but are better placed in other instruments than in the present decision. let me thank you once again for the report. at this stage it is expected that the telecoms council of 22 december will reach a political agreement on the proposal. this is necessary in order to start the action early in 2001. thank you very much for your attention.
- mr president, spain has supported and supports the policy of combating noise in general and this community directive in particular, as well as the meritorious work of mr de roo. despite the spanish interest and willingness to establish community standards in this area, a fundamental problem remains which deeply affects the way of life in spain. the proposal for a directive is to introduce a noise nuisance factor for noise from 7 p.m. onwards, which is called evening noise in the proposal. the commission proposal, in point 1 of annex i, provides for a systematic addition of five decibels to all noise generated between 7 p.m. and 11 p.m. for climatic and cultural reasons, life in spain is longer than in many other parts of europe. it is obvious that the nuisance that noise can cause between 7 and 10 pm varies according to the different forms of life in each place . in spain and in many mediterranean countries, the normal daytime hours are well beyond the 19 hours stipulated in this directive. i therefore do not conceal the fact that my country will have great difficulty in accepting the commission's proposal unless it incorporates a mechanism of sufficient flexibility to enable the way of life inherited from our ancestors and, on the other hand, so much appreciated by spaniards themselves and by our foreign visitors, to be maintained. the flexibility formulae offered so far consist in shifting part of the four hours of compulsory evening time towards nap time. but this mechanism does not work, because, unfortunately, the siesta is not slept all year round in spain, nor is it even slept in all of spain. elements of flexibility may be the possibility of reducing either the number of hours or the degree of nuisance which the proposal assigns to this evening time. it would be for the member states to determine the length of such a period in a specific way, depending on the customs of each country. in this respect, we of course support amendment no 48 by mr oomen-ruijten and mr florenz.

- mr president, as the rapporteur very well recalls, the precautionary principle - although the rapporteur differentiates between the two - is enshrined in several international conventions, from rio in 1992 to the protection of the north sea and, more recently, the montreal protocol on biosafety. as other speakers have said, it is essential that this principle be used properly and that there be legal guarantees for the parties concerned, but i would like to take up three ideas which are in mrs patrie's report and in some of the amendments and which i think are perhaps the most important in the report. first, there is no minimum risk threshold below which the precautionary principle should not apply and, therefore, even in cases where there is a low risk, it should be used. secondly, transparency and consumer information throughout the risk assessment and management process are very important and necessary. and finally, that public health and the environment must take precedence over other considerations, especially economic ones. if this had been done, mr president, i do not think we would be lamenting mad cow disease today, or any other food contamination whose future effects we do not yet know. there is a great deal of sensitivity and concern about the use of gm products in food. another example of this is the great sensitivity to information, whether scientifically based or not, about the effect that mobile phones, electromagnetic waves and also electromagnetic wave transmission columns can have. i think, mr president, that this is a very important principle if it is used properly and wherever necessary.

- mr president, i too would like to begin by expressing my condolences to the family of the murdered councillor and to my comrades in the popular party, and to condemn this fascist barbarity of eta and the groups that are supporting it. i want to give due weight to the pact signed between the people's party and the socialist party against terrorism, and i think it is important that the european union should move in this direction. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's fishing fleet is not disrupted. in it it stated that the damage to the submarine, which had occurred since 12 may in sicilian waters, could not be repaired in the port of gibraltar, since the italian and nato authorities had refused to receive the submarine in their ports. in that speech he also pointed out the lack of seriousness and respect shown by the british government in reclassifying the gibraltar wharf on paper, from category z to x, in order to be able to carry out the repair in the best colonial style. it also indicated alarm among the more than 200,000 people living within a ten-kilometer radius of the area. the evasive response i received from the commission on that occasion obliged me to ask a second question on 21 september, urging the commission to request the british government to drive the tireless to a british port and to follow up on this matter. the answer received from the commission was disappointing and unsatisfactory. i would like to think that this feeling of dissatisfaction with the answer has nothing to do with the fact that commissioner patten is british, but on the one hand, on the most important issue - the repair of the submarine in a dock of the european union which does not meet the minimum conditions - he said that it was an internal matter of the united kingdom, when, according to the euratom treaty, this is not the case; and on the other hand, he merely said that he would keep parliament informed. and yet, since that time, the european parliament has not received any information from the commission, despite its commitment to do so. so, in these months we have attended a dance of futility. we have heard claims from british naval officials that the damage was insignificant, and others that it was quite the opposite, that it was extensive and needed long and difficult repairs. we have heard statements from the spanish government that there was no need to worry, and others, fortunately recent ones, from minister piqué, urging that the submarine be taken as soon as possible - it is true that they have set a deadline of three months - so that it can be repaired in the united kingdom. we have also heard, after visits by spanish nuclear safety technicians to the submarine, that there was no danger, until further statements, noting that they were not allowed to actually see, observe and inspect the site of the failure. i therefore believe that the commission must be aware of the very anomalous situation we are living in and that it must first demand the immediate cessation of any reparations in gibraltar. secondly, it must require that all the necessary information be given to the public, as the euratom treaty requires. thirdly, i think that the british government should be reprimanded for the irresponsibility and recklessness with which it has made this reclassification, so that the port of gibraltar can be returned to its original classification. i also think it would be appropriate to take the tireless submarine to britain for repairs as soon as possible, as soon as the weather conditions are right. i think it is clear that there is a general alarm about this type of nuclear submarine from all the countries of the european union and from all over the world, and therefore i think that we should recommend that this type of nuclear submarine disappear from the map, from the oceans. i would also point out that, given the ineffectiveness of the commission, a delegation of technicians should be sent to the field, since we cannot trust what the government has done so far. and finally, i think it would be appropriate for the british government to compensate the area economically, because there have been losses in tourism and in fishing activity, for which the british government is responsible.
- thank you, commissioner, for your reply which contains very important and new information for us. the situation we are talking about is of extraordinary gravity. a nuclear-powered ship with a major breakdown is to be repaired in a small, unprepared port, in the vicinity of which more than 300,000 people live. and decisions about repair and about safety must be made by a government that is alien to those inhabitants. this situation can in no way be a bilateral matter between two states belonging to a political union. the commission, in its clear reply two months ago and in its reply today, has had the responsibility to recognise this, although the motion for a resolution by the group of the european people's party has not, which, together with other trivializations of the matter, has prevented us from sharing it. the commission must exercise its powers with the same responsibility, mr commissioner, without concealing them behind an approach of diplomatic prudence and submission to the council. i am not an alarmist, i am not against nuclear energy, i would never advocate, as i believe no one in spain would, that the submarine be moved at any cost if this meant an objective increase in risk, but it is not in the spirit of european democracies, nor in the treaty on european union, that decision-making is alien to human security and, in short, that the population should take risks in exchange for greater technical, budgetary or diplomatic comfort. so far, despite the information mr patten has given us, the public is unaware of the risks in scientific terms, of the date of repair, of what the repair will consist of, of the plans to be made in the event of a radiological emergency, of whether the risk of moving the submarine is greater than the risk of repair there. can the commission accept this situation? i do not make this a matter of national dignity, nor is this the time to denounce the territorial anachronism of gibraltar. the specific matter is more serious than all that, since it affects hundreds of thousands of human beings in the community, not only spaniards, of course, but also of all nationalities and especially british. we believe that these citizens have found the protection to which they are entitled in their most modest territorial representation, which is their town halls. today we are joined by municipal and social representatives of those citizens. whether or not they have found him in the government of their nation is a matter for the spanish parliament. there is debate there, but the citizens, based on their knowledge or intuition, turn their attention to the european institutions. it is their responsibility that the citizens, in relation to the european union, stop thinking only in terms of when my agricultural subsidy will arrive or when my community funds will arrive and think instead about the degree of security that my community institutions offer me. i therefore ask you, ladies and gentlemen, to adopt the proposals contained in the joint resolution which will be voted on first, or at least those proposed by the socialist group. and in any case, i trust that the commission will not only fulfil its obligations, but will also ensure that the two states concerned fulfil theirs.

- mr president, i will begin by saying that i am an andalusian and that i live in andalusia, although i do not claim to represent the whole of the andalusian people, as our colleague mr bautista has done here - although that arrogance is based on very few votes. i would like to see him feel as strongly andalusian as he did when he signed the condemnation of this house against terrorism - precisely this afternoon, without so much hesitation and without so much reticence - especially since more than 70% of the members of the security forces killed by eta were andalusians. that said, it should be remembered that there has been a lot of conflicting information since the british navy nuclear submarine tireless chose the port of gibraltar - where the british flag is flying - in may for a repair of the cooling system of its nuclear reactor, which, as the british authorities initially reported, was not particularly difficult and did not pose any danger to the inhabitants of the area. since then, explanations have followed and concern has grown over what was happening to the tireless. the spanish government has from the outset maintained a position based on two points: the need for transparent information, based on technical and scientific criteria, to assess the extent of the repair and its potential for risk; and also that any decision, whether on its repair in gibraltar or on its transfer to a naval base in the british isles, be taken in accordance with rigorous technical criteria. this is, and remains, in our view the most coherent approach and the one which best safeguards the interests and security of all the parties involved. what has certainly not been appropriate and consistent has been the intentional creation of a climate of social alarm in the area, with the obvious purpose of turning this problem into a drain on the spanish government. and in this case, we must say to our spanish socialist colleagues - with the utmost respect - that they have allowed party interests to override the interests of the state. that is reflected in the curious agreement they reached with their british labour colleagues to discharge from responsibility who owns the submarine, who is responsible for its mooring and stay in gibraltar and who is in charge of its repair, and who is also the owner of the port in which it is moored. the important thing at the moment is that good, transparent and scientifically sound information is available on the scope and consequences of the repair and that the possibilities and risks of moving the submarine, if necessary, are seriously considered. what is left are demagogic positions, which are justified only by the purest partisan opportunism and which produce, among other consequences, the alarm and anxiety of a population which has every right to be safe, to be informed, but which does not have to endure, in addition to all this, being manipulated.

- mr president, for months now the news from côte d'ivoire has been causing justified alarm in european public opinion and corresponding concern in our parliament. this turbulent situation has surprised many because it was in a peaceful, relatively prosperous country with institutions that functioned reasonably and a society of satisfactory coexistence. the traumatic events that have occurred there clearly reflect the process of degradation that the entire african continent is going through. in côte d'ivoire this degradation has been dramatic in terms of the economy. the collapse in cocoa prices, the crushing weight of the external debt, the rise in fuel prices and other factors have led to an internal situation of growing tensions, with a marked deterioration in the social climate, with increased unemployment and poverty. xenophobia found in this panorama a suitable breeding ground with political forces willing to use it in an interesting way, around the concept of ivoirité and making it the object of their odious hostility to radical immigrants of decades ago. in this context, the military seized power, which, as always, only contributed to worsening the situation. violence became widespread, particularly against immigrants or citizens from the north or neighbouring countries. the political process articulated to restore democratic legitimacy has not lived up to the hopes that some had placed in its procedures. after a more than dubious presidential election, the european parliament insisted that the legislative elections on 10 december were free, fair and pluralist. today, we must acknowledge that our demands have not been met. the worst part is that in 32 constituencies there have not even been elections, making the crisis of legitimacy even more evident. the political conditions must therefore be created to put an end to the exclusion, to allow the rdr and other political forces to participate in the democratic process and to ensure, at least in these circumstances, pending the elections in january, that a certain path back to democratic normality can be opened. the problem is not to call a general election at any cost. in order to really unblock the current situation, the conditions must first be created so that such elections can take place in a climate of civil peace and reconciliation. the conditions for this are that no one should feel excluded, that the supreme court established by military power should disappear, that the head of state should be implicated unambiguously in the process of democratic restoration and that the opinions of the committee for national reconciliation should be heard.
